questions.answerText: Red blood cells need room for hemoglobin; neurons must maintain themselves for life

questions.q: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the plasma membrane freely, while proteins and charged ions need a transport mechanism. Which term describes a membrane like this?
options: Hydrophobic
Semipermeable
Permeable
Impermeable
questions.why: A semipermeable membrane lets some substances cross and holds back others, based on their size, charge, and solubility. Small lipid-soluble molecules and gases such as O2 and CO2 diffuse through freely, while larger or charged substances rely on transport proteins. The plasma membrane is the main example, and this selectivity lets the cell control what enters and leaves.
notes: Hydrophobic means water-fearing and describes the phospholipid tails in the core of the bilayer. It explains part of why the membrane is selective, but it is not the term for the membrane's overall permeability.
Correct. Letting some substances through and not others is semipermeable.
A permeable barrier lets substances pass freely without restriction. It describes something like water moving through open water channels (aquaporins), not a membrane that sorts what crosses.

An impermeable barrier blocks movement unless a specific mechanism carries the substance across. It describes how the membrane treats proteins or ions with no transporter, but not the membrane as a whole, which lets gases through.
questions.answerText: Semipermeable
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the cytoplasm and the cytosol?
options: The cytoplasm is fluid inside the nucleus; the cytosol is fluid outside it
The cytoplasm is organelles plus fluid; the cytosol is only the fluid
The cytosol is organelles plus fluid; the cytoplasm is only the fluid
The cytoplasm includes the nucleus; the cytosol excludes the nucleus
questions.why: The cytoplasm is everything inside the plasma membrane except the nucleus, which means the organelles together with the fluid they float in. The cytosol is just that fluid: water with dissolved ions, enzymes, and small molecules. So the cytosol is one part of the cytoplasm, not another name for it.
notes: The fluid inside the nucleus is the nucleoplasm, a separate term. This option would be correct for a question comparing the nucleoplasm with the cytosol.
Correct. The cytosol is the fluid part of the cytoplasm.
This reverses the two terms. Students mix them up because both start with cyto-, but the cytosol is the fluid alone, and the cytoplasm is the larger region that contains it.
Neither term includes the nucleus. The cytoplasm stops at the nuclear envelope, and the material inside the nucleus has its own name.
questions.answerText: The cytoplasm is organelles plus fluid; the cytosol is only the fluid
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which model describes the plasma membrane as a fluid sea of phospholipids with proteins floating in it and drifting sideways?
options: The endomembrane system
The generalized cell model
The sliding filament model
The fluid mosaic model
questions.why: The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as a flexible sheet of phospholipids in which proteins and other molecules float like tiles in a mosaic. The phospholipids and proteins can drift sideways within the layer, so the membrane is not a rigid wall. This movement gives the membrane flexibility and lets its parts interact.
notes: The endomembrane system is the network of membranous organelles, such as the ER, Golgi apparatus, and vesicles, that make and ship proteins and lipids. It is a group of organelles, not a model of the plasma membrane.
The generalized cell model is a composite drawing of a whole cell that shows the features shared by most body cells. It describes the entire cell, not the structure of the membrane.
The sliding filament model explains how thick and thin filaments slide past each other when a muscle fiber contracts. It belongs to muscle tissue, which comes up in Module 3.
Correct. The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane this way.
questions.answerText: The fluid mosaic model
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: The flattened membrane sacs that make up the Golgi apparatus are called what?
options: Cisternae
Microvilli
Lacunae
Cristae
questions.why: The Golgi apparatus is built from a stack of flattened membrane sacs called cisternae. Products arriving from the ER are modified within the cisternae and then leave in vesicles that bud from the edges of the stack. The stacked cisternae are the feature to look for when identifying the Golgi.
notes: Correct. The Golgi's flattened sacs are cisternae.
Microvilli are finger-like folds of the plasma membrane on the outer surface of absorptive cells. They are the answer for a question about increasing surface area for absorption.
Lacunae are small spaces in the matrix of cartilage and bone where chondrocytes and osteocytes sit. They belong to connective tissue, not to an organelle.
Cristae are the folds of the inner membrane of a mitochondrion, which increase surface area for making ATP. The names look alike, so pick cristae only for a question about mitochondria.
questions.answerText: Cisternae
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares free ribosomes and ribosomes bound to the rough ER?
options: Free ones make proteins for export or membranes; bound ones make proteins for inside the cell
Free ones work inside the nucleus; bound ones work in the cytoplasm
Free ones make lipids; bound ones make proteins
Free ones make proteins for inside the cell; bound ones make proteins for export or membranes
questions.why: All ribosomes build proteins, but where they sit decides where the protein goes. Free ribosomes in the cytosol make proteins that stay in the cell and work in the cytosol. Ribosomes bound to the rough ER make proteins that will be secreted or placed into membranes, because those proteins must travel through the ER and Golgi apparatus first.
notes: This swaps the two jobs. Proteins headed out of the cell must enter the endomembrane route, which starts at the rough ER, so they are made by bound ribosomes.
Ribosomal subunits are assembled in the nucleolus, but finished ribosomes work in the cytoplasm. Free ribosomes float in the cytosol, not inside the nucleus.
Ribosomes make only proteins. Lipids are made by the smooth ER, which has no ribosomes at all.
Correct. Location decides the protein's destination.
questions.answerText: Free ones make proteins for inside the cell; bound ones make proteins for export or membranes
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: What is the viscous fluid inside the nucleus that supports the chromatin and nucleolus called?
options: Nucleolus
Cytosol
Nucleoplasm
Chromatin
questions.why: The nucleoplasm is the thick fluid enclosed by the nuclear envelope. The chromatin and the nucleolus sit within it, much as organelles sit in the cytosol outside the nucleus. Keeping the two fluids separate is one of the jobs of the nuclear envelope.
notes: The nucleolus is a dense region suspended in the nucleoplasm where ribosomal subunits are assembled. It is a structure within the fluid, not the fluid itself.
The cytosol is the fluid of the cytoplasm, outside the nucleus, where the organelles are suspended. Pick it for a question about the fluid between the plasma membrane and the nuclear envelope.
Correct. The fluid of the nucleus is the nucleoplasm.
Chromatin is the loose network of DNA and histone proteins in the nucleus. It is supported by the nucleoplasm and is the answer for a question about the form DNA takes between divisions.
questions.answerText: Nucleoplasm
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares cilia and flagella?
options: Cilia absorb nutrients; flagella secrete mucus
Cilia have a 9 plus 0 core; flagella have a 9 plus 2 core
Cilia move the whole cell; a flagellum moves substances across the surface
Cilia move substances across the surface; a flagellum moves the whole cell
questions.why: Cilia and flagella share the same internal design, a core of microtubules in a 9 plus 2 arrangement that lets them move. Cilia are short and numerous and sweep substances such as mucus across the surface of a cell that stays in place, as in the respiratory tract. A flagellum is long and single and propels the cell itself, and in humans the only example is the sperm tail.
notes: Absorbing nutrients is the job of microvilli, and mucus is secreted by goblet cells. Neither description fits cilia or flagella, which are projections built for movement.
Both cilia and flagella have the 9 plus 2 arrangement. The 9 plus 0 arrangement belongs to centrioles, which organize rather than move.
This reverses their jobs. Cells with cilia, like those lining the trachea, stay in place while their cilia move mucus past them.
Correct. Cilia move material past the cell, and a flagellum moves the cell.
questions.answerText: Cilia move substances across the surface; a flagellum moves the whole cell

questions.q: Which cytoskeletal component is made of tubulin and forms the core of centrioles, cilia, and flagella?
options: Intermediate filaments
Microfilaments
Microtubules
Collagen fibers
questions.why: Microtubules are hollow tubes built from the protein tubulin, the thickest of the three cytoskeletal fibers. Besides acting as tracks for vesicles, they are the building blocks of centrioles (9 plus 0 arrangement) and of cilia and flagella (9 plus 2 arrangement). That makes microtubules important for both cell division and cell movement.
notes: Intermediate filaments are rope-like fibers made of various tough proteins that resist tension. Pick them for a question about mechanical strength.
Microfilaments are thin fibers made of actin that support the cell's shape and allow movement at its surface. They are the answer for a question about actin.
Correct. Microtubules are made of tubulin and build centrioles, cilia, and flagella.

Collagen fibers are strong fibers in the matrix of connective tissue, outside the cells. They are not part of the cytoskeleton and are the answer for a question about the most abundant connective tissue fiber.
questions.answerText: Microtubules
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which of these organelles is part of the endomembrane system?
options: The nucleolus
The mitochondrion
The centrosome
The lysosome
questions.why: The endomembrane system is the connected group of membranous organelles that make, modify, and move proteins and lipids. It includes the nuclear envelope, rough and smooth ER, the Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, and vesicles, all linked directly or by vesicles. Lysosomes belong because their enzymes are made on the rough ER and packaged by the Golgi apparatus.
notes: The nucleolus is a dense region inside the nucleus with no membrane of its own. It is the answer for a question about assembling ribosomal subunits.
The mitochondrion has its own double membrane, DNA, and ribosomes and is not connected to the ER and Golgi by vesicles. It is the answer for a question about ATP production.
The centrosome has no membrane, so it cannot be part of a membrane system. It is the answer for a question about organizing microtubules.
Correct. Lysosomes are part of the endomembrane system.
questions.answerText: The lysosome
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which membrane component provides stability and moderates the membrane's fluidity as temperature changes?
options: Integral proteins
Glycoproteins
Cholesterol
Peripheral proteins
questions.why: Cholesterol molecules are wedged between the phospholipids of the bilayer. They keep the membrane from becoming too stiff when cold or too loose when warm, which stabilizes it. This is why cholesterol is listed as a membrane component even though the bilayer itself is the main fabric.
notes: Integral proteins span the bilayer and form channels, carriers, and receptors. Choose them for a question about how substances or signals pass through the membrane.
Glycoproteins carry the sugar chains of the glycocalyx and are used for cell recognition and immune responses. Pick them for a question about how cells identify one another.
Correct. Cholesterol stabilizes the membrane and moderates its fluidity.
Peripheral proteins rest on one face of the membrane and act as enzymes or link the membrane to the cytoskeleton. They are the answer for a protein that is not embedded in the bilayer.
questions.answerText: Cholesterol

questions.q: Which of these is a standard example of a multinucleated cell?
options: A skeletal muscle fiber
A smooth muscle cell
A neuron
A mature red blood cell
questions.why: A multinucleated cell has more than one nucleus, and skeletal muscle fibers are the standard example, with many nuclei along each long fiber. Liver cells (hepatocytes) can also have more than one nucleus. Most body cells have a single nucleus, and mature red blood cells have none.
notes: Correct. Skeletal muscle fibers have many nuclei.
Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus. They would be the answer for a question about non-striated muscle in the walls of hollow organs.
A neuron has a single nucleus in its cell body. Pick it for a question about cells that carry electrical signals.
A mature red blood cell is anucleated, meaning it has no nucleus at all. It is the answer for a question about a cell that gives up its nucleus to make room for hemoglobin.
questions.answerText: A skeletal muscle fiber
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which structure has microtubules in a 9 plus 0 arrangement and organizes rather than moves?
options: Cilia
Centrioles
Flagella
Microvilli
questions.why: Centrioles are short cylinders of microtubules in a 9 plus 0 arrangement, meaning nine sets around the edge and none in the center. This pattern goes with organizing, and centrioles help build the spindle during cell division. Cilia and flagella use a 9 plus 2 arrangement, with two extra microtubules in the center, and that pattern goes with movement.
notes: Cilia have the 9 plus 2 arrangement and beat to move mucus across the cell surface. They would be the answer for a question about the moving projections of the airway lining.
Correct. Centrioles have the 9 plus 0 arrangement and organize the spindle.
Flagella also have the 9 plus 2 arrangement and propel the whole cell, as in the sperm tail. Pick them for a question about the single long projection that moves a cell.
Microvilli are supported by actin microfilaments, not microtubules, and they do not move. They are the answer for a question about increasing surface area for absorption.
questions.answerText: Centrioles
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: After the Golgi apparatus finishes a protein for export, which structure carries it to the plasma membrane?
options: A lysosome
A transport vesicle
A secretory vesicle
A nuclear pore
questions.why: The Golgi apparatus packs finished products into secretory vesicles, which bud from its edge and travel to the plasma membrane along microtubules. There the vesicle fuses with the membrane and releases its contents by exocytosis. This is the last leg of the secretory pathway, after a transport vesicle has already carried the protein from the ER to the Golgi.
notes: A lysosome is a sac of digestive enzymes that the Golgi supplies, but it does not carry products to the cell surface. It is the answer for a question about digestion inside the cell.
A transport vesicle carries the protein from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus, the leg before this one. Choose it for the step that leaves the ER.
Correct. Secretory vesicles carry finished products from the Golgi to the membrane.
A nuclear pore is a channel through the nuclear envelope for messenger RNA and proteins. It is at the very start of the route, not at the step after the Golgi.
questions.answerText: A secretory vesicle

questions.q: Which organelle breaks down hydrogen peroxide and helps detoxify alcohol, and is plentiful in liver and kidney cells?
options: The ribosome
The lysosome
The peroxisome
The Golgi apparatus
questions.why: Peroxisomes are small membrane sacs of enzymes that break down fatty acids, amino acids, and hydrogen peroxide, a harmful by-product of metabolism. They also help detoxify alcohol, which is why liver and kidney cells contain many of them. They look similar to lysosomes, so their contents and job are what tell them apart.
notes: A ribosome builds proteins and has no membrane or detoxifying enzymes. Choose it for a protein synthesis question.
A lysosome is also an enzyme-filled sac, but its enzymes digest worn-out organelles, debris, and engulfed bacteria. Pick it for a question about the cell's digestion and recycling.
Correct. Peroxisomes break down hydrogen peroxide and help detoxify alcohol.
The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids. It is the answer for a question about the cell's shipping center.
questions.answerText: The peroxisome
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A mature red blood cell has no nucleus. Which term describes a cell like this?
options: Uninucleated
Anucleated
Binucleated
Multinucleated
questions.why: Anucleated means without a nucleus. Mature red blood cells are the standard example: they lose their nucleus as they develop, which makes room for hemoglobin to carry oxygen. Because they have no nucleus, they cannot divide or make new proteins, and they are replaced after a few months.
notes: Uninucleated cells have a single nucleus, which describes most body cells, including cardiac and smooth muscle cells. It is the opposite of what a mature red blood cell shows.
Correct. A cell with no nucleus is anucleated.
Binucleated cells have exactly two nuclei, which some liver cells show. The term still describes a cell that has nuclei, so it cannot fit a cell with none.
Multinucleated cells have more than one nucleus, as in skeletal muscle fibers and some liver cells. Pick this term for a long muscle fiber with many nuclei.
questions.answerText: Anucleated
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A liver cell must detoxify drugs and make lipids. Which organelle would you expect to be especially well developed in it?
options: Lysosomes
Smooth ER
The Golgi apparatus
Rough ER
questions.why: Smooth ER is the organelle that makes lipids, detoxifies drugs, and stores calcium, and it has no ribosomes. A liver cell that clears drugs from the blood and makes lipids therefore carries a large amount of smooth ER. Matching the amount of each organelle to the cell's job is the same idea that explains why protein-exporting cells are full of rough ER.
notes: Lysosomes digest worn-out parts and engulfed debris. They would be well developed in a phagocytic cell such as a macrophage, not in a cell built for detoxifying drugs.
Correct. Drug detoxification and lipid production call for abundant smooth ER.
The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins and lipids made elsewhere. It is the answer for a question about sorting and shipping products.
Rough ER makes proteins for secretion and membranes on its ribosomes. It would be the answer for a cell that exports large amounts of protein, such as a pancreatic enzyme-secreting cell.
questions.answerText: Smooth ER
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Rough ER sends its newly made proteins onward in transport vesicles. Which organelle receives them next?
options: A lysosome
The nucleus
The Golgi apparatus
A mitochondrion
questions.why: Transport vesicles carry newly made proteins from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus, the next stop on the endomembrane route. The Golgi modifies the proteins, sorts them, and tags them for their final destinations. From there, secretory vesicles carry products to the plasma membrane, and other vesicles carry enzymes to lysosomes.
notes: A lysosome can be a final destination for enzymes, but they reach it only after passing through the Golgi apparatus. It is the answer for a question about where digestive enzymes end up.
The nucleus is where messenger RNA is made, before the protein is built at the rough ER. Proteins leaving the ER do not travel backward to the nucleus.
Correct. The Golgi apparatus is the next stop after the rough ER.
Mitochondria make ATP and have their own ribosomes for some of their proteins. They are not a stop on the endomembrane route.
questions.answerText: The Golgi apparatus
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: What are the folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane called?
options: Cristae
Microvilli
Cisternae
Rugae
questions.why: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion folds back and forth into shelves called cristae. These folds multiply the surface area on which ATP is produced, so a mitochondrion can make more energy without getting larger. The same idea of folding to gain surface area shows up in microvilli on absorptive cells.
notes: Correct. The inner mitochondrial folds are cristae.
Microvilli are finger-like folds of the plasma membrane on the outer surface of absorptive cells. They are the answer for a question about absorption, not ATP production.
Cisternae are the flattened membrane sacs stacked to form the Golgi apparatus. The two words sound alike, so match cisternae with the Golgi and cristae with the mitochondrion.
Rugae are large folds in the wall of organs such as the stomach that let the organ expand. They are a whole-organ feature, not part of an organelle.
questions.answerText: Cristae
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Lysosomes take part in both phagocytosis and autophagy. Which statement correctly compares the two?
options: Phagocytosis builds proteins; autophagy builds lipids
Phagocytosis takes in outside debris; autophagy recycles the cell's own parts
Phagocytosis recycles the cell's own parts; autophagy takes in outside debris
Phagocytosis releases products; autophagy brings fluid into the cell
questions.why: In phagocytosis, a cell engulfs bacteria or debris from outside, and lysosomes then digest the captured material. In autophagy, the cell wraps up its own worn-out organelles and sends them to lysosomes to be broken down and recycled. Both rely on lysosomal enzymes, but one handles material from outside and the other handles the cell's own parts.
notes: Building proteins is the job of ribosomes, and building lipids is the job of smooth ER. Phagocytosis and autophagy are both about breaking things down.
Correct. Phagocytosis handles outside material and autophagy handles the cell's own parts.
This swaps the two processes. The prefix phago- refers to eating something taken in, while auto- means self, which points to the cell's own components.
Releasing products from the cell is exocytosis, the last step of the secretory pathway. Neither phagocytosis nor autophagy sends material out of the cell.
questions.answerText: Phagocytosis takes in outside debris; autophagy recycles the cell's own parts
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which cell junction uses cadherins linked to intermediate filaments to bind neighboring cells firmly, and is abundant in the outer epidermis and cardiac muscle?
options: The gap junction
The hemidesmosome
The desmosome
The tight junction
questions.why: A desmosome is a spot of strong adhesion between two neighboring cells. Cadherin proteins hold the two cells together, and on the inside they connect to intermediate filaments, which resist pulling. That is why desmosomes are abundant in tissues under constant tension, such as the epidermis and cardiac muscle.
notes: A gap junction is a protein channel connecting neighboring cells so ions and small molecules can pass. It is the answer for a question about cell-to-cell communication.
A hemidesmosome anchors a cell to the basement membrane below it rather than to another cell, using integrins. Pick it for a question about attaching the epidermis to the basement membrane.
Correct. Desmosomes bind cell to cell under tension.

A tight junction seals neighboring cells together so substances cannot leak between them, using claudins and occludins. It is the answer for a question about preventing leakage, as in the stomach and bladder lining.
questions.answerText: The desmosome

questions.q: Which cell junction is built from connexin proteins that form channels between neighboring cells?
options: The gap junction
The tight junction
The desmosome
The adherens junction
questions.why: Gap junctions are clusters of channels made from connexin proteins that link the cytoplasm of two neighboring cells. Small ions and molecules pass directly through them, which lets cells share nutrients and lets electrical impulses spread from cell to cell. They are found in places such as cardiac muscle, the GI tract, the uterus, and some neurons.
notes: Correct. Gap junctions are connexin channels.
Tight junctions use claudins and occludins to seal neighboring cells so nothing leaks between them. They block passage rather than create channels.
Desmosomes use cadherins attached to intermediate filaments to bind cells firmly under tension. They anchor cells together and do not let molecules pass between them.
Adherens junctions use cadherins attached to microfilaments to form adhesion belts that hold cells together. They give mechanical stability, not a passage between cells.
questions.answerText: The gap junction
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A patient has a disorder in which the hemidesmosomes of the skin fail. Which separation is most likely?
options: Cardiac muscle cells stop passing impulses to each other
Fluid leaks between the cells of the bladder lining
The epidermis lifts away from the basement membrane
Neighboring epidermal cells pull apart from each other
questions.why: Hemidesmosomes rivet the basal cells of the epidermis to the basement membrane beneath them. When they fail, the whole epidermis can lift off the basement membrane, producing a deep blister. Loss of desmosomes causes a different blister, because there the cells separate from one another instead.
notes: Impulses pass between cardiac muscle cells through gap junctions in the intercalated discs. Failure of gap junctions, not hemidesmosomes, would disrupt that communication.
Leakage between lining cells follows failure of tight junctions, which seal epithelia such as the bladder and stomach lining. It does not describe a hemidesmosome problem.
Correct. Without hemidesmosomes, the epidermis separates from the basement membrane.
Cells pulling apart from each other is what happens when desmosomes fail, since desmosomes bind cell to cell. Pick this outcome for a disorder of desmosomal adhesion.
questions.answerText: The epidermis lifts away from the basement membrane
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which junctions seal neighboring epithelial cells so substances cannot leak between them?
options: Desmosomes
Tight junctions
Basement membranes
Gap junctions
questions.why: Tight junctions are made of transmembrane proteins (claudins and occludins) that fuse the membranes of neighboring cells together, sealing the space between them. This stops substances from leaking between cells, so anything crossing the epithelium has to pass through the cells themselves. They are prominent in the linings of the stomach, intestines, and urinary bladder, and in the blood-brain barrier.
notes: Desmosomes bind neighboring cells strongly so they do not pull apart under tension. They hold cells together but do not seal the gaps between them.
Correct. Tight junctions seal the space between cells.
Basement membranes anchor the whole epithelium to the connective tissue below. They are a sheet under the tissue, not a junction between neighboring cells.
Gap junctions are channels that let ions and small molecules pass between neighboring cells. They connect cells for communication rather than sealing the space between them.
questions.answerText: Tight junctions
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which junctions are channels that let neighboring cells pass ions and small molecules directly to each other?
options: Gap junctions
Tight junctions
Desmosomes
Microvilli
questions.why: Gap junctions are clusters of protein channels that connect the cytoplasm of neighboring cells. Ions and small molecules pass directly through them, which lets cells share nutrients and lets electrical signals spread from cell to cell. In cardiac muscle they help the heart contract in a coordinated way, and they are found in many other tissues too.
notes: Correct. Gap junctions are channels between cells.
Tight junctions seal neighboring cells so nothing leaks between them. They block passage rather than create a channel.
Desmosomes anchor neighboring cells strongly against mechanical stress. They hold cells together but do not let molecules pass between them.
Microvilli are finger-like folds of the plasma membrane that increase surface area for absorption. They are not junctions between cells.
questions.answerText: Gap junctions
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which cell junction forms an adhesion belt of cadherins tied to actin microfilaments, just deep to the tight junctions?
options: The gap junction
The hemidesmosome
The adherens junction
The tight junction
questions.why: An adherens junction forms a continuous belt around the cell, just below the tight junctions. Transmembrane cadherin proteins link neighboring cells, and inside each cell they attach to actin microfilaments. This belt gives mechanical stability and helps epithelial surfaces resist being pulled apart, as in the cells lining the intestine.
notes: A gap junction is a channel of connexin proteins that lets ions and small molecules pass between cells. It is the answer for cell-to-cell communication.
A hemidesmosome anchors the base of a cell to the basement membrane using integrins. It is the answer for attaching cells to the sheet beneath them.
Correct. The adherens junction is the cadherin and actin adhesion belt.
A tight junction seals neighboring cells with claudins and occludins so nothing leaks between them. It sits just above the adherens junction and is the answer for preventing leakage.
questions.answerText: The adherens junction
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which junction anchors the basal surface of an epithelial cell to the underlying basement membrane?
options: The hemidesmosome
The desmosome
The gap junction
The adherens junction
questions.why: A hemidesmosome looks like half of a desmosome and anchors the basal surface of an epithelial cell to the basement membrane below it. Its main proteins are integrins. It keeps the epidermis from separating from the basement membrane under mechanical stress.
notes: Correct. Hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the basement membrane.
A desmosome binds two neighboring cells to each other, side to side. It is the answer for cell-to-cell adhesion, not cell-to-basement membrane attachment.
A gap junction is a channel between neighboring cells for ions and small molecules. It does not anchor cells to anything.
An adherens junction forms an adhesion belt between neighboring cells near their apical ends. It holds cells to each other, not to the basement membrane.
questions.answerText: The hemidesmosome
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A desmosome and a hemidesmosome both anchor cells. What does each one bind?
options: A desmosome binds two adjacent cells; a hemidesmosome binds a cell to the basement membrane
Both bind two adjacent cells
A desmosome binds a cell to the basement membrane; a hemidesmosome binds two cells
Both bind a cell to the basement membrane
questions.why: A desmosome is a spot weld between two neighboring cells, while a hemidesmosome attaches the base of one cell to the basement membrane below it. The name helps: hemi means half, so the half-desmosome has only one cell taking part and binds to a sheet instead. That is why hemidesmosomes are found only on the basal surface, while desmosomes are found between cells throughout an epithelium.
notes: Correct. Desmosomes join cells, and hemidesmosomes join a cell to the basement membrane.
Only the desmosome binds two neighboring cells. If both did, nothing would anchor the epithelium to the basement membrane, and the whole layer could lift off.
This reverses the two. Desmosomes join cell to cell, and the half-named hemidesmosome joins a cell to the basement membrane.
Only the hemidesmosome binds to the basement membrane. If both did, nothing would hold neighboring cells together under tension.
questions.answerText: A desmosome binds two adjacent cells; a hemidesmosome binds a cell to the basement membrane
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A cell diagram shows a dark nucleus surrounded by a granular region packed with small organelles, all enclosed by a thin outer boundary. A student labels the granular region cytosol. What is the better label, and why?
options: Nucleoplasm, because the region surrounds the nucleus and supports it.
Cytosol, because the organelles are not counted as part of any region.
Cytoplasm, because the region includes the organelles as well as the cytosol.
Plasma membrane, because the region lies just inside the outer boundary.
questions.why: The cytoplasm is everything between the plasma membrane and the nucleus, the cytosol plus the organelles. Cytosol is only the fluid part. A region drawn with organelles in it is the cytoplasm, so cytosol is too narrow a label.
notes: Nucleoplasm is the fluid inside the nucleus, not around it. It supports the chromatin and the nucleolus.
Organelles are part of the cytoplasm. Cytosol would be right only for the fluid between the organelles.
Correct. Cytoplasm is the cytosol plus the organelles, which is what the region shows.
The plasma membrane is the thin outer boundary itself. The granular region inside it is the cytoplasm.
questions.answerText: Cytoplasm, because the region includes the organelles as well as the cytosol.

questions.q: A mature red blood cell and a skeletal muscle fiber are compared. Which of the three cell regions is missing from one of them, and how many does each cell have?
options: The nucleus: the red blood cell has none, and the muscle fiber has many.
The cytoplasm: the muscle fiber has cytoplasm, and the red blood cell has none.
The nucleus: the red blood cell has one, and the muscle fiber has none.
The nucleus: the red blood cell has many, and the muscle fiber has none.
questions.why: Every cell has a plasma membrane and cytoplasm, but the number of nuclei varies. A mature red blood cell is anucleated, because losing the nucleus makes room for hemoglobin. A skeletal muscle fiber is multinucleated, with many nuclei. So the nucleus is the region present in one cell and missing from the other.
notes: Correct. The red blood cell is anucleated, and the skeletal muscle fiber is multinucleated.
Both cells have cytoplasm. The red blood cell's cytoplasm is packed with hemoglobin, so it is the nucleus, not the cytoplasm, that the red blood cell lacks.
Neither count is right. A mature red blood cell has no nucleus, and a skeletal muscle fiber has many, so it is the standard multinucleated example.
This is reversed. The red blood cell is the anucleated cell, and the skeletal muscle fiber is the multinucleated one.
questions.answerText: The nucleus: the red blood cell has none, and the muscle fiber has many.

questions.q: A liver cell on a slide has two nuclei. A student decides it must be abnormal because the generalized cell has one nucleus. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Liver cells normally have no nucleus, so any nucleus at all is a sign of damage.
Liver cells can have more than one nucleus, and the generalized cell is only a model.
The generalized cell has two nuclei, so every normal body cell has two.
Only red blood cells can have extra nuclei, so this cell must be a red blood cell.
questions.why: The generalized cell is a composite model that shows features shared by most cells, and no real cell looks exactly like it. Hepatocytes in the liver are a standard example of a multinucleated cell, along with skeletal muscle fibers. Two nuclei in a liver cell is normal.
notes: Hepatocytes do have nuclei, sometimes more than one. The cell with no nucleus is the mature red blood cell.
Correct. Hepatocytes are a standard multinucleated example, and the generalized cell is a composite.
The generalized cell shows one nucleus. The number of nuclei varies by cell type, so it is not a rule for every cell.
Mature red blood cells have no nucleus at all. The standard multinucleated examples are hepatocytes and skeletal muscle fibers.
questions.answerText: Liver cells can have more than one nucleus, and the generalized cell is only a model.
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: An electron micrograph shows a protein on the inner face of the membrane. It is not embedded in the bilayer and is attached only to the end of a protein that spans the bilayer. Which two protein types are shown?
options: An integral protein bound to a peripheral protein.
A peripheral protein bound to an integral protein.
Two integral proteins joined across the bilayer.
Two peripheral proteins joined on the inner face.
questions.why: Integral proteins are firmly embedded in the bilayer, and most span it completely. Peripheral proteins are not embedded. They attach loosely to one face of the membrane or to an integral protein. The loose protein is peripheral and the spanning one it holds is integral.
notes: This reverses the two. The protein that spans the bilayer is the integral one, and the loosely attached one is peripheral.
Correct. The loose protein is peripheral, and the one spanning the bilayer is integral.
Only one protein spans the bilayer. The other is not embedded, which makes it peripheral, not integral.
The protein that spans the bilayer is embedded, so it is integral. Only the loosely attached one is peripheral.
questions.answerText: A peripheral protein bound to an integral protein.

questions.q: A slide of the small intestine shows a dense border of short finger-like extensions on the free surface. A slide of the trachea shows longer hair-like extensions. Which extensions are these, and which of them has a 9 plus 2 microtubule core?
options: Cilia on the intestine and microvilli on the trachea; only the microvilli have the 9 plus 2 core.
Microvilli on the intestine and cilia on the trachea; both have the 9 plus 2 core.
Microvilli on the intestine and flagella on the trachea; only the flagella have the 9 plus 2 core.
Microvilli on the intestine and cilia on the trachea; only the cilia have the 9 plus 2 core.
questions.why: Microvilli are finger-like extensions that increase surface area for absorption, which fits the intestinal lining. Cilia are short hair-like extensions that sweep mucus across the airway surface. Cilia and flagella are built on a 9 plus 2 microtubule core, and microvilli are not.
notes: The surfaces are swapped. The intestine's finger-like border is microvilli, and the trachea's hair-like extensions are cilia, which are the ones with the 9 plus 2 core.
The labels are right, but microvilli do not have the 9 plus 2 microtubule core. That core belongs to cilia and flagella, the extensions that move.
The trachea's many hair-like extensions are cilia. A flagellum is a single long extension, and the only human example is the sperm tail.
Correct. Absorptive intestine carries microvilli, the airway carries cilia, and only cilia have the 9 plus 2 core.
questions.answerText: Microvilli on the intestine and cilia on the trachea; only the cilia have the 9 plus 2 core.

questions.q: A membrane protein forms a channel that lets ions pass from outside the cell to the inside. Which protein type must it be, and why could the other type not form this channel?
options: Peripheral, because only it touches the fluid; an integral protein is buried inside.
Integral, because it is loosely attached; a peripheral protein is fixed in place.
Integral, because only it spans the bilayer; a peripheral protein sits on one face.
Peripheral, because it spans the bilayer; an integral protein sits on one face.
questions.why: A channel has to reach from one side of the membrane to the other. Integral proteins are firmly embedded, most span the bilayer completely, and they form the channels, carriers, and receptors. Peripheral proteins attach to only one face, so they cannot open a path through the membrane.
notes: Peripheral proteins sit on one face, so they cannot open a path all the way through. Integral proteins span the bilayer and are exposed on both sides.
Integral is right, but integral proteins are firmly embedded, not loosely attached. Loose attachment describes peripheral proteins.
Correct. A channel must cross the whole bilayer, and only integral proteins do.
This swaps the two types. Integral proteins span the bilayer, and peripheral proteins sit on one face.
questions.answerText: Integral, because only it spans the bilayer; a peripheral protein sits on one face.

questions.q: A micrograph of a cell that is not dividing shows no rod-shaped chromosomes in the nucleus. A student concludes the cell has lost its DNA. What is the error?
options: The DNA has moved out through the nuclear pores and will return during division.
The DNA is present as loose chromatin and coils into chromosomes only during division.
The DNA is stored in the nucleolus, which hides it until the cell divides.
The DNA is dissolved in the nucleoplasm and is never visible in any form.
questions.why: Chromatin is the loose, threadlike form of DNA wound on proteins, present when the cell is not dividing. When the cell divides, chromatin coils tightly into rod-shaped chromosomes that can be seen. A nondividing cell with no visible chromosomes still has all its DNA, in the chromatin form.
notes: The DNA stays inside the nucleus. Nuclear pores let messenger RNA and ribosomal subunits out and proteins in, not the cell's DNA.
Correct. Between divisions the DNA stays as chromatin, which is why no chromosomes are visible.
The nucleolus is where ribosomal subunits are assembled, not where the DNA is stored. The DNA is spread through the nucleus as chromatin.
The nucleoplasm is the fluid that supports the chromatin and nucleolus. The DNA is visible as chromatin and condenses into chromosomes during division.
questions.answerText: The DNA is present as loose chromatin and coils into chromosomes only during division.
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A ribosomal subunit has to reach the cytoplasm, where it will help build proteins. Where in the nucleus is it assembled, and which structure does it leave through?
options: It is assembled in the chromatin and leaves through the nuclear envelope membrane.
It is assembled in the nucleoplasm and leaves through the rough ER.
It is assembled in the nucleolus and leaves through the plasma membrane.
It is assembled in the nucleolus and leaves through a nuclear pore.
questions.why: The nucleolus is the dense region inside the nucleus where ribosomal subunits are assembled. The nuclear envelope is a double membrane, so material crosses it through the nuclear pores, the protein-lined channels that let ribosomal subunits and messenger RNA move out to the cytoplasm.
notes: Chromatin is the DNA itself, not the site where subunits are built. Material crosses the envelope through its pores, not directly through the membrane.
The nucleoplasm is the supporting fluid, and the nucleolus inside it is the assembly site. The rough ER lies outside the nucleus, so it is not an exit from it.
The nucleolus is right, but the plasma membrane is the outer boundary of the whole cell. Passing through it would put the subunit outside the cell, not in the cytoplasm.
Correct. Subunits are built in the nucleolus and exit through the nuclear pores.
questions.answerText: It is assembled in the nucleolus and leaves through a nuclear pore.

questions.q: An electron micrograph shows ribosome-studded membranes running directly off the outer surface of the nuclear envelope. Which organelle is this, and what does it show about the envelope?
options: The Golgi apparatus, showing the envelope is a single membrane joined to it.
The rough ER, showing the envelope's outer membrane is continuous with it.
The smooth ER, showing the envelope's inner membrane is continuous with it.
The rough ER, showing the envelope is a single membrane with no pores.
questions.why: The rough ER is a membrane network studded with ribosomes. The nuclear envelope is a double membrane, and its outer membrane is continuous with the rough ER. Ribosome-covered membranes running straight off the envelope show that connection.
notes: The Golgi is a stack of flattened sacs with no ribosomes, and the envelope is a double membrane, not a single one.
Correct. Ribosomes mark the rough ER, and it joins the outer membrane of the double nuclear envelope.
Smooth ER has no ribosomes, so it would not look studded. It is the outer membrane of the envelope that joins the ER, not the inner one.
Rough ER is right, but the envelope is a double membrane with nuclear pores running through it.
questions.answerText: The rough ER, showing the envelope's outer membrane is continuous with it.

questions.q: A toxin breaks down the claudins and occludins between cells of the intestinal lining. Which junction fails, and what can now happen?
options: Gap junctions fail, so the cells can no longer pass ions to each other.
Desmosomes fail, so the cells pull apart under tension.
Hemidesmosomes fail, so the lining lifts off the basement membrane.
Tight junctions fail, so substances can leak between the cells.
questions.why: Claudins and occludins are the proteins of tight junctions. Tight junctions fuse the membranes of neighboring cells and seal the gap between them, which keeps organ contents from leaking into the surrounding tissue. When they fail, material can pass between the cells.
notes: Gap junctions are built from connexins, not claudins and occludins. They are the channels that let ions and small molecules pass between cells.
Desmosomes are built from cadherins linked to intermediate filaments. They resist pulling forces, and their loss causes blistering in the epidermis.
Hemidesmosomes use integrins to anchor cells to the basement membrane. The toxin targets the proteins of tight junctions instead.
Correct. Claudins and occludins build tight junctions, which seal the space between cells.
questions.answerText: Tight junctions fail, so substances can leak between the cells.
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: On a slide of cardiac muscle, an intercalated disc joins two cells. One junction there holds the cells together under pulling force, and another lets ions pass from cell to cell. Which pair is it?
options: Tight junctions hold the cells together, and desmosomes pass the ions.
Gap junctions hold the cells together, and desmosomes pass the ions.
Desmosomes hold the cells together, and gap junctions pass the ions.
Hemidesmosomes hold the cells together, and tight junctions pass the ions.
questions.why: Desmosomes rivet cells together against pulling forces, and cardiac muscle cells are one of their main locations. Gap junctions are protein channels that pass ions and small molecules between neighboring cells, and they are found in cardiac tissue. The intercalated disc uses both.
notes: Tight junctions seal gaps between epithelial cells, and desmosomes do not form channels. The ion channels at the disc are gap junctions.
These are reversed. Gap junctions are the channels for ions, and desmosomes are the ones that hold the cells together.
Correct. Desmosomes resist tension and gap junctions let ions pass between the cardiac cells.
Hemidesmosomes anchor a cell to a basement membrane, not to another cell, and tight junctions seal rather than pass ions.
questions.answerText: Desmosomes hold the cells together, and gap junctions pass the ions.

questions.q: Which tissue type covers body surfaces, lines cavities and vessels, and forms glands?
options: Muscle tissue
Connective tissue
Epithelial tissue
Nervous tissue
questions.why: Epithelial tissue covers the body's outer surface, lines internal cavities, tubes, and vessels, and forms glands. Its cells are packed tightly with very little material between them, and one surface always faces open space. Its main jobs are acting as a selective barrier, secreting products, and protecting against wear.
notes: Muscle tissue contracts to produce movement and generate force. It is the answer for a tissue that moves bones, pumps blood, or pushes material through hollow organs.
Connective tissue binds, supports, and protects other tissues and is found beneath epithelium, never on a body surface. It is the answer for the most widespread and diverse tissue.
Correct. Epithelium covers, lines, and forms glands.
Nervous tissue detects changes and generates nerve impulses. It is the answer for the tissue of the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.
questions.answerText: Epithelial tissue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which structure anchors an epithelium to the connective tissue below it?
options: A gap junction
A desmosome
The glycocalyx
The basement membrane
questions.why: The basement membrane is a thin sheet under the basal surface of every epithelium. It is made of a basal lamina (collagen, laminin, and glycoproteins) and a reticular lamina (collagen and glycoproteins), and it anchors and supports the epithelium on the connective tissue below. It also restricts large molecules and helps with wound healing.
notes: A gap junction is a channel between neighboring cells that lets ions and small molecules pass. It is the answer for a question about cell-to-cell communication.
A desmosome binds two neighboring cells to each other with cadherins and intermediate filaments. It holds cells together side to side, not the epithelium to the tissue below.
The glycocalyx is the sugar coat on the outside of individual cells, used for recognition. It is on the cell surface, not a sheet that anchors the whole epithelium.
Correct. The basement membrane anchors epithelium to connective tissue.
questions.answerText: The basement membrane
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Epithelia are classified on two features. One is the shape of the surface cells. What is the other?
options: The number of cell layers
The germ layer of origin
The fiber type in the matrix
The presence of a duct
questions.why: Epithelium is named using two features: the number of cell layers and the shape of the cells at the free surface. One layer is simple and more than one is stratified, and the surface cells are squamous (flat), cuboidal (cube-shaped), or columnar (tall). Putting the two together gives names such as simple squamous or stratified columnar.
notes: Correct. Layers plus surface cell shape name an epithelium.
The germ layer of origin describes where a tissue comes from in the embryo. It is not part of an epithelium's name.
Fiber type is used to describe connective tissue, such as dense regular tissue with parallel collagen. Epithelium has very little matrix and no fiber-based naming.
Whether a duct is present separates exocrine glands, which have ducts, from endocrine glands, which do not. It classifies glands, not covering and lining epithelium.
questions.answerText: The number of cell layers
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An epithelium classified as simple has how many cell layers?
options: One
Many
Three
Two
questions.why: A simple epithelium has a single layer of cells, with every cell resting on the basement membrane. A single layer keeps the path across the tissue short, so simple epithelia are built for diffusion, filtration, absorption, and secretion. Epithelia with more than one layer are called stratified and are built for protection.
notes: Correct. Simple means one layer.
Many layers describes a stratified epithelium, such as the stratified squamous epithelium of the skin. Choose it for a question about an epithelium built to resist wear.
Three layers would also make an epithelium stratified. No category of epithelium is defined by exactly three layers, so students pick this only when guessing a number.
Two layers is common in stratified cuboidal epithelium, found in the ducts of sweat and salivary glands. Any epithelium with two or more layers is stratified, not simple.
questions.answerText: One
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Squamous cells, used to name an epithelium, have which shape?
options: Flat and thin
Tall and column-like
Cube-shaped
Spindle-shaped
questions.why: Squamous cells are flat and thin, like scales or floor tiles, so their nuclei often look flattened too. Because they are so thin, a layer of squamous cells gives substances a very short path to cross, which suits diffusion and filtration. In a stratified epithelium, the name squamous refers to the flat cells at the free surface.
notes: Correct. Squamous cells are flat and thin.
Tall, column-like cells are columnar, with nuclei usually near the base. They are the answer for the lining of the stomach and intestines.
Cube-shaped cells are cuboidal, about as tall as they are wide, with round central nuclei. They are the answer for kidney tubules and small glands.
Spindle-shaped cells, thick in the middle and tapered at the ends, describe smooth muscle cells. That shape belongs to muscle tissue, not to epithelium.
questions.answerText: Flat and thin
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A gland releases its product through a duct onto a surface. Which gland is an example of this type?
options: The thyroid gland
The pituitary gland
A sweat gland
The adrenal gland
questions.why: Glands that release their product into a duct that carries it onto a surface or into a lumen are exocrine glands. Sweat glands are a clear example: sweat travels up a duct and out onto the skin surface. Salivary and sebaceous glands are other exocrine examples, while endocrine glands have no ducts and release hormones into the blood.
notes: The thyroid gland is an endocrine gland with no duct; it releases hormones directly into the bloodstream. Pick it for a question about a ductless gland.
The pituitary gland is an endocrine gland that releases hormones into the blood without a duct. It is the answer for a question about endocrine glands.
Correct. A sweat gland is an exocrine gland with a duct.
The adrenal gland is an endocrine gland that secretes hormones into the blood. It would be the answer for a question about ductless glands, not glands with ducts.
questions.answerText: A sweat gland
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which epithelial classification term describes one cell layer that looks layered and often lines the airways?
options: Pseudostratified
Stratified
Transitional
Simple squamous
questions.why: Pseudostratified epithelium looks layered because its nuclei sit at different heights, but every cell actually touches the basement membrane, so it is truly a single layer. Pseudo means false, so the name says it only seems stratified. It usually carries cilia and goblet cells and lines the trachea and bronchi.
notes: Correct. Pseudostratified is one layer that looks layered.
A stratified epithelium truly has two or more layers, and only the deepest cells touch the basement membrane. Choose it for a tissue built for protection, such as the epidermis.
Transitional epithelium has several true layers whose surface cells change from dome-shaped to flat as the organ stretches. It is the answer for the urinary bladder and ureters.
Simple squamous epithelium is one layer of flat cells and does not look layered. It is the answer for the air sacs of the lungs and the lining of blood vessels.
questions.answerText: Pseudostratified
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which general structural feature is true of epithelial tissue?
options: It is richly vascular with abundant matrix between cells
It has cells spaced widely apart in a fluid matrix
It has little capacity to regenerate after injury
It is avascular but innervated, with a free apical surface
questions.why: Epithelial tissue has no blood vessels of its own (it is avascular) and depends on diffusion from the connective tissue beneath it, but it does have nerve endings (it is innervated). Its cells are tightly packed with very little matrix, and each epithelium has one free apical surface facing open space. It also regenerates quickly because its cells divide often.
notes: Being richly vascular with abundant matrix describes most connective tissue, not epithelium. Epithelium has no blood vessels and very little matrix.
Cells widely spaced in a fluid matrix describes blood, a connective tissue. Epithelial cells are packed tightly side by side.
Epithelium actually regenerates well, which is why skin wounds and the gut lining heal quickly. Slow healing is typical of cartilage, which is avascular.
Correct. Epithelium is avascular, innervated, and has a free surface.
questions.answerText: It is avascular but innervated, with a free apical surface
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide shows a tissue with many cell layers and flat cells at its free surface. Which epithelial type is it?
options: Simple squamous epithelium
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium
questions.why: Name an epithelium by counting the layers first and then looking at the cells at the free surface. Many layers make it stratified, and flat surface cells make it squamous, so this is stratified squamous epithelium. It protects against abrasion and is found in the skin (keratinized) and in the mouth, esophagus, and vagina (non-keratinized).
notes: Simple squamous epithelium has flat cells but only one layer. It is the answer for the air sacs of the lungs and the lining of blood vessels.
Pseudostratified epithelium only looks layered; all of its cells touch the basement membrane, and its surface cells are columnar. It is the answer for the lining of the trachea.
Correct. Many layers with flat surface cells is stratified squamous.
Simple columnar epithelium is one layer of tall cells. It is the answer for the lining of the stomach and intestines.
questions.answerText: Stratified squamous epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide shows a single layer of cube-shaped cells lining a kidney tubule. Which epithelial type is it?
options: Simple squamous epithelium
Stratified cuboidal epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium
questions.why: One layer of cells makes the epithelium simple, and cells about as tall as they are wide, with round central nuclei, make it cuboidal. Simple cuboidal epithelium handles secretion and absorption and lines kidney tubules, small glands, and the surface of the ovary. In the kidney tubules it reabsorbs substances from the fluid passing through.
notes: Simple squamous epithelium has flat, thin cells, not cube-shaped ones. It is the answer for the air sacs of the lungs and capillary walls.
Stratified cuboidal epithelium has two or more layers of cube-shaped cells and lines the ducts of sweat, salivary, and mammary glands. It would need more than one layer.
Simple columnar epithelium has tall cells with nuclei near the base. It is the answer for the lining of the stomach and intestines.
Correct. One layer of cube-shaped cells is simple cuboidal.
questions.answerText: Simple cuboidal epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A tissue lines the urinary tract and stretches and recoils as the bladder fills and empties. Which epithelial type is it?
options: Stratified columnar epithelium
Transitional epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
questions.why: Transitional epithelium lines the urinary bladder, the ureters, and part of the urethra. It has several layers, and its surface cells change from dome-shaped to flat as the organ fills and stretches, then return to dome-shaped as it empties. This lets the lining expand without tearing while still keeping urine in.
notes: Stratified columnar epithelium has several layers with tall surface cells and is found in the male urethra and some large gland ducts. It does not stretch the way the bladder lining must.
Correct. The stretchy urinary lining is transitional epithelium.
Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer of flat cells built for diffusion and filtration. It is the answer for the air sacs of the lungs and blood vessel linings.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium is one layer that looks layered and lines the trachea and bronchi. It is the answer for an airway lining that moves mucus.
questions.answerText: Transitional epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide shows a single layer of tall cells lining the intestine, suited to absorption. Which epithelial type is it?
options: Simple columnar epithelium
Stratified columnar epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium
questions.why: One layer of tall, column-shaped cells with nuclei near the base identifies simple columnar epithelium. Its tall cells have room for the machinery of absorption and secretion, and they often carry microvilli and goblet cells. It lines the digestive tract from the stomach to the rectum, and the gallbladder.
notes: Correct. One layer of tall cells is simple columnar.
Stratified columnar epithelium has several layers and is found in places like the male urethra. It is too thick to suit absorption.
Simple cuboidal epithelium has cube-shaped cells with round central nuclei. It is the answer for kidney tubules and small glands.
Simple squamous epithelium is one layer of flat, thin cells. It is the answer for the air sacs of the lungs and the lining of blood vessels.
questions.answerText: Simple columnar epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide shows a single layer of very flat, thin cells forming the lining of a blood vessel. Which epithelial type is it?
options: Simple cuboidal epithelium
Transitional epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium
questions.why: A single layer of very flat, thin cells is simple squamous epithelium. It gives substances the shortest possible path to cross, so it is used wherever diffusion or filtration must be fast. It lines blood vessels, the air sacs (alveoli) of the lungs, and the filtering capillaries of the kidney, and it forms the serous membranes.
notes: Simple cuboidal epithelium has cube-shaped cells. It is the answer for kidney tubules and small glands.
Transitional epithelium has several layers that stretch and flatten as an organ fills. It is the answer for the urinary bladder and ureters.
Stratified squamous epithelium has many layers with flat surface cells and is built to resist abrasion. It is the answer for the skin and the lining of the mouth and esophagus.
Correct. One layer of flat cells is simple squamous.
questions.answerText: Simple squamous epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Sort these epithelia by their number of true cell layers: simple squamous, pseudostratified ciliated columnar, stratified squamous, transitional.
options: One layer: simple squamous and pseudostratified. More than one: stratified squamous and transitional
One layer: simple squamous and transitional. More than one: pseudostratified and stratified squamous
One layer: pseudostratified and transitional. More than one: simple squamous and stratified squamous
One layer: simple squamous only. More than one: pseudostratified, stratified squamous, and transitional
questions.why: Simple squamous epithelium is one layer of flat cells. Pseudostratified epithelium also has only one true layer, because every cell touches the basement membrane even though the nuclei sit at different heights. Stratified squamous and transitional epithelia both have several true layers, with only the deepest cells touching the basement membrane.
notes: Correct. Simple squamous and pseudostratified are one layer; the other two are layered.
Transitional epithelium has several true layers, which is part of what lets the bladder lining stretch. Pseudostratified is the one that only looks layered.
Simple squamous is one layer by definition, and transitional has several layers. This sort reverses those two.
This sort treats pseudostratified epithelium as layered because it looks layered. The prefix pseudo means false: all of its cells reach the basement membrane, so it is one layer.
questions.answerText: One layer: simple squamous and pseudostratified. More than one: stratified squamous and transitional
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A tissue must protect a surface against constant wear. Which epithelial arrangement best suits this job?
options: Simple epithelium
Pseudostratified epithelium
Stratified epithelium
Transitional epithelium
questions.why: Stratified epithelium has several layers of cells, so the surface cells can be worn away and replaced from below without exposing the tissue underneath. That makes it the right design for surfaces that face constant friction, such as the skin, mouth, and esophagus. Simple epithelium, with only one layer, would be damaged quickly by the same wear.
notes: Simple epithelium has a single layer built for diffusion, absorption, and secretion. It is the answer for thin exchange surfaces like the lung air sacs, not for resisting wear.
Pseudostratified epithelium is one true layer that looks layered and usually carries cilia and goblet cells. It is the answer for the airway lining that moves mucus.
Correct. Several replaceable layers suit a surface that faces wear.
Transitional epithelium is layered and stretches as the bladder fills. It is the answer for a lining that must change shape, not one that faces abrasion.
questions.answerText: Stratified epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A gland releases its product into the blood rather than onto a surface. How is this gland classified?
options: An endocrine gland
A sebaceous gland
An exocrine gland
A merocrine gland
questions.why: Endocrine glands have no ducts. They release their products, hormones, into the bloodstream, which carries them throughout the body. The thyroid, adrenal, and pituitary glands are examples, while glands that use ducts to deliver products to a surface are exocrine.
notes: Correct. A ductless gland that releases into the blood is endocrine.
A sebaceous (oil) gland is an exocrine gland that releases its oily product into a hair follicle. It is the classic example of holocrine secretion, not a gland that empties into the blood.
An exocrine gland releases its product into a duct that carries it onto a surface or into a lumen, as sweat and salivary glands do. It is the answer for a gland with a duct.

Merocrine describes how many exocrine gland cells release their product, by exocytosis, leaving the cell unharmed. It is the answer for salivary glands and the pancreas, not for release into the blood.
questions.answerText: An endocrine gland
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A small cut that stays within the epidermis heals quickly and hurts noticeably. Which two structural features of epithelium explain this?
options: Gap junctions and a rich blood supply
Many dividing cells and a nerve supply
An abundant matrix and a nerve supply
A rich blood supply and many dividing cells
questions.why: Epithelium regenerates quickly because its cells divide often to replace those lost at the surface. It is also innervated, with nerve endings among its cells, so even a shallow cut is felt. It has no blood vessels of its own, which is why a cut that stays in the epidermis may not bleed.
notes: Gap junctions let cells share ions and small molecules but do not explain fast healing or pain. Epithelium also lacks blood vessels, so this option has both parts wrong.
Correct. Frequent cell division and nerve endings explain fast healing and pain.
Epithelium has very little matrix; its cells are packed tightly together. A nerve supply is right, but abundant matrix describes connective tissue.
Epithelium is avascular, so it has no blood supply of its own. Dividing cells are right, but blood vessels belong to the connective tissue beneath it.
questions.answerText: Many dividing cells and a nerve supply
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Most cancers are carcinomas, which arise from one tissue type. Which tissue is it, and why is it a common origin?
options: Muscle tissue, because it contracts constantly
Epithelium, because its cells divide often
Connective tissue, because it is the most widespread
Nervous tissue, because it processes signals
questions.why: Carcinomas are cancers that arise from epithelium, and they make up the majority of cancers. Epithelial cells divide often to replace cells lost from surfaces, and each division is a chance for a mistake in copying DNA. Epithelium also lines the surfaces most exposed to damaging agents, such as the skin, lungs, and gut.
notes: Contraction does not damage DNA, and most muscle cells rarely divide in adults. Muscle cancers are rare and are a type of sarcoma.
Correct. Carcinomas come from epithelium, which divides often.
Cancers of connective tissue are called sarcomas, and they are much less common than carcinomas. Being widespread does not make a tissue the most frequent source of cancer.
Neurons in the adult rarely divide, so they offer few chances for copying errors. Processing signals does not make a tissue more likely to become cancerous.
questions.answerText: Epithelium, because its cells divide often
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Simple squamous epithelium lines the air sacs of the lungs and the inner walls of capillaries. Why is this flat, single-layer design used in both places?
options: Both face heavy abrasion, which flat cells resist best
Both secrete large amounts of mucus, which flat cells produce
Both move material across the wall, and one thin layer shortens the path
Both need a thick barrier to block material from crossing
questions.why: The air sacs of the lungs and the walls of capillaries both exist to let materials cross quickly: oxygen and carbon dioxide in the lungs, and nutrients, gases, and wastes in capillaries. A single layer of flat cells gives the shortest possible path, so diffusion is fast. The trade-off is fragility, which is why the alveoli are so easily damaged.
notes: Resisting abrasion is the job of stratified squamous epithelium, which sheds its top layers. A single flat layer is easily damaged by friction.
Mucus is made by goblet cells and mucous glands, usually in columnar or pseudostratified epithelium. Flat squamous cells are not built for heavy secretion.
Correct. A single flat layer gives the shortest path for diffusion.
A thick barrier would slow the crossing of materials, the opposite of what lungs and capillaries need. Thick, protective layers are found where blocking is the goal, as in the skin.
questions.answerText: Both move material across the wall, and one thin layer shortens the path
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The epidermis is stratified squamous epithelium, while the lining of the stomach is simple columnar. Why does each location get a different number of cell layers?
options: The stomach faces more abrasion, so it needs more layers than skin
Skin faces abrasion and needs replaceable layers; the stomach needs one layer for secretion
Skin absorbs nutrients and needs one layer; the stomach needs many layers
Both have many layers, but the stomach's are hidden under mucus
questions.why: Many layers protect against surface wear because the top cells can be lost and replaced from below, which fits the skin. A single layer of tall cells keeps the path for secretion and absorption short and leaves room in each cell for that work, which fits the stomach lining. The trade is protection versus exchange, so the two sites are built differently on purpose.
notes: The stomach lining is protected by mucus and is built for secretion, not for heavy friction. The skin actually faces far more abrasion than the stomach lining.
Correct. Protection calls for layers, and secretion calls for a single layer.
This reverses the two sites. The skin does not absorb nutrients, and a thick layered lining in the stomach would get in the way of its secretion.

The stomach lining really is a single layer of simple columnar epithelium; mucus covers it but does not hide extra layers. Students choose this when they cannot reconcile a thin lining with a harsh environment.
questions.answerText: Skin faces abrasion and needs replaceable layers; the stomach needs one layer for secretion
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lines much of the airway. Why is its ciliated, mucus-trapping design suited to that location?
options: It traps debris in mucus and sweeps it away from the lungs
It absorbs oxygen directly into the blood across the cilia
It forms a thick, waterproof seal that blocks airflow
It secretes digestive enzymes onto food passing through
questions.why: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lines the trachea and bronchi. Its goblet cells secrete mucus that traps inhaled dust and microbes, and its cilia beat to sweep that mucus up toward the throat, away from the lungs. This keeps debris from reaching the delicate air sacs, where gas exchange happens across thin simple squamous epithelium.
notes: Correct. Mucus traps debris and cilia sweep it out.
Gas exchange happens deeper in the lungs, across the simple squamous epithelium of the air sacs. Cilia move mucus; they do not absorb oxygen.
A waterproof seal that blocked airflow would stop breathing. Waterproofing is the job of the keratinized epidermis of the skin.
Digestive enzymes are secreted into the digestive tract by glands such as the pancreas, not into the airways. The airway lining secretes mucus, not enzymes.
questions.answerText: It traps debris in mucus and sweeps it away from the lungs
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Why does an endocrine gland not need a duct, while an exocrine gland does?
options: Endocrine cells burst to release their product, so no duct is needed
Endocrine glands are too large for a duct to fit inside them
Endocrine products enter the blood; exocrine products need a duct to reach a surface
Exocrine glands make hormones that can travel only through ducts
questions.why: Endocrine glands release hormones into the surrounding tissue fluid, where they enter the bloodstream and travel throughout the body, so no tube is needed. Exocrine products such as sweat, saliva, and digestive enzymes must reach one specific surface or cavity, and the duct is the path that carries them there. The pancreas does both, sending enzymes through a duct and hormones into the blood.
notes: A cell that bursts to release its product describes holocrine secretion, a type of exocrine secretion seen in sebaceous glands. It is not why endocrine glands lack ducts.
Gland size has nothing to do with having a duct. Tiny sweat glands have ducts, while the larger adrenal glands do not.
Correct. The blood carries endocrine products, while ducts carry exocrine products.
Hormones are the products of endocrine glands, and they travel in the blood, not in ducts. Exocrine products include sweat, saliva, and digestive enzymes.
questions.answerText: Endocrine products enter the blood; exocrine products need a duct to reach a surface
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Transitional epithelium lines the urinary bladder. Why is this tissue type, rather than simple squamous, the right choice there?
options: It is keratinized to resist abrasion from urine
It is one thin layer that lets urine diffuse back into the blood
It changes shape as the bladder fills, stretching without tearing
It carries cilia that sweep urine toward the urethra
questions.why: The bladder repeatedly fills and empties, so its lining must change its surface area without tearing. Transitional epithelium has several layers whose surface cells are dome-shaped when the bladder is empty and flatten out as it fills. Simple squamous epithelium is a single fragile layer that would tear when stretched and would let material cross too easily.
notes: Keratinized epithelium is found in the skin, where it resists abrasion and drying. The bladder lining is not keratinized; it needs to stretch rather than toughen.

Letting urine diffuse back into the blood would undo the work of the kidneys, so the bladder lining must act as a barrier. A single thin layer is the design for exchange surfaces such as the lung air sacs.
Correct. Transitional epithelium stretches as the bladder fills.
The bladder lining does not have cilia, and urine is moved by the muscular wall, not by beating projections. Ciliated epithelium is the answer for the airways.
questions.answerText: It changes shape as the bladder fills, stretching without tearing
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which germ layer forms the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts?
options: Mesoderm
Endoderm
Mesenchyme
Ectoderm
questions.why: The endoderm is the innermost of the three germ layers. It forms the epithelial lining of the digestive tract and the respiratory tract, which fits its position on the inside of the early embryo. The muscle and connective tissue around those linings come from the mesoderm.
notes: The mesoderm is the middle layer and forms muscle, bone, cartilage, blood, and most connective tissue. It forms the walls around the gut and airways, but not their inner epithelial lining.
Correct. The endoderm forms the lining of the gut and airways.
Mesenchyme is an embryonic connective tissue that develops into all types of connective tissue. It is a tissue, not one of the three germ layers.
The ectoderm is the outer layer and forms the epidermis of the skin and all nervous tissue. Pick it for the outer covering of the body or the brain.
questions.answerText: Endoderm
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide of the esophagus lining shows several cell layers, with cuboidal cells in the deep layers and flat cells at the free surface. How is this epithelium named?
options: Stratified squamous epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium
Stratified cuboidal epithelium
questions.why: Stratified epithelia are named for the shape of the cells at the free (apical) surface, not the deep cells. In stratified squamous epithelium the deepest cells are cuboidal or columnar, but they flatten as they are pushed toward the surface, so the name is squamous. Name the layers first, then the shape of the surface cells.
notes: Correct. Several layers with flat surface cells is stratified squamous.
Simple squamous has only one layer of flat cells. This tissue has several layers, so it must be stratified.
