Simple cuboidal is a single layer of cube-shaped cells, as in kidney tubules. This tissue has several layers and flat surface cells, so neither part of the name fits.
Stratified cuboidal would need cube-shaped cells at the surface. Students pick it when they name the tissue from its deep cells rather than its surface cells.
questions.answerText: Stratified squamous epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which location is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium?
options: The epidermis of the skin
The trachea
The esophagus
The kidney tubules
questions.why: Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium has many layers for protection, but its surface cells stay alive and moist rather than filling with keratin. It lines surfaces that face friction but must stay wet, such as the mouth, esophagus, and vagina. The skin uses the keratinized form, which is dry and tough.
notes: The epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, with dead keratin-filled cells at the surface that make it dry and water-resistant. Pick it for the keratinized version.
The trachea is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium that moves mucus. It is the answer for an airway lining.
Correct. The esophagus is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
Kidney tubules are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium, built for secretion and absorption. It is a single layer, not a stratified one.
questions.answerText: The esophagus
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In which mode of exocrine secretion does the entire cell rupture to release its product, as in sebaceous glands?
options: Apocrine
Endocrine
Merocrine
Holocrine
questions.why: In holocrine secretion, the product builds up inside the cell until the whole cell ruptures and becomes part of the secretion. Sebaceous (oil) glands work this way, and new cells must keep dividing to replace those lost. A simple memory aid is that holocrine sounds like whole, and the whole cell is secreted.
notes: Apocrine secretion pinches off the apical part of the cell with the product, and the cell then repairs itself. It is the answer for mammary glands.
Endocrine describes ductless glands that release hormones into the blood. It is a gland category, not a way an exocrine cell releases its product.
Merocrine secretion releases the product by exocytosis and leaves the cell unharmed. It is the most common type and is the answer for salivary glands and the pancreas.
Correct. In holocrine secretion the whole cell is released.
questions.answerText: Holocrine
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which mode of exocrine secretion releases the product by exocytosis and leaves the cell unharmed?
options: Endocrine
Holocrine
Apocrine
Merocrine
questions.why: In merocrine secretion, the product is packed into secretory vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane and release their contents by exocytosis. The cell loses nothing but the product, so it can keep secreting. It is the most common type of exocrine secretion and is used by salivary glands and the pancreas.
notes: Endocrine refers to ductless glands that release hormones into the blood. It does not describe how an exocrine cell releases its product.
Holocrine secretion releases the product by rupturing the entire cell, so the cell is destroyed. It is the answer for sebaceous glands.
Apocrine secretion releases the product by pinching off the top of the cell, which then repairs itself. It is the answer for mammary glands.
Correct. Merocrine secretion uses exocytosis and spares the cell.
questions.answerText: Merocrine
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which cell is a unicellular gland that secretes mucus?
options: The goblet cell
The mast cell
The adipocyte
The plasma cell
questions.why: A goblet cell is a single-celled exocrine gland shaped like a wine goblet, with a swollen top full of mucus. Goblet cells are scattered among the cells of simple columnar and pseudostratified epithelium in the intestines and airways. The mucus they release lubricates and protects the lining and traps particles.
notes: Correct. Goblet cells are single-celled mucus glands.
A mast cell sits in connective tissue along blood vessels and secretes histamine during inflammation. It is the answer for a question about allergic and inflammatory responses.
An adipocyte is a connective tissue cell that stores fat. It is the answer for adipose tissue, not mucus secretion.
A plasma cell develops from a B lymphocyte and secretes antibodies. It is the answer for antibody production in connective tissue.
questions.answerText: The goblet cell
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which gland is the classic example of a mixed gland, with both exocrine and endocrine parts?
options: The pancreas
The pituitary gland
The thyroid gland
A sweat gland
questions.why: The pancreas is a mixed gland. Its exocrine part secretes digestive enzymes into a duct that empties into the small intestine, and its endocrine part releases insulin and glucagon directly into the blood. One organ therefore uses both delivery routes.
notes: Correct. The pancreas is both exocrine and endocrine.
The pituitary gland is purely endocrine, releasing hormones into the blood. Pick it for a question about endocrine glands at the base of the brain.
The thyroid gland is purely endocrine, releasing its hormones into the blood with no duct. It is the answer for a ductless gland in the neck.
A sweat gland is purely exocrine, sending sweat through a duct onto the skin surface. It is the answer for a gland with a duct.
questions.answerText: The pancreas
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which epithelium, made of two or more layers of cube-shaped cells, lines the ducts of sweat glands?
options: Transitional epithelium
Stratified cuboidal epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium
questions.why: Stratified cuboidal epithelium has two or more layers of cube-shaped cells. It is fairly uncommon and is found mainly in the ducts of sweat, mammary, and salivary glands, where it gives some protection and limited secretion. The extra layer makes the duct wall sturdier than a single layer would be.
notes: Transitional epithelium has several layers that stretch as the organ fills and lines the urinary bladder. It is not found in gland ducts.
Correct. Sweat gland ducts are lined by stratified cuboidal epithelium.
Simple cuboidal epithelium has cube-shaped cells but only one layer. It is the answer for kidney tubules and small glands.
Stratified squamous epithelium has flat surface cells and many layers. It is the answer for the skin and the esophagus.
questions.answerText: Stratified cuboidal epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A multicellular exocrine gland has a branching duct and rounded secretory portions. What is its structural name?
options: Simple acinar
Simple tubular
Compound tubular
Compound acinar
questions.why: Gland names combine two features. The duct is simple if it does not branch and compound if it branches, and the secretory portion is tubular if it is tube-shaped and acinar if it is rounded. A branching duct with rounded secretory portions is therefore a compound acinar gland.
notes: Simple acinar gets the rounded secretory portion right but describes an unbranched duct. The branching duct makes this gland compound.
Simple tubular would mean an unbranched duct with a tube-shaped secretory part. Both features are the opposite of this gland.
Compound tubular gets the branching duct right but describes a tube-shaped secretory portion. Rounded secretory portions make it acinar.
Correct. Branching duct plus rounded secretory portions is compound acinar.
questions.answerText: Compound acinar
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In which mode of secretion does the apical part of the cell pinch off with the product, after which the cell repairs itself, as in mammary glands?
options: Holocrine
Endocrine
Apocrine
Merocrine
questions.why: In apocrine secretion, the product collects at the apical (top) end of the cell, and that part of the cell pinches off to release it. The rest of the cell survives, repairs itself, and secretes again. Mammary glands are the standard example.
notes: Holocrine secretion destroys the whole cell to release its product. It is the answer for sebaceous glands.
Endocrine describes ductless glands that release hormones into the blood. It is not a way that an exocrine cell releases its product.
Correct. Apocrine secretion pinches off the top of the cell.
Merocrine secretion releases the product by exocytosis without losing any of the cell. It is the answer for salivary glands and the pancreas.
questions.answerText: Apocrine
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. What does keratinized tell you about its surface cells?
options: They are cube-shaped cells that secrete sweat
They are dead cells filled with keratin
They are living cells with cilia on top
They are cells that stretch and change shape
questions.why: Keratinized means the surface cells have filled with the tough protein keratin and died, forming a dry, durable, water-resistant layer. This is the form of stratified squamous epithelium found in the epidermis. The nonkeratinized form, with living moist surface cells, lines wet surfaces such as the mouth, esophagus, and vagina.
notes: Cube-shaped cells describe cuboidal epithelium, which lines the ducts of sweat glands. This would be the answer for the tissue forming sweat gland ducts, not the skin surface.
Correct. Keratinized surface cells are dead and packed with keratin.
Living ciliated cells are found in pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lining the airways. Pick this description if the question asked about the tissue that sweeps mucus in the trachea.
Cells that stretch and change shape describe transitional epithelium of the urinary bladder. Choose it if the question asked which epithelium lets the bladder expand.
questions.answerText: They are dead cells filled with keratin
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Sebaceous glands release sebum by which mode of secretion, in which the whole cell fills with product and ruptures?
options: Merocrine secretion
Holocrine secretion
Apocrine secretion
Endocrine secretion
questions.why: In holocrine secretion, product builds up in the cytoplasm until the entire cell ruptures, so the dead cell becomes part of the secretion. Sebaceous glands work this way, and new cells from the base of the gland replace those that are lost. The prefix holo means whole, which matches the whole cell being released.
notes: Merocrine secretion releases product by exocytosis and leaves the cell unharmed; it is the most common type. Pick it if the question asked how salivary glands or eccrine sweat glands secrete.
Correct. Holocrine secretion releases whole ruptured cells, as sebaceous glands do.

Apocrine secretion releases product by pinching off the apical (top) part of the cell, which then repairs itself. The course notes give mammary glands as the example, so choose it for a question about milk release.
Endocrine is not a mode of exocrine secretion; it describes ductless glands that release hormones into the blood. It would be the answer for glands such as the thyroid.
questions.answerText: Holocrine secretion
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An eccrine sweat gland and a sebaceous gland release their products in different ways. Which pairing is correct?
options: Both glands are merocrine
The eccrine gland is merocrine, and the sebaceous gland is holocrine
Both glands are holocrine
The eccrine gland is holocrine, and the sebaceous gland is merocrine
questions.why: Eccrine sweat glands release watery sweat by exocytosis, leaving the secretory cells intact, which is merocrine secretion. Sebaceous glands fill whole cells with sebum and then rupture them, which is holocrine secretion. The two glands sit side by side in the dermis but use opposite strategies.
notes: Eccrine glands are merocrine, but sebaceous glands are not, because their cells rupture. This would be right for two glands like a salivary gland and an eccrine sweat gland.
Correct. Eccrine glands are merocrine and sebaceous glands are holocrine.
Sebaceous glands are holocrine, but eccrine glands keep their cells intact. Students choose this when they assume all skin glands secrete the same way.
This pairing reverses the two modes. Sweat glands do not destroy their cells to make sweat, while sebaceous cells do burst to release sebum.
questions.answerText: The eccrine gland is merocrine, and the sebaceous gland is holocrine
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which surface of an epithelial cell faces the lumen or the free surface of the tissue?
options: The basal surface
The basement membrane
The apical surface
The lateral surface
questions.why: Every epithelial cell has three surfaces. The apical surface faces the open space, either a lumen (the hollow inside of a tube or organ) or the outside of the body, and it is where you find cilia, microvilli, or keratin when a tissue has them. Because epithelium is named by the shape of its apical cells, finding this surface is the first step in identifying a slide.
notes: The basal surface is the opposite side of the cell, resting on the basement membrane. Pick it if the question asked which surface is anchored to the connective tissue below.
The basement membrane is not part of the cell at all. It is the thin layer beneath the basal surface that anchors the epithelium to the connective tissue below.
Correct. The apical surface faces the lumen or free surface.
The lateral surfaces are the sides of the cell that face its neighbors, where most cell junctions sit. Pick them if the question asked which surface connects one epithelial cell to the next.
questions.answerText: The apical surface
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which surface of an epithelial cell faces the neighboring cells and holds most of the cell junctions?
options: The lateral surface
The basal surface
The free surface
The apical surface
questions.why: The lateral surfaces are the sides of an epithelial cell, where it presses against the cells beside it. Junctions such as tight junctions and desmosomes are concentrated here, which is how epithelial cells stay tightly packed and form a continuous sheet with very little material between them.
notes: Correct. The lateral surfaces face neighboring cells and carry the junctions that hold the sheet together.
The basal surface rests on the basement membrane. Pick it if the question asked which surface anchors the cell to the tissue below, the site of hemidesmosomes.
The free surface is another name for the exposed apical side of the tissue, which faces a lumen or the outside rather than neighboring cells.
The apical surface faces the lumen or the outside, not other cells. Pick it if the question asked where cilia or microvilli are found.
questions.answerText: The lateral surface
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What do microvilli on the apical surface of an epithelial cell do?
options: They increase the surface area for absorption
They waterproof the surface with keratin
They sweep mucus along the surface
They anchor the cell to the basement membrane
questions.why: Microvilli are tiny, finger-like folds of the plasma membrane on the apical surface. They do not move; instead, they greatly increase the amount of membrane in contact with the lumen, so more material can be absorbed. That is why they are common on simple columnar cells lining the small intestine and on simple cuboidal cells of kidney tubules.
notes: Correct. Microvilli add surface area so the cell can absorb more.
Keratin is a tough protein that fills the surface cells of the epidermis. It belongs to keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, not to microvilli.
Sweeping mucus is the job of cilia, which are longer, motile projections. Pick this if the question were about the projections on the cells lining the trachea.
Anchoring to the basement membrane is done on the basal surface by hemidesmosomes. It is the opposite end of the cell from microvilli.
questions.answerText: They increase the surface area for absorption
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What do cilia on the apical surface of an epithelium do?
options: They store fat for energy
They absorb nutrients from the lumen
They move mucus along the surface
They secrete hormones into the blood
questions.why: Cilia are hair-like projections on the apical surface that beat together in waves. Their motion pushes a layer of mucus, or other material, across the surface in one direction. In the airways this carries trapped dust and microbes up and away from the lungs.
notes: Fat storage is the job of adipocytes in adipose connective tissue. It has nothing to do with projections on an epithelial surface.
Absorption is helped by microvilli, which increase surface area but do not beat. Pick this if the question asked about the brush border of intestinal cells.
Correct. Cilia beat in waves to move mucus and particles along the surface.
Hormones are released into the blood by endocrine glands, which have no ducts. Pick this if the question asked what an endocrine gland does.
questions.answerText: They move mucus along the surface
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Goblet cells are scattered among the cells of which two epithelia?
options: Simple columnar and pseudostratified ciliated columnar
Transitional epithelium and stratified cuboidal epithelium
Keratinized and non-keratinized stratified squamous
Simple squamous and simple cuboidal
questions.why: Goblet cells are single-celled glands that secrete mucus, and on a slide they look like pale, cup-shaped cells tucked between taller neighbors. They appear in simple columnar epithelium of the digestive tract and in pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium of the airways. Both linings need a protective, moist coat of mucus over their surface.
notes: Correct. Goblet cells sit in the columnar linings of the gut and the airways.
Transitional epithelium lines the bladder and stratified cuboidal lines sweat gland ducts. Neither one carries goblet cells.
Stratified squamous epithelium protects the skin, mouth, and esophagus by layering cells. Its surface is protected by layers or keratin, not by goblet cells.
Simple squamous and simple cuboidal cells are too short to house goblet cells. These tissues are built for diffusion and for secretion or absorption in places such as the alveoli and kidney tubules.
questions.answerText: Simple columnar and pseudostratified ciliated columnar
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What are the main functions of simple squamous epithelium?
options: Diffusion and filtration
Moving mucus with cilia
Protection against abrasion
Stretching as an organ fills
questions.why: Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer of very thin, flat cells, so substances only have to cross one thin cell to get through. That makes it ideal for diffusion, as in the alveoli of the lungs, and for filtration, as in the glomeruli of the kidneys. It also lines blood vessels and forms the surface of serous membranes.
notes: Correct. A single thin layer is built for diffusion and filtration.
Moving mucus with cilia is the job of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium in the trachea and bronchi.
Protection against abrasion needs many layers, which is the job of stratified squamous epithelium in the skin, mouth, and esophagus. A single thin layer would wear through.
Stretching as an organ fills is the job of transitional epithelium in the urinary bladder and ureters.
questions.answerText: Diffusion and filtration
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which epithelium, uncommon in the body, is found in parts of the male urethra and in the ducts of some glands?
options: Simple squamous epithelium
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium
Stratified columnar epithelium
questions.why: Stratified columnar epithelium has several layers, and the cells at the free surface are tall and column-shaped. It is rare in the body, found mainly in parts of the male urethra and in the ducts of some glands, where it gives both protection and some secretion.
notes: Simple squamous epithelium is a single flat layer used for diffusion. Pick it if the question asked about the alveoli or the lining of blood vessels.
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium is the epidermis of the skin, the most exposed surface in the body. Pick it if the question asked about a dry, outer surface.
Simple cuboidal epithelium is a single layer of cube-shaped cells. Pick it if the question asked about kidney tubules or the surface of the ovary.
Correct. Stratified columnar is the rare type found in the male urethra and some gland ducts.
questions.answerText: Stratified columnar epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide of the small intestine lining shows a single layer of tall cells with a fuzzy, brush-like edge on their apical surface. What forms this brush border?
options: Cilia
Microvilli
Goblet cells
Keratin
questions.why: The brush border is the fuzzy band you see along the apical surface of absorptive cells, and it is made of thousands of microvilli. In the small intestine, the job is absorbing nutrients, so the extra membrane surface area that microvilli provide fits that location. Cilia can also look fuzzy, but they are longer and are found in the airways, not on intestinal absorptive cells.
notes: Cilia are longer, motile projections that move mucus. Pick them if the slide came from the trachea, where the lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar.
Correct. Microvilli form the brush border and add surface area for absorption.
Goblet cells are present in the intestinal lining, but they are whole cells that look like pale cups, not a fuzzy edge. Pick them if the question asked which cells secrete mucus.
Keratin is the tough protein in the dead surface layers of the epidermis. Pick it if the slide showed a thick, layered skin surface.
questions.answerText: Microvilli
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide shows many cell layers. The deep cells are cuboidal, but the top layers are flat, dead, and lack nuclei, forming a compact pink band. Which tissue is it?
options: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Stratified cuboidal epithelium
Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Transitional epithelium
questions.why: Many layers with flat surface cells make this stratified squamous epithelium. The deciding clue is the surface: cells that have filled with keratin, lost their nuclei, and died form a compact layer at the top, which marks it as keratinized. This is the epidermis of the skin.
notes: Correct. Dead, flat, anucleate surface cells filled with keratin mark the keratinized type found in the epidermis.
Stratified cuboidal epithelium usually has just two layers of cube-shaped cells around a small lumen. Pick it for the duct of a sweat gland.
Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium also has flat surface cells, but they are alive and still have nuclei. Pick it for a moist lining such as the esophagus, mouth, or vagina.
Transitional epithelium has rounded, dome-shaped surface cells in a relaxed organ. Pick it for a slide of the urinary bladder or ureter.
questions.answerText: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide of the trachea shows nuclei at several different heights, cilia on the apical surface, and goblet cells, yet every cell touches the basement membrane. Which tissue is it?
options: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
Transitional epithelium
Stratified columnar epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium
questions.why: Pseudo means false. The nuclei sit at different heights, so the tissue looks layered, but every cell rests on the basement membrane, which makes it truly a single layer. Add cilia, goblet cells, and a location in the trachea, and the tissue is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.
notes: Correct. Staggered nuclei with every cell on the basement membrane, plus cilia and goblet cells, mark pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.
Transitional epithelium has true layers with dome-shaped surface cells and no cilia. Pick it for the urinary bladder.
Stratified columnar epithelium has true layers, with only the deepest cells on the basement membrane. Pick it for the rare lining of parts of the male urethra.
Simple columnar epithelium is one layer of tall cells whose nuclei line up in a single row near the base. Pick it for the stomach or intestine.
questions.answerText: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The serosa is the outer covering of many organs inside the ventral body cavity. Which epithelium forms its surface?
options: Transitional epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium
questions.why: The serosa is the visceral layer of a serous membrane, and its surface is a single layer of flat cells. A thin, smooth, moist sheet lets organs slide against the body wall with little friction, which suits the serous membranes. This is why the serosa is listed among the locations of simple squamous epithelium, along with the alveoli and the lining of blood vessels.
notes: Transitional epithelium lines the inside of the bladder and ureters so they can stretch. It is not found on the outer surface of organs.
Correct. A single sheet of flat cells forms the smooth surface of the serosa.
Simple columnar epithelium lines the inside of the digestive tract from the stomach to the rectum. It forms the inner lining of the gut, not its outer covering.
Stratified squamous epithelium is thick and built to resist abrasion. Pick it for the skin, mouth, or esophagus, not a slippery organ covering.
questions.answerText: Simple squamous epithelium
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide shows a single layer of cube-shaped cells with round, central nuclei. Besides the kidney tubules, where else would you expect to find this tissue?
options: Lining the trachea
On the surface of the ovary
Lining the urinary bladder
Lining the alveoli of the lungs
questions.why: A single layer of cube-shaped cells with round central nuclei is simple cuboidal epithelium. It handles secretion and absorption and is found in kidney tubules, in small glands, and on the surface of the ovary.
notes: The trachea is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, with tall cells, cilia, and goblet cells. Pick it for a slide with staggered nuclei and cilia.
Correct. Simple cuboidal epithelium covers the surface of the ovary as well as lining kidney tubules.
The urinary bladder is lined by transitional epithelium, which has several layers that stretch. Pick it for a layered tissue with dome-shaped surface cells.
The alveoli are lined by simple squamous epithelium, which is flat and thin for gas exchange. Pick it for a slide of very thin, flat cells.
questions.answerText: On the surface of the ovary
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In a heavy smoker, part of the ciliated lining of the bronchi can be replaced by stratified squamous epithelium. What does the airway lose with this change?
options: The cilia that sweep mucus out of the airway
Its ability to stretch as the airway fills
Its blood supply, since epithelium becomes vascular
Its basement membrane anchoring the epithelium
questions.why: The normal bronchial lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, where goblet cells make mucus and cilia beat to carry trapped particles upward and out. Stratified squamous epithelium is tougher against irritation but has no cilia or goblet cells. So the airway gains protection at that spot but loses its cleaning action, and mucus and debris collect instead of being swept away.
notes: Correct. Stratified squamous epithelium has no cilia, so the airway loses its mucus-clearing action at that spot.
Stretching as an organ fills is the special feature of transitional epithelium in the urinary bladder. The bronchial lining was never built to stretch like that.
All epithelium is avascular, both before and after this change. It always relies on the connective tissue underneath for nutrients, so blood supply is not what changes.
Every epithelium, simple or stratified, rests on a basement membrane. The new tissue still has one, so this is not what is lost.
questions.answerText: The cilia that sweep mucus out of the airway
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide from a full, stretched urinary bladder shows a few layers of fairly flat surface cells, and a student labels it stratified squamous. Which tissue is it really, and why do the surface cells look flat?
options: Transitional, because its surface cells flatten when stretched
Stratified cuboidal, because its cells shrink as urine collects
Keratinized stratified squamous, because the surface is dead
Simple squamous, because one thin layer allows diffusion
questions.why: Transitional epithelium lines the urinary bladder and ureters. Its surface cells are dome-shaped when the bladder is empty, but as the bladder fills and stretches they flatten out, and the layers thin. That is exactly why a full-bladder slide can be mistaken for stratified squamous, so the location is the clue that settles it.
notes: Correct. Transitional surface cells change from dome-shaped to flat as the bladder stretches.
Stratified cuboidal epithelium lines sweat gland ducts and does not change shape with filling. The idea that its cells shrink is a made-up explanation.
The bladder lining is not keratinized, and its surface cells are alive. Keratinized stratified squamous is the epidermis of the skin.
Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer, but this slide shows a few layers. Pick it for a slide of the alveoli or a blood vessel lining.
questions.answerText: Transitional, because its surface cells flatten when stretched
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, but the lining of the esophagus is non-keratinized. What best explains this difference?
options: The esophagus needs cilia on its surface to push food downward
Skin is avascular, while the esophageal lining has its own blood vessels
The esophagus lacks a basement membrane, so it cannot hold keratin
Skin faces dry air, while the esophagus surface stays moist
questions.why: Both tissues are many layers thick with flat surface cells, because both face rubbing and wear. Skin is exposed to dry air, so its surface cells fill with keratin and die, forming a tough layer that resists water loss. The esophagus is kept moist by mucus and saliva, so its surface cells stay alive and the lining stays soft and flexible as food passes.
notes: The esophagus has no cilia; food is moved by muscle contractions in its wall. Cilia belong to the airway lining, such as the trachea.
All epithelium is avascular, including both the epidermis and the esophageal lining. Each one gets its nutrients by diffusion from the connective tissue below.
Every epithelium, including the esophageal lining, rests on a basement membrane. This is not a real difference between the two tissues.
Correct. A dry outer surface gets keratin, while a moist inner lining stays non-keratinized.
questions.answerText: Skin faces dry air, while the esophagus surface stays moist
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which tissue type is the most diverse and widespread, binding and supporting other tissues?
options: Epithelial tissue
Muscle tissue
Nervous tissue
Connective tissue
questions.why: Connective tissue is the most diverse and widespread tissue type, ranging from fluid blood to hard bone. It binds and supports other tissues, protects and insulates organs, stores energy as fat, and transports materials in the blood. What these different forms share is a plan of scattered cells within a large extracellular matrix.
notes: Epithelial tissue covers surfaces, lines cavities, and forms glands, with tightly packed cells and little matrix. It is the answer for a tissue that forms coverings and linings.
Muscle tissue contracts to produce movement and force. It is the answer for a tissue specialized for movement, not for binding and support.
Nervous tissue detects changes and carries nerve impulses. It is the answer for the tissue of the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.
Correct. Connective tissue is the most diverse and widespread type.
questions.answerText: Connective tissue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which three ingredients make up every connective tissue?
options: Neurons, fibers, and plasma
Cells, junctions, and ducts
Cells, fibers, and ground substance
Cells, fibers, and a basement membrane
questions.why: Every connective tissue is built from the same three ingredients: cells, protein fibers, and ground substance. The fibers and ground substance together form the extracellular matrix, which makes up most of the tissue's volume. Changing the proportions of these ingredients is what makes blood liquid, cartilage firm, and bone hard.
notes: Neurons are the signaling cells of nervous tissue, and plasma is the fluid matrix of blood only. This list mixes nervous tissue with one specific connective tissue.
Cell junctions and ducts are features of epithelium and glands. Epithelial cells are joined tightly by junctions, while connective tissue cells are scattered in matrix.
Correct. Cells, fibers, and ground substance.
The basement membrane belongs to epithelium; it anchors the epithelium to the connective tissue below. Cells and fibers are correct, but the third ingredient of connective tissue is ground substance.
questions.answerText: Cells, fibers, and ground substance
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which connective tissue fiber type is strong, ropelike, and the most abundant?
options: Muscle fibers
Collagen fibers
Elastic fibers
Reticular fibers
questions.why: Collagen fibers are thick, strong, ropelike fibers that resist pulling forces. Collagen is the most abundant protein in the body, about 25 percent of all protein, and it is found in most connective tissues, including bone, tendon, and cartilage. When collagen fibers run in parallel bundles, as in a tendon, they give great strength in one direction.
notes: Muscle fibers are muscle cells, not fibers in a connective tissue matrix. Students pick this because the word fiber is shared, but muscle fibers are living cells that contract.
Correct. Collagen fibers are the strong, abundant, ropelike fibers.
Elastic fibers are made of elastin and can stretch to about 150 percent of their relaxed length and then recoil. They are the answer for skin, lungs, and artery walls that must spring back.

Reticular fibers are fine, branching collagen fibers coated with glycoprotein that form delicate networks. They are the answer for the supporting framework of soft organs such as lymph nodes and the spleen.
questions.answerText: Collagen fibers
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which cell builds the fibers and ground substance of connective tissue proper?
options: The macrophage
The chondrocyte
The fibroblast
The adipocyte
questions.why: Fibroblasts are the most common cells of connective tissue proper. They migrate through the tissue and secrete both the protein fibers and the ground substance that make up the matrix. In the blast and cyte naming pattern, fibroblasts are the active, matrix-building form, while fibrocytes are the mature cells that maintain it.
notes: Macrophages are phagocytic cells, derived from monocytes, that engulf bacteria and debris. They defend connective tissue rather than build its matrix.

Chondrocytes are mature cartilage cells sitting in lacunae, where they maintain the cartilage matrix. They are the answer for cartilage, which is a supporting connective tissue rather than connective tissue proper.
Correct. Fibroblasts secrete the fibers and ground substance.
Adipocytes are connective tissue cells that store fat as triglycerides. They are the answer for adipose tissue, not for the cell that builds fibers.
questions.answerText: The fibroblast
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which tissue is the most common type of cartilage, with fine collagen fibers and a glassy-looking matrix?
options: Elastic cartilage
Fibrocartilage
Dense regular connective tissue
Hyaline cartilage
questions.why: Hyaline cartilage is the most common cartilage in the body. Its collagen fibers are so fine they are not visible with ordinary staining, which gives the matrix a smooth, glassy look, and its chondrocytes sit in small spaces called lacunae. It covers the ends of long bones and forms the costal cartilages, the nose, and the rings of the trachea.
notes: Elastic cartilage looks similar but has many elastic fibers that let it bend and spring back. It is the answer for the external ear and the epiglottis.
Fibrocartilage has thick, visible collagen bundles that resist compression and absorb shock. It is the answer for intervertebral discs, the pubic symphysis, and the knee menisci.
Dense regular connective tissue has densely packed parallel collagen fibers with fibroblasts between them, not chondrocytes in lacunae. It is the answer for tendons and ligaments.
Correct. Hyaline cartilage is the most common, glassy cartilage.
questions.answerText: Hyaline cartilage
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Compact bone is built around repeating structural units called what?
options: Lacunae
Trabeculae
Lamellae
Osteons
questions.why: Compact bone is built from repeating cylindrical units called osteons. Each osteon is a set of concentric rings of bone matrix, called lamellae, around a central canal that carries blood vessels and nerves. Osteocytes sit in small spaces called lacunae between the rings.
notes: Lacunae are the small spaces where osteocytes sit within an osteon. They are parts of the unit, not the repeating unit itself.
Trabeculae are the thin bony struts of spongy bone, arranged as an open lattice with marrow in the spaces. Pick them for a question about the inner bone tissue at the ends of long bones.
Lamellae are the concentric rings of matrix that make up each osteon. They are the layers of the unit, so choose them for a question about the rings around the central canal.
Correct. Osteons are the repeating units of compact bone.
questions.answerText: Osteons
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which connective tissue consists of cells and cell fragments suspended in a fluid matrix called plasma?
options: Blood
Adipose tissue
Areolar tissue
Reticular tissue
questions.why: Blood is a fluid connective tissue. Its cells and cell fragments (red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets) are suspended in a fluid matrix called plasma. It counts as connective tissue because it follows the same plan of cells within an extracellular matrix, and it connects the body by transporting materials.
notes: Correct. Blood is cells and fragments in plasma.
Adipose tissue is made mostly of fat-storing adipocytes with very little matrix. It is the answer for energy storage, insulation, and cushioning.

Areolar tissue is loose connective tissue with a gel-like ground substance and a mix of collagen, elastic, and reticular fibers. It is the answer for the soft packing beneath epithelium and around organs.
Reticular tissue is a network of fine reticular fibers that forms the framework of soft organs such as lymph nodes and the spleen. Its matrix is not fluid.
questions.answerText: Blood
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Muscle, bone, cartilage, blood, and most connective tissue all develop from which germ layer?
options: Endoderm
Mesoderm
Ectoderm
Ectoderm and endoderm together
questions.why: The mesoderm is the middle germ layer. It forms muscle, bone, cartilage, blood, and most connective tissue, which together make up much of the body's bulk. Embryonic mesenchyme, the tissue that develops into all types of connective tissue, comes mainly from this layer.
notes: The endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts. Pick it for a question about the inner lining of the gut or airways.
Correct. The mesoderm forms the supporting and moving tissues.
The ectoderm forms the epidermis and all nervous tissue. It would be the answer for the brain, spinal cord, and outer skin.
These two layers form coverings, linings, and nervous tissue, not the supporting and moving tissues listed here. Students choose this when they forget the middle layer.
questions.answerText: Mesoderm
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The extracellular matrix of a connective tissue is made of which two components together?
options: Cells and fibers
Cells and ground substance
Fibers and ground substance
Fibers and a basement membrane
questions.why: The extracellular matrix is the nonliving material between connective tissue cells, made of protein fibers plus ground substance. The fibers give strength and stretch, and the ground substance fills the spaces and holds tissue fluid. In most connective tissues the matrix takes up far more of the volume than the cells do.
notes: Cells are a separate ingredient of connective tissue; they live in the matrix but are not part of it. Fibers are half right, but ground substance completes the matrix.
Ground substance is half right, but the cells are not part of the matrix. The second matrix component is the protein fibers.
Correct. The matrix is fibers plus ground substance.
The basement membrane is the anchoring sheet beneath an epithelium. Fibers are half right, but the other matrix component is ground substance.
questions.answerText: Fibers and ground substance
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Dense regular connective tissue is built of parallel collagen and forms which structures?
options: The walls of large arteries
Tendons and ligaments
Lymph nodes and the spleen
The dermis and organ capsules
questions.why: Dense regular connective tissue is packed with collagen fibers that all run parallel, with rows of fibroblasts squeezed between them. This arrangement makes it extremely strong when pulled along the line of the fibers, which is exactly what tendons and ligaments need. Tendons connect muscle to bone, and ligaments connect bone to bone.
notes: The walls of large arteries contain elastic connective tissue, rich in elastic fibers that let the wall stretch and recoil with each heartbeat.
Correct. Parallel collagen forms tendons and ligaments.
Lymph nodes and the spleen are supported by reticular connective tissue, a fine branching network of reticular fibers.
The dermis and organ capsules are made of dense irregular connective tissue, whose collagen runs in many directions to resist forces from all sides.
questions.answerText: Tendons and ligaments
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which connective tissue fiber type forms fine branching networks that support soft organs such as lymph nodes and the spleen?
options: Muscle fibers
Elastic fibers
Collagen fibers
Reticular fibers
questions.why: Reticular fibers are thin collagen fibers coated with glycoprotein that branch to form a fine, delicate mesh. This mesh forms the internal framework, or stroma, of soft organs such as lymph nodes, the spleen, and bone marrow, where it holds cells in place. Reticular fibers also help form the basement membrane.
notes: Muscle fibers are muscle cells that contract, not fibers in a connective tissue matrix. Students pick this because the word fiber is shared.
Elastic fibers stretch and recoil because they contain elastin. They are the answer for skin, lungs, and artery walls.
Collagen fibers are thick, strong, ropelike fibers that resist pulling. They are the answer for tendons, ligaments, and most connective tissues, not a fine branching mesh.
Correct. Reticular fibers form the supporting mesh of soft organs.
questions.answerText: Reticular fibers
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the material that fills the space between connective tissue cells and fibers and holds tissue fluid?
options: The basement membrane
Plasma
Ground substance
Collagen
questions.why: Ground substance is the material that fills the space between connective tissue cells and fibers. It can be fluid, gel-like, or calcified, and it is made of water and organic molecules such as chondroitin sulfate. It holds tissue fluid, supports and binds cells, and lets nutrients and wastes move between the blood and the cells.
notes: The basement membrane is the anchoring sheet beneath an epithelium. It lies between epithelium and connective tissue rather than filling spaces within connective tissue.
Plasma is the fluid matrix of blood specifically. It would be the answer for a question about what blood cells are suspended in.
Correct. Ground substance fills the space between cells and fibers.
Collagen is a protein fiber in the matrix, not the material between the fibers. It is the answer for the strong, ropelike component of connective tissue.
questions.answerText: Ground substance
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide shows cells in lacunae surrounded by a firm matrix, and the tissue has no blood vessels. Which tissue is it?
options: Compact bone
Cartilage
Dense regular connective tissue
Areolar tissue
questions.why: Cells sitting in small spaces called lacunae, surrounded by a firm matrix with no blood vessels running through it, identify cartilage. Its cells are chondrocytes, and because cartilage is avascular, nutrients must diffuse through the matrix to reach them. This lack of blood vessels is why cartilage heals so slowly.
notes: Compact bone also has cells (osteocytes) in lacunae, but its matrix is calcified and arranged in osteons around central canals that carry blood vessels. Pick it when the slide shows concentric rings around canals.
Correct. Cells in lacunae with no blood vessels is cartilage.
Dense regular connective tissue has parallel collagen fibers with rows of fibroblasts, not cells in lacunae. It is the answer for a tendon or ligament slide.
Areolar tissue is loose, with a mix of fibers and scattered cells in a soft, gel-like matrix. It is the answer for the packing tissue under epithelium, and it has blood vessels.
questions.answerText: Cartilage
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A connective tissue shows densely packed collagen fibers all running parallel in one direction. Which subtype is it?
options: Dense irregular connective tissue
Dense regular connective tissue
Reticular connective tissue
Areolar connective tissue
questions.why: Collagen fibers packed tightly and all running in the same direction identify dense regular connective tissue. Rows of flattened fibroblast nuclei lie between the fiber bundles. This arrangement resists pulling along one line, which is why it forms tendons and ligaments.
notes: Dense irregular connective tissue also has densely packed collagen, but its bundles run in many directions. It is the answer for the dermis and organ capsules.
Correct. Parallel collagen is dense regular connective tissue.
Reticular connective tissue is a fine branching network of reticular fibers. It is the answer for the framework of lymph nodes and the spleen.
Areolar connective tissue is loose, with scattered fibers of several types and lots of open space. It is the answer for the soft packing beneath epithelium.
questions.answerText: Dense regular connective tissue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cartilage slide from an intervertebral disc shows a tough matrix dominated by thick collagen bundles. Which cartilage type is it?
options: Fibrocartilage
Hyaline cartilage
Dense regular connective tissue
Elastic cartilage
questions.why: A cartilage matrix dominated by thick bundles of collagen identifies fibrocartilage. Those collagen bundles let it resist compression and absorb shock, which is why it is found in intervertebral discs, the pubic symphysis, and the menisci of the knee. Its chondrocytes often sit in rows between the collagen bundles.
notes: Correct. Thick collagen bundles in cartilage mean fibrocartilage.

Hyaline cartilage has fine collagen fibers that are not visible with ordinary staining, giving a smooth, glassy matrix. It is the answer for the ends of long bones, the costal cartilages, and the trachea.
Dense regular connective tissue also has thick parallel collagen, but its cells are fibroblasts between fibers, not chondrocytes in lacunae. It is the answer for tendons and ligaments.
Elastic cartilage is packed with elastic fibers that let it bend and spring back. It is the answer for the external ear and the epiglottis.
questions.answerText: Fibrocartilage
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide shows an open lattice of thin bony struts with marrow in the spaces. Which tissue is it?
options: Hyaline cartilage
Spongy bone
Compact bone
Dense regular connective tissue
questions.why: Spongy bone is an open lattice of thin bony struts called trabeculae, with marrow filling the spaces between them. The lattice makes bone lighter while still supporting stress along the lines of the struts. It fills the ends of long bones and the inside of flat bones, beneath a shell of compact bone.
notes: Hyaline cartilage has chondrocytes in lacunae within a smooth, glassy matrix and no marrow. It is the answer for the ends of long bones at the joint surface.
Correct. An open lattice with marrow is spongy bone.
Compact bone is the dense outer layer of bone, built from tightly packed osteons with no large open spaces. Pick it for a slide showing concentric rings around central canals.
Dense regular connective tissue is parallel collagen fibers with fibroblasts, forming tendons and ligaments. It is not mineralized and has no marrow spaces.
questions.answerText: Spongy bone
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A connective tissue slide shows large, empty-looking cells that store fat. Which subtype is it?
options: Reticular tissue
Adipose tissue
Dense irregular tissue
Areolar tissue
questions.why: Adipose tissue is made of adipocytes, cells almost completely filled by a large fat droplet that pushes the nucleus to the edge. On a slide the fat is dissolved during preparation, so the cells look empty, like a net of rings. Adipose tissue stores energy, insulates the body, and cushions organs such as the kidneys and heart.
notes: Reticular tissue is a fine branching mesh of reticular fibers. It is the answer for the framework of lymph nodes and the spleen.
Correct. Fat-filled, empty-looking cells are adipose tissue.
Dense irregular tissue is thick collagen bundles running in many directions with few cells. It is the answer for the dermis and organ capsules.
Areolar tissue is loose connective tissue with scattered fibers and a variety of cells in a soft matrix. It is the answer for the packing tissue beneath epithelium.
questions.answerText: Adipose tissue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide from the dermis of the skin shows thick collagen bundles running in all directions. Which subtype is it?
options: Dense irregular connective tissue
Elastic connective tissue
Dense regular connective tissue
Areolar connective tissue
questions.why: Dense irregular connective tissue is packed with thick collagen bundles running in many directions. Because the fibers point every way, the tissue resists pulling from any direction, which suits the dermis of the skin and the capsules around organs and joints. Fibroblasts are scattered among the bundles.
notes: Correct. Collagen in all directions is dense irregular connective tissue.
Elastic connective tissue is dominated by elastic fibers that stretch and recoil. It is the answer for the walls of large arteries.
Dense regular connective tissue has collagen bundles that all run parallel, giving strength in one direction. It is the answer for tendons and ligaments.
Areolar connective tissue is loose, with thin scattered fibers and a lot of open ground substance. It is the answer for the soft packing beneath epithelium.
questions.answerText: Dense irregular connective tissue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cartilage slide from the external ear shows a matrix packed with elastic fibers. Which tissue is it?
options: Hyaline cartilage
Elastic cartilage
Fibrocartilage
Elastic connective tissue
questions.why: Elastic cartilage has chondrocytes in lacunae like other cartilage, but its matrix is packed with dark-staining elastic fibers. These fibers let it bend and spring back into shape, which is why it forms the external ear (pinna) and the epiglottis. Hyaline cartilage would be too stiff for these structures.
notes: Hyaline cartilage has a smooth, glassy matrix with fine collagen fibers that do not show with ordinary staining. It is the answer for the ends of long bones, the nose, and the trachea.
Correct. Cartilage with elastic fibers in the ear is elastic cartilage.
Fibrocartilage is dominated by thick collagen bundles that resist compression. It is the answer for intervertebral discs and the knee menisci.
Elastic connective tissue is also rich in elastic fibers, but it has fibroblasts rather than chondrocytes in lacunae. It is the answer for the walls of large arteries, not the ear.
questions.answerText: Elastic cartilage
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide shows a soft, loosely arranged connective tissue with scattered fibers that wraps and cushions organs and holds tissue fluid. Which subtype is it?
options: Fibrocartilage
Dense regular connective tissue
Areolar connective tissue
Adipose connective tissue
questions.why: Areolar connective tissue is loose connective tissue with a mix of collagen, elastic, and reticular fibers scattered through a soft, gel-like ground substance. That open structure holds tissue fluid and gives support with some stretch. It lies under epithelia and wraps around organs and blood vessels, cushioning them and holding them in place.
notes: Fibrocartilage is a tough cartilage with chondrocytes in lacunae among thick collagen bundles. It is the answer for intervertebral discs and the knee menisci.
Dense regular connective tissue has tightly packed parallel collagen fibers. It is the answer for tendons and ligaments.
Correct. Soft, loose packing tissue is areolar connective tissue.
Adipose tissue is dominated by large fat-filled adipocytes and stores energy and insulates. It is the answer for a slide of empty-looking cells packed together.
questions.answerText: Areolar connective tissue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A tissue has cells in lacunae, a firm matrix with fine collagen, no blood vessels, and covers the ends of bones at a joint. Which tissue is it?
options: Fibrocartilage
Hyaline cartilage
Dense regular connective tissue
Compact bone
questions.why: Chondrocytes in lacunae and an avascular matrix mark the tissue as cartilage. A firm matrix with fine collagen fibers points to hyaline cartilage, and its location covering the ends of bones, as articular cartilage, confirms it. Hyaline cartilage gives a smooth surface for joint movement.
notes: Fibrocartilage is also avascular with cells in lacunae, but its matrix is dominated by thick collagen bundles. It is the answer for intervertebral discs and the knee menisci, not the ends of long bones.
Correct. All four features point to hyaline cartilage.
Dense regular connective tissue has fibroblasts between parallel collagen fibers rather than cells in lacunae. It is the answer for tendons and ligaments.
Compact bone also has cells in lacunae, but it is well supplied with blood vessels running through the central canals of its osteons. An avascular tissue cannot be bone.
questions.answerText: Hyaline cartilage
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A torn knee meniscus barely repairs itself. Which structural feature of cartilage explains this slow healing?
options: Cartilage has a rich blood supply
Cartilage is avascular, with no blood vessels
Cartilage contains only elastic fibers
Cartilage is made of many cell layers
questions.why: Cartilage, including the fibrocartilage of the knee meniscus, has no blood vessels of its own. Repair depends on blood bringing oxygen, nutrients, and repair cells, so in cartilage these must slowly diffuse in through the matrix instead. That is why a torn meniscus heals poorly, while a skin wound closes in days.
notes: Cartilage has no blood supply; a rich blood supply describes bone and most other connective tissue. A rich blood supply would speed healing, not slow it.
Correct. Without blood vessels, cartilage heals slowly.
Only elastic cartilage is dominated by elastic fibers, and the meniscus is fibrocartilage with thick collagen bundles. Fiber type is not what slows healing; the lack of blood vessels is.
Many cell layers describe a stratified epithelium, not cartilage. Cartilage is made of scattered chondrocytes in a firm matrix.
questions.answerText: Cartilage is avascular, with no blood vessels
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A tendon tears when it is twisted sideways rather than pulled along its length. Which structural property of dense regular connective tissue explains this?
options: It is avascular like cartilage
Its collagen runs in all directions
It contains mostly elastic fibers
Its collagen runs parallel in one direction
questions.why: In dense regular connective tissue, the collagen bundles all run parallel along the length of the tendon. That makes the tendon very strong when pulled in that one direction but much weaker against forces from other angles, such as twisting. Dense irregular tissue, with fibers in every direction, trades some of that one-way strength for resistance from all sides.
notes: Tendons do have a poor blood supply, which slows their healing, but that does not explain why twisting tears them. Their weakness to twisting comes from the parallel fiber direction.
Collagen running in all directions describes dense irregular connective tissue, such as the dermis. That arrangement would resist twisting better, not worse.
Mostly elastic fibers describes elastic connective tissue in artery walls. Tendons are dominated by collagen, not elastic fibers.
Correct. Parallel collagen gives strength in one direction only.
questions.answerText: Its collagen runs parallel in one direction
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A large artery wall must stretch with each heartbeat and then spring back. Which connective tissue fiber should dominate there, and why?
options: Reticular fibers, because they form a soft supporting mesh
Collagen fibers, because they resist stretch with great strength
Keratin fibers, because they make a tissue tough and waterproof
Elastic fibers, because they stretch and then recoil to shape
questions.why: Elastic fibers are made of elastin and can stretch to about 150 percent of their resting length and then return to their original shape. A large artery wall is stretched by every surge of blood from the heart, and elastic fibers let it expand and then recoil. This is why the walls of large arteries contain elastic connective tissue.
notes: Reticular fibers form a fine supporting mesh in soft organs such as lymph nodes and the spleen. They hold cells in place but do not provide stretch and recoil.
Collagen fibers resist stretching and give tensile strength, but they do not spring back after being stretched. They are the answer for tendons and ligaments.
Keratin is a protein inside epidermal cells, not a connective tissue fiber. It is the answer for what makes the skin's surface tough and water-resistant.
Correct. Elastic fibers let the artery wall stretch and recoil.
questions.answerText: Elastic fibers, because they stretch and then recoil to shape
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Adipose tissue stores fat, cushions organs, and insulates the body. Why is its cell structure, a large lipid droplet pushing the nucleus to the edge, well matched to that job?
options: The droplet conducts heat away from the body to cool it
The droplet holds water that cushions the organs
The droplet is empty space that keeps the cell light
One large droplet stores the most fat per cell
questions.why: An adipocyte is almost completely filled by one large lipid droplet, with its nucleus and cytoplasm squeezed into a thin rim at the edge. Packing the cell this way stores the most fat in the least space, which is ideal for a tissue whose main jobs are energy storage, insulation, and cushioning. The fat also conducts heat poorly, so it helps hold in body heat.
notes: Fat conducts heat poorly, which is why adipose tissue insulates and helps hold heat in. This option reverses that property.
The droplet holds lipid (triglycerides), not water. Adipose does cushion organs, but it does so with fat, which also stores energy.
The droplet looks empty on slides only because the fat dissolves during slide preparation. In the living tissue it is full of lipid.
Correct. One large droplet maximizes fat storage per cell.
questions.answerText: One large droplet stores the most fat per cell
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Connective tissue has cells scattered within a large amount of nonliving material. Why does this abundant matrix suit connective tissue's roles?
options: Connective tissue has almost no material between its cells
The matrix gives the support, cushioning, and connection
The matrix lets the cells absorb nutrients from a free surface
The matrix keeps the tissue from supporting anything
questions.why: In connective tissue, most of the work is done by the matrix the cells secrete rather than by the cells themselves. The fibers and ground substance give bone its hardness, cartilage its firm cushioning, and tendons their strength. That is the opposite of epithelium, where tightly packed cells with little matrix form the working surface.
notes: Having almost no material between cells describes epithelium, where cells are packed tightly. Connective tissue is defined by its large amount of matrix.
Correct. The matrix does most of connective tissue's work.
A free surface that faces open space is a feature of epithelium. Connective tissue lies beneath epithelium and never forms a body surface.
The matrix is what does the supporting, so it cannot prevent support. Students choose this when they think of nonliving material as filler with no function.
questions.answerText: The matrix gives the support, cushioning, and connection
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares blast cells (such as fibroblasts) with cyte cells (such as fibrocytes)?
options: Blasts occur only in bone; cytes occur only in cartilage
Blasts divide and secrete matrix; cytes are mature and maintain it
Blasts are mature and maintain matrix; cytes divide and secrete it
Blasts break down matrix; cytes build new matrix
questions.why: In connective tissue, cell names ending in -blast mark immature, active cells that divide and secrete new extracellular matrix. Names ending in -cyte mark the mature form, which maintains and repairs the matrix already in place. The same pattern applies to fibroblasts and fibrocytes, osteoblasts and osteocytes, and chondroblasts and chondrocytes.
notes: Both forms occur in several connective tissues. Fibroblasts and fibrocytes are in connective tissue proper, osteoblasts and osteocytes in bone, and chondroblasts and chondrocytes in cartilage.
Correct. Blasts build matrix, and cytes maintain it.
This reverses the two. The -blast form is the builder, and the -cyte form is the mature maintainer.
Breaking down matrix is not the job of either form. In bone, that job belongs to a separate cell type, the osteoclast, which comes up in Module 2.
questions.answerText: Blasts divide and secrete matrix; cytes are mature and maintain it
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which connective tissue cell, found along blood vessels, secretes histamine that widens blood vessels during inflammation?
options: The adipocyte
The mast cell
The fibroblast
The plasma cell
questions.why: Mast cells sit along the small blood vessels that supply connective tissue. When tissue is injured or exposed to an allergen, they release histamine, which widens nearby blood vessels and helps start inflammation. They are one of the cells to identify on a slide of loose areolar connective tissue.
notes: Adipocytes store fat as triglycerides. They are the answer for adipose tissue, not inflammation.
Correct. Mast cells release histamine.
Fibroblasts are the most common connective tissue cells and secrete fibers and ground substance. They build matrix rather than releasing histamine.
Plasma cells develop from B lymphocytes and secrete antibodies. They are the answer for antibody production in the connective tissue of the gut and airways.
questions.answerText: The mast cell
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which connective tissue cell develops from a monocyte and engulfs bacteria and debris by phagocytosis?
options: The macrophage
The mast cell
The plasma cell
The fibroblast
questions.why: Macrophages are large phagocytic cells that develop from monocytes, a type of white blood cell. They engulf and digest bacteria, dead cells, and debris. Fixed macrophages stay in one tissue, such as the liver, lungs, or spleen, while wandering macrophages move to sites of infection or inflammation.
notes: Correct. Macrophages come from monocytes and engulf debris.
Mast cells release histamine during inflammation rather than engulfing debris. They are the answer for the cell that widens blood vessels.
Plasma cells come from B lymphocytes, not monocytes, and they secrete antibodies. They fight infection with antibodies rather than by engulfing it.
Fibroblasts build connective tissue fibers and ground substance. They are the answer for the cell that makes matrix.
questions.answerText: The macrophage
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which connective tissue cell develops from a B lymphocyte and secretes antibodies?
options: The fibroblast
The mast cell
The macrophage
The plasma cell
questions.why: Plasma cells develop from B lymphocytes and secrete antibodies, proteins that tag specific invaders for destruction. They are common in the connective tissue beneath the linings of the digestive and respiratory tracts and in lymphatic tissue, where invaders are most likely to enter. Their name refers to the cell type, not to blood plasma.
notes: Fibroblasts secrete fibers and ground substance, not antibodies. They are the answer for the cell that builds the matrix.
Mast cells release histamine to widen blood vessels during inflammation. They are the answer for the cell involved in allergic responses.
Macrophages come from monocytes and engulf bacteria and debris. They fight infection by phagocytosis, not by secreting antibodies.
Correct. Plasma cells secrete antibodies.
questions.answerText: The plasma cell
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the fluid extracellular matrix of blood called?
options: Plasma
Ground substance
Lymph
Synovial fluid
questions.why: Blood is a connective tissue whose matrix is a fluid called plasma. The red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets are suspended in it, and it carries dissolved nutrients, gases, hormones, and wastes. A fluid matrix is what lets blood flow through the vessels.
notes: Correct. The matrix of blood is plasma.
Ground substance is the general term for the material between cells and fibers in connective tissue, often a gel. Blood's fluid matrix has its own name, plasma.
Lymph is the fluid carried in lymphatic vessels after it drains from the tissues. It is not the matrix of blood.
Synovial fluid is secreted by the synovial membrane and lubricates joint cavities. It is not part of blood.
questions.answerText: Plasma
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which embryonic connective tissue, with widely scattered fibroblasts in a jelly-like matrix, supports the umbilical cord?
options: Areolar connective tissue
Hyaline cartilage
Embryonic mesenchyme
Mucous connective tissue
questions.why: Mucous connective tissue has widely scattered fibroblasts in a jelly-like matrix, and it is found in the umbilical cord, where it supports the cord's blood vessels. It is one of the two embryonic connective tissues. The other, mesenchyme, is the tissue that gives rise to all connective tissues.
notes: Areolar connective tissue is adult loose connective tissue found beneath epithelium and around organs. It is not the jelly-like tissue of the umbilical cord.
Hyaline cartilage has chondrocytes in lacunae within a firm, glassy matrix. It is the answer for the ends of long bones, not the umbilical cord.
Embryonic mesenchyme has irregular cells in a semifluid matrix and is found in the embryo under the skin and along developing bones. It differentiates into all types of connective tissue.
Correct. Mucous connective tissue supports the umbilical cord.
questions.answerText: Mucous connective tissue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Most connective tissue is highly vascular. Which two connective tissues are the main exceptions, with little or no blood supply?
options: Dense irregular and reticular tissue
Bone and blood
Cartilage and tendon
Areolar and adipose tissue
questions.why: Most connective tissues have a rich blood supply, but cartilage has no blood vessels and tendons have very few. Without a good blood supply, oxygen, nutrients, and repair cells reach these tissues slowly. That is why injuries such as a torn meniscus or a ruptured calcaneal (Achilles) tendon heal slowly.
notes: Dense irregular and reticular connective tissue both have a good blood supply. The dermis, made of dense irregular tissue, bleeds readily when cut.
Bone is well supplied with blood vessels that run through the central canals of its osteons, and blood is itself the fluid inside vessels. Neither lacks a blood supply.
Correct. Cartilage and tendon are the exceptions.
Areolar and adipose tissue are both well supplied with blood vessels, and blood vessels are one of the structures to find on an adipose slide.
questions.answerText: Cartilage and tendon
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which type of cartilage forms the costal cartilages that connect the ribs to the sternum?
options: Elastic cartilage
Dense regular connective tissue
Hyaline cartilage
Fibrocartilage
questions.why: The costal cartilages are made of hyaline cartilage, the most common type, with fine collagen fibers in a glassy matrix. Hyaline cartilage gives firm but flexible support, which lets the rib cage move slightly during breathing. Hyaline cartilage also covers the ends of long bones and forms the nose, trachea, and larynx.
notes: Elastic cartilage is packed with elastic fibers and is very bendable. It is the answer for the external ear and the epiglottis.
Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments, which are made of parallel collagen and fibroblasts. It does not have chondrocytes in lacunae and is not cartilage.
Correct. Costal cartilage is hyaline cartilage.
Fibrocartilage has thick collagen bundles that resist compression. It is the answer for intervertebral discs, the pubic symphysis, and the knee menisci.
questions.answerText: Hyaline cartilage
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which embryonic tissue differentiates into all types of connective tissue?
options: Mucous connective tissue
Embryonic mesenchyme
Ectoderm
Endoderm
questions.why: Embryonic mesenchyme is a connective tissue of the embryo with irregular cells in a semifluid matrix and delicate reticular fibers. It is found under the developing skin and along developing bones, and it gives rise to every type of connective tissue, from blood to bone. Most mesenchyme comes from the mesoderm.
notes: Mucous connective tissue is the jelly-like embryonic tissue of the umbilical cord. It supports the cord but does not give rise to the other connective tissues.
Correct. Mesenchyme gives rise to all connective tissues.
The ectoderm is the outer germ layer and forms the epidermis and nervous tissue. It is not the source of connective tissue in general.
The endoderm is the inner germ layer and forms the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts. It does not form connective tissue.
questions.answerText: Embryonic mesenchyme
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Elastic fibers in connective tissue are built mainly from which protein?
options: Keratin
Collagen
Elastin
Actin
questions.why: Elastic fibers are made mostly of the protein elastin, supported by a glycoprotein called fibrillin. Elastin lets the fiber stretch to about 150 percent of its relaxed length and then spring back. That is why elastic fibers are plentiful in the skin, lungs, and blood vessel walls, which all stretch and recoil.
notes: Keratin is the tough protein that fills the surface cells of the epidermis, hair, and nails. It belongs to epithelial cells, not to connective tissue fibers.
Collagen is the protein of collagen fibers and, coated with glycoproteins, of reticular fibers. It resists pulling but does not stretch and recoil, so pick it for the strong fibers of tendons.
Correct. Elastin is the stretchy protein of elastic fibers.
Actin is a protein of the cytoskeleton and of the thin filaments in muscle cells. It is found inside cells, not in the fibers of the extracellular matrix.
questions.answerText: Elastin
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which fibers are found in loose areolar connective tissue?
options: Only reticular fibers, forming a fine mesh
Collagen, elastic, and reticular, loosely mixed
Only elastic fibers, packed in wavy sheets
Only collagen fibers, packed in parallel bundles
questions.why: Areolar connective tissue is the general packing tissue of the body. It has a loose arrangement of all three fiber types with cells scattered among them and plenty of ground substance, which gives it strength, elasticity, and support. It sits under epithelia and around organs and blood vessels.
notes: A mesh of reticular fibers alone is the signature of reticular connective tissue. Pick it for the framework of lymph nodes and the spleen.
Correct. Areolar tissue has all three fiber types in a loose arrangement.
A tissue dominated by elastic fibers is elastic connective tissue. Pick it for the wall of a large artery such as the aorta.
Parallel, tightly packed collagen bundles describe dense regular connective tissue. Pick it for tendons and ligaments.
questions.answerText: Collagen, elastic, and reticular, loosely mixed
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Besides the subcutaneous tissue under the skin, where is adipose tissue commonly found?
options: In the tendons of the limbs
In the walls of the trachea
Around the kidneys and the heart
At the ends of long bones
questions.why: Adipose tissue is connective tissue made of fat-storing cells called adipocytes. It stores energy, insulates the body, and cushions organs. Besides the subcutaneous layer, it collects around organs such as the kidneys and the heart, where it pads and protects them.
notes: Tendons are dense regular connective tissue with parallel collagen bundles. Pick dense regular connective tissue if the question asked about tendons.
The trachea is held open by rings of hyaline cartilage and lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. Adipose is not what builds its wall.
Correct. Adipose tissue pads organs such as the kidneys and the heart.
The ends of long bones are covered by hyaline cartilage, which gives a smooth joint surface. Pick hyaline cartilage for that location.
questions.answerText: Around the kidneys and the heart
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On a cartilage slide, what is the perichondrium?
options: The small space in the matrix that holds a chondrocyte
A dense connective tissue layer around the cartilage
The gel-like ground substance between the cartilage cells
The membrane that covers the outer surface of bone
questions.why: Peri means around and chondr means cartilage, so the perichondrium is the layer around cartilage. It is a band of dense connective tissue at the edge of hyaline and elastic cartilage, and because it has blood vessels, the avascular cartilage inside relies on it for nutrients. Fibrocartilage is the cartilage type listed in lab as having no perichondrium.
notes: The small space that holds a chondrocyte is a lacuna. Pick lacuna if the question asked where cartilage cells sit.
Correct. The perichondrium is the dense connective tissue layer around cartilage.
The gel-like material between cells is part of the extracellular matrix, the ground substance. It fills the cartilage rather than wrapping its outside.
The membrane covering bone is the periosteum. The name is similar, but oste means bone, so pick it for a bone slide.
questions.answerText: A dense connective tissue layer around the cartilage
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Besides the external ear, which structure is made of elastic cartilage?
options: The epiglottis
The costal cartilages
The pubic symphysis
The intervertebral discs
questions.why: Elastic cartilage looks like hyaline cartilage but has many elastic fibers in its matrix. That lets it bend and then return to its shape. It is found in the external ear (the pinna) and in the epiglottis, the flap that tips over the airway when you swallow.
notes: Correct. The epiglottis is elastic cartilage, like the external ear.
The costal cartilages that join the ribs to the sternum are hyaline cartilage. Pick hyaline for them.
The pubic symphysis is a pad of fibrocartilage, built to resist compression. Pick fibrocartilage for this joint.
The intervertebral discs are made with fibrocartilage, which absorbs shock between vertebrae. Pick fibrocartilage for a disc.
questions.answerText: The epiglottis
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The pubic symphysis, where the two hip bones meet at the front, contains which type of cartilage?
options: Dense regular connective tissue
Elastic cartilage
Fibrocartilage
Hyaline cartilage
questions.why: Fibrocartilage has thick bundles of collagen fibers running through its matrix, which makes it the toughest cartilage. It resists compression and absorbs shock, so it is found where bones are pushed together under load, such as the pubic symphysis, the intervertebral discs, and the menisci of the knee.
notes: Dense regular connective tissue is not cartilage at all; it has fibroblasts instead of chondrocytes in lacunae. Pick it for tendons and ligaments.
Elastic cartilage bends and springs back. Pick it for the external ear or the epiglottis.
Correct. The pubic symphysis contains a pad of fibrocartilage.
Hyaline cartilage has a smooth, glassy matrix with fine collagen fibers. Pick it for the ends of long bones, the costal cartilages, or the trachea.
