questions.answerText: Fibrocartilage
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The C-shaped rings that hold the trachea open are made of which type of cartilage?
options: Elastic cartilage
Fibrocartilage
Dense irregular connective tissue
Hyaline cartilage
questions.why: Hyaline cartilage is the most common cartilage. It is firm but flexible, with fine collagen fibers that do not show with ordinary staining, which gives the matrix its glassy look. That combination keeps the trachea open while still letting it bend, and the same tissue is found in the larynx, nose, costal cartilages, and the ends of long bones.
notes: Elastic cartilage is more flexible and springs back after bending. Pick it for the epiglottis or the external ear.
Fibrocartilage resists heavy compression. Pick it for the intervertebral discs, the pubic symphysis, or the knee menisci.
Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen running in many directions but is not cartilage. Pick it for the dermis of the skin.
Correct. The tracheal rings are hyaline cartilage.
questions.answerText: Hyaline cartilage
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where is connective tissue found in relation to epithelium?
options: Between the epithelial cells, holding them together
Only inside bones, separate from any epithelium
Below the epithelium, never on a free body surface
On the free surface, above the epithelium
questions.why: Epithelium covers surfaces and lines cavities, while connective tissue supports and connects other tissues from beneath. Connective tissue is found below epithelial tissue and never forms a free surface. Because epithelium has no blood vessels, it depends on the blood supply of the connective tissue underneath for its nutrients.
notes: Epithelial cells are held to each other by cell junctions such as tight junctions and desmosomes, not by connective tissue between them.
Connective tissue is found throughout the body, not only in bone. It includes areolar tissue, adipose, cartilage, blood, and more.
Correct. Connective tissue lies beneath epithelium and does not form free surfaces.
Free surfaces are covered by epithelium, not connective tissue. This choice reverses the two tissues.
questions.answerText: Below the epithelium, never on a free body surface
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide from a lymph node shows a fine, dark-staining network of branching fibers forming a mesh, with many cells sitting in its spaces. Which tissue is it?
options: Reticular connective tissue
Areolar connective tissue
Dense irregular connective tissue
Adipose connective tissue
questions.why: Reticular connective tissue is built around a fine, branching mesh of reticular fibers, which take up dark stains. This mesh forms the stroma, the internal framework, of soft organs such as lymph nodes and the spleen, and blood cells sit in its open spaces. The location in a lymph node plus the mesh pattern is the giveaway.
notes: Correct. A dark-staining branching mesh in a lymph node is reticular connective tissue.
Areolar connective tissue has a loose mix of thick collagen and thin elastic fibers with scattered cells. Pick it for tissue found just under an epithelium or around vessels.
Dense irregular connective tissue has thick collagen bundles running in many directions. Pick it for the dermis of the skin.
Adipose tissue is made of large, empty-looking fat cells with little matrix. Pick it for the subcutaneous tissue or the fat around the kidneys.
questions.answerText: Reticular connective tissue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide from the wall of the aorta shows a connective tissue dominated by wavy, dark-staining elastin fibers, with no lacunae. Which tissue is it?
options: Dense regular connective tissue
Reticular connective tissue
Elastic connective tissue
Elastic cartilage
questions.why: Elastic connective tissue is a dense connective tissue in which elastin fibers dominate. It is found where a wall must stretch and recoil, such as the large arteries that expand with every heartbeat. The absence of lacunae tells you it is not cartilage, even though elastic cartilage also has many elastic fibers.
notes: Dense regular connective tissue is dominated by parallel collagen bundles with fibroblasts between them. Pick it for a tendon or ligament.
Reticular connective tissue has a fine mesh of reticular fibers holding cells. Pick it for a lymph node or the spleen.
Correct. Dominant elastin fibers without lacunae, from an artery wall, mark elastic connective tissue.
Elastic cartilage has elastic fibers too, but its cells sit in lacunae. Pick it for a slide of the external ear or the epiglottis.
questions.answerText: Elastic connective tissue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On a loose areolar slide you see thick, pink, ribbon-like fibers and thin, dark, branching threads. What are the thick pink fibers?
options: Reticular fibers
Elastic fibers
Smooth muscle fibers
Collagen fibers
questions.why: Collagen fibers are the thickest and strongest connective tissue fibers, and on a typical areolar slide they appear as broad, pink, wavy ribbons. The thin, dark, branching threads are elastic fibers. Learning to tell these two apart is one of the lab structures for the areolar slide.
notes: Reticular fibers are very fine and form a mesh. They are the defining fiber of reticular connective tissue in lymph nodes and the spleen.
Elastic fibers are the thin, dark, branching threads on the same slide. Pick them if the question asked about the thin dark fibers.
Smooth muscle fibers are whole spindle-shaped cells with a central nucleus, not extracellular fibers. Pick them for a slide of the wall of the intestine.
Correct. The thick pink ribbons are collagen fibers.
questions.answerText: Collagen fibers
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On an areolar slide, a few large cells sit along small blood vessels, and each is packed with dark-staining granules. Which cells are they?
options: Adipocytes
Fibroblasts
Chondrocytes
Mast cells
questions.why: Mast cells sit along the blood vessels that supply connective tissue. Their granules hold histamine, which widens blood vessels during inflammation, and the packed granules are why the cells stain so darkly. Mast cells are one of the structures you identify on the areolar slide.
notes: Adipocytes are fat cells that look empty because a single large fat droplet fills them. Pick them for an adipose slide.
Fibroblasts are the common cells that make fibers and ground substance. They look like slender cells with oval nuclei, without dark granules.
Chondrocytes are cartilage cells sitting in lacunae within a firm matrix. Pick them for a cartilage slide.
Correct. Large, granule-packed cells along blood vessels are mast cells.
questions.answerText: Mast cells
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On a dense regular connective tissue slide, which cells have the flattened nuclei squeezed in rows between the parallel collagen bundles?
options: Mast cells
Fibroblasts
Osteocytes
Macrophages
questions.why: Fibroblasts make the collagen fibers and ground substance of connective tissue proper. In dense regular connective tissue the collagen is packed in parallel bundles, so the fibroblasts get pressed into thin rows between them, and you see their nuclei as flattened dark streaks running in the same direction as the fibers.
notes: Mast cells are larger cells packed with dark granules, found along blood vessels. Pick them on an areolar slide.
Correct. The flattened nuclei in rows between collagen bundles belong to fibroblasts.
Osteocytes are mature bone cells sitting in lacunae within a hard, calcified matrix. Pick them on a compact bone slide.
Macrophages are phagocytic cells that develop from monocytes and engulf debris. They are not the cells that line up between tendon fibers.
questions.answerText: Fibroblasts
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide shows concentric rings of hard matrix around a central canal, with small cells in lacunae linked by tiny channels. Which tissue is it?
options: Dense regular connective tissue
Compact bone
Hyaline cartilage
Spongy bone
questions.why: The concentric rings are lamellae arranged around a central (Haversian) canal, and together they form an osteon, the repeating unit of compact bone. The cells in lacunae are osteocytes, and the tiny channels connecting them are canaliculi. This ring pattern is what sets compact bone apart from every other connective tissue on a slide.
notes: Dense regular connective tissue has parallel collagen bundles and fibroblasts, with no lacunae or rings. Pick it for a tendon.
Correct. Concentric lamellae around a central canal form the osteons of compact bone.
Hyaline cartilage also has cells in lacunae, but its matrix is glassy and smooth with no rings or canals. Pick it for the trachea or the ends of long bones.
Spongy bone is an open lattice of thin bony struts with marrow between them and no osteons. Pick it for the interior of a bone end.
questions.answerText: Compact bone
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares bone with cartilage?
options: Bone is calcified and vascular, while cartilage is flexible and avascular
Bone is avascular, while cartilage has a rich supply of blood vessels
Bone has no cells, while cartilage has chondrocytes in lacunae
Both have cells in lacunae, and both are flexible tissues
questions.why: Bone and cartilage are both supporting connective tissues with cells in lacunae, but their matrix and blood supply differ. Bone matrix is calcified, which makes it hard and inflexible, and bone is well supplied with blood vessels. Cartilage matrix is firm but pliable, and cartilage has no blood vessels, so it heals slowly.
notes: Correct. Bone is hard and vascular, while cartilage is flexible and avascular.
This reverses the two tissues. Cartilage is the avascular one, which is why a torn meniscus heals slowly, while bone has a good blood supply.
Bone does have cells. Osteocytes live in lacunae in bone just as chondrocytes live in lacunae in cartilage.
The first half is true, since both have cells in lacunae, but bone is hard and inflexible because its matrix is calcified. Only cartilage is flexible.
questions.answerText: Bone is calcified and vascular, while cartilage is flexible and avascular
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Slide one shows tightly packed cells with almost no material between them and a free surface. Slide two shows scattered cells in a large amount of matrix. Which statement identifies them?
options: Slide one is connective tissue and slide two is epithelium
Both slides are epithelium at different magnifications
Slide one is epithelium and slide two is connective tissue
Both slides are connective tissue from different organs
questions.why: The amount of matrix is the quickest way to separate the two tissue types. Epithelium has tightly packed cells with very little extracellular matrix and a free apical surface. Connective tissue has relatively few cells spread through a large extracellular matrix of fibers and ground substance, and it never forms a free surface.
notes: This reverses the two. A large matrix with scattered cells is the mark of connective tissue, not epithelium.
Changing the magnification does not create a large matrix between cells. Slide two has a feature epithelium lacks.
Correct. Packed cells with a free surface is epithelium, and scattered cells in matrix is connective tissue.
Connective tissue does not form a free surface with tightly packed cells. Slide one has the features of epithelium.
questions.answerText: Slide one is epithelium and slide two is connective tissue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In osteoarthritis, the smooth tissue covering the ends of the bones in a joint wears away. Which tissue is being lost?
options: Elastic cartilage
Dense regular connective tissue
Fibrocartilage
Hyaline cartilage
questions.why: The ends of long bones in a joint are covered by hyaline cartilage, which gives a smooth, slick surface for joint movement. In osteoarthritis this articular cartilage gradually wears down. Because cartilage has no blood vessels, it repairs itself poorly, so the damage tends to build over time.
notes: Elastic cartilage is found in the external ear and epiglottis, not in weight-bearing joints.
Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments, which attach structures at a joint but do not cover the bone ends.
Fibrocartilage forms shock-absorbing pads such as the menisci and intervertebral discs. Pick it if the question asked about a torn meniscus rather than the bone-end surface.
Correct. The smooth covering of bone ends at a joint is hyaline cartilage.
questions.answerText: Hyaline cartilage
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Blood is a liquid, yet it is classified as a connective tissue. What best supports that classification?
options: It covers body surfaces and lines the inside of the blood vessels
Its cells sit in a matrix, plasma, and it arises from mesenchyme
Its cells are joined by intercalated discs and contract together
It is built from neurons and the glial cells that support them
questions.why: Every connective tissue is cells plus an extracellular matrix. In blood, the cells and cell fragments are suspended in plasma, which is a fluid matrix, so blood fits that plan even though it flows. Blood also develops from embryonic mesenchyme, the tissue that gives rise to all connective tissues, and it serves as the body's major transport system.
notes: Covering surfaces and lining vessels is the job of epithelium. The lining of blood vessels is simple squamous epithelium, not blood.
Correct. Cells in a fluid matrix, with an origin in mesenchyme, place blood among the connective tissues.
Intercalated discs and contraction describe cardiac muscle tissue. Pick this for the heart wall, not for blood.
Neurons and glial cells make up nervous tissue. Pick this for the brain, spinal cord, or nerves.
questions.answerText: Its cells sit in a matrix, plasma, and it arises from mesenchyme
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: After an ankle sprain, the area under the skin becomes puffy with excess fluid (edema). Which connective tissue's loose, fluid-holding matrix soaks up most of this fluid?
options: Dense regular connective tissue
Compact bone
Hyaline cartilage
Areolar connective tissue
questions.why: Areolar connective tissue has loosely arranged fibers and a large amount of watery ground substance, so it acts as a reservoir for tissue fluid. When an area is injured or inflamed, extra fluid leaks into this loose tissue, and it swells like a sponge. That swelling is called edema.
notes: Dense regular connective tissue is packed tightly with parallel collagen and has little room for fluid. Pick it for the tendons and ligaments that may be strained in a sprain.
Compact bone has a hard, calcified matrix that cannot soak up fluid. Pick it for the dense outer layer of a bone.
Hyaline cartilage has a firm matrix and no blood vessels. It covers joint surfaces and does not swell like a sponge under the skin.
Correct. Loose areolar tissue holds tissue fluid and swells in edema.
questions.answerText: Areolar connective tissue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: You can fold the external ear forward and it springs right back into shape. Which feature of its tissue explains this?
options: Its matrix is calcified like compact bone
Its cartilage has a rich blood supply
Its cartilage is filled with thick collagen bundles
Its cartilage matrix is packed with elastic fibers
questions.why: The external ear is made of elastic cartilage, which has the same basic plan as hyaline cartilage but with many elastic fibers in its matrix. Elastic fibers stretch and then return to their original shape, so the ear can bend without breaking and then recoil. The same tissue in the epiglottis lets it flip down over the airway and back up again.
notes: A calcified matrix is hard and inflexible, the opposite of what the ear does. Pick it for bone.
All cartilage is avascular, including the ear. A blood supply would not explain the springiness anyway.
Thick collagen bundles describe fibrocartilage, which is tough and resists compression rather than springing back. Pick it for an intervertebral disc.
Correct. Elastic fibers in the matrix let the ear bend and recoil.
questions.answerText: Its cartilage matrix is packed with elastic fibers
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A slide shows chondrocytes in lacunae and a tough matrix crowded with thick collagen bundles. No perichondrium wraps the edge of the tissue. Which structure could this sample have come from?
options: A knee meniscus.
Articular cartilage.
The epiglottis.
A tracheal ring.
questions.why: Work it in two steps. Thick bundles of collagen mark fibrocartilage, and fibrocartilage is the type with no perichondrium on your lab list. Fibrocartilage is found in the intervertebral discs, the knee menisci, and the pubic symphysis, so the meniscus is the only structure here that fits.
notes: Correct. Thick collagen bundles with no perichondrium mark fibrocartilage, and the knee menisci are made of it.
Articular cartilage, which caps the bone ends at a joint, is hyaline cartilage, with fine collagen and a glassy matrix, so it would not show thick collagen bundles.
The epiglottis is elastic cartilage. Its matrix is packed with elastic fibers, and it has a perichondrium around it.
The tracheal rings are hyaline cartilage, with fine collagen you cannot see on ordinary staining and a perichondrium around the edge.
questions.answerText: A knee meniscus.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An unlabeled slide shows chondrocytes in lacunae, a perichondrium at the edge, and a matrix packed with elastic fibers. A student labels it as tissue from the trachea. What is wrong with the label?
options: It is hyaline cartilage, so the trachea label is correct.
It is elastic cartilage, so it came from the ear or epiglottis.
It is fibrocartilage, so it came from the pubic symphysis.
It is hyaline cartilage, so it came from the nose instead.
questions.why: First name the tissue from what you see: a matrix full of elastic fibers is elastic cartilage. Then match the tissue to its locations. Elastic cartilage is found in the external ear and the epiglottis, while the trachea is built from hyaline cartilage, so the label points to the wrong tissue.
notes: Hyaline cartilage has fine collagen and a glassy matrix, not a matrix packed with elastic fibers. The trachea is hyaline, but this slide is not.
Correct. Many elastic fibers mean elastic cartilage, which is found in the external ear and the epiglottis.
Fibrocartilage shows thick collagen bundles and has no perichondrium. This slide has both a perichondrium and elastic fibers.
The nose is hyaline cartilage, but the elastic fibers on this slide rule hyaline out. The mix-up is knowing the nose is cartilage without checking the fiber type.
questions.answerText: It is elastic cartilage, so it came from the ear or epiglottis.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which germ layer is the outer layer of the early embryo?
options: The epidermis
Endoderm
Mesoderm
Ectoderm
questions.why: The early embryo forms three germ layers, and the ectoderm is the outermost. It gives rise to the epidermis of the skin and to all nervous tissue, including the brain and spinal cord, which develop from the ectodermal neural tube. The mesoderm lies in the middle and the endoderm lies innermost.
notes: The epidermis is a tissue that develops from the ectoderm, not a germ layer itself. Students pick it because the names sound alike, but it is the product of the outer layer, not the layer.
The endoderm is the innermost germ layer. It forms the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts.
The mesoderm is the middle germ layer. It forms muscle, bone, cartilage, blood, and most connective tissue.
Correct. The ectoderm is the outer germ layer.
questions.answerText: Ectoderm

questions.q: Which tissue has long, cylindrical, striated cells with many nuclei?
options: Smooth muscle
Skeletal muscle
Cardiac muscle
Dense regular connective tissue
questions.why: Skeletal muscle cells are long, cylindrical, and contain many nuclei, and they show striations (stripes) under the microscope. Each cell forms when many embryonic cells fuse together, which is why it has so many nuclei. Skeletal muscle is attached to bones and produces voluntary movement.
notes: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus and no striations. They are the answer for the walls of hollow organs such as the intestines and bladder.
Correct. Long, cylindrical, multinucleated cells are skeletal muscle.
Cardiac muscle cells are striated but branched, usually with one nucleus, and joined by intercalated discs. They are the answer for the muscle of the heart wall.

Dense regular connective tissue also shows long parallel structures, but they are collagen fibers with flattened fibroblast nuclei squeezed between them. Pick it for a tendon or ligament slide, not a muscle.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscle
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which two cell types make up nervous tissue?
options: Neuroglia and chondrocytes
Neurons and adipocytes
Neurons and fibroblasts
Neurons and neuroglia
questions.why: Nervous tissue has two kinds of cells. Neurons are the signaling cells that carry electrical impulses, with a cell body and long processes. Neuroglia, or glial cells, are smaller supporting cells that protect, nourish, and insulate the neurons, and they far outnumber them.
notes: Chondrocytes are cartilage cells sitting in lacunae. Neuroglia are half right, but the signaling cells of nervous tissue are neurons, not chondrocytes.
Adipocytes are fat-storing cells of adipose connective tissue. Neurons are half right, but adipocytes do not belong in nervous tissue.
Fibroblasts are the cells that build connective tissue fibers and matrix. Neurons are half right, but fibroblasts belong to connective tissue, not nervous tissue.
Correct. Nervous tissue is neurons plus neuroglia.
questions.answerText: Neurons and neuroglia
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which body membrane lines joint cavities and is made of connective tissue only, with no epithelium?
options: The serous membrane
The cutaneous membrane
The synovial membrane
The mucous membrane
questions.why: The synovial membrane lines the cavities of synovial joints and is the only body membrane made entirely of connective tissue, with no epithelium. It secretes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint. The other three membranes, mucous, serous, and cutaneous, each pair an epithelium with an underlying layer of connective tissue.
notes: A serous membrane is simple squamous epithelium over a thin layer of connective tissue and lines closed ventral cavities, such as the pleura, pericardium, and peritoneum. It is the answer for membranes around the lungs, heart, and abdominal organs.
The cutaneous membrane is the skin, a keratinized stratified squamous epithelium over dense connective tissue. It is the answer for the body's dry outer membrane.
Correct. The synovial membrane is connective tissue only.
A mucous membrane has an epithelium over loose connective tissue and lines cavities open to the outside, such as the digestive and respiratory tracts. Pick it for a moist lining that secretes mucus.
questions.answerText: The synovial membrane

questions.q: Nervous tissue and the epidermis of the skin both arise from which germ layer?
options: Mesoderm
Both mesoderm and endoderm
Ectoderm
Endoderm
questions.why: The ectoderm is the outermost of the three germ layers. It gives rise to the epidermis of the skin and to all nervous tissue, because the brain and spinal cord develop from a tube of ectoderm called the neural tube. This shared origin links the outer skin and the nervous system in development.
notes: The mesoderm forms muscle, bone, cartilage, blood, and most connective tissue. It would be the answer for the connective tissue of the dermis, but not for the epidermis or nervous tissue.
Neither the mesoderm nor the endoderm forms nervous tissue or the epidermis. Students choose this when they are unsure and hedge across layers.
Correct. Both come from the ectoderm.
The endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts. Pick it for a question about the inner lining of the gut or airways.
questions.answerText: Ectoderm
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Cardiac muscle cells are joined end to end by which structures?
options: Synapses
Tight junctions
Hemidesmosomes
Intercalated discs
questions.why: Cardiac muscle cells are joined end to end by intercalated discs, which show up as dark lines across the fibers under the microscope. Each disc contains desmosomes, which hold the cells together as the heart contracts, and gap junctions, which let the contraction signal pass directly from cell to cell. Together they let the heart muscle contract as a coordinated unit.
notes: Synapses are where a neuron passes its signal to another neuron, a muscle, or a gland. They connect nerve cells to their targets, not cardiac muscle cells to each other.
Tight junctions seal neighboring epithelial cells so substances cannot leak between them, as in the stomach and bladder lining. They are not the end-to-end connections of cardiac muscle.
Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to the basement membrane beneath them. They attach cells to a sheet, not cardiac cells to each other.
Correct. Intercalated discs join cardiac muscle cells.
questions.answerText: Intercalated discs
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which body membrane is made of a keratinized epithelium over dense connective tissue and is a dry membrane?
options: The cutaneous membrane
The mucous membrane
The serous membrane
The synovial membrane
questions.why: The cutaneous membrane is the skin. Its surface layer is the epidermis, a keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, and beneath it is the dermis, made of dense connective tissue. It is the only dry membrane in the body, because keratin makes its surface tough and water-resistant.
notes: Correct. The cutaneous membrane is the skin.
A mucous membrane is kept moist by mucus and lines cavities that open to the outside, such as the mouth, airways, and gut. It is the answer for a wet lining, not a dry one.
A serous membrane is simple squamous epithelium over thin connective tissue that lines closed body cavities and secretes a watery fluid. It is the answer for the pleura, pericardium, and peritoneum.
The synovial membrane lines joint cavities and has no epithelium at all. It is the answer for the membrane made of connective tissue only.
questions.answerText: The cutaneous membrane

questions.q: A muscle slide shows branching striated cells with one nucleus each, joined end to end by dark crossbands. Which muscle type is it?
options: Skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle
Dense regular connective tissue
questions.why: Branching, striated cells with a single central nucleus, joined end to end by dark lines called intercalated discs, identify cardiac muscle. The discs are where neighboring cells connect, and they contain desmosomes and gap junctions. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart wall and contracts involuntarily.
notes: Skeletal muscle is striated too, but its cells are long, unbranched cylinders with many nuclei at the edge, and it has no intercalated discs.
Smooth muscle has spindle-shaped cells with one central nucleus and no striations. It is the answer for the walls of hollow organs such as the intestines and bladder.
Correct. Branching cells with intercalated discs are cardiac muscle.
Dense regular connective tissue shows parallel collagen fibers with flattened fibroblast nuclei. It has no branching cells or crossbands and is the answer for a tendon slide.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle

questions.q: A muscle slide from the wall of a hollow organ shows spindle-shaped cells, each with a single nucleus and no striations. Which muscle type is it?
options: Skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle
Dense regular connective tissue
questions.why: Spindle-shaped cells, thick in the middle and tapered at both ends, each with one central nucleus and no striations, identify smooth muscle. It forms the walls of hollow organs such as the intestines, bladder, and blood vessels, where it contracts involuntarily to move contents along. The lack of striations is what gives it the name smooth.
notes: Skeletal muscle has long cylindrical cells with many nuclei and visible striations. It is the answer for muscle attached to bones under voluntary control.
Correct. Spindle-shaped, non-striated cells are smooth muscle.
Cardiac muscle has branching striated cells joined by intercalated discs. It is the answer for the heart wall.
Dense regular connective tissue has parallel collagen fibers with flattened fibroblast nuclei, which can look wavy. It is the answer for a tendon slide, not the wall of a hollow organ.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle

questions.q: A body membrane lines the airways, is kept moist, and is an epithelium over loose connective tissue. Which membrane is it?
options: A serous membrane
A synovial membrane
A mucous membrane
A cutaneous membrane
questions.why: A mucous membrane lines body cavities and passages that open to the outside, such as the airways and the digestive, urinary, and reproductive tracts. It is made of an epithelium resting on loose connective tissue called the lamina propria, and it is kept moist by mucus. That moist surface traps particles and protects the lining.
notes: A serous membrane lines closed ventral cavities and covers the organs inside them, producing a thin watery fluid. It is the answer for the pleura, pericardium, and peritoneum.
A synovial membrane lines joint cavities and has no epithelium. It is the answer for the membrane made only of connective tissue.
Correct. A moist lining of an open passage is a mucous membrane.
The cutaneous membrane is the skin, a keratinized epithelium over dense connective tissue that stays dry. It is the answer for the body's outer covering.
questions.answerText: A mucous membrane

questions.q: Which chain correctly links a germ layer to a tissue it forms and then to a location of that tissue?
options: Ectoderm forms nervous tissue, found in the brain
Mesoderm forms the epidermis, found in the skin
Endoderm forms nervous tissue, found in the brain
Ectoderm forms bone, found in the skeleton
questions.why: The ectoderm, the outer germ layer, forms all nervous tissue, and the brain is made of nervous tissue, so this chain links correctly at every step. Checking each link separately is how to catch the errors in the other chains. The ectoderm also forms the epidermis, the mesoderm forms bone and most connective tissue, and the endoderm forms the linings of the gut and airways.
notes: Correct. Ectoderm forms nervous tissue, which builds the brain.
The epidermis comes from the ectoderm, not the mesoderm. The mesoderm would be correct for the dermis or for bone.
The endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts, not nervous tissue. The second and third links are right, but the chain starts from the wrong layer.
Bone develops from the mesoderm, not the ectoderm. The chain would be correct if it started with the mesoderm.
questions.answerText: Ectoderm forms nervous tissue, found in the brain
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Match each membrane to its composition: cutaneous, serous, and synovial. Which set of pairings is correct?
options: Cutaneous is keratinized epithelium over dense connective tissue; serous is simple squamous over thin connective tissue; synovial is connective tissue only
Cutaneous is simple squamous over thin connective tissue; serous is connective tissue only; synovial is keratinized epithelium
Cutaneous is connective tissue only; serous is keratinized epithelium; synovial is simple squamous over thin connective tissue
Cutaneous is simple squamous epithelium; serous is connective tissue only; synovial is keratinized epithelium over dense connective tissue
questions.why: The cutaneous membrane, the skin, is a keratinized stratified squamous epithelium over dense connective tissue. A serous membrane is simple squamous epithelium over a thin layer of connective tissue and lines closed body cavities. The synovial membrane lines joint cavities and has no epithelium at all, only connective tissue.
notes: Correct. Each membrane is matched to its real composition.
This set gives the skin a simple squamous epithelium, which describes a serous membrane. It also puts keratinized epithelium in a joint, when the synovial membrane has no epithelium.
This set calls the skin connective tissue only, but the skin has an epidermis, a keratinized epithelium. Connective tissue only describes the synovial membrane.

This set gives the skin a simple squamous epithelium, which belongs to a serous membrane, and gives the synovial membrane the keratinized epithelium over dense connective tissue that belongs to the skin. It also calls the serous membrane connective tissue only, which describes the synovial membrane.
questions.answerText: Cutaneous is keratinized epithelium over dense connective tissue; serous is simple squamous over thin connective tissue; synovial is connective tissue only

questions.q: Match each muscle type to its cell description: skeletal, cardiac, and smooth. Which set is correct?
options: Skeletal is spindle-shaped with one nucleus; cardiac is long and cylindrical; smooth is branched
Skeletal is long, cylindrical, and multinucleate; cardiac is branched with intercalated discs; smooth is spindle-shaped
Skeletal is branched with intercalated discs; cardiac is spindle-shaped; smooth is long and cylindrical
Skeletal is long and cylindrical; cardiac is spindle-shaped; smooth is branched with intercalated discs
questions.why: Skeletal muscle cells are long, cylindrical, and multinucleated. Cardiac muscle cells are branched and joined by intercalated discs, and smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus. Shape, number of nuclei, and the presence of intercalated discs are the quickest features for telling the three apart on a slide.
notes: This set gives skeletal muscle the spindle shape of smooth muscle and gives smooth muscle the branching of cardiac muscle. Each description is real but attached to the wrong tissue.
Correct. Each muscle type is matched to its cell shape.
This set gives skeletal muscle the intercalated discs that only cardiac muscle has. It also gives smooth muscle the long cylindrical shape of skeletal muscle.
This set gets skeletal muscle right but swaps the other two. Intercalated discs belong to cardiac muscle, and the spindle shape belongs to smooth muscle.
questions.answerText: Skeletal is long, cylindrical, and multinucleate; cardiac is branched with intercalated discs; smooth is spindle-shaped
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which description fits skeletal muscle tissue?
options: Non-striated and involuntary
Striated and involuntary
Non-striated and voluntary
Striated and voluntary
questions.why: Skeletal muscle is striated, meaning its cells show light and dark bands under the microscope, and it is voluntary, meaning it is under conscious control. It is attached to bones (and occasionally to skin) and produces body movement and heat. Of the three muscle types, it is the only one that is both striated and voluntary.
notes: Non-striated and involuntary describes smooth muscle in the walls of hollow organs such as the intestines and bladder. It would be the answer for a question about smooth muscle.
Striated and involuntary describes cardiac muscle, which has bands like skeletal muscle but contracts without conscious control. Pick it for the muscle of the heart wall.
No muscle tissue in the body is both non-striated and voluntary. Students choose this when they remember that skeletal muscle is voluntary but mix up which muscle lacks striations.
Correct. Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary.
questions.answerText: Striated and voluntary
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Cardiac muscle is striated, involuntary, and made of branching cells joined by intercalated discs. Which of these features is unique to cardiac muscle among the three muscle types?
options: Involuntary control
Intercalated discs joining cells
A spindle-shaped cell body
Striations across the cells
questions.why: Intercalated discs joining branching cells are found only in cardiac muscle. Its striations are shared with skeletal muscle, and its involuntary control is shared with smooth muscle, so neither feature identifies cardiac muscle alone. Looking for the one feature no other tissue has is the fastest way to identify it on a slide.
notes: Involuntary control is shared with smooth muscle, so it does not single out cardiac muscle. It would separate cardiac from skeletal muscle only.
Correct. Only cardiac muscle has intercalated discs.
A spindle-shaped cell body is the feature of smooth muscle, not cardiac muscle. Pick it for a question about what is unique to smooth muscle.
Striations are also present in skeletal muscle, so they cannot identify cardiac muscle by themselves. They would help separate cardiac from smooth muscle, but not from skeletal.
questions.answerText: Intercalated discs joining cells
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which body membrane lines closed ventral body cavities and covers the organs within them, such as the pleura around the lungs?
options: A mucous membrane
A cutaneous membrane
A serous membrane
A synovial membrane
questions.why: A serous membrane is a thin layer of simple squamous epithelium over a small amount of connective tissue. Its parietal layer lines the cavity wall and its visceral layer covers the organs, and it secretes a watery fluid that lets organs slide with little friction. The pleura, pericardium, and peritoneum are the three serous membranes.
notes: A mucous membrane lines passages that open to the outside, such as the airways and digestive tract. It is the answer for a moist lining that secretes mucus, not a closed cavity.
The cutaneous membrane is the skin, the body's dry outer covering. It does not line any internal cavity.
Correct. Serous membranes line closed ventral cavities.
The synovial membrane lines joint cavities and has no epithelium. It is the answer for a membrane inside a joint, not around the lungs.
questions.answerText: A serous membrane

questions.q: Which two cell junctions are found in the intercalated discs of cardiac muscle?
options: Tight junctions and desmosomes
Tight junctions and hemidesmosomes
Hemidesmosomes and gap junctions
Desmosomes and gap junctions
questions.why: Intercalated discs, where cardiac muscle cells meet end to end, contain desmosomes and gap junctions. The desmosomes keep the cells from pulling apart as the heart contracts, and the gap junctions let the contraction signal pass directly from one cell to the next. Together they let the heart wall work as one coordinated unit.
notes: Desmosomes are right, but tight junctions seal epithelial linings against leakage. The signaling junction in the discs is the gap junction.
Tight junctions seal epithelial cells, and hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to the basement membrane. Neither is part of the intercalated discs.
Gap junctions are right, but hemidesmosomes attach a cell to a basement membrane, not to a neighboring muscle cell. The anchoring junction in the discs is the desmosome.
Correct. Desmosomes hold the cells together and gap junctions pass the signal.
questions.answerText: Desmosomes and gap junctions

questions.q: Which muscle tissue is striated but usually has only one nucleus per cell?
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Skeletal muscle
Dense regular connective tissue
questions.why: Cardiac muscle cells are striated like skeletal muscle cells, but each usually has a single, centrally placed nucleus. Skeletal muscle cells are striated with many nuclei, and smooth muscle cells have one nucleus but no striations. Checking striations and nuclei together separates all three muscle types.
notes: Correct. Cardiac muscle is striated with one nucleus per cell.
Smooth muscle cells have a single nucleus but no striations. It is the answer for a non-striated tissue in the walls of hollow organs.
Skeletal muscle is striated, but each long cell has many nuclei. It is the answer for a striated, multinucleated tissue.
Dense regular connective tissue has wavy parallel collagen fibers that can look banded, but it is not muscle and its fibroblasts are not striated cells. It is the answer for a tendon slide.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle

questions.q: A nervous tissue slide shows a large cell body with a prominent nucleus and several long processes branching from it, surrounded by many small nuclei. What is the large cell?
options: A fibroblast
A neuroglial cell
A multipolar neuron
A smooth muscle cell
questions.why: A large cell body with a prominent nucleus and several long processes extending from it is a multipolar neuron, the most common type of neuron. Its processes are many dendrites and a single axon. The many small nuclei scattered around it belong to neuroglia, the smaller supporting cells that far outnumber neurons.
notes: A fibroblast is a connective tissue cell with an elongated nucleus that builds fibers. It does not have a large cell body with long branching processes.
Neuroglia are the small cells whose nuclei surround the neuron on this slide. They support and protect neurons and are much smaller than a neuron's cell body.
Correct. A large cell body with many processes is a multipolar neuron.
A smooth muscle cell is spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus and no branching processes. It is the answer for a slide of a hollow organ wall.
questions.answerText: A multipolar neuron

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how cardiac muscle is controlled?
options: It is voluntary, contracting only when we decide to move
It is involuntary, contracting without conscious control
It is involuntary only while the vagus nerve stimulates it
It is voluntary at rest and involuntary during exercise
questions.why: Cardiac muscle is involuntary, which means we cannot make it contract or stop by choosing to. The heart sets its own beat through its conduction system, and autonomic nerves only speed it up or slow it down. Skeletal muscle is the only muscle tissue under voluntary control.
notes: This describes skeletal muscle, the voluntary muscle attached to bones that contracts when you decide to move. Choose voluntary if the question asked about a muscle such as the deltoid, not the heart.
Correct. Cardiac muscle contracts on its own, without conscious control.

This confuses starting the beat with adjusting it. The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic fibers that slow the heart rate, but the heart beats involuntarily whether or not the vagus is active, as a transplanted heart with its nerves cut shows.
This is a made-up mix. Cardiac muscle never switches to voluntary control; exercise changes the heart rate through autonomic nerves, but the muscle stays involuntary the whole time.
questions.answerText: It is involuntary, contracting without conscious control
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Cardiac muscle is striated. What produces these stripes under the microscope?
options: Many nuclei along each cell
Intercalated discs between cells
Branching of the cells
Ordered sarcomeres in each cell
questions.why: Striations are the alternating light and dark bands seen across a muscle cell. They come from sarcomeres, the repeating contractile units, lined up in order along the cell. Cardiac muscle is striated for the same reason skeletal muscle is, because both are built of ordered sarcomeres, while smooth muscle lacks this arrangement and looks unstriped.
notes: Many nuclei per cell is a feature of skeletal muscle fibers, not cardiac muscle, which usually has one central nucleus. The number of nuclei also has nothing to do with the stripes.

Intercalated discs are the dark junction lines where neighboring cardiomyocytes meet end to end. They mark cell boundaries, and they are the answer if the question asked which feature identifies cardiac muscle and sets it apart from skeletal muscle.
Branching describes the shape of cardiomyocytes, which split and connect to several neighbors. It would be the answer for how cardiac cells form a network, but it does not create the stripes.
Correct. Sarcomeres lined up in order produce the striations, in both cardiac and skeletal muscle.
questions.answerText: Ordered sarcomeres in each cell
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares cardiac muscle with skeletal muscle?
options: Both are voluntary, but only skeletal muscle has visible striations
Both are involuntary, but cardiac muscle cells contain many nuclei
Both are striated, but cardiac muscle is involuntary with branched cells
Neither is striated, but both have cells joined by intercalated discs
questions.why: Cardiac and skeletal muscle are both striated because both are built of ordered sarcomeres. They differ in control and cell shape. Skeletal muscle is voluntary, with long, cylindrical, unbranched cells that each hold many nuclei, while cardiac muscle is involuntary, with short, branched cells that usually have one central nucleus and are joined by intercalated discs.
notes: Only skeletal muscle is voluntary, and cardiac muscle is striated too. This statement would fit only if the heart were under conscious control, which it is not.
Skeletal muscle is voluntary, and the cell with many nuclei is the skeletal muscle fiber, not the cardiomyocyte. This choice swaps the nucleus feature between the two tissues.
Correct. Both are striated; cardiac muscle is involuntary and its cells are short and branched.
Both tissues are clearly striated, and intercalated discs are found only in cardiac muscle. Pick intercalated discs for a question about the feature that identifies cardiac muscle on a slide.
questions.answerText: Both are striated, but cardiac muscle is involuntary with branched cells
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Where are the nuclei located in a skeletal muscle fiber?
options: No nuclei, since the fibers are dead cells
One nucleus in the center of the cell
Many nuclei along the edge, under the membrane
Two nuclei, one at each tapered end
questions.why: A skeletal muscle fiber is one very long cell formed when many embryonic cells fuse, so it ends up with many nuclei. These nuclei are pushed to the periphery, just under the sarcolemma (the fiber's plasma membrane), because the inside of the cell is packed with contractile myofibrils. Multiple peripheral nuclei are one of the lab structures for identifying skeletal muscle.
notes: Skeletal muscle fibers are living cells. Dead cells without nuclei describe the keratinized surface of the epidermis, not muscle.
One central nucleus fits cardiac and smooth muscle cells. Pick it if the question asked about either of those tissues.
Correct. Skeletal muscle fibers have many nuclei at the periphery.
No muscle type has one nucleus at each end. This is a made-up pattern, perhaps from picturing the tapered ends of smooth muscle cells.
questions.answerText: Many nuclei along the edge, under the membrane
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: How many nuclei does a smooth muscle cell have, and where are they?
options: Many nuclei along the edge
No nucleus at all
Several nuclei at the cell junctions
A single nucleus in the center
questions.why: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped, wide in the middle and tapering at both ends, and each one has a single nucleus in its thick central region. On a slide the nuclei often look like elongated ovals lying in the middle of each cell. A single central nucleus with no striations is how you recognize smooth muscle.
notes: Many nuclei along the edge describe skeletal muscle fibers. Pick this for a slide of long, striated, cylindrical fibers.
Smooth muscle cells are living cells and each has a nucleus. Cells without nuclei, such as mature red blood cells, belong to other tissues.
Nuclei are not located at cell junctions in any muscle tissue. This mixes up nuclei with the intercalated discs that join cardiac cells.
Correct. Each smooth muscle cell has one central nucleus.
questions.answerText: A single nucleus in the center

questions.q: What is the plasma membrane of a skeletal muscle fiber called?
options: The perichondrium
The sarcolemma
The neurolemma
The basement membrane
questions.why: Sarco means flesh, and lemma means husk or covering, so the sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of a muscle fiber. On a skeletal muscle slide it is the thin outer boundary of each fiber, with the peripheral nuclei lying just beneath it. It is one of the structures listed for identification on the skeletal muscle slide.
notes: The perichondrium is the dense connective tissue layer that surrounds cartilage. Pick it for a hyaline or elastic cartilage slide.
Correct. The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of a muscle fiber.
The neurolemma is the outer layer of a Schwann cell wrapped around a peripheral axon. Pick it for a question about nerve fibers, not muscle.
The basement membrane is the layer that anchors an epithelium to the connective tissue below. It is not the membrane of a muscle cell.
questions.answerText: The sarcolemma

questions.q: Where is smooth muscle tissue found?
options: In the walls of the intestines and bladder
Attached to the bones of the skeleton
In the walls of the heart
Covering the ends of long bones
questions.why: Smooth muscle forms the walls of hollow organs, such as the intestines and the urinary bladder. Its slow, involuntary contractions squeeze and propel substances along, which is why food moves through the gut without any conscious effort.
notes: Correct. Smooth muscle lines the walls of hollow organs such as the intestines and bladder.
Muscle attached to bones is skeletal muscle, which is striated and voluntary. Pick it for the biceps or quadriceps.
The walls of the heart are cardiac muscle, which is striated and has intercalated discs. Pick it for the myocardium.
The ends of long bones are covered by hyaline cartilage, which is connective tissue, not muscle.
questions.answerText: In the walls of the intestines and bladder
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Skeletal muscle is usually attached to bones. To which other structure is it occasionally attached?
options: The stomach wall
The heart wall
The skin
The lining of blood vessels
questions.why: Most skeletal muscles pull on bones, but some attach to the skin. The muscles of facial expression are the classic example: they pull on the skin of the face to make expressions such as a smile or a frown. These muscles are still skeletal muscle, striated and under voluntary control.
notes: The stomach wall contains smooth muscle, which is involuntary. Pick it if the question asked where smooth muscle is found.
The heart wall is made of cardiac muscle, not skeletal muscle attached to it. Pick it if the question asked where cardiac muscle is found.
Correct. Some skeletal muscles, such as those of facial expression, attach to the skin.
The lining of blood vessels is simple squamous epithelium. It is not an attachment point for skeletal muscle.
questions.answerText: The skin
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A cross section of muscle shows large, rounded-to-angular fiber profiles, each with several nuclei at its edge and none in its center. Which tissue is it?
options: Skeletal muscle
Dense regular connective tissue
Smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle
questions.why: In a cross section you see each muscle fiber cut across like a slice of a cylinder. Skeletal muscle fibers are large and have many nuclei pushed to the periphery, so each profile shows nuclei around its edge and none in the middle. Cardiac and smooth muscle cells would show a single nucleus near the center when the cut passes through it.
notes: Correct. Large fibers with several peripheral nuclei mark skeletal muscle.
Dense regular connective tissue has collagen bundles and fibroblasts rather than muscle fibers. Pick it for a tendon.
Smooth muscle cells are small and have one central nucleus. Pick it for a slide of the wall of the intestine.
Cardiac muscle cells have a single central nucleus, so a cross section would show nuclei in the middle of the profiles. Pick it for a slide of the heart wall.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscle
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: You need a sample of smooth muscle tissue to make a slide. Which location would give you one?
options: The wall of the small intestine
The wall of the left ventricle
The biceps brachii
The tongue
questions.why: Smooth muscle lives in the walls of hollow organs, and the small intestine has layers of it that squeeze food along. Each of the other locations contains striated muscle instead. Matching each muscle tissue to its typical location is part of identifying it in lab.
notes: Correct. The wall of the small intestine contains smooth muscle.
The wall of the left ventricle is cardiac muscle. It would give you a slide of branching, striated cells joined by intercalated discs.
The biceps brachii is a skeletal muscle that moves the forearm. It would give you a slide of long, striated, multinucleated fibers.
The tongue is made of skeletal muscle, which lets you move it voluntarily when you speak and swallow.
questions.answerText: The wall of the small intestine
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which feature do cardiac and smooth muscle share that skeletal muscle does not?
options: Involuntary control
Attachment to bones
Many peripheral nuclei
Striations
questions.why: Cardiac muscle pumps blood and smooth muscle moves material through hollow organs, and neither one is under conscious control. Skeletal muscle is the only voluntary muscle tissue. Grouping features this way, which are shared and which are unique, makes the three tissues easier to tell apart.
notes: Correct. Cardiac and smooth muscle are both involuntary.
Attachment to bones is a feature of skeletal muscle alone. Cardiac muscle forms the heart wall and smooth muscle lines hollow organs.
Many peripheral nuclei are found only in skeletal muscle. Pick this if the question asked what is unique to skeletal muscle.
Striations are shared by skeletal and cardiac muscle. Smooth muscle is the one without them, so this feature does not fit.
questions.answerText: Involuntary control
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which feature do skeletal and cardiac muscle share that smooth muscle does not?
options: Spindle-shaped cells
Intercalated discs
Striations
Voluntary control
questions.why: Skeletal and cardiac muscle both show striations, the alternating light and dark bands across the cells, because their contractile proteins are lined up in regular repeating units. Smooth muscle has the same kinds of proteins but not in that orderly arrangement, so it looks smooth. That is how it got its name.
notes: Spindle-shaped cells are the mark of smooth muscle. Pick this if the question asked how smooth muscle cells are shaped.
Intercalated discs are found only in cardiac muscle. Pick this if the question asked what is unique to cardiac muscle.
Correct. Skeletal and cardiac muscle are both striated, while smooth muscle is not.
Voluntary control belongs only to skeletal muscle. Cardiac muscle is involuntary.
questions.answerText: Striations
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Two cell junctions are found in the intercalated discs of cardiac muscle. Which one holds neighboring cells together so they do not pull apart as the heart contracts?
options: Tight junctions
Hemidesmosomes
Gap junctions
Desmosomes
questions.why: Intercalated discs contain desmosomes and gap junctions, and each has a different job. Desmosomes strongly bind one cell to the next and keep them from separating under tension, which matters in a muscle that contracts with every heartbeat. Gap junctions are channels that let the impulse pass from cell to cell so the heart contracts as a unit.
notes: Tight junctions seal the space between cells so contents cannot leak, as in the lining of the stomach and bladder. They are not part of intercalated discs.
Hemidesmosomes anchor a cell to a basement membrane, not to a neighboring cell. Pick them for the attachment of the epidermis to its basement membrane.

Gap junctions are also in the intercalated discs, but they are channels that let impulses spread between cells. Pick them if the question asked how the signal passes from one cardiac cell to the next.
Correct. Desmosomes hold cardiac cells together under the tension of contraction.
questions.answerText: Desmosomes

questions.q: After a heart attack, the dead area of heart muscle is replaced by scar tissue rather than new muscle. What best explains this?
options: Cardiac muscle lacks nuclei, so it cannot make new proteins
Cardiac muscle cells divide very little, so scar tissue fills the gap
Cardiac muscle has no blood supply, so nothing can reach the area
Cardiac muscle is voluntary, so it heals only with exercise
questions.why: Mature cardiac muscle cells have very limited ability to divide, so the heart cannot replace large numbers of lost cells. Instead, fibroblasts lay down collagen, and the area becomes a scar of dense connective tissue. Scar tissue holds the wall together, but it cannot contract, so the heart pumps less strongly.
notes: Cardiac muscle cells do have nuclei, usually one central nucleus per cell. This choice confuses them with cells that lack nuclei, such as mature red blood cells.
Correct. Cardiac cells divide very little, so dense connective tissue forms a scar in their place.
Cardiac muscle has a rich blood supply through the coronary arteries. A heart attack happens when that supply is blocked, but normal heart muscle is not avascular.
Cardiac muscle is involuntary, not voluntary. Exercise does not regrow cardiac muscle that has already died.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle cells divide very little, so scar tissue fills the gap
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A slide labeled tongue shows striated, multinucleated fibers running in several directions. Which tissue is it, and how is it controlled?
options: Skeletal muscle, under voluntary control
Smooth muscle, under involuntary control
Cardiac muscle, under involuntary control
Smooth muscle, under voluntary control
questions.why: Striations together with many nuclei per fiber mark skeletal muscle. The tongue is skeletal muscle, which is why you can move it at will to speak, chew, and swallow. Its fibers run in several directions, which lets the tongue change shape as well as position.
notes: Correct. The tongue is skeletal muscle and moves voluntarily.
Smooth muscle has no striations and only one nucleus per cell. Pick it for the wall of the stomach or intestine.
Cardiac muscle is striated but has one central nucleus and intercalated discs, and it is found only in the heart wall.
Smooth muscle is involuntary, and it lacks the striations seen on this slide. Neither half of this choice fits the tongue.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscle, under voluntary control
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: An unknown slide shows striated fibers that branch, each with one central nucleus. A student calls it skeletal muscle because of the striations. What is the error?
options: Branching cells are the mark of skeletal muscle, so the student is right
A central nucleus is found only in nervous tissue, so it must be a neuron
Striations appear only in smooth muscle, so it must be smooth
Cardiac muscle is also striated, and branching cells mark cardiac
questions.why: Striations narrow the choice to skeletal or cardiac muscle but cannot settle it, because both are striated. The deciding features are branching cells and one central nucleus, which belong to cardiac muscle. Skeletal fibers are unbranched and have many nuclei at their edges.
notes: Skeletal muscle fibers are long and unbranched. Branching is a feature of cardiac muscle, so the student is not right.
Many cells, including cardiac and smooth muscle cells, have a central nucleus. A striated fiber is muscle, not a neuron.
Smooth muscle is the one muscle tissue without striations. This choice reverses the rule.
Correct. Both striated types have stripes, and the branching cells with central nuclei point to cardiac muscle.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle is also striated, and branching cells mark cardiac

questions.q: Which part of a neuron receives incoming signals from other cells?
options: The axon
The axon hillock
The synaptic bulb
The dendrites
questions.why: Dendrites are the short, branched, tree-like processes that extend from the cell body. Their job is to receive incoming signals and carry them toward the cell body. A multipolar neuron has many dendrites but only one axon, which is how you tell them apart on a slide.
notes: The axon carries the impulse away from the cell body toward other cells. Pick it if the question asked which process sends the signal out.
The axon hillock is the cone-shaped region where the cell body joins the axon. Pick it if the question asked where the axon begins.
The synaptic bulb is the swollen tip at the end of an axon terminal, where the signal is passed to the next cell. It sends signals rather than receiving them.
Correct. Dendrites receive incoming signals.
questions.answerText: The dendrites
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which part of a neuron carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body toward other cells?
options: The cell body
The nucleolus
The axon
The dendrite
questions.why: The axon is the single long process of a neuron. It carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body, and at its far end it branches into axon terminals that contact the next cell. A neuron can have many dendrites, but it has only one axon.
notes: The cell body holds the nucleus and is the neuron's metabolic center. It is where the axon starts, not the process that carries the impulse away.
The nucleolus is a small dark spot inside the nucleus, visible in the cell body on a neuron slide. It is not a process and does not carry impulses.
Correct. The axon carries the impulse away from the cell body.
Dendrites carry signals toward the cell body, the opposite direction. Pick them if the question asked which processes receive incoming signals.
questions.answerText: The axon
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which part of a neuron contains the nucleus and serves as the cell's metabolic center?
options: The dendrites
The cell body
The synaptic bulb
The axon
questions.why: The cell body, also called the soma, holds the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm, so it is where the neuron makes its proteins and keeps itself alive. On a multipolar neuron slide it is the large central part of the cell, often with a clearly visible nucleus and a dark nucleolus inside.
notes: Dendrites are branched processes that receive signals. They extend from the cell body but do not hold the nucleus.
Correct. The cell body holds the nucleus and is the neuron's metabolic center.
The synaptic bulb is the swollen tip of an axon terminal that passes the signal to the next cell. It is far from the nucleus.
The axon is the single long process that carries impulses away. It contains no nucleus.
questions.answerText: The cell body

questions.q: On a neuron, what is the synaptic bulb?
options: The swollen tip at the end of an axon terminal
A short, branched process that receives signals
The cone-shaped region where the axon begins
A gap in the myelin sheath along the axon
questions.why: At its far end, the axon splits into fine branches called axon terminals, and each one ends in a small swelling, the synaptic bulb (also called the synaptic end bulb). The bulb holds the machinery that passes the signal to the next cell. It is one of the three nerve tissue structures listed for the Module 1 lab.
notes: Correct. The synaptic bulb is the swollen tip of an axon terminal.
A short, branched process that receives signals is a dendrite. Pick it if the question asked what brings signals toward the cell body.
The cone-shaped region where the axon begins is the axon hillock, at the junction with the cell body. Pick it if the question asked where the axon starts.
A gap in the myelin sheath is a node of Ranvier. Pick it for a question about a myelinated axon in a nerve.
questions.answerText: The swollen tip at the end of an axon terminal
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Where in the body is nervous tissue found?
options: The walls of the intestines and bladder
The tendons and ligaments
The heart wall and blood vessels
The brain, spinal cord, and nerves
questions.why: Nervous tissue is made of neurons and neuroglia, and its job is to detect changes and carry electrical signals. It is found in the brain and spinal cord, which make up the central nervous system, and in the nerves that branch out to the rest of the body.
notes: The walls of the intestines and bladder are mainly smooth muscle, lined by epithelium. Pick smooth muscle for that location.
Tendons and ligaments are dense regular connective tissue. Pick them for a slide of parallel collagen bundles.
The heart wall is cardiac muscle, and blood vessel walls are mostly smooth muscle and connective tissue. Nerves reach these organs, but the walls themselves are not nervous tissue.
Correct. Nervous tissue makes up the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.
questions.answerText: The brain, spinal cord, and nerves
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: On a nervous tissue slide, one large neuron with long processes is surrounded by many small, dark nuclei that have no visible processes. What are the small nuclei?
options: Synaptic bulbs
Dendrites
Neuroglia
Smooth muscle cells
questions.why: Neuroglia are the supporting cells of nervous tissue. They are much smaller and far more numerous than neurons, so on a slide they appear as many small, dark nuclei scattered around the large neuron cell bodies. Telling neurons from neuroglia under the microscope is a listed lab skill.
notes: Synaptic bulbs are swellings at the tips of axon terminals. They are parts of a neuron, not separate cells with nuclei.
Dendrites are processes of the neuron itself and do not have their own nuclei. Pick them if the question asked about the branches coming off the cell body.
Correct. The many small nuclei around the neuron belong to neuroglia.
Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped muscle cells in the walls of hollow organs. They are not found scattered among neurons in nervous tissue.
questions.answerText: Neuroglia
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares neurons with neuroglia?
options: Neuroglia carry impulses, while neurons only support and protect
Neurons and neuroglia are the same size and both carry impulses
Neuroglia are smaller and more numerous, and only neuroglia can divide
Neurons are smaller and more numerous, and only neurons can divide
questions.why: Neurons are the excitable cells that receive and transmit nerve impulses, and mature neurons cannot divide. Neuroglia are the support cells that nourish, support, and protect neurons. They are smaller and far more numerous, and they keep the ability to divide.
notes: This swaps the two roles. Neurons carry impulses, while neuroglia support and protect them.
Neurons are generally much larger than neuroglia, and carrying impulses is the job of neurons, not glia.
Correct. Neuroglia are smaller, more numerous, and still able to divide.
This reverses the two cells. Neurons are the larger cells, and mature neurons cannot divide.
questions.answerText: Neuroglia are smaller and more numerous, and only neuroglia can divide
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A glioma is a brain tumor that arises from glial cells. Why do tumors like this arise from glia rather than from mature neurons?
options: Glial cells can still divide, while mature neurons cannot
Glial cells are larger than neurons, so they have more room to grow
Neurons are protected by intercalated discs that stop growth
Neurons are found only in nerves, not inside the brain
questions.why: A tumor is a mass of cells dividing out of control, so it can only arise from cells that are still able to divide. Mature neurons have lost that ability, but neuroglia keep it. That is why tumors of brain tissue come from glial cells rather than from mature neurons.
notes: Correct. Tumors come from dividing cells, and glia can divide while mature neurons cannot.
Glial cells are smaller than neurons, not larger. Size is not what lets a cell form a tumor anyway.
Intercalated discs are junctions between cardiac muscle cells, not structures in nervous tissue.
Neurons are found throughout the brain and spinal cord as well as in ganglia. Their cell bodies are plentiful inside the brain.
questions.answerText: Glial cells can still divide, while mature neurons cannot
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which body membrane lines the cavities that open to the outside of the body, such as the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and reproductive tracts?
options: The mucous membrane
The cutaneous membrane
The synovial membrane
The serous membrane
questions.why: Mucous membranes, also called mucosae, line the body cavities and tubes that open to the exterior. They are an epithelium resting on a layer of loose connective tissue, and their surface is kept moist, often by mucus. The lining of the mouth, stomach, trachea, and bladder are all mucous membranes.
notes: Correct. Mucous membranes line the tracts that open to the exterior.
The cutaneous membrane is the skin, a dry membrane covering the outside of the body rather than lining an internal tract.
The synovial membrane lines the cavities of freely movable joints. Pick it for the knee or shoulder joint.
Serous membranes line closed cavities with no opening to the outside, such as the pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal cavities.
questions.answerText: The mucous membrane

questions.q: What does serous fluid do in the space between the parietal and visceral layers of a serous membrane?
options: It carries oxygen to the organs
It reduces friction as organs move
It traps dust and microbes
It waterproofs the body surface
questions.why: A serous membrane is a double layer, with the parietal layer lining the body wall and the visceral layer covering the organ. The thin film of serous fluid between them acts as a lubricant, so the heart, lungs, and abdominal organs can slide against the wall as they beat, expand, and move without rubbing damage.
notes: Carrying oxygen to organs is the job of red blood cells in the blood, not of serous fluid.
Correct. Serous fluid lubricates the layers so organs move with little friction.
Trapping dust and microbes is the job of mucus on mucous membranes, such as the lining of the airways.
Waterproofing the body surface is done by the keratinized cutaneous membrane, the skin.
questions.answerText: It reduces friction as organs move

questions.q: In a mucous membrane, what is the lamina propria?
options: The basement membrane between the epithelial cells
The loose connective tissue layer under the epithelium
The film of mucus that goblet cells spread over the epithelium
The single layer of flat cells on its surface
questions.why: A mucous membrane has two parts: an epithelium on the surface and a layer of loose (areolar) connective tissue beneath it. That connective tissue layer is the lamina propria. It supports the epithelium and carries the blood vessels that the avascular epithelium depends on, and it appears on epithelial slides as one of the structures to identify when present.
notes: The basement membrane sits below the epithelium, not between its cells, and it is a thin anchoring layer rather than a full layer of connective tissue.
Correct. The lamina propria is the loose connective tissue under the epithelium of a mucous membrane.
Mucus is a secretion on top of the epithelium, made by goblet cells. It is not a tissue layer.
A single layer of flat surface cells is simple squamous epithelium, which forms the surface of serous membranes rather than the lamina propria.
questions.answerText: The loose connective tissue layer under the epithelium

questions.q: What does the synovial membrane secrete?
options: Sebum, which oils the skin and hair
Synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint
Serous fluid, which lubricates organs in a cavity
Mucus, which traps particles in the airway
questions.why: The synovial membrane lines the cavity of a freely movable joint, such as the knee or shoulder. It is made of connective tissue only, with no epithelium, and it secretes synovial fluid. This fluid lubricates the joint and nourishes the avascular cartilage covering the bone ends.
notes: Sebum is secreted by sebaceous glands in the skin by the holocrine mode. Pick it for a question about oil on the skin and hair.
Correct. The synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid into the joint cavity.
Serous fluid is secreted by serous membranes such as the pleura and peritoneum. Pick it for the fluid around the lungs or abdominal organs.
Mucus is secreted by goblet cells and glands of mucous membranes. Pick it for the lining of the airway or gut.
questions.answerText: Synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares serous and mucous membranes?
options: Serous membranes line closed cavities, and mucous membranes line open tracts
Mucous membranes line closed cavities, and serous membranes line open tracts
Both line joint cavities and secrete synovial fluid
Both are dry membranes covered by keratinized epithelium
questions.why: The deciding feature is whether the space opens to the outside. Serous membranes, such as the pleura, pericardium, and peritoneum, line closed cavities and cover the organs inside them. Mucous membranes line the tracts that do open to the exterior, such as the digestive and respiratory tracts. Both are moist membranes.
notes: Correct. Serous membranes line closed cavities and mucous membranes line tracts open to the outside.
This reverses the two. The pleural and peritoneal cavities are closed and lined by serous membranes, while the gut and airways are open tracts lined by mucous membranes.
Joint cavities are lined by the synovial membrane, which secretes synovial fluid. Neither serous nor mucous membranes do this.
A dry membrane with keratinized epithelium is the cutaneous membrane, the skin. Serous and mucous membranes are both moist.
questions.answerText: Serous membranes line closed cavities, and mucous membranes line open tracts

questions.q: A patient has an infection of the inner lining of the urinary bladder. Which type of body membrane is infected?
options: A synovial membrane
The cutaneous membrane
A serous membrane
A mucous membrane
questions.why: The urinary tract opens to the outside of the body through the urethra, so the inner lining of the bladder is a mucous membrane. Its epithelium is transitional epithelium, resting on a lamina propria of connective tissue. Infections that enter from the outside travel up along this mucous lining.
notes: The synovial membrane lines joint cavities. Pick it for an infected knee or shoulder joint.
The cutaneous membrane is the skin on the outside of the body. Pick it for a skin infection.

Serous membranes line closed cavities such as the peritoneal cavity. Pick a serous membrane if the question asked about the covering on the outside of an organ in that cavity, not the inner lining of a tract.
Correct. The bladder lining is a mucous membrane because the urinary tract opens to the exterior.
questions.answerText: A mucous membrane

questions.q: Rheumatoid arthritis attacks the membrane that lines the cavity of freely movable joints. Which membrane is it, and what is it made of?
options: The serous membrane, made of simple squamous epithelium
The cutaneous membrane, made of keratinized epithelium
The mucous membrane, made of epithelium over loose connective tissue
The synovial membrane, made of connective tissue only
questions.why: Freely movable joints are lined by the synovial membrane, the one body membrane made of connective tissue alone, with no epithelial layer. It secretes synovial fluid into the joint cavity. In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks this membrane and the joint cartilage, starting with the small joints.
notes: Serous membranes line closed body cavities such as the pleural and peritoneal cavities. Pick a serous membrane for pleurisy or peritonitis.
The cutaneous membrane is the skin. It covers the body surface and is not found inside joints.
Mucous membranes line tracts open to the exterior, such as the gut and airways. They do not line joints.
Correct. The synovial membrane lines joint cavities and is made of connective tissue only.
questions.answerText: The synovial membrane, made of connective tissue only

questions.q: Which germ layer is the middle layer of the early embryo?
options: Ectoderm.
Endoderm.
Mesoderm.
Epidermis.
questions.why: The early embryo forms three primary germ layers. Ectoderm is the outer layer, mesoderm the middle layer, and endoderm the inner layer. Every tissue in the body traces back to one of them.
notes: Ectoderm is the outer germ layer. It forms the epidermis and all nervous tissue.
Endoderm is the inner germ layer. It forms the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts.
Correct. Mesoderm is the middle germ layer, the source of muscle, bone, cartilage, and blood.
The epidermis is the outer layer of the skin, not a germ layer. It develops from the ectoderm.
questions.answerText: Mesoderm.

questions.q: Melanocytes, the pigment cells of the epidermis, develop from which germ layer?
options: Mesoderm.
Endoderm.
Dermis.
Ectoderm.
questions.why: Melanocytes develop from the ectoderm of the embryo. The ectoderm is the outer germ layer, the same layer that forms the epidermis and all nervous tissue.
notes: Mesoderm forms muscle, bone, cartilage, blood, and most connective tissue, not the pigment cells of the epidermis.
Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts and their glands, not skin pigment cells.
The dermis is the deep layer of the skin, not a germ layer. Melanocytes sit in the epidermis, above it.
Correct. Melanocytes develop from the ectoderm, the outer germ layer.
questions.answerText: Ectoderm.

questions.q: A biopsy of the stomach shows simple columnar epithelium lining the inside, with a layer of smooth muscle deeper in the wall. Which germ layer formed each tissue?
options: Ectoderm formed the lining, and mesoderm formed the smooth muscle.
