Positive feedback is normal in these settings, so calling it always pathological is wrong. Osmolarity is defended by negative feedback through antidiuretic hormone and thirst. A setpoint comparison is a feature of negative feedback, not positive.
questions.answerText: It is used for processes that should go to completion quickly

questions.q: Blood pressure falls, baroreceptors fire less, and heart rate rises to bring pressure back up. Which type of feedback is this?
options: Positive feedback, because heart rate rose
Positive feedback, because two variables changed together
Feedforward, because the heart acted before pressure changed
Negative feedback, because the response opposes the fall
questions.why: The sign of a loop is judged by whether the response opposes or amplifies the original change, and here a fall in pressure produced a correction that raises pressure. Heart rate rising is the mechanism of the correction, not evidence of amplification. The response came after the pressure fell, so it is not anticipatory. Two variables changing together says nothing about the sign of the loop.
questions.answerText: Negative feedback, because the response opposes the fall

questions.q: During the upstroke of an action potential, sodium entry depolarizes the membrane, which opens more voltage gated sodium channels. Classify this loop.
options: Negative feedback, because the membrane returns to rest afterward
Feedforward, because the cell anticipates the stimulus
Positive feedback, because the response increases the stimulus
Neither, because ion movement is passive
questions.why: Depolarization opens channels whose current causes further depolarization, which is why the upstroke is so fast and all or none. The later return to rest is caused by different channels and does not change the sign of the upstroke loop. Nothing about this is anticipatory. Passive ion movement can still form a feedback loop, since the loop is defined by the causal chain rather than by the energy source.
questions.answerText: Positive feedback, because the response increases the stimulus

questions.q: Plasma osmolarity rises, antidiuretic hormone is released, the kidney conserves water, and osmolarity falls back toward normal. Classify this loop.
options: Positive feedback
Negative feedback
Feedforward control
Acclimatization
questions.why: The response lowered the variable that had risen, which is opposition and therefore negative feedback. Positive feedback would have driven osmolarity higher still. Feedforward would act before osmolarity changed, for instance thirst triggered by the taste of salty food. Acclimatization is a slow adaptive change over days, not a single corrective loop.
questions.answerText: Negative feedback

questions.q: Stretch of the cervix during labor increases oxytocin secretion, which strengthens uterine contractions, which stretches the cervix further. What finally ends this cycle?
options: Delivery of the infant, which removes the stretch stimulus
Oxytocin receptors reaching their maximum firing rate
A negative feedback loop within the uterus that limits contraction
The pituitary running out of stored oxytocin
questions.why: Because each turn of the loop increases the stimulus, the cycle can only stop when the stimulus is physically removed, and birth accomplishes that. Receptor saturation would slow the acceleration but would not remove the ongoing stretch. There is no internal opposing loop that halts labor once it is established. Oxytocin supply is not the limiting factor in a normal delivery.
questions.answerText: Delivery of the infant, which removes the stretch stimulus

questions.q: A control system is described as having a very low gain, meaning the effector response to a given error is weak. What is the predicted effect on the regulated variable?
options: Elimination of the setpoint from the integrating center
Perfectly flat control with no deviation at all
Conversion of the loop from negative to positive feedback
Larger swings away from the setpoint before correction occurs
questions.why: Gain determines how forcefully the system pushes back per unit of error, so a weak response lets the variable drift further before it is brought under control. Low gain cannot produce tighter control than high gain. The sign of the loop is unchanged, since the response still opposes the deviation. The setpoint remains in place; only the strength of the correction has changed.
questions.answerText: Larger swings away from the setpoint before correction occurs

questions.q: Which of these responses would be classified as positive feedback?
options: A damaged vessel wall attracts platelets that release chemicals attracting still more platelets
Rising body temperature increases sweating, which cools the body
A drop in plasma calcium triggers parathyroid hormone that raises calcium
A rise in carbon dioxide increases ventilation, which lowers carbon dioxide
questions.why: Platelet recruitment builds on itself, with each arriving platelet increasing the signal that brings in more, so the plug forms rapidly. Sweating, parathyroid hormone secretion, and the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide all reverse the change that triggered them, which makes them negative feedback.
questions.answerText: A damaged vessel wall attracts platelets that release chemicals attracting still more platelets

questions.q: Why would positive feedback be a poor design for controlling body temperature?
options: It would respond too slowly to be useful for temperature
A small rise would drive temperature higher and higher instead of correcting it
It would require a sensor, which the thermoregulatory system does not have
It would prevent the hypothalamus from changing the setpoint during illness
questions.why: Positive feedback amplifies deviation, so a warm day would push core temperature away from the survivable range rather than defend it, which is fatal within a narrow margin. Speed is not the problem; positive feedback is fast. The thermoregulatory system does have sensors in the skin and the hypothalamus. Setpoint resetting during fever is unrelated to the sign of the loop.
questions.answerText: A small rise would drive temperature higher and higher instead of correcting it

questions.q: In severe hemorrhage, cardiac output falls, coronary blood flow falls, the heart weakens, and cardiac output falls further. What is happening, and what does it imply for treatment?
options: Equilibrium has been reached, so cardiac output will hold at its new value
A negative feedback loop is correcting the problem, so no intervention is needed
The setpoint for cardiac output has been reset downward and the patient is stable
A positive feedback cycle has taken over, so an outside intervention such as restoring volume is required to break it
questions.why: Each fall in output worsens perfusion of the heart itself, which worsens output again, so the loop feeds itself and nothing internal can stop it. The baroreceptor reflex is trying to help, but once the vicious cycle dominates, the response no longer opposes the change. Cardiac output has no defended setpoint of its own that could be reset in this way. Equilibrium implies a stable resting state, which is not what a spiraling decline is.
questions.answerText: A positive feedback cycle has taken over, so an outside intervention such as restoring volume is required to break it

questions.q: The sodium positive feedback of the action potential upstroke does not run forever. Which pair of events stops it?
options: Inactivation of the sodium channels and delayed opening of potassium channels
A rise in extracellular sodium and closure of potassium channels
Activation of the Na+ K+ ATPase, which reverses the upstroke within a millisecond
A negative feedback sensor in the membrane detecting the peak voltage
questions.why: Sodium channels have a separate inactivation gate that closes shortly after opening, and voltage gated potassium channels open with a delay, so two processes outside the amplifying loop terminate it. Extracellular sodium does not change during a single spike, and closing potassium channels would prolong depolarization. The pump restores gradients over many cycles and is far too slow to end one upstroke. There is no voltage sensing comparator that halts the spike the way a homeostatic center would.
questions.answerText: Inactivation of the sodium channels and delayed opening of potassium channels

questions.q: A person with a fever of 39.5 C is given a drug that lowers the hypothalamic setpoint back to 37 C. Predict what the negative feedback loop does next.
options: Temperature rises further because lowering the setpoint amplifies the error
The person shivers harder because the body is still trying to reach 39.5 C
Nothing happens until the infection clears, since the setpoint cannot drive a response
The system now reads 39.5 C as too high, so sweating and skin vasodilation begin and temperature falls
questions.why: The integrating center compares actual temperature against the current setpoint, so lowering the target creates an error in the hot direction and triggers heat loss responses. Shivering would occur only if actual temperature were below the target, which is now not the case. The setpoint is precisely what drives the response, so the loop does not wait for the infection. Lowering a setpoint cannot amplify a deviation in a negative feedback system.
questions.answerText: The system now reads 39.5 C as too high, so sweating and skin vasodilation begin and temperature falls

questions.q: Compare the ends of two loops: labor contractions and the baroreceptor response to standing up. Which statement is correct?
options: Labor ends when the stimulus is physically removed, while the baroreceptor response shuts itself off as pressure returns to normal
Both stop when their responses restore the original value of the variable
Both require an outside event, since no loop can stop on its own
The baroreceptor response ends only when the person lies back down, and labor stops on its own
questions.why: A negative feedback loop is self limiting because the response erases the error that drove it, while a positive feedback loop keeps building until something external interrupts it. Labor never restores the original state, so it cannot end by returning the variable to where it began. Negative feedback loops do stop on their own, which is exactly the difference. The baroreceptor reflex maintains pressure while standing rather than waiting for the person to lie down.
questions.answerText: Labor ends when the stimulus is physically removed, while the baroreceptor response shuts itself off as pressure returns to normal

questions.q: What is feedforward control?
options: A slow structural change that develops over weeks in a new environment
A response triggered only after a sensor detects an error
A response made in anticipation of a change, before the regulated variable actually moves
A loop in which the response amplifies the original stimulus
questions.why: Feedforward uses a cue that predicts a disturbance and starts the correction early, which keeps the eventual deviation small. Responding after a detected error is ordinary negative feedback. A slow structural change over weeks is acclimatization. A response that amplifies the stimulus is positive feedback.
questions.answerText: A response made in anticipation of a change, before the regulated variable actually moves

questions.q: What is acclimatization?
options: An immediate reflex correction of a deviation
An anticipatory response triggered by a predictive cue
A permanent genetic change passed to offspring
A reversible physiological adjustment to a sustained change in the natural environment, developing over days to weeks
questions.why: Acclimatization involves changes in gene expression, hormone levels, and tissue properties that improve function in a new environment and fade when the person returns home. An immediate reflex correction is negative feedback and happens in seconds. Genetic change across generations is adaptation, which is evolutionary rather than physiological. An anticipatory response is feedforward.
questions.answerText: A reversible physiological adjustment to a sustained change in the natural environment, developing over days to weeks

questions.q: When does a feedforward response occur relative to the change in the regulated variable?
options: At the same instant the variable changes
Before the variable changes
Only after the variable has fully returned to its setpoint
Only when the variable moves outside its normal range
questions.why: The defining feature of feedforward is timing: the body reads a predictive cue and acts in advance, so the disturbance is blunted before it arrives. Acting at the same instant or after the deviation describes feedback. Waiting until the variable is back at the setpoint would leave nothing to correct. Waiting for the variable to leave its normal range is again feedback, and a late one.
questions.answerText: Before the variable changes

questions.q: Which change occurs during acclimatization to high altitude over several weeks?
options: Plasma volume rises steadily above sea level values
Hemoglobin loses its ability to bind oxygen
Resting ventilation falls below sea level values
Red blood cell production increases
questions.why: Low arterial PO2 stimulates erythropoietin from the kidney, which raises red cell number and therefore oxygen carrying capacity over weeks. Hemoglobin continues to bind oxygen normally; its affinity shifts slightly but binding is not lost. Ventilation rises rather than falls at altitude. Plasma volume actually falls in the early days at altitude, which contributes to the rise in hematocrit.
questions.answerText: Red blood cell production increases

questions.q: The smell and taste of food trigger a small release of insulin before any glucose has been absorbed. What is this response called?
options: Feedforward control
Negative feedback
Acclimatization
Positive feedback
questions.why: The sensory cue predicts an incoming glucose load, so insulin is released early and the rise in blood glucose after the meal is smaller. Negative feedback insulin release comes later, driven by glucose actually reaching the beta cell. Acclimatization takes days to weeks and is not involved in a single meal. Nothing here amplifies the stimulus.
questions.answerText: Feedforward control

questions.q: Which statement about acclimatization is accurate?
options: It is permanent once it has developed
It reverses over time once the person returns to the original environment
It occurs within seconds of the environmental change
It requires a mutation in the genes of the exposed person
questions.why: Acclimatization is a reversible shift in physiological function, so a climber who returns to sea level slowly loses the extra red cells and the higher ventilatory drive. Permanence would make it adaptation rather than acclimatization. Responses within seconds are reflexes. No genetic mutation is involved, only changes in expression and regulation of existing genes.
questions.answerText: It reverses over time once the person returns to the original environment

questions.q: An athlete's heart rate rises from 65 to 90 beats per minute in the moments before a race begins, while still standing still. Which mechanism is operating?
options: Acclimatization
Feedforward control
Negative feedback triggered by rising carbon dioxide
Positive feedback in the sinoatrial node
questions.why: No exercise has occurred yet, so no metabolic error has been detected; the nervous system is acting on the expectation of exercise to prepare the circulation. Acclimatization would take days and would not appear in a single moment. Carbon dioxide has not yet risen, so a feedback response to it is not possible. The sinoatrial node is being driven by autonomic input rather than by an amplifying loop.
questions.answerText: Feedforward control

questions.q: A person who moves to a city at 3500 meters has a hematocrit of 52 percent after three weeks, compared with 44 percent on arrival. Which mechanism explains the change?
options: Acclimatization
Feedforward control
Positive feedback
A reset of the oxygen setpoint by the medulla
questions.why: Weeks of sustained low arterial PO2 raised erythropoietin and red cell production, which is a reversible adjustment to a new environment. Feedforward would require an anticipatory cue and would act in seconds to minutes. Nothing in the sequence amplifies the original stimulus. Arterial oxygen is not defended around a setpoint in the way temperature or pressure are.
questions.answerText: Acclimatization

questions.q: After ten days of outdoor work in the desert, a laborer sweats sooner, sweats more, and the sweat contains less Na+. Which mechanism is this?
options: Acclimatization
Negative feedback within a single work shift
Feedforward control
Positive feedback driving sweat production
questions.why: Repeated heat exposure over days raises aldosterone driven sodium reabsorption in the sweat duct and lowers the threshold for sweating, both of which improve heat tolerance and reverse after weeks indoors. Feedforward would be an anticipatory response to a cue rather than a change in gland behavior over days. A single shift of negative feedback cannot change the composition of sweat. Nothing about sweating amplifies the heat load.
questions.answerText: Acclimatization

questions.q: A person steps into cold water and immediately begins to shiver. Which mechanism is operating?
options: Feedforward, since the person expected the water to be cold
Acclimatization, since the body is adjusting to a new environment
Negative feedback, since the response follows a detected drop in temperature
Positive feedback, since shivering makes the person feel colder
questions.why: Skin thermoreceptors detected the cooling and the hypothalamus ordered heat production, which is a correction after the fact and therefore feedback. Feedforward would be the shiver that begins while the person is still on the pool deck, before contact. Acclimatization requires repeated exposure over days. Shivering generates heat and opposes the cooling rather than amplifying it.
questions.answerText: Negative feedback, since the response follows a detected drop in temperature

questions.q: Which pairing correctly matches the mechanism to the timescale on which it acts?
options: Feedforward acts over days to weeks, acclimatization in seconds
Feedforward acts in seconds to minutes, acclimatization over days to weeks
Both act within seconds of the triggering cue
Both require weeks of repeated exposure before they appear
questions.why: Feedforward is a fast nervous or hormonal response to a predictive cue, while acclimatization requires changes in gene expression and tissue composition that take much longer to build and to fade. Assigning days to weeks to feedforward and seconds to acclimatization reverses the two. Acclimatization cannot occur in seconds because protein synthesis and cell production are involved. Feedforward needs no prior exposure period, only a recognized cue.
questions.answerText: Feedforward acts in seconds to minutes, acclimatization over days to weeks

questions.q: A runner who has lived at 3000 meters for a month steps to the starting line and her ventilation increases before the gun fires. During the race her arterial oxygen content is higher than it was on her first day at altitude. Which mechanisms explain each observation?
options: Acclimatization explains the ventilation rise at the line, and feedforward explains the better oxygen content
Both observations are explained by feedforward acting on different organs
Both observations are explained by negative feedback from chemoreceptors
Feedforward explains the ventilation rise at the line, and acclimatization explains the better oxygen content
questions.why: Breathing harder before the race starts is an anticipatory response to a cue with no error yet detected, while a higher oxygen content after a month reflects more red cells and other slow adjustments to sustained hypoxia. Reversing the two ignores their very different timescales. Chemoreceptor feedback cannot act before any change in blood gases occurs. A single month long change in blood composition is not a feedforward response.
questions.answerText: Feedforward explains the ventilation rise at the line, and acclimatization explains the better oxygen content

questions.q: A patient loses the cephalic phase of insulin secretion, so no insulin is released until glucose actually reaches the beta cell. Predict the effect on blood glucose after a meal.
options: The peak glucose is lower, because the beta cell now responds only to a real signal
Blood glucose never rises, because feedforward is the only route to insulin release
The peak glucose is higher and returns to baseline more slowly, because the correction starts later
Blood glucose becomes unregulated and stays elevated permanently
questions.why: Feedforward exists to shrink the coming deviation, so losing it leaves the feedback loop to correct a larger error that it did not get a head start on. Feedback insulin release is intact, so insulin is still secreted and glucose does eventually rise and fall. Removing an early corrective response cannot lower the peak. Regulation continues, just less tightly, so a permanent elevation overstates the defect.
questions.answerText: The peak glucose is higher and returns to baseline more slowly, because the correction starts later

questions.q: Two workers do identical labor in 38 C heat. One has worked there for two weeks and the other started today. Predict the difference and give the reason.
options: The experienced worker holds a lower core temperature because acclimatization raised sweat rate and lowered sweat Na+ loss
The new worker holds a lower core temperature because unacclimatized sweat glands work at maximum from the first day
Both hold identical core temperatures, since sweating capacity is fixed at birth
The experienced worker holds a higher core temperature because acclimatization raises the thermal setpoint
questions.why: Two weeks of heat exposure increases plasma volume, starts sweating at a lower core temperature, and conserves sodium, all of which improve evaporative cooling and reduce the thermal strain. An unacclimatized worker sweats later and loses more salt, so heat storage is greater. Sweating capacity is plastic rather than fixed at birth. Acclimatization improves defense of the normal setpoint rather than shifting the setpoint upward.
questions.answerText: The experienced worker holds a lower core temperature because acclimatization raised sweat rate and lowered sweat Na+ loss

questions.q: What defines a local control pathway?
options: The response is always slower than a reflex pathway
The response requires a signal carried by the bloodstream to a distant organ
The response is restricted to the tissue where the change was detected
The response is coordinated by the medulla oblongata
questions.why: In local control, the cell or tissue that senses the change also produces the response, using chemicals that diffuse only a short distance. Signals carried in blood to distant organs are long distance reflexes. Local control is usually faster than a reflex because there is no travel time. Involvement of the medulla means the nervous system is coordinating a long distance pathway.
questions.answerText: The response is restricted to the tissue where the change was detected

questions.q: What defines a long distance reflex pathway?
options: Chemicals diffuse a few micrometers to neighboring cells
The response occurs only in cells that lack receptors
The nervous system or endocrine system carries a signal from the site of the stimulus to a distant effector
The stimulus and the response occur in the same cell
questions.why: Long distance reflexes use neurons, hormones, or both to link a sensor in one place with an effector somewhere else, allowing the whole body to respond together. Diffusion over micrometers is paracrine signaling and is local. Receptors are required for any response, not absent from it. Stimulus and response in the same cell is autocrine signaling.
questions.answerText: The nervous system or endocrine system carries a signal from the site of the stimulus to a distant effector

questions.q: What is a paracrine signal?
options: A chemical carried in the blood to distant target cells
A chemical that acts on the same cell that released it
A chemical released from an axon terminal onto a muscle fiber
A chemical that diffuses to act on nearby cells in the same tissue
questions.why: Paracrine signals travel only across the interstitial fluid to neighbors, which makes them a hallmark of local control. Blood borne chemicals acting at a distance are hormones. Release from an axon terminal onto a target is neurotransmission. Acting on the cell of origin is autocrine signaling.
questions.answerText: A chemical that diffuses to act on nearby cells in the same tissue

questions.q: What is an autocrine signal?
options: A chemical that acts on receptors of the cell that secreted it
A chemical released into the blood by an endocrine gland
A chemical that acts only on cells of a different tissue type
A chemical that requires a nerve to carry it to its target
questions.why: An autocrine signal feeds back onto its own cell, often to reinforce or limit its own secretion, and it is a form of local control. A chemical released into the blood is a hormone. Acting on a different tissue type describes many signals but is not what defines autocrine action. No chemical signal is carried inside a nerve to its target in this sense.
questions.answerText: A chemical that acts on receptors of the cell that secreted it

questions.q: Which is an example of local control?
options: The medulla increases heart rate when arterial pressure falls
Arterioles in an active muscle dilate in response to metabolites released by the muscle
The pancreas releases insulin that acts on liver and muscle
The hypothalamus triggers shivering in cold weather
questions.why: Metabolites such as carbon dioxide, adenosine, and K+ accumulate in the working tissue and act on the vessels right there, with no involvement of nerves or hormones. The medullary response to falling pressure, insulin release, and hypothalamic shivering all send signals from one location to effectors elsewhere, which makes them long distance reflexes.
questions.answerText: Arterioles in an active muscle dilate in response to metabolites released by the muscle

questions.q: Which is an example of a long distance reflex pathway?
options: Endothelial cells releasing nitric oxide onto adjacent smooth muscle
A mast cell releasing histamine that dilates the vessel beside it
Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus signaling the medulla, which changes heart rate
Damaged tissue releasing chemicals that make nearby capillaries leaky
questions.why: The sensor sits in the neck, the integrating center is in the brainstem, and the effector is the heart, so the signal must travel a long way through the nervous system. Nitric oxide from endothelium, histamine from a mast cell, and inflammatory mediators from damaged tissue all act on immediate neighbors and are local control.
questions.answerText: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus signaling the medulla, which changes heart rate

questions.q: In an endocrine reflex, what carries the signal from the integrating center to the effector?
options: Direct electrical coupling through gap junctions
A paracrine molecule diffusing through interstitial fluid
A motor neuron with its cell body in the spinal cord
A hormone traveling in the blood
questions.why: Endocrine reflexes use the bloodstream as the efferent pathway, which lets one gland reach every tissue with the right receptor. Diffusion through interstitial fluid limits a signal to its neighbors and is therefore local. A motor neuron is the efferent limb of a neural reflex, not an endocrine one. Gap junction coupling passes current between adjacent cells only.
questions.answerText: A hormone traveling in the blood

questions.q: Compared with an endocrine reflex, a neural reflex is generally which of the following?
options: Faster in onset and shorter in duration
Slower in onset and longer in duration
Identical in speed but broader in the tissues reached
Faster in onset and longer in duration
questions.why: Action potentials travel in milliseconds and neurotransmitter is cleared quickly, so neural reflexes start and stop fast. Hormones take seconds to minutes to reach targets and persist while they circulate, which gives endocrine reflexes the slower and longer profile. The two systems are not identical in speed. A neural reflex does not combine fast onset with long duration; that combination is unusual outside sustained autonomic tone.
questions.answerText: Faster in onset and shorter in duration

questions.q: During exercise, adenosine and carbon dioxide accumulate in a working muscle and the arterioles inside that muscle dilate. Classify this response.
options: Local control, because the signal never leaves the tissue
Long distance reflex, because blood flow changes
Long distance reflex, because the muscle is far from the heart
Neither, because chemicals cannot control vessel diameter
questions.why: The metabolites are produced by the same tissue whose vessels respond, and no nerve or hormone is required, which is the definition of local control. A change in blood flow does not by itself imply a distant pathway. The distance from the heart is irrelevant, since what matters is the distance the signal travels. Metabolic chemicals are among the most powerful controllers of arteriolar diameter.
questions.answerText: Local control, because the signal never leaves the tissue

questions.q: Blood pressure falls when a person stands, and within seconds arterioles throughout the body constrict. Classify this pathway.
options: Local control by each arteriole sensing its own pressure
A long distance neural reflex
A paracrine response of endothelial cells
Acclimatization to the upright posture
questions.why: Baroreceptors in the great vessels detect the fall, the medulla integrates it, and sympathetic nerves reach vessels all over the body, so a signal travels a long way to widespread effectors. Local sensing could not produce a coordinated body wide response within seconds. Paracrine signals cannot reach vessels in distant limbs. Acclimatization takes days and would not appear in a single act of standing.
questions.answerText: A long distance neural reflex

questions.q: A mast cell in the skin releases histamine after an insect bite, and the capillaries a few micrometers away become leaky. Classify this response.
options: Long distance endocrine reflex
Autocrine feedback on the mast cell
Long distance neural reflex
Local control through paracrine signaling
questions.why: Histamine diffuses a very short distance to act on neighboring vessels, which is paracrine signaling and therefore local. An endocrine reflex would require histamine to travel in blood to distant targets. No sensor, nerve, or brain center is involved in this step. The response occurs on vessels rather than on the mast cell itself, so it is not autocrine.
questions.answerText: Local control through paracrine signaling

questions.q: Blood glucose falls to 60 mg/dL, alpha cells secrete glucagon, and the liver releases glucose into the blood. Classify this pathway.
options: Local control within the pancreas
A long distance neural reflex
A long distance endocrine reflex
Paracrine signaling between liver cells
questions.why: The sensor sits in the pancreas, the signal travels in blood, and the effector is the liver, so the pathway spans two organs using a hormone. Local control would keep both sensing and response inside the pancreas. No neuron is required for this loop, although the nervous system can modulate it. Liver cells respond to glucagon rather than signaling one another.
questions.answerText: A long distance endocrine reflex

questions.q: Endothelial cells lining an arteriole release nitric oxide, which relaxes the smooth muscle directly beneath them. Classify this control.
options: Local, because the signal acts on immediately adjacent cells
Endocrine, because nitric oxide enters the blood
Neural, because vessel diameter is controlled by nerves
Autocrine, because the endothelium relaxes itself
questions.why: Nitric oxide is short lived and diffuses only a few cell widths, so its target is the muscle layer right next to the endothelium, making this a textbook paracrine and local mechanism. Nitric oxide is destroyed too quickly in blood to act as a circulating hormone. Sympathetic nerves also affect diameter, but they are not involved in this described step. The relaxing cell is smooth muscle, not the endothelial cell itself.
questions.answerText: Local, because the signal acts on immediately adjacent cells
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which feature most reliably tells you a response used a long distance pathway rather than local control?
options: The effector is in a different organ from the sensor
The response involved a chemical signal
The response was fast
The response corrected a deviation from a setpoint
questions.why: Distance between where the change is detected and where the response occurs is the defining test, because bridging that gap requires nerves or hormones. Speed does not separate the two, since local responses are often the faster of the pair. Chemical signals occur in both categories, as paracrines and as hormones. Correcting a deviation describes negative feedback, which both local and long distance pathways can perform.
questions.answerText: The effector is in a different organ from the sensor

questions.q: During heavy exercise, sympathetic nerves order vasoconstriction throughout the body, yet the arterioles inside working muscle dilate. What does this show about the two kinds of control?
options: Long distance control always overrides local control, so the muscle vessels must actually be constricting
The sympathetic nerves do not reach skeletal muscle vessels at all
Local metabolic control can override the long distance neural signal in the tissue that needs flow
The two pathways cannot operate at the same time in one tissue
questions.why: Accumulating metabolites in active muscle blunt the constrictor signal locally, so blood is directed to the tissue doing the work while other beds are constricted, which is a beautifully efficient arrangement. Sympathetic fibers do innervate muscle arterioles, which is why the conflict exists in the first place. The observed dilation contradicts the claim that neural control always wins. Both pathways act on the same vessels simultaneously, and the outcome is their sum.
questions.answerText: Local metabolic control can override the long distance neural signal in the tissue that needs flow

questions.q: A segment of small intestine is removed, placed in a warm oxygenated bath, and stretched. It still produces coordinated peristaltic contractions. What does this experiment establish?
options: Peristalsis can be generated by local control within the intestinal wall, without input from the brain or spinal cord
Peristalsis requires hormones circulating in the blood
Peristalsis is a long distance reflex mediated by the vagus nerve only
The bath is providing an artificial stimulus that does not occur in the body
questions.why: With every long distance connection cut and no blood supply present, the coordinated response must arise from sensors, neurons, and muscle contained in the gut wall itself. Circulating hormones are absent in the bath, so they cannot be required. Vagal input is also absent, which rules out an exclusively vagal reflex. Stretch is the normal stimulus for peristalsis in the intact gut, so it is not an artifact.
questions.answerText: Peristalsis can be generated by local control within the intestinal wall, without input from the brain or spinal cord

questions.q: A heart transplant recipient has no autonomic nerves to the new heart, yet heart rate still rises during exercise, though more slowly than normal. What accounts for the rise?
options: Circulating epinephrine from the adrenal medulla acting as a long distance endocrine signal
Sympathetic nerves regrowing within minutes of exercise starting
Local paracrine signals from the coronary arteries setting the pacemaker rate
The absence of any control, since the intrinsic rate cannot change
questions.why: Exercise raises adrenal epinephrine, which reaches the pacemaker in the blood and speeds it, and the slower onset reflects the time hormones need compared with nerves. Nerves do not regrow within a single exercise bout. Coronary paracrine signals adjust vessel diameter rather than setting pacemaker rate. The observed rise itself proves that some control remains.
questions.answerText: Circulating epinephrine from the adrenal medulla acting as a long distance endocrine signal

questions.q: An investigator wants to prove that a given vasodilation in a tissue is locally controlled. Which result would provide the strongest evidence?
options: The dilation is abolished when the spinal cord is cut
The dilation occurs at the same time in several distant organs
The dilation still occurs after all nerves to the tissue are cut and the tissue is perfused with blood free of hormones
The dilation is larger when the person is emotionally stressed
questions.why: Removing both possible long distance routes, nerves and blood borne hormones, and still seeing the response leaves only signals generated within the tissue. Abolition after a cord transection would argue for a neural reflex instead. Simultaneous dilation in distant organs points to a shared systemic signal. Sensitivity to emotional stress suggests central nervous input rather than local control.
questions.answerText: The dilation still occurs after all nerves to the tissue are cut and the tissue is perfused with blood free of hormones

questions.q: Which expression states the mass balance principle for a substance in the body?
options: Amount in the body equals intake divided by output
Amount in the body equals intake multiplied by the time of exposure
Amount in the body equals output minus intake
Amount in the body equals intake plus metabolic production minus output minus metabolic removal
questions.why: Everything that enters or is made must be balanced against everything that leaves or is consumed, and whatever remains is what the body holds. A ratio of intake to output has no units of amount and does not track accumulation. Output minus intake reverses the sign, so it would predict growth during starvation. Multiplying intake by time gives a cumulative dose, not the amount currently present.
questions.answerText: Amount in the body equals intake plus metabolic production minus output minus metabolic removal

questions.q: When intake plus production exactly equals output, what happens to the amount of the substance in the body?
options: It rises steadily
It falls steadily
It stays constant
It oscillates between two values
questions.why: Equal gains and losses mean nothing accumulates and nothing is depleted, which is the definition of being in balance. A steady rise would require intake to exceed output, and a steady fall the reverse. Oscillation would require the two terms to alternate rather than match.
questions.answerText: It stays constant

questions.q: Which of these is a route of water input to the body?
options: Insensible loss from the skin
Metabolic water produced by oxidation of nutrients
Evaporation from the airways
Water lost in feces
questions.why: Oxidizing carbohydrate, fat, and protein generates water inside the body, which counts as production in the mass balance equation along with what is eaten and drunk. Insensible skin loss, evaporation from airways, and fecal water are all output terms. Recognizing metabolic water as a gain is the point of the production term.
questions.answerText: Metabolic water produced by oxidation of nutrients

questions.q: Which route accounts for the largest single loss of water in a resting adult on a temperate day?
options: Urine
Sweat
Feces
Tears
questions.why: Urine typically accounts for roughly 1.5 L of the 2.5 L lost each day at rest, and it is also the route the body can adjust most precisely. Fecal water loss is normally around 100 mL per day. Sweat is small at rest, though it dominates during heat or exercise. Tear production is a trivial fraction of daily loss.
questions.answerText: Urine

questions.q: Why does the production term of the mass balance equation equal zero for sodium?
options: Sodium leaves only in urine, which cancels the production term
Sodium is destroyed by cells as fast as it is produced
Sodium is stored in bone and therefore never enters the equation
The body cannot synthesize sodium, so all of it must come from the diet
questions.why: Elements cannot be made or destroyed by metabolism, so for an ion like sodium the only inputs are dietary and the only changes are in distribution and excretion. Cells cannot destroy sodium atoms. Bone stores participate in internal distribution but do not remove sodium from the balance equation. Sodium also leaves in sweat and feces, and output terms do not cancel production.
questions.answerText: The body cannot synthesize sodium, so all of it must come from the diet

questions.q: What does negative balance for a substance mean?
options: The substance carries a negative electrical charge
Intake exceeds output, so the amount in the body is rising
Output exceeds intake plus production, so the amount in the body is falling
The substance is present at less than its normal plasma concentration
questions.why: Balance refers to the direction of change in total body content, so negative balance means losses are winning and stores are shrinking. Electrical charge is unrelated to the accounting. Intake exceeding output is positive balance. A low plasma concentration describes one measurement at one moment and can occur with any direction of balance.
questions.answerText: Output exceeds intake plus production, so the amount in the body is falling

questions.q: A person is in positive water balance. What is happening?
options: Total body water is constant
Total body water is decreasing
Total body water is increasing
Water is moving from the intracellular to the extracellular compartment
questions.why: Positive balance means gains exceed losses, so the body is accumulating water and body weight rises. Decreasing water is negative balance. A constant amount is zero balance. Movement between compartments is redistribution, which changes where water sits without changing the total.
questions.answerText: Total body water is increasing

questions.q: Which organ makes the largest adjustable contribution to water and solute output, and is therefore the main site of mass balance regulation?
options: The skin
The kidney
The large intestine
The lung
questions.why: Renal excretion can be varied over a wide range under hormonal control, which is how the body matches output to whatever was taken in. Skin loss is driven mainly by temperature rather than by regulatory need. The large intestine reabsorbs efficiently but handles a small volume. The lung loses water as an unavoidable consequence of breathing, not as a regulated output.
questions.answerText: The kidney

questions.q: An adult takes in 2200 mL of water in food and drink and produces 300 mL of metabolic water. Losses are 1500 mL urine, 800 mL from skin and lungs, and 100 mL in feces. What is the daily water balance?
options: Negative by 100 mL
Positive by 400 mL
Balanced at zero
Positive by 100 mL
questions.why: Total input is 2200 plus 300, which is 2500 mL, and total output is 1500 plus 800 plus 100, which is 2400 mL, leaving a gain of 100 mL. Getting a negative answer means the terms were subtracted in the wrong order. Zero would require the two totals to match exactly. Four hundred milliliters results from forgetting the fecal and insensible losses.
questions.answerText: Positive by 100 mL

questions.q: A person eats 150 mmol of sodium per day and loses 5 mmol in sweat and 5 mmol in feces. How much sodium must appear in the urine each day to stay in balance?
options: 140 mmol
160 mmol
150 mmol
145 mmol
questions.why: Output must equal the 150 mmol taken in, and 10 mmol already leaves by non renal routes, so the kidney must excrete the remaining 140 mmol. Excreting 150 mmol would put the person in negative balance by 10 mmol a day. One hundred sixty would add the non renal losses instead of subtracting them. One hundred forty five accounts for only one of the two other routes.
questions.answerText: 140 mmol

questions.q: A patient drinks 3.0 L of water per day and loses 1.0 L per day through skin, lungs, and feces combined. What urine output holds total body water constant?
options: 1.0 L per day
3.0 L per day
4.0 L per day
2.0 L per day
questions.why: Total output must match the 3.0 L input, and 1.0 L is already accounted for elsewhere, so the kidney must produce 2.0 L. Producing 1.0 L would leave a gain of 1.0 L per day. Three liters of urine on top of the other losses would create a 1.0 L daily deficit. Four liters would deepen that deficit further.
questions.answerText: 2.0 L per day

questions.q: A person takes in 100 mmol of potassium per day, excretes 80 mmol in urine and 10 mmol in feces, and has no other losses. What is happening to total body potassium?
options: It is falling by 10 mmol per day
It is rising by 10 mmol per day
It is constant
It is rising by 20 mmol per day
questions.why: Input of 100 mmol against total output of 90 mmol leaves 10 mmol retained each day, which is positive balance. A falling total would require output to exceed input. Constancy would require output of exactly 100 mmol. Twenty results from ignoring the fecal loss.
questions.answerText: It is rising by 10 mmol per day

questions.q: A hospitalized patient loses 1.5 kg of body weight in 24 hours with no change in food intake. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: A water deficit of about 1.5 L, since tissue mass cannot change that fast
A loss of about 1.5 kg of fat
A gain of sodium that displaced body water
No change in body fluid, since weight varies randomly
questions.why: One liter of water weighs about one kilogram, and fat or protein stores cannot be lost at that rate, so rapid weight change is a direct readout of fluid balance. Losing 1.5 kg of fat in a day would require an impossible energy deficit. Gaining sodium tends to hold water and raise weight rather than lower it. Day to day weight in a controlled hospital setting is a sensitive fluid measure, not random noise.
questions.answerText: A water deficit of about 1.5 L, since tissue mass cannot change that fast

questions.q: A substance is neither produced nor destroyed by the body, and its plasma concentration is stable while the person eats 200 mg of it daily. What must the total output be?
options: Zero, since a stable concentration means nothing is leaving
200 mg per day
More than 200 mg per day, since some is always stored
Less than 200 mg per day, since some is metabolized
questions.why: With no production and no destruction, a constant body content requires output to match intake exactly. Zero output with continued intake would cause steady accumulation. Output above intake would mean stores are shrinking, contradicting stability. The problem states the substance is not metabolized, so no removal term exists.
questions.answerText: 200 mg per day

questions.q: During a marathon a runner loses 4.0 L in sweat and 0.3 L in urine, drinks 2.0 L, and produces 0.4 L of metabolic water. What is the net change in body water, and what happens to plasma osmolarity?
options: A deficit of 1.9 L, and plasma osmolarity falls because salt was lost in sweat
A deficit of 1.9 L, and plasma osmolarity rises because sweat is hypo-osmotic to plasma
A deficit of 2.3 L, and plasma osmolarity is unchanged
A gain of 1.9 L, and plasma osmolarity falls
questions.why: Inputs total 2.4 L and outputs total 4.3 L, so 1.9 L is lost, and because sweat contains less salt per liter than plasma does, more water than solute leaves and the remaining fluid becomes more concentrated. Osmolarity falling would require sweat to be saltier than plasma, which it is not. A deficit of 2.3 L ignores the metabolic water. The runner clearly lost fluid rather than gaining it.
questions.answerText: A deficit of 1.9 L, and plasma osmolarity rises because sweat is hypo-osmotic to plasma

questions.q: A person in sodium balance on 100 mmol per day abruptly increases intake to 250 mmol per day. The kidneys take about two days to raise excretion to match. Roughly how much extra sodium is retained, and what does it do to extracellular volume?
options: About 150 mmol is retained, and extracellular volume is unchanged because sodium stays in cells
About 300 mmol is retained, and intracellular volume expands because sodium enters cells
About 300 mmol is retained, and extracellular volume expands by roughly 2 L as water follows the sodium
No sodium is retained, because the kidney matches intake immediately
questions.why: An excess of 150 mmol per day for two days leaves about 300 mmol in the body, and since extracellular sodium concentration is held near 150 mEq/L, that load holds about 2 L of water in the extracellular space. Retaining only 150 mmol counts a single day. Sodium is excluded from cells by the Na+ K+ ATPase, so the intracellular option is wrong. The renal response to a step change in intake takes days, not minutes.
questions.answerText: About 300 mmol is retained, and extracellular volume expands by roughly 2 L as water follows the sodium

questions.q: A patient in potassium balance takes in 100 mmol per day, excreting 90 mmol in urine and 10 mmol in feces. A new drug reduces urinary potassium excretion to 60 mmol per day, with diet and fecal losses unchanged. Predict the daily balance and the trend in plasma potassium.
options: Negative balance of 30 mmol per day, and plasma potassium will trend downward
Positive balance of 40 mmol per day, and plasma potassium will trend upward
Balance is unchanged, because the feces will compensate automatically
Positive balance of 30 mmol per day, and plasma potassium will trend upward
questions.why: Output falls to 70 mmol against an unchanged intake of 100 mmol, so 30 mmol accumulates each day and the excess eventually shows up in plasma. Negative balance would require output to rise, not fall. The colon can increase potassium secretion somewhat but does not automatically match a renal deficit of this size. Forty results from ignoring the fecal loss entirely.
questions.answerText: Positive balance of 30 mmol per day, and plasma potassium will trend upward

questions.q: A patient was in water balance with an intake of 2.5 L per day and a urine output of 1.5 L per day. A diuretic raises urine output to 3.5 L per day with intake unchanged. What happens, and how can a new steady state be reached?
options: Body water falls by about 2.0 L per day until thirst raises intake or urine output falls as volume declines
Body water falls by about 1.0 L per day, the difference between urine output and intake
Body water stays constant, because the kidney cannot alter total body water
Body water rises by about 1.0 L per day, because diuretics increase filtration and retention
questions.why: Balance at the start means the other 1.0 L of daily loss was already matched, so adding 2.0 L of urine creates a deficit of 2.0 L per day, and balance returns only when intake rises or output falls again. Simply subtracting intake from urine output ignores the skin, lung, and fecal losses that were part of the original balance. The kidney is the main organ that adjusts total body water. Increased urine output removes water rather than adding it.
questions.answerText: Body water falls by about 2.0 L per day until thirst raises intake or urine output falls as volume declines

questions.q: Approximately how much total body water does a 70 kg adult contain?
options: About 28 L
About 70 L
About 14 L
About 42 L
questions.why: Water makes up roughly 60 percent of body weight, and 60 percent of 70 kg is about 42 L. Twenty eight liters is the intracellular portion of that total. Fourteen liters is the extracellular portion. Seventy liters would mean the body is entirely water, which is impossible given bone, fat, and protein.
questions.answerText: About 42 L

questions.q: About how much of the 42 L of total body water in a 70 kg adult is intracellular fluid?
options: About 14 L
About 21 L
About 28 L
About 3 L
questions.why: Roughly two thirds of body water sits inside cells, and two thirds of 42 L is about 28 L. Fourteen liters is the extracellular fluid, which is the other third. Twenty one liters would be an even split, which is not how the compartments divide. Three liters is plasma volume alone.
questions.answerText: About 28 L

questions.q: About how large is the extracellular fluid volume in a 70 kg adult?
options: About 28 L
About 14 L
About 42 L
About 7 L
questions.why: Extracellular fluid is about one third of the 42 L of total body water, which comes to roughly 14 L. Twenty eight liters is the intracellular compartment. Forty two liters is the whole of body water. Seven liters is too small and matches no standard compartment.
questions.answerText: About 14 L

questions.q: About how much plasma does a 70 kg adult have?
options: About 3 L
About 5 L
About 11 L
About 14 L
questions.why: Plasma is roughly one quarter of the 14 L extracellular volume, which is about 3 L. Eleven liters is interstitial fluid, the other three quarters. Five liters is the total blood volume, which includes red cells as well as plasma. Fourteen liters is the entire extracellular compartment.
questions.answerText: About 3 L

questions.q: About how much interstitial fluid does a 70 kg adult have?
options: About 3 L
About 28 L
About 11 L
About 6 L
questions.why: Interstitial fluid is about three quarters of the 14 L extracellular volume, or roughly 11 L, and it is the fluid that actually bathes the cells. Three liters is plasma. Twenty eight liters is intracellular fluid. Six liters matches no standard compartment in a 70 kg adult.
questions.answerText: About 11 L

questions.q: Which cation is present at the highest concentration in extracellular fluid?
options: K+
Mg2+
Ca2+
Na+
questions.why: Extracellular Na+ sits near 140 mEq/L and is the main determinant of extracellular osmolarity and volume. Extracellular K+ is only about 4 mEq/L, since potassium is concentrated inside cells. Ionized Ca2+ is near 1 mEq/L range in plasma and Mg2+ is lower still, so neither contributes much to osmolarity.
questions.answerText: Na+

questions.q: Which cation is present at the highest concentration in intracellular fluid?
options: Cl-
Na+
K+
Ca2+
questions.why: Intracellular K+ is roughly 140 to 150 mEq/L, maintained by the Na+ K+ ATPase, and it sets the resting membrane potential. Intracellular Na+ is low, near 12 mEq/L, because it is pumped out continuously. Chloride is an anion rather than a cation and is also low inside most cells. Free intracellular Ca2+ is kept extremely low, in the micromolar range, so it can serve as a signal.
questions.answerText: K+

questions.q: Which anions dominate inside the cell?
options: Chloride and bicarbonate
Lactate and acetate
Sulfate and nitrate
Phosphates and negatively charged proteins
questions.why: Organic phosphates such as ATP and the negative charges on cytosolic proteins balance the large intracellular potassium load, and they are too large or too charged to leave the cell. Chloride and bicarbonate are the dominant extracellular anions. Sulfate and nitrate are present in trace amounts. Lactate and acetate rise only in particular metabolic states and never dominate.
questions.answerText: Phosphates and negatively charged proteins

questions.q: Using 60 percent of body weight as total body water, how much water does a 50 kg adult have?
options: About 20 L
About 25 L
About 42 L
About 30 L
questions.why: Sixty percent of 50 kg is 30 kg of water, which is about 30 L because a liter of water weighs about a kilogram. Twenty liters would be 40 percent, and 25 L would be 50 percent, both below the usual fraction. Forty two liters is the value for a 70 kg adult and cannot apply to a smaller person.
questions.answerText: About 30 L

questions.q: A patient has 36 L of total body water. Using the usual two thirds to one third split, what is the intracellular volume?
options: 9 L
questions.why: Two thirds of 36 L is 24 L inside cells, leaving 12 L outside. Twelve liters is the extracellular volume, which is the other third. Eighteen liters would be half, which is not the standard division. Nine liters corresponds to a quarter and matches no compartment here.

questions.q: A patient has an extracellular fluid volume of 12 L. Using the usual proportions, what is the plasma volume?
options: 3 L
6 L
9 L
questions.why: Plasma is about one quarter of extracellular fluid, and one quarter of 12 L is 3 L, leaving 9 L in the interstitium. Six liters would be half of the extracellular volume, far more plasma than the circulation holds. Nine liters is the interstitial share. One point five liters would be an eighth, which is too small.
questions.answerText: 3 L

questions.q: Which body fluid compartment is the largest by volume?
options: Interstitial fluid
Plasma
Intracellular fluid
Extracellular fluid
questions.why: The intracellular compartment holds about two thirds of body water, roughly 28 L in a 70 kg adult, more than everything outside cells combined. Interstitial fluid is about 11 L and plasma about 3 L. Extracellular fluid at 14 L is the sum of those two and is still only half the intracellular volume.
questions.answerText: Intracellular fluid

questions.q: A marker that cannot cross the capillary wall is injected into the blood. Which volume does its distribution measure?
options: Plasma volume
Extracellular fluid volume
Total body water
Intracellular fluid volume
questions.why: A marker confined by the capillary wall stays in the vascular space and dilutes only into plasma, so its distribution volume is plasma volume. Measuring extracellular fluid requires a marker that crosses capillaries but not cell membranes, such as inulin. Total body water requires a marker that crosses both barriers, such as labeled water. No marker distributes only inside cells, so intracellular volume is always obtained by subtraction.
questions.answerText: Plasma volume

questions.q: Why is the protein concentration of plasma much higher than that of interstitial fluid?
options: Interstitial cells destroy any protein that reaches them
Proteins are actively pumped from interstitial fluid back into plasma
The capillary wall restricts the movement of large proteins out of the blood
Plasma proteins are too dense to leave the vessel by gravity
questions.why: Capillary clefts pass water and small solutes freely but hold back albumin and larger proteins, which is what creates the colloid osmotic gradient that pulls fluid back into the capillary. Interstitial protein is returned by lymphatics rather than destroyed on the spot. There is no pump that carries protein back across the capillary wall. Density and gravity have nothing to do with the distribution.
questions.answerText: The capillary wall restricts the movement of large proteins out of the blood

questions.q: Which pair of compartments has nearly the same concentration of Na+, K+, and Cl-?
options: Plasma and intracellular fluid
Plasma and interstitial fluid
Interstitial fluid and intracellular fluid
Intracellular fluid and total body water
questions.why: Only a leaky capillary wall separates plasma from interstitial fluid, so small ions equilibrate across it and the two subcompartments of extracellular fluid are nearly identical apart from protein. Intracellular fluid differs sharply from both because the cell membrane and the Na+ K+ ATPase maintain steep gradients. Total body water is a calculated total rather than a compartment with its own composition.
questions.answerText: Plasma and interstitial fluid

questions.q: A 300 mg dose of a marker that stays inside blood vessels is injected. After mixing, its plasma concentration is 100 mg/L. What is the plasma volume?
options: 3 L
questions.why: Volume equals the amount given divided by the resulting concentration, so 300 mg divided by 100 mg/L is 3 L, which matches the expected plasma volume in an adult. Zero point three liters would come from dividing by 1000 mg/L. Thirty liters would come from a concentration of 10 mg/L. Ten liters matches no plausible plasma volume and does not follow from these numbers.
questions.answerText: 3 L

questions.q: In one subject, labeled water gives a total body water of 42 L and inulin gives an extracellular volume of 14 L. What is the intracellular volume, and why must it be obtained this way?
options: 14 L, because intracellular and extracellular volumes are always equal
56 L, found by adding the two measured volumes
28 L, because no marker distributes only into cells, so it is found by subtraction
28 L, measured directly by a marker that enters only cells
questions.why: Subtracting the 14 L outside cells from the 42 L of total water leaves 28 L inside them, and this indirect approach is necessary because any substance that enters cells also passes through the extracellular space first. Adding the volumes double counts the extracellular water. The two compartments are not equal; the intracellular one is about twice as large. No practical marker is confined to the intracellular space.
questions.answerText: 28 L, because no marker distributes only into cells, so it is found by subtraction

questions.q: A subject has a measured extracellular volume of 15 L and a measured plasma volume of 3 L. What is the interstitial volume, and what separates it from plasma?
options: 18 L, separated from plasma by the cell membrane
15 L, separated from plasma by the lymphatic vessels
12 L, separated from plasma by the cell membrane
12 L, separated from plasma by the capillary wall
questions.why: Interstitial fluid is what remains of the extracellular compartment after plasma is subtracted, so 15 minus 3 gives 12 L, and the barrier between them is the capillary endothelium. Adding rather than subtracting gives 18 L. The cell membrane separates extracellular from intracellular fluid, not plasma from interstitium. Lymphatics return interstitial fluid to blood but are not the barrier between the two.
questions.answerText: 12 L, separated from plasma by the capillary wall

questions.q: Two adults both weigh 90 kg, but one has much more adipose tissue than the other. How do their total body water values compare?
options: The leaner person has more total body water, because adipose tissue contains little water
They are identical, because total body water depends only on body weight
The person with more adipose tissue has more total body water, because fat stores water
Neither can have measurable total body water without knowing their height
questions.why: Muscle is roughly three quarters water while adipose tissue is only about one tenth water, so body composition, not weight alone, determines the fraction of body weight that is water. Using a single percentage for everyone is an approximation that breaks down at the extremes of body composition. Fat is the least hydrated major tissue, so claiming that more adipose tissue brings more body water is backward. Height is not needed to measure total body water by dilution.
questions.answerText: The leaner person has more total body water, because adipose tissue contains little water

questions.q: What is the normal osmolarity of plasma?
options: About 140 mOsm/L
About 40 mOsm/L
About 580 mOsm/L
About 290 mOsm/L
questions.why: Plasma osmolarity is defended in a narrow band near 290 mOsm/L, mostly by sodium and its accompanying anions plus small contributions from glucose and urea. One hundred forty is the plasma Na+ concentration in mEq/L, which contributes only about half of the total osmolarity. Five hundred eighty would be roughly double normal and incompatible with life. Forty is far too low to support cell function.
questions.answerText: About 290 mOsm/L

questions.q: In osmosis, which way does water move?
options: Toward the compartment with the lower concentration of solute
Toward the compartment with the higher concentration of nonpenetrating solute
Toward the compartment with the higher hydrostatic pressure
Toward the compartment with the larger volume
questions.why: Water follows solute that cannot cross the barrier, moving down its own concentration gradient into the more concentrated compartment. Moving toward the more dilute side is the reverse of osmosis. Water moves away from higher hydrostatic pressure, which is filtration rather than osmosis. Compartment size does not determine the direction of osmotic flow.
questions.answerText: Toward the compartment with the higher concentration of nonpenetrating solute

questions.q: What separates the intracellular fluid from the extracellular fluid, and how does water cross it?
options: The capillary wall, which water crosses through clefts between cells
The cell membrane, which is impermeable to water in all tissues
The basement membrane, which water crosses only by active transport
The cell membrane, which water crosses freely through aquaporins and the lipid bilayer
questions.why: Water equilibrates rapidly across cell membranes, so osmolarity is essentially equal inside and outside cells at steady state. The capillary wall separates plasma from interstitial fluid, which are two parts of the extracellular compartment. Basement membranes are not the osmotic barrier and water is never actively transported. Membranes are quite permeable to water, especially where aquaporins are abundant.
questions.answerText: The cell membrane, which water crosses freely through aquaporins and the lipid bilayer
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which solute is the main determinant of extracellular fluid osmolarity?
options: K+ together with intracellular phosphate
Na+ together with its accompanying anions
Albumin and the other plasma proteins
Urea produced by the liver
questions.why: Sodium and the chloride and bicarbonate that accompany it account for most of the roughly 290 mOsm/L outside cells, which is why changes in plasma Na+ track changes in extracellular osmolarity. Potassium and phosphate dominate inside cells, not outside. Plasma proteins contribute only a couple of mOsm/L, although that small share matters for capillary exchange. Urea contributes a few mOsm/L and crosses membranes freely, so it does not drive water shifts at steady state.
questions.answerText: Na+ together with its accompanying anions

questions.q: Why is urea called an ineffective osmole for most cells?
options: It is present at too low a concentration to be measured
It crosses the cell membrane, so it does not create a lasting water gradient
It is electrically neutral, and only charged particles cause osmosis
It is removed by the kidney before it can reach cells
questions.why: A solute drives water movement only if it is held on one side of the membrane, and urea equilibrates across membranes so its concentration ends up similar inside and out. Urea is easily measured and contributes to total osmolarity. Electrical charge is irrelevant to osmosis, since glucose is an effective osmole for many cells and is uncharged. Urea circulates throughout body water before it is excreted.
questions.answerText: It crosses the cell membrane, so it does not create a lasting water gradient
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: What term describes an extracellular fluid whose osmolarity is above 290 mOsm/L?
options: Hypo-osmotic
Iso-osmotic
Hyperosmotic
Isotonic
questions.why: Hyperosmotic simply means a higher total solute concentration than the reference fluid. Hypo-osmotic means lower and iso-osmotic means equal. Isotonic describes what a solution does to cell volume rather than what its measured osmolarity is, and the two do not always agree because penetrating solutes are counted in osmolarity but not in tonicity.
questions.answerText: Hyperosmotic

questions.q: What are aquaporins?
options: Pumps that move water against its concentration gradient
Transporters that carry sodium and water together
Membrane channels that let water cross the cell membrane rapidly
Proteins that hold water inside the cell by binding it
questions.why: Aquaporins are passive channels, and their number in a membrane sets how quickly water can follow an osmotic gradient. Water is never pumped directly against a gradient anywhere in the body. Carrying sodium and water together describes cotransporters, which are a different family. Aquaporins conduct water rather than bind and store it.
questions.answerText: Membrane channels that let water cross the cell membrane rapidly
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: What does osmolarity measure?
options: The electrical charge carried by solutes in a solution
The mass of solute per liter of solution
The number of osmotically active particles per liter of solution
The pressure a solution exerts against a rigid container
questions.why: Osmolarity counts particles, so one mole of NaCl contributes about two osmoles because it dissociates while one mole of glucose contributes one. Mass per liter is concentration by weight and ignores particle number and size. Charge per liter is closer to what mEq/L expresses. Pressure against a container is hydrostatic pressure, which is a different quantity.
questions.answerText: The number of osmotically active particles per liter of solution

questions.q: Extracellular osmolarity rises from 290 to 310 mOsm/L. Which way does water move, and what happens to cell volume?
options: Water enters the cells and cell volume rises
Water leaves the cells and cell volume falls
Water does not move because the cell membrane blocks it
Water leaves the cells and cell volume rises
questions.why: Water follows the nonpenetrating solute, so a more concentrated extracellular fluid pulls water out of cells until osmolarity is equal again, and the cells shrink. Water entering cells would require the outside to be more dilute, not more concentrated. Membranes are highly permeable to water, so it does move. Losing water and gaining volume at the same time is a contradiction.
questions.answerText: Water leaves the cells and cell volume falls

questions.q: Extracellular osmolarity falls from 290 to 270 mOsm/L. What happens to the cells?
options: They shrink as water moves out of them
They shrink because low osmolarity dehydrates the cytoplasm
They stay the same size because osmolarity affects only plasma
They swell as water moves into them
questions.why: With the outside now more dilute than the inside, water moves into the cells until the two osmolarities match, and the cells swell, which is dangerous in the fixed volume of the skull. Shrinkage requires the extracellular fluid to be the more concentrated side. Osmolarity changes reach interstitial fluid and therefore every cell in the body. Low extracellular osmolarity adds water to cells rather than removing it.
questions.answerText: They swell as water moves into them

questions.q: Which clinical situation produces a fall in extracellular osmolarity and swelling of cells?
options: Excess water retention, as in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
Heavy sweating without fluid replacement
Untreated severe hyperglycemia
Loss of an isotonic fluid through a fistula
questions.why: Retaining water without proportionate solute dilutes the extracellular fluid, lowers osmolarity, and drives water into cells, which is the danger of hyponatremia. Heavy sweating loses more water than salt and therefore raises osmolarity. Severe hyperglycemia adds an effective osmole outside cells and also raises osmolarity. Losing isotonic fluid removes water and solute in equal proportion, leaving osmolarity unchanged.
questions.answerText: Excess water retention, as in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

questions.q: Which clinical situation raises extracellular osmolarity and shrinks cells?
options: Prolonged sweating in the heat with no fluid intake
Drinking several liters of plain water quickly
Infusion of a large volume of isotonic saline
A slow bleed that removes whole blood
questions.why: Sweat is dilute compared with plasma, so sweating loses proportionally more water than salt and concentrates the extracellular fluid, pulling water out of cells. Drinking plain water dilutes the extracellular fluid and swells cells. Isotonic saline expands the extracellular volume without changing osmolarity. Whole blood loss removes fluid at the osmolarity of plasma, so it lowers volume without shifting water between compartments.
questions.answerText: Prolonged sweating in the heat with no fluid intake

questions.q: A liter of isotonic saline is infused into a vein. What happens to cell volume?
options: Cells swell, because any infusion adds water to the body
Cell volume is unchanged, because extracellular osmolarity did not change
Cells shrink, because saline adds sodium to the extracellular fluid
Cells swell and then shrink as the sodium is excreted
questions.why: An isotonic solution has the same effective osmolarity as body fluid, so it expands the extracellular compartment without creating any osmotic gradient across cell membranes. Water alone would swell cells, but this fluid carries solute in matching proportion. The added sodium comes with enough water to keep concentration constant, so no shrinkage occurs. There is no transient swelling, because osmolarity never departs from normal.
questions.answerText: Cell volume is unchanged, because extracellular osmolarity did not change

questions.q: In uncontrolled diabetes, plasma glucose rises sharply and glucose cannot readily enter many cells without insulin. What is the effect on cell volume?
options: Cells shrink, because the added extracellular glucose acts as an effective osmole
Cells swell, because glucose pulls water into the cytoplasm
Cell volume is unchanged, because glucose is not an osmotically active particle
Cells swell, because high glucose opens more aquaporins
questions.why: Glucose that stays outside cells adds to extracellular osmolarity, and water follows it out of the cells, which is why severe hyperglycemia causes cellular dehydration. Glucose would only pull water into cells if it accumulated inside them. Glucose is very much osmotically active, contributing one osmole per mole. Aquaporin number does not change acutely with glucose, and more channels would only speed the movement, not reverse its direction.
questions.answerText: Cells shrink, because the added extracellular glucose acts as an effective osmole

questions.q: A person drinks 2 L of plain water in a short period. Trace what happens to extracellular osmolarity and to both compartment volumes before the kidney responds.
options: Extracellular osmolarity rises, water leaves cells, and the extracellular volume alone expands
Extracellular osmolarity is unchanged and only the extracellular volume expands
Extracellular osmolarity falls, water moves into cells, and both compartments end up larger
Extracellular osmolarity falls, water leaves cells, and the intracellular volume shrinks
questions.why: Water enters the extracellular fluid first and dilutes it, and because the cell membrane is permeable to water, some of the load then moves into cells until osmolarity is equal again, leaving both compartments expanded and slightly dilute. Osmolarity cannot rise when pure water is added. It also cannot stay unchanged, since water was added without solute. Water moves toward the more concentrated side, which after drinking is the intracellular fluid.
questions.answerText: Extracellular osmolarity falls, water moves into cells, and both compartments end up larger

questions.q: A hiker sweats heavily for hours and drinks nothing. Predict the change in each compartment and explain the direction of the shift.
options: Extracellular osmolarity rises, water leaves cells, and both compartments shrink while the intracellular fluid partly defends extracellular volume
Extracellular osmolarity falls, water enters cells, and only the intracellular volume rises
Only the extracellular volume falls, because water cannot leave cells once osmolarity changes
Both compartments shrink equally, because sweat is isotonic to plasma
questions.why: Sweat is hypo-osmotic, so more water than solute is lost, the remaining extracellular fluid becomes concentrated, and water moves out of cells, which cushions the fall in circulating volume at the cost of cellular dehydration. Osmolarity cannot fall when dilute fluid is removed. Water leaves cells readily, so the extracellular compartment is not the only one to shrink. Sweat is not isotonic, which is precisely why the shift occurs.
questions.answerText: Extracellular osmolarity rises, water leaves cells, and both compartments shrink while the intracellular fluid partly defends extracellular volume

questions.q: A patient loses 2 L of fluid that has the same osmolarity as plasma, through severe vomiting of gastric contents replaced by isotonic secretions. Predict the compartment changes.
options: Intracellular volume rises because the extracellular fluid became more dilute
Extracellular volume falls by 1 L and intracellular volume falls by 1 L, since losses are shared equally
Extracellular osmolarity rises and water moves out of cells to replace the loss
Extracellular volume falls by 2 L, osmolarity is unchanged, and intracellular volume stays the same
questions.why: Removing fluid at the same osmolarity as plasma leaves the concentration of the remaining fluid unchanged, so there is no gradient to move water across cell membranes and the entire loss falls on the extracellular compartment. An equal split would require an osmotic gradient to redistribute the loss. Osmolarity cannot rise when the fluid removed is iso-osmotic. Nothing here dilutes the extracellular fluid, so cells do not swell.
questions.answerText: Extracellular volume falls by 2 L, osmolarity is unchanged, and intracellular volume stays the same

questions.q: A patient with very high plasma glucose has a measured plasma Na+ of 130 mEq/L, yet total body sodium is not low. What explains the low sodium reading?
options: Sodium moved into cells to replace the glucose that entered them
Glucose interferes chemically with the measurement of sodium in the laboratory
The kidney excreted sodium rapidly in response to the glucose load
Glucose drew water out of cells into the extracellular fluid, diluting the sodium that is there
questions.why: Extracellular glucose is an effective osmole, so water leaves the cells and expands the extracellular fluid, and the same amount of sodium spread through more water gives a lower concentration even with normal total body sodium. The Na+ K+ ATPase keeps sodium out of cells, so a sodium shift inward does not explain it. Renal sodium loss would lower total body sodium, which the question rules out. This is a real dilution rather than a measurement artifact.
questions.answerText: Glucose drew water out of cells into the extracellular fluid, diluting the sodium that is there

questions.q: What makes a water molecule polar?
