options: Oxygen gains a full negative charge and each hydrogen loses an electron completely
The hydrogens sit on opposite sides of the oxygen, so the charges line up end to end
Oxygen holds the shared electrons more strongly, so oxygen is partly negative and the hydrogens partly positive
The oxygen and hydrogens share their electrons equally, and only the bent shape creates a charge
questions.why: Polarity comes from unequal sharing in the covalent bonds plus the bent shape, which keeps the partial charges from canceling. Full charges would make water an ion pair, not a polar molecule, and water does not transfer electrons outright. A linear arrangement would cancel the dipoles and leave water nonpolar, and equal sharing would remove the partial charges altogether.
questions.answerText: Oxygen holds the shared electrons more strongly, so oxygen is partly negative and the hydrogens partly positive

questions.q: What type of bond forms between the partially negative oxygen of one water molecule and the partially positive hydrogen of a neighboring water molecule?
options: A hydrogen bond
An ionic bond
A nonpolar covalent bond
A polar covalent bond
questions.why: A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between molecules, not a sharing of electrons, and it is what gives water its cohesion and high heat capacity. Polar covalent bonds are the strong bonds inside a single water molecule, between its own oxygen and hydrogens. Ionic bonds require full charges, and nonpolar covalent bonds involve equal sharing, neither of which describes the attraction between two water molecules.
questions.answerText: A hydrogen bond

questions.q: A solute is described as hydrophilic. What does that tell you about it?
options: It is uncharged and nonpolar, so it separates from water
It has one polar end and one nonpolar end
It dissolves only in lipid, not in water
It is polar or charged, so it interacts with water and dissolves
questions.why: Hydrophilic literally means water loving, and the physical basis is that polar or charged groups can form hydrogen bonds or ion dipole attractions with water. An uncharged nonpolar solute is hydrophobic and is excluded from the water network. A molecule with one polar end and one nonpolar end is amphipathic, a separate category, and dissolving only in lipid describes a hydrophobic solute.
questions.answerText: It is polar or charged, so it interacts with water and dissolves

questions.q: What is the term for a molecule that has both a polar region and a nonpolar region?
options: Amphipathic
Hydrophilic
Hydrophobic
Nonpolar
questions.why: Amphipathic molecules such as phospholipids and bile salts carry both kinds of region, which is exactly why they line up at oil and water boundaries and form membranes and micelles. Hydrophilic and hydrophobic each describe a molecule that is one way throughout. Nonpolar is a description of bonding, and a nonpolar molecule by definition lacks the polar region an amphipathic molecule has.
questions.answerText: Amphipathic

questions.q: Which of these blood solutes is hydrophobic and therefore travels bound to a carrier protein rather than dissolved freely in plasma?
options: Glucose
Na+
Urea
Cholesterol
questions.why: Cholesterol is a largely nonpolar steroid ring structure, so plasma water will not dissolve it and it is carried inside lipoproteins. Glucose carries many hydroxyl groups and hydrogen bonds well with water. Na+ is a charged ion surrounded by a hydration shell, and urea is a small polar molecule, so both dissolve directly in plasma without a carrier.
questions.answerText: Cholesterol

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of total body weight is water in a typical adult?
options: About 20 percent
About 40 percent
About 85 percent
About 60 percent
questions.why: Roughly 60 percent of adult body weight is water, split about two thirds intracellular and one third extracellular, which is why water chemistry sets the rules for nearly every physiological process. About 40 percent is close to the intracellular fraction alone, and 20 percent is close to the extracellular fraction alone. Values near 85 percent describe individual cells or an embryo, not whole body composition.
questions.answerText: About 60 percent

questions.q: A newly synthesized drug is a nonpolar steroid similar in structure to cortisol. Predict how it will be carried in the bloodstream.
options: Dissolved freely in the water of the plasma at a high concentration
Mostly bound to plasma carrier proteins, with only a small fraction free
Trapped inside red blood cell cytoplasm and unable to leave
Converted into an ion by plasma enzymes so that it dissolves
questions.why: A nonpolar molecule cannot form the hydrogen bonds needed to stay dissolved in plasma water, so the body solves the problem with binding proteins, exactly as it does for steroid hormones and thyroid hormone. Free dissolution at high concentration is what a polar solute like glucose does. Red cell cytoplasm is also mostly water, so it offers no better solvent, and plasma has no mechanism to ionize a steroid ring.
questions.answerText: Mostly bound to plasma carrier proteins, with only a small fraction free

questions.q: Sweat evaporating from the skin cools the body far more effectively than an equal mass of most other liquids would. Which property of water explains this?
options: Its low density as a solid, since ice floats on liquid water
Its polarity, since polar solutes dissolve in it very easily
Its high heat of vaporization, since many hydrogen bonds break as a molecule escapes
Its cohesion, since water molecules stick to one another in a continuous column
questions.why: Each water molecule leaving the liquid must break several hydrogen bonds, and the energy for that comes from the skin, which is why evaporative loss removes so much heat. Ice floating matters for lakes, not for thermoregulation in a 37 C body. Polarity explains solubility rather than heat removal, and cohesion explains surface tension and columns of water, not the energy cost of evaporation.
questions.answerText: Its high heat of vaporization, since many hydrogen bonds break as a molecule escapes

questions.q: A metabolite has a six carbon backbone carrying five hydroxyl groups. Predict its behavior in plasma.
options: It stays as an undissolved droplet on the surface of the plasma
It dissolves readily, because its hydroxyl groups hydrogen bond with water
It inserts into the lipid core of cell membranes and stays there
It must be carried by albumin because water cannot surround it
questions.why: Hydroxyl groups are polar and hydrogen bond with water, so a sugar like molecule dissolves easily, which is why glucose travels free in plasma. Forming a separate droplet is what a nonpolar lipid does. Inserting into the membrane core requires a nonpolar surface, and albumin binding is the solution for hydrophobic solutes, not for a molecule that water already surrounds well.
questions.answerText: It dissolves readily, because its hydroxyl groups hydrogen bond with water

questions.q: Oil droplets shaken into water quickly merge back into a single layer. What drives this?
options: The oil molecules are attracted to one another by strong ionic bonds
Water hydrogen bonds with itself and excludes the nonpolar oil, forcing it together
Water forms covalent bonds with the oil surface and pulls the droplets in
Oil is denser than water and settles into one mass at the bottom
questions.why: The hydrophobic effect is really about water, not about oil: water gains stability by maximizing hydrogen bonds with itself, and the cheapest way to do that is to minimize the oil water surface. Oil molecules attract each other only weakly and by van der Waals forces, not ionic bonds. Water does not form covalent bonds with oil, and oil is less dense than water, so it rises rather than settles.
questions.answerText: Water hydrogen bonds with itself and excludes the nonpolar oil, forcing it together

questions.q: When NaCl dissolves in water, which part of the water molecule faces the Na+ ion?
options: The hydrogens, because they carry the partial positive charge
Either end, since water is not oriented around dissolved ions
The oxygen, because it carries the partial negative charge
The oxygen, because it carries the partial positive charge
questions.why: Na+ is positive, so it attracts the partially negative oxygen ends of surrounding water molecules, forming a hydration shell that keeps the ion in solution. The hydrogens orient toward Cl- instead, since that ion is negative. Water molecules are strongly oriented around ions rather than randomly arranged, and the oxygen is partially negative, not positive.
questions.answerText: The oxygen, because it carries the partial negative charge

questions.q: A patient with liver disease has a plasma albumin of 2.0 g/dL instead of the usual 4.0 g/dL. Thyroid hormone is hydrophobic and normally travels mostly bound to plasma proteins. Predict what happens to the free hormone fraction and to hormone delivery to tissues at first.
options: The free fraction falls and tissue delivery falls, because less hormone is dissolved in plasma water
Both the free fraction and total hormone rise, because hormone no longer has anywhere to bind
The free fraction rises, so more hormone is available to tissues even though total plasma hormone falls
Neither changes, because hydrophobic hormones dissolve directly in plasma water
questions.why: Fewer carrier sites means a smaller reservoir, so total hormone falls, but the hormone that remains is a larger percentage unbound, and only unbound hormone crosses into cells. The answer that has the free fraction falling reverses the relationship between binding and free fraction. Total hormone cannot rise when the carrier pool that holds it has shrunk, and a hydrophobic hormone cannot dissolve freely in plasma water, which is the whole reason carriers exist.
questions.answerText: The free fraction rises, so more hormone is available to tissues even though total plasma hormone falls

questions.q: A general anesthetic is highly lipid soluble. It is given to two patients of the same weight, one with a large adipose mass and one with very little body fat. Predict how recovery time compares and why.
options: Recovery is faster in the patient with more adipose tissue, because fat destroys the drug quickly
Recovery is slower in the patient with more adipose tissue, because drug stored in fat leaks back into plasma
Recovery is identical, because plasma water content is what determines how any drug distributes
Recovery is slower in the leaner patient, because the drug stays dissolved in the plasma water
questions.why: A nonpolar drug distributes into the largest nonpolar compartment available, so adipose acts as a reservoir that fills during dosing and empties slowly afterward, prolonging the effect. Fat stores the drug, it does not metabolize it, so the claim that fat destroys the drug confuses storage with clearance. Distribution depends on lipid solubility rather than plasma water, and a lean patient has less reservoir, so the drug clears sooner rather than later.
questions.answerText: Recovery is slower in the patient with more adipose tissue, because drug stored in fat leaks back into plasma

questions.q: A runner in hot, very humid air is sweating heavily but her core temperature keeps climbing. Trace the reason, starting from the property of water that normally makes sweating work.
options: Cooling depends on evaporation, which removes heat as hydrogen bonds break, and humid air slows it, so sweat drips off
Sweat cools by conducting heat into the liquid film, so humidity has no effect on the amount of heat removed
Humid air blocks sweat gland secretion, so no sweat reaches the skin surface and no cooling occurs
Water in humid air has a lower heat of vaporization, so each gram of sweat carries away less heat
questions.why: The heat leaves the body only at the moment water changes from liquid to vapor, so sweat that runs off the skin removes almost nothing. Warming the liquid film accounts for only a small amount of heat compared with vaporization. Sweat glands keep secreting in humid air, which is why she loses fluid without benefit, and the heat of vaporization of water is a property of water itself and does not change with the humidity of the surrounding air.
questions.answerText: Cooling depends on evaporation, which removes heat as hydrogen bonds break, and humid air slows it, so sweat drips off

questions.q: What does pH measure?
options: The total number of acid molecules dissolved in a solution
The negative logarithm of the OH- concentration
The ratio of strong acid to weak acid in a solution
The negative logarithm of the H+ concentration
questions.why: pH is defined from free H+ only, and the logarithm is why small pH numbers correspond to large H+ concentrations. Total acid molecules is a different quantity, since a weak acid holds most of its H+ undissociated. The OH- concentration defines pOH, which is related to pH but is not the same number, and the ratio of strong to weak acid is not part of the definition at all.
questions.answerText: The negative logarithm of the H+ concentration

questions.q: What is the normal pH range of arterial blood?
questions.why: Arterial blood is held in a narrow slightly alkaline window of 7.35 to 7.45, and values outside roughly 6.8 to 7.8 are not compatible with life for long. A pH of 7.00 to 7.10 is severe acidemia, not normal. The range 6.80 to 7.20 spans the survivable acid extreme, and 7.60 to 7.80 is severe alkalemia.

questions.q: Which buffer pair is the most important one in extracellular fluid?
options: Ammonia and ammonium
Carbonic acid and bicarbonate
Dihydrogen phosphate and monohydrogen phosphate
Hemoglobin and oxyhemoglobin
questions.why: The carbonic acid and bicarbonate pair dominates extracellular buffering because both members are present in quantity and both ends are under physiological control, CO2 by the lungs and HCO3- by the kidneys. The phosphate pair matters mainly inside cells and in urine, where its concentration is much higher. The ammonia system is a renal mechanism for excreting acid, and hemoglobin is a major buffer inside red cells rather than in extracellular fluid.
questions.answerText: Carbonic acid and bicarbonate

questions.q: A solution moves from pH 7.4 to pH 6.4. How has the H+ concentration changed?
options: It is two times higher
It is ten times lower
It is ten times higher
It is one hundred times higher
questions.why: The pH scale is logarithmic, so each whole unit is a tenfold change in H+, and a falling pH means more H+. A tenfold decrease would correspond to pH rising by one unit, not falling. A hundredfold change would require two pH units, and a doubling of H+ corresponds to a pH change of only about 0.3 units.
questions.answerText: It is ten times higher

questions.q: What is the term for an arterial blood pH below 7.35?
options: Acidemia
Alkalemia
Hypercapnia
Hypoxemia
questions.why: Acidemia names the measured state of blood that is too acidic, while the underlying process producing it is called acidosis. Alkalemia is the opposite, a pH above 7.45. Hypercapnia is a raised PCO2, which is one common cause of acidemia but is not the same measurement, and hypoxemia refers to low blood oxygen, a separate parameter entirely.
questions.answerText: Acidemia

questions.q: Which organ eliminates the volatile acid load by excreting CO2?
options: The kidneys
The liver
The lungs
The stomach
questions.why: CO2 produced by metabolism combines with water to form carbonic acid, so exhaling CO2 is literally acid excretion, and the lungs handle a far larger daily acid load than any other route. The kidneys excrete the fixed, nonvolatile acids such as sulfuric and phosphoric acid and regenerate bicarbonate, a slower process. The liver produces acid loads through metabolism rather than excreting them, and the stomach secretes HCl into its lumen without removing acid from the body.
questions.answerText: The lungs

questions.q: What is a buffer?
options: A strong acid that neutralizes any base added to a solution
A weak acid and its conjugate base together, which resist change in pH
A protein that transports H+ out of the body
A solution that holds its H+ concentration exactly constant no matter what is added
questions.why: The pair matters: the weak acid can donate H+ when base is added and the conjugate base can accept H+ when acid is added, so the system works in both directions. A strong acid dissociates completely and would drive pH down rather than stabilize it. Transport proteins move H+ but are not themselves buffers, and a buffer only minimizes pH change, it never holds pH perfectly constant.
questions.answerText: A weak acid and its conjugate base together, which resist change in pH

questions.q: What is the normal plasma bicarbonate concentration?
options: About 4 mEq/L
About 24 mEq/L
About 12 mEq/L
About 40 mEq/L
questions.why: Plasma HCO3- runs about 22 to 26 mEq/L, and holding that against a dissolved CO2 level of about 1.2 mmol/L gives the 20 to 1 ratio that sets pH at 7.4. About 12 mEq/L is the kind of value seen in metabolic acidosis, not in health. About 4 mEq/L is closer to normal plasma K+, and 40 mEq/L is the usual normal arterial PCO2 in mmHg, a different quantity entirely.
questions.answerText: About 24 mEq/L

questions.q: A strong acid is added to plasma. What happens to the bicarbonate concentration and the amount of CO2 formed?
options: Bicarbonate rises and CO2 formation falls
Both bicarbonate and CO2 rise
Both bicarbonate and CO2 fall
Bicarbonate is consumed and CO2 formation rises
questions.why: Added H+ is mopped up by HCO3-, forming carbonic acid that breaks down to CO2 and water, so the buffer is spent as bicarbonate falls and CO2 is generated for the lungs to blow off. Bicarbonate cannot rise while it is being consumed by the added acid. The reaction converts one into the other, so they move in opposite directions, which rules out both rising or both falling.
questions.answerText: Bicarbonate is consumed and CO2 formation rises

questions.q: A person hyperventilates during a panic attack. Predict the direction of change in arterial PCO2 and in blood pH.
options: PCO2 rises and pH falls
PCO2 falls and pH falls
PCO2 rises and pH rises
PCO2 falls and pH rises
questions.why: Blowing off CO2 removes the acid side of the carbonic acid and bicarbonate pair, so H+ is consumed as the reaction shifts back toward CO2 and pH rises, a respiratory alkalosis. Rising PCO2 with falling pH describes hypoventilation, the opposite situation. Any answer that has PCO2 and pH moving in the same direction misreads a respiratory change, since a change in CO2 always moves pH the other way.
questions.answerText: PCO2 falls and pH rises

questions.q: An arterial sample from a patient reads pH 7.28. How would you classify this value?
options: Acidemia, since it is below the lower limit of 7.35
Normal, since it is still above 7.0
Alkalemia, since it is above 7.0
Normal, since arterial pH is expected to sit near 7.2
questions.why: The reference point is the physiological range, not chemical neutrality, so anything below 7.35 in arterial blood counts as acidemia even though 7.28 is still alkaline on the chemistry scale. Comparing to 7.0 is the classic error: 7.0 is neutral water, not the body's set point. Alkalemia would require a pH above 7.45, and 7.2 is a value seen in illness, not a normal expectation.
questions.answerText: Acidemia, since it is below the lower limit of 7.35

questions.q: You have four weak acids with pKa values of 3.1, 4.8, 6.8, and 9.2. Which one makes the most effective buffer at pH 7.0?
options: pKa 3.1
pKa 9.2
pKa 6.8
pKa 4.8
questions.why: A buffer is strongest when pH is near its pKa, because that is where the weak acid and conjugate base are present in comparable amounts and can absorb H+ or OH- equally well. At pH 7.0 the acid with pKa 3.1 or 4.8 is almost entirely dissociated, leaving little undissociated acid to donate H+. The acid with pKa 9.2 is almost entirely undissociated, leaving little conjugate base to accept added H+.
questions.answerText: pKa 6.8

questions.q: A patient vomits repeatedly and loses a large volume of gastric HCl. Predict the effect on arterial pH.
options: pH falls, because vomiting removes bicarbonate
pH rises, because H+ has been lost from the body
pH is unchanged, because the stomach contents are outside the body already
pH falls, because the loss of fluid concentrates the remaining H+
questions.why: Gastric juice is rich in HCl, so vomiting it removes H+ from the body and leaves bicarbonate behind unopposed, producing a metabolic alkalosis. Bicarbonate loss is what happens with severe diarrhea, since intestinal secretions are alkaline, and that would lower pH instead. The H+ was secreted from body stores, so losing it does count, and the fluid loss is small compared with the shift in the acid base balance.
questions.answerText: pH rises, because H+ has been lost from the body

questions.q: The free H+ concentration in a patient's blood doubles. By approximately how much does pH change?
options: It falls by about 1.0 unit
It falls by about 0.3 units
It falls by about 2.0 units
It rises by about 0.3 units
questions.why: Because pH is a negative logarithm, doubling H+ subtracts log 2, which is about 0.3, from the pH. A fall of one full unit means a tenfold rise in H+, and two units means a hundredfold rise, both far more than doubling. pH rises only when H+ falls, so any answer with pH rising has the direction backward.
questions.answerText: It falls by about 0.3 units

questions.q: A small amount of NaOH is added to a solution buffered with acetic acid and acetate. Which component of the buffer is consumed?
options: The acetate, which donates H+ to the added base
The acetic acid, which donates H+ to neutralize the added OH-
Neither, because the added OH- simply dilutes
Both are consumed equally, since the pair reacts as a unit
questions.why: Added base is neutralized by the proton donor, so acetic acid is used up and acetate accumulates, and pH rises only slightly. Acetate is the conjugate base and has no H+ to donate, so it works only against added acid. Dilution alone would not remove the OH-, and the two members of a buffer pair are consumed one at a time depending on whether acid or base was added.
questions.answerText: The acetic acid, which donates H+ to neutralize the added OH-

questions.q: A patient with severe diarrhea loses large volumes of alkaline intestinal fluid. Trace the change in plasma bicarbonate, then the change in ventilation, then the effect on PCO2.
options: Bicarbonate falls, ventilation decreases, and PCO2 rises
Bicarbonate rises, ventilation increases, and PCO2 falls
Bicarbonate rises, ventilation decreases, and PCO2 rises
Bicarbonate falls, ventilation increases, and PCO2 falls
questions.why: Losing bicarbonate leaves acid unbuffered, pH falls, and chemoreceptors respond by driving deeper and faster breathing, which blows off CO2 and pulls pH partway back toward normal. Decreasing ventilation would worsen the acidosis, so any answer with ventilation falling compensates in the wrong direction. Bicarbonate cannot rise when it is being lost in the stool, which rules out both answers that start with a rise in bicarbonate.
questions.answerText: Bicarbonate falls, ventilation increases, and PCO2 falls

questions.q: Use the relationship pH = 6.1 + log (HCO3- divided by 0.03 times PCO2). A patient has HCO3- of 12 mEq/L and PCO2 of 40 mmHg. What is the approximate pH?
options: About 7.4
About 7.1
About 7.3
About 6.8
questions.why: Dissolved CO2 is 0.03 times 40, which is 1.2, so the ratio is 12 divided by 1.2, or 10, and log 10 is 1, giving 6.1 plus 1, or 7.1. A pH of 7.4 comes from the normal 20 to 1 ratio, which needs a bicarbonate near 24. A value of 7.3 would require a ratio of about 16, and 6.8 would require a ratio of about 5, well below what these numbers give.
questions.answerText: About 7.1

questions.q: A patient has a completely obstructed airway and cannot exhale. Lactic acid accumulates and is buffered by bicarbonate. Why does bicarbonate buffering fail to hold the pH in this situation?
options: The CO2 made by the buffering reaction cannot be exhaled, so it builds up and drives the reaction back toward H+
The obstruction prevents the kidney from making bicarbonate, so no buffer is available at all
Bicarbonate stops binding H+ once the pH has fallen below 7.35
Lactic acid is a strong acid, and strong acids cannot be buffered by any system
questions.why: Bicarbonate buffering is only powerful because the CO2 it generates is removed by ventilation, which is what pulls the reaction forward; in a closed system the product accumulates and the buffer stalls. The kidney is not blocked by an airway obstruction, and in any case renal compensation takes days. Bicarbonate continues to bind H+ at low pH, it simply runs out, and any acid can be buffered, strong or weak, as long as buffer remains and the products can be cleared.
questions.answerText: The CO2 made by the buffering reaction cannot be exhaled, so it builds up and drives the reaction back toward H+

questions.q: In lab, adding 1 mL of strong acid to pure water drops the pH from 7.0 to 4.0, but adding the same 1 mL to a phosphate buffer at pH 6.8 drops the pH only to 6.75. What accounts for the difference?
options: The buffer chemically destroys the added acid, removing it from the solution
The buffer is more dilute, so the added acid is spread through a larger volume
Most of the added H+ is bound by the conjugate base in the buffer, so free H+ changes very little
The buffer raises the pKa of the added acid so that it no longer dissociates
questions.why: pH reflects free H+ only, and the conjugate base converts most of the added H+ into undissociated weak acid, so the free concentration rises only slightly. Nothing is destroyed, the protons are simply held in a different chemical form. Both solutions received the same acid in the same volume, so dilution is not the explanation, and the pKa of the added strong acid is a fixed property that the buffer cannot change.
questions.answerText: Most of the added H+ is bound by the conjugate base in the buffer, so free H+ changes very little

questions.q: What is the primary structure of a protein?
options: The coiling of the backbone into an alpha helix
The overall three dimensional folded shape of one chain
The sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds
The assembly of several folded chains into one functional unit
questions.why: Primary structure is the order of amino acids, and because that order dictates which R groups end up next to each other, it determines every higher level of folding. Coiling into an alpha helix is secondary structure. The full three dimensional shape of a single chain is tertiary structure, and combining several chains is quaternary structure.
questions.answerText: The sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds

questions.q: Which bonds stabilize secondary structure such as the alpha helix and beta pleated sheet?
options: Disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains
Peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids
Hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms
Ionic bonds between charged side chains
questions.why: Secondary structure is a backbone phenomenon: the carbonyl oxygen of one residue hydrogen bonds to the amide hydrogen of another, and repeating that pattern produces a helix or a sheet. Peptide bonds hold the chain together and define primary structure rather than its folding. Disulfide and ionic bonds involve R groups and belong to tertiary structure.
questions.answerText: Hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms

questions.q: In a globular protein dissolved in cytosol, where do the nonpolar amino acid side chains typically end up?
options: On the outer surface, in contact with cytosolic water
Distributed evenly between surface and interior
Buried in the interior, away from water
Attached to the peptide backbone hydrogen bonds
questions.why: The hydrophobic effect drives nonpolar side chains inward so that water can maximize hydrogen bonding with itself, and this buried core is a major force holding tertiary structure together. Polar and charged side chains are the ones that face the water on the outside. An even distribution would leave nonpolar groups exposed and destabilize the fold, and side chains project from the backbone rather than participating in its hydrogen bonds.
questions.answerText: Buried in the interior, away from water

questions.q: Which covalent bond helps lock a protein's tertiary structure in place?
options: A hydrogen bond between two hydroxyl side chains
An ionic bond between a positive and a negative side chain
A disulfide bond between two cysteine side chains
A van der Waals interaction between two nonpolar side chains
questions.why: The disulfide bridge is the only covalent link among the tertiary interactions, which is why it resists heat and pH change far better than the others. Hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, and van der Waals interactions all help fold the protein but each is a weak, noncovalent attraction that is broken easily. Those weak bonds are exactly what denaturation disrupts first.
questions.answerText: A disulfide bond between two cysteine side chains

questions.q: What is denaturation?
options: Breaking of the peptide bonds so the chain falls into single amino acids
Removal of a phosphate group from a protein by a phosphatase
Loss of three dimensional shape while the amino acid sequence stays intact
Joining of two polypeptides into a quaternary structure
questions.why: Denaturation disrupts the weak interactions that hold the folded shape, so function is lost, but the covalent backbone and therefore the primary sequence survive. Breaking peptide bonds is hydrolysis or digestion, a different and more destructive process. Dephosphorylation is a regulated chemical modification, and joining chains builds structure rather than destroying it.
questions.answerText: Loss of three dimensional shape while the amino acid sequence stays intact

questions.q: Why can a binding site accept one ligand and reject a similar looking one?
options: The site accepts whichever ligand is present in the highest concentration
The site is complementary to that ligand in both shape and charge distribution
The site accepts whichever ligand is smallest
The site forms permanent covalent bonds with the first ligand it meets
questions.why: Specificity comes from a three dimensional fit in which the ligand's shape, charges, and polar groups all match the pocket, so a molecule that is close but not identical binds poorly or not at all. Concentration influences how often binding happens but not whether the fit exists. Size alone does not confer fit, and most physiological binding is reversible and noncovalent so that the site can be reused.
questions.answerText: The site is complementary to that ligand in both shape and charge distribution

questions.q: How many polypeptide subunits make up one hemoglobin molecule?
options: One
Two
Four
Six
questions.why: Hemoglobin has four subunits, two alpha and two beta, and that quaternary arrangement is what allows the cooperative binding that shapes the oxygen dissociation curve. A single chain protein such as myoglobin has no quaternary structure and binds oxygen without cooperativity. Two or six subunits do not match hemoglobin, and its four heme groups correspond one to each chain.
questions.answerText: Four

questions.q: Which level of protein structure exists only in proteins built from more than one polypeptide chain?
options: Quaternary structure
Secondary structure
Tertiary structure
Primary structure
questions.why: Quaternary structure describes how separate folded chains fit together, so a single chain protein simply does not have it. Primary, secondary, and tertiary structure all describe features within one chain and are present in every protein. Tertiary structure in particular is often confused with quaternary, but it refers to the folding of one chain, not the assembly of several.
questions.answerText: Quaternary structure

questions.q: A purified receptor protein is heated to 65 C for ten minutes. Predict what happens to its ability to bind its hormone.
options: Binding rises, because heat increases molecular motion and collisions
Binding is unchanged, because the amino acid sequence is unaffected by heat
Binding falls sharply, because heat disrupts the weak bonds holding the site in shape
Binding falls only if the hormone itself is heated along with the receptor
questions.why: Heat adds kinetic energy that shakes apart hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, and hydrophobic packing, so the pocket loses the shape the hormone must fit. Faster collisions cannot help once the site no longer matches the ligand. The sequence does survive, which is exactly the point of denaturation, but sequence alone does not produce binding, and the receptor's own shape is what is lost regardless of the hormone's condition.
questions.answerText: Binding falls sharply, because heat disrupts the weak bonds holding the site in shape

questions.q: A mutation replaces a nonpolar amino acid buried in a protein's hydrophobic core with a charged one. Predict the most likely consequence.
options: No effect, because only surface residues have any influence on folding
The protein folds normally but is degraded faster by the stomach
The protein gains a second binding site where the new charge sits
The protein misfolds, because a charged residue is unstable in the water free core
questions.why: Burying a charge is energetically costly, so the chain folds differently or not at all, and function is usually lost even though only one residue changed. Interior residues drive folding more strongly than surface residues, so the claim that only the surface matters is backward. Gastric digestion is irrelevant to a protein working inside a cell, and a random new charge does not create an organized binding pocket.
questions.answerText: The protein misfolds, because a charged residue is unstable in the water free core

questions.q: Dietary protein reaching the stomach is exposed to a pH near 2. Which level of protein structure survives that exposure intact?
options: Quaternary structure
Primary structure
Tertiary structure
Secondary structure
questions.why: Extreme pH changes the charge on side chains and breaks ionic and hydrogen bonds, so the higher levels of folding unravel while the covalent peptide bonds of the primary sequence hold. Quaternary and tertiary structure depend heavily on those side chain interactions and go first. Secondary structure depends on backbone hydrogen bonds and is also disrupted, even though the backbone itself remains a continuous chain until pepsin cleaves it.
questions.answerText: Primary structure

questions.q: How does a shift in pH away from a protein's normal range disrupt its shape?
options: It changes the protonation of side chains, breaking ionic bonds between R groups
It hydrolyzes the peptide bonds that run along the backbone
It replaces amino acids in the sequence with differently charged ones
It removes the disulfide bridges by oxidizing cysteine side chains
questions.why: Adding or removing H+ changes whether a carboxyl or amino side chain carries a charge, and a pair that used to attract may now repel, so the fold collapses. Peptide bond hydrolysis needs an enzyme or prolonged harsh treatment and is digestion, not denaturation. pH cannot rewrite a sequence, and disulfide bridges are covalent and relatively resistant to pH change.
questions.answerText: It changes the protonation of side chains, breaking ionic bonds between R groups

questions.q: A patient produces normal amounts of a hormone, but the receptor for that hormone has an altered binding site shape. Predict the result.
options: Target cells respond normally, since hormone levels are normal
Hormone levels fall because the hormone is destroyed by the altered receptor
Target cells respond more strongly, since unbound hormone accumulates
Target cells fail to respond even though hormone levels measure normal or high
questions.why: Signaling requires the hormone to bind, so a distorted pocket blocks the response no matter how much hormone circulates, and the unused hormone often accumulates as the feedback loop calls for more. Normal hormone levels alone do not guarantee a response, since the receptor is half of the system. The receptor does not degrade the hormone, and a hormone that cannot bind cannot produce a stronger effect.
questions.answerText: Target cells fail to respond even though hormone levels measure normal or high

questions.q: An egg white turns opaque and solid when heated. In protein terms, what has happened?
options: The proteins were hydrolyzed into free amino acids
The proteins gained new peptide bonds linking them into a solid network
The proteins lost their primary sequence and reformed as a gel
The proteins denatured and their exposed hydrophobic regions clumped together
questions.why: Heat unfolds the chains, and the newly exposed nonpolar surfaces stick to each other rather than to water, which is what makes the mass opaque and firm and why it never turns clear again on cooling. Hydrolysis would break the chains into amino acids and produce a liquid, not a solid. No new peptide bonds are formed, and the primary sequence is preserved throughout denaturation.
questions.answerText: The proteins denatured and their exposed hydrophobic regions clumped together

questions.q: A patient runs a core temperature of 41.5 C for several hours. Predict the effect on cellular enzyme function and explain why cooling the patient may not fully restore it.
options: Enzyme activity rises steadily with temperature, and cooling simply returns the rate to baseline
Enzymes are unaffected by temperature as long as pH stays normal
Enzymes progressively denature, and because unfolded chains aggregate, cooling does not refold many of them
Enzymes are destroyed by cleavage of their peptide bonds, which cooling cannot reverse
questions.why: Rate does climb with temperature up to an optimum near 37 C, but past that the weak bonds holding the fold give way, and once exposed hydrophobic surfaces clump together the process is effectively one way. Treating the rise as purely a rate effect ignores denaturation entirely. pH is not the only variable that unfolds proteins, and the irreversibility comes from aggregation, not from broken peptide bonds, which stay intact in denaturation.
questions.answerText: Enzymes progressively denature, and because unfolded chains aggregate, cooling does not refold many of them

questions.q: In sickle cell disease a single change in the beta globin sequence puts valine, a nonpolar amino acid, on the surface of hemoglobin where glutamate, a charged one, normally sits. Trace how this leads to distorted red cells at low PO2.
options: The nonpolar patch lets deoxygenated hemoglobin molecules stick together into fibers that deform the cell
The change breaks the peptide backbone, so hemoglobin falls apart and the cell collapses
The change prevents heme from being inserted, so the cell has no hemoglobin and shrinks
The change makes hemoglobin bind oxygen irreversibly, so the cell stiffens while fully loaded
questions.why: A hydrophobic residue on a water facing surface is unstable, and in the deoxygenated shape it fits a complementary pocket on a neighboring hemoglobin, so the molecules chain together and the growing fibers push the membrane out of shape. A single substitution does not break the backbone, and the chain is made normally. Heme insertion still occurs, which is why these cells carry oxygen at all, and the problem appears when hemoglobin releases oxygen rather than when it holds it.
questions.answerText: The nonpolar patch lets deoxygenated hemoglobin molecules stick together into fibers that deform the cell

questions.q: A transport protein binds its ligand normally at 37 C but loses most binding at 39 C, and regains it when returned to 37 C. What does this reversibility tell you about the bonds holding the binding site together?
options: The site depends on disulfide bridges, which break and reform with small temperature changes
The site depends on peptide bonds, which are unstable near body temperature
The site depends mainly on weak noncovalent bonds, which come apart with mild heating and reform on cooling
The site depends on the primary sequence, which changes with temperature
questions.why: Full recovery of function means nothing permanent was broken, which points to hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions, and hydrophobic packing, all weak enough to be disturbed by a couple of degrees. Disulfide bridges are covalent and would not open and close over a 2 degree range. Peptide bonds are stable at body temperature, and the primary sequence is fixed once the protein is made.
questions.answerText: The site depends mainly on weak noncovalent bonds, which come apart with mild heating and reform on cooling

questions.q: Two secreted proteins have the same size and similar folds, but one contains several disulfide bridges and the other is held together only by hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic packing. Predict which retains function longer in the harsh extracellular environment, and why.
options: The one with only weak bonds, because flexible proteins tolerate stress better
Both fail at the same rate, because folding stability depends only on the amino acid sequence
The one with disulfide bridges, because covalent cross links resist unfolding from heat and pH shifts
The one with disulfide bridges, because those bonds allow it to refold instantly after full denaturation
questions.why: Covalent cross links tie distant parts of the chain together, so even when weak bonds are disturbed the overall fold is pinned in place, which is why extracellular and digestive proteins are rich in disulfides. Flexibility helps a protein change shape during function but does not protect against denaturation. Sequence does determine stability, but it does so precisely by specifying which cross links exist, and the advantage of disulfides lies in resisting unfolding rather than in refolding after it.
questions.answerText: The one with disulfide bridges, because covalent cross links resist unfolding from heat and pH shifts

questions.q: How does an enzyme speed up a chemical reaction?
options: By adding energy to the substrate so it can react
By making the products more stable than they would otherwise be
By raising the temperature of the surrounding solution
By lowering the activation energy needed to reach the transition state
questions.why: Binding the substrate in the active site positions and strains it so that less energy is needed to get over the barrier, and more molecules per second have enough energy to cross it. Enzymes do not supply energy to the substrate, they lower the cost of the step. They also leave the energy of the products unchanged, and they do not heat the solution.
questions.answerText: By lowering the activation energy needed to reach the transition state

questions.q: What does an enzyme do to the equilibrium position of the reaction it catalyzes?
options: Nothing, it changes only how fast equilibrium is reached
It shifts equilibrium toward the products
It shifts equilibrium toward the reactants
It prevents the reverse reaction from occurring at all
questions.why: An enzyme lowers the barrier in both directions equally, so forward and reverse rates both increase and the final ratio of products to reactants is unchanged. Shifting the equilibrium requires changing concentrations or the free energy of the reaction, which catalysis does not do. Enzymes catalyze the reverse reaction as readily as the forward one, which is why the same enzyme often runs in either direction depending on substrate levels.
questions.answerText: Nothing, it changes only how fast equilibrium is reached

questions.q: What is the molecule an enzyme acts on called?
options: The cofactor
The product
The substrate
The inhibitor
questions.why: The substrate is the starting molecule that binds in the active site and is converted. The product is what leaves after the reaction, so it comes later in the sequence. A cofactor is a nonprotein helper such as a metal ion or a vitamin derived coenzyme, and an inhibitor slows the enzyme rather than being converted by it.
questions.answerText: The substrate

questions.q: What is the active site of an enzyme?
options: The region of the enzyme that binds substrate and catalyzes its conversion
A separate regulatory pocket where allosteric modulators bind
The portion of the enzyme that anchors it in the cell membrane
The section of the gene that codes for the enzyme protein
questions.why: The active site is a small pocket formed by tertiary folding, and its shape and charge pattern give the enzyme its specificity. A separate regulatory pocket is the allosteric site, which is a different location on the same protein. Membrane anchoring involves other regions of the protein, and the coding sequence is in DNA, not in the enzyme itself.
questions.answerText: The region of the enzyme that binds substrate and catalyzes its conversion

questions.q: What is a coenzyme?
options: A second protein subunit that helps bind the substrate
A metal ion that is permanently bound in the active site
A molecule that binds the active site and blocks substrate entry
A small organic helper molecule, often vitamin derived, that the enzyme needs
questions.why: Coenzymes such as NAD+ and coenzyme A carry chemical groups or electrons and are not proteins, which is one reason vitamin deficiencies impair metabolism. A metal ion helper is usually called a cofactor rather than a coenzyme. A second protein subunit is part of quaternary structure, and a molecule that blocks the active site is a competitive inhibitor.
questions.answerText: A small organic helper molecule, often vitamin derived, that the enzyme needs

questions.q: What happens to an enzyme molecule after it converts its substrate to product?
options: It is consumed along with the substrate molecule
It is released unchanged and can catalyze the reaction again
It stays permanently bound to the product it just made
It is broken down into amino acids for later reuse
questions.why: A catalyst emerges from the reaction as it went in, which is why a small number of enzyme molecules can process a large amount of substrate. Being consumed would make the enzyme a reactant, not a catalyst. Staying bound to product would block the active site permanently, and routine breakdown after each cycle would waste enormous amounts of protein.
questions.answerText: It is released unchanged and can catalyze the reaction again

questions.q: What does Vmax describe?
options: The substrate concentration at which the rate is half maximal
The rate observed when substrate concentration is zero
The amount of product formed before the enzyme denatures
The maximum rate reached when every active site is occupied by substrate
questions.why: Vmax is a plateau: once every active site is busy, adding more substrate cannot make the enzyme work faster, so the rate stops climbing. The substrate concentration at half maximal rate is Km, a separate constant. Rate at zero substrate is zero, and the total product formed over time is not a rate at all.
questions.answerText: The maximum rate reached when every active site is occupied by substrate

questions.q: What does Km tell you about an enzyme?
options: The number of substrate molecules converted per second at saturation
The temperature at which the enzyme works fastest
The total amount of enzyme present in the sample
The substrate concentration giving half maximal rate, a measure of binding affinity
questions.why: A low Km means the enzyme reaches half speed at low substrate, so it binds substrate tightly, while a high Km means it needs a lot of substrate to get going. Molecules converted per second at saturation is the turnover number, related to Vmax rather than Km. Optimum temperature and enzyme quantity are separate properties that Km does not report.
questions.answerText: The substrate concentration giving half maximal rate, a measure of binding affinity

questions.q: An enzyme is already saturated with substrate. Predict what happens to the reaction rate if you double the substrate concentration again.
options: The rate stays essentially the same, because every active site is already occupied
The rate doubles, because rate is proportional to substrate concentration
The rate falls, because excess substrate inhibits the enzyme directly
The rate rises by half, because binding becomes more likely
questions.why: Past saturation the limiting factor is how fast the enzyme can turn over, not how much substrate is available, so the curve has flattened at Vmax. Rate is roughly proportional to substrate only at low concentrations, on the steep early part of the curve. Ordinary substrate does not inhibit the enzyme, and no partial increase occurs once every site is filled.
questions.answerText: The rate stays essentially the same, because every active site is already occupied

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme reaction. Predict its effect on apparent Km and on Vmax.
options: Apparent Km falls and Vmax is unchanged
Apparent Km is unchanged and Vmax falls
Apparent Km rises and Vmax is unchanged
Both apparent Km and Vmax fall
questions.why: A competitive inhibitor occupies the active site, so more substrate is needed to reach half maximal rate, but flooding the system with substrate still outcompetes the inhibitor and Vmax is eventually reached. A falling Km would mean tighter binding, the opposite of competition. Unchanged Km with reduced Vmax is the signature of a noncompetitive or allosteric inhibitor, which binds elsewhere and cannot be outcompeted.
questions.answerText: Apparent Km rises and Vmax is unchanged

questions.q: A molecule binds an enzyme at a site away from the active site and changes the shape of that site so catalysis slows. Can this inhibition be overcome by adding more substrate?
options: No, because the inhibitor occupies a different site and is unaffected by substrate levels
Yes, because added substrate outcompetes any inhibitor for the enzyme
Yes, but only once substrate concentration climbs well above the Km
No, because substrate can no longer bind an enzyme that is already folded
questions.why: This is allosteric or noncompetitive inhibition, and since the two molecules occupy different pockets, raising substrate does not push the inhibitor off, so Vmax stays reduced. Adding substrate helps only when the two are competing for the same site. Exceeding Km changes how full the active sites are but does not touch the allosteric site, and substrate does bind normally to a properly folded enzyme.
questions.answerText: No, because the inhibitor occupies a different site and is unaffected by substrate levels

questions.q: A human enzyme is assayed at 37 C and then at 55 C. Predict the rate at 55 C.
options: Roughly double, because rate rises with temperature
Much lower, because the enzyme denatures above its optimum
Slightly higher, because molecules collide more often
Unchanged, because enzymes are temperature independent
questions.why: Rate does rise with temperature up to about 37 C for human enzymes, but past that the added kinetic energy breaks the weak bonds holding the fold and the active site is destroyed, so activity drops steeply. Doubling or a modest increase would only apply below the optimum. Enzymes are strongly temperature dependent, which is why body temperature is regulated so tightly.
questions.answerText: Much lower, because the enzyme denatures above its optimum

questions.q: Pepsin has a pH optimum near 2. Predict its activity if it is carried into the small intestine, where pH is about 8.
options: Activity falls to near zero, because its active site shape depends on acidic pH
Activity rises, since most enzymes work best in alkaline conditions
Activity is unchanged, since pH affects only the substrate
Activity doubles, since the intestine has more substrate available
questions.why: Pepsin's fold and the charges in its active site are tuned to a very acidic environment, so raising the pH changes side chain protonation and the enzyme loses its shape and its activity. Enzymes have individual optima rather than a shared alkaline preference, and pancreatic enzymes take over digestion in the intestine for exactly this reason. pH acts on the enzyme protein itself, and extra substrate cannot rescue an inactive enzyme.
questions.answerText: Activity falls to near zero, because its active site shape depends on acidic pH

questions.q: With substrate held at a saturating concentration, the amount of enzyme in the tube is doubled. Predict the reaction rate.
options: It stays at the same Vmax as before
It roughly doubles
It rises only slightly, because substrate is limiting
It falls, because enzyme molecules compete for substrate
questions.why: Vmax is set by how much enzyme is present, so twice as many active sites working at full speed convert twice as much substrate per minute. The rate would stay flat only if something other than enzyme quantity were limiting. Substrate is saturating here rather than limiting, and enzyme molecules working in parallel do not interfere with one another.
questions.answerText: It roughly doubles

questions.q: An allosteric activator binds its regulatory site on an enzyme. Predict what happens to the active site and to the reaction rate.
options: The active site is blocked directly by the activator, and the rate falls
The active site is unchanged, but the substrate is chemically altered so it reacts faster
The active site shifts to a shape that binds substrate better, and the rate rises
The active site is destroyed, and the enzyme must be replaced
questions.why: Allosteric regulation works through shape: binding at one site propagates a conformational change to the active site, in this case improving substrate binding or catalysis. The activator never enters the active site itself, which is what distinguishes it from a competitive molecule. It also does not modify the substrate, and the change is reversible rather than destructive, which is what makes it useful for moment to moment regulation.
questions.answerText: The active site shifts to a shape that binds substrate better, and the rate rises

questions.q: In a four step pathway, the end product inhibits the first enzyme allosterically. The cell suddenly accumulates a large amount of end product. Predict what happens to flux through the pathway and to the concentration of the first intermediate.
options: Flux falls and the first intermediate accumulates, because it can no longer be used
Flux falls and the first intermediate becomes less abundant, because the entry step is slowed
Flux rises and the first intermediate accumulates, because inhibition speeds the entry step
Flux is unchanged, because allosteric inhibition affects only the final step
questions.why: Blocking the first committed step means fewer molecules enter the pathway at all, so both throughput and the downstream intermediates drop, which is the point of end product feedback: stop making what is already in surplus. The intermediate would accumulate only if a later enzyme were blocked while entry continued. Inhibition cannot raise flux, and inhibiting the first enzyme necessarily affects the whole pathway rather than the last step alone.
questions.answerText: Flux falls and the first intermediate becomes less abundant, because the entry step is slowed

questions.q: An enzyme is assayed with and without an unknown compound. Without it, Km is 2 mM and Vmax is 100 units. With it, Km is 8 mM and Vmax is still 100 units. What is the compound, and what happens if substrate is raised sharply?
options: A noncompetitive inhibitor, and raising substrate will not restore the rate
A competitive inhibitor, and raising substrate restores the rate toward Vmax
An allosteric activator, and raising substrate will push the rate above Vmax
A denaturing agent, and raising substrate will not help because enzyme has been destroyed
questions.why: The fingerprint of competition is a higher apparent Km with Vmax preserved, since the inhibitor and substrate contend for the same pocket and enough substrate wins the contest. A noncompetitive inhibitor would have lowered Vmax while leaving Km alone. An activator would lower apparent Km rather than raise it, and denaturation would reduce the amount of working enzyme and therefore lower Vmax.
questions.answerText: A competitive inhibitor, and raising substrate restores the rate toward Vmax

questions.q: Methanol becomes toxic only after alcohol dehydrogenase converts it to formaldehyde and then formic acid. Ethanol binds the same enzyme with much higher affinity. Explain the mechanism by which giving ethanol reduces formic acid production.
options: Ethanol denatures alcohol dehydrogenase, stopping all conversion permanently
Ethanol binds an allosteric site and lowers the Vmax of the enzyme for every substrate
Ethanol competes for the same active site, so fewer enzyme molecules are available to convert methanol
Ethanol chemically neutralizes formic acid after it has been formed
questions.why: This is classic competitive inhibition using a preferred substrate: with ethanol occupying most active sites, methanol passes through slowly enough to be excreted before it is converted to acid. Ethanol does not denature the enzyme, which would be nonspecific and permanent. It binds the active site rather than an allosteric one, and it has no chemical action on formic acid once that acid exists.
questions.answerText: Ethanol competes for the same active site, so fewer enzyme molecules are available to convert methanol

questions.q: A patient is both febrile at 40 C and acidotic at pH 7.10. Consider the effect of each variable on a typical cytosolic enzyme with an optimum near 37 C and pH 7.4, then predict the combined effect on reaction rate.
options: The higher temperature and the lower pH cancel out, leaving the rate near normal
Only the pH change matters, because temperature affects only extracellular enzymes
Both changes push the enzyme off its optimum, so the rate falls more than either alone
The rate rises, because higher temperature always increases reaction rate
questions.why: Optimum curves peak at one set of conditions, so moving off the peak on two axes at once compounds the loss of activity, and this is part of why very sick patients decompensate quickly. The two changes do not cancel, since neither one corrects the other's departure from the optimum. Temperature acts on every protein regardless of location, and rate rises with temperature only up to the optimum, not past it.
questions.answerText: Both changes push the enzyme off its optimum, so the rate falls more than either alone

questions.q: What are the products when ATP is hydrolyzed in a typical energy releasing step?
options: ADP and inorganic phosphate
AMP and two inorganic phosphates
Adenosine and three inorganic phosphates
ADP and glucose phosphate
questions.why: Most cellular work removes the terminal phosphate, leaving ADP and free Pi, and the released energy is captured by the protein doing the work. Hydrolysis to AMP plus pyrophosphate happens in a few reactions such as amino acid activation, but it is not the usual step. Stripping all three phosphates to adenosine is not a normal energy yielding reaction, and glucose phosphate is a product of a transfer reaction, not of plain hydrolysis.
questions.answerText: ADP and inorganic phosphate

questions.q: Where in the ATP molecule is the energy released during hydrolysis stored?
options: In the bond that links the terminal phosphate group to the molecule
In the carbon to nitrogen bonds of the adenine ring
In the ring structure of the ribose sugar
In the hydrogen bonds between the adenine and the ribose
questions.why: The phosphate groups carry closely spaced negative charges that repel each other, so breaking the terminal phosphoanhydride bond and letting the products separate releases usable energy. Adenine and ribose form the structural backbone that identifies the molecule but do not store the transferable energy. The adenine and ribose are joined by a stable covalent bond rather than a hydrogen bond, and that link holds the molecule together instead of powering cellular work.
questions.answerText: In the bond that links the terminal phosphate group to the molecule

questions.q: What is an exergonic reaction?
options: One that releases free energy and can proceed spontaneously
One that requires an input of free energy to proceed
One that neither releases nor requires energy
One that always requires an enzyme to occur at all
questions.why: Exergonic reactions have a negative free energy change, so they are thermodynamically downhill and can be used to drive other reactions. A reaction that needs energy put in is endergonic, the opposite category. Reactions with no net energy change are at equilibrium, and spontaneity is about thermodynamics while enzymes govern only speed.
questions.answerText: One that releases free energy and can proceed spontaneously

questions.q: Muscle contraction is an example of which category of cellular work powered by ATP?
options: Mechanical work
Chemical work
Transport work
Osmotic work
questions.why: Mechanical work is movement produced by motor proteins, and myosin walking along actin is the clearest example in the body. Chemical work is building larger molecules from smaller ones, such as making protein from amino acids. Transport work is moving solutes against a gradient by pumps, and osmotic movement of water follows those gradients passively rather than consuming ATP directly.
questions.answerText: Mechanical work

questions.q: The Na+/K+ ATPase moving ions against their concentration gradients is an example of which category of cellular work?
options: Mechanical work
Transport work
Chemical work
Electrical work performed without ATP
questions.why: Transport work is the use of ATP to move a solute up its electrochemical gradient, and the sodium potassium pump is the standard example, consuming a large share of resting energy expenditure. Mechanical work moves whole structures rather than solutes across a membrane. Chemical work builds bonds in new molecules, and the pump is very much ATP dependent, which is why it stops when ATP falls.
questions.answerText: Transport work

questions.q: Linking amino acids into a new protein is an example of which category of cellular work?
options: Transport work
Chemical work
Mechanical work
Thermal work
questions.why: Chemical or synthetic work uses ATP to form bonds that would not form on their own, and building polymers from monomers is the main example. Transport work moves substances across membranes, and mechanical work produces movement of structures. Heat is a byproduct of metabolism rather than a category of work the cell purchases with ATP.
questions.answerText: Chemical work

questions.q: In an aerobic cell, where is the great majority of ATP produced?
options: In the mitochondria, by oxidative phosphorylation
In the cytosol, by glycolysis
In the rough endoplasmic reticulum
In the nucleus, alongside transcription
questions.why: Oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane yields far more ATP per glucose than any other route, which is why oxygen delivery is so central to physiology. Glycolysis in the cytosol produces a small net yield and becomes the main source only when oxygen is scarce. The rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesizes protein and the nucleus houses DNA, and neither generates significant ATP.
questions.answerText: In the mitochondria, by oxidative phosphorylation
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which molecule is the immediate energy currency that cells actually spend on work?
options: Glycogen
ATP
Glucose
Triglyceride
questions.why: ATP is the molecule that couples directly to pumps, motors, and synthetic enzymes, so all other fuels must first be converted into it. Glucose is a fuel that must be metabolized before its energy can be used. Glycogen and triglyceride are storage forms that are broken down to fuel molecules first, putting them two steps away from doing work.
questions.answerText: ATP

questions.q: ATP hydrolysis releases about 7.3 kcal/mol. It is coupled to a reaction that requires 3.4 kcal/mol. What is the net free energy change of the coupled reaction, and is it spontaneous?
options: About positive 3.9 kcal/mol, so it is not spontaneous
About positive 10.7 kcal/mol, so it is not spontaneous
About zero, so the reaction sits at equilibrium
About negative 3.9 kcal/mol, so it is spontaneous
questions.why: The two free energy changes add: negative 7.3 plus positive 3.4 gives negative 3.9, and a negative total means the coupled reaction can proceed. A positive 3.9 would come from subtracting in the wrong direction. Adding the two magnitudes gives 10.7, which treats an energy releasing step as if it also cost energy, and a value of zero would require the two to be equal in size.
questions.answerText: About negative 3.9 kcal/mol, so it is spontaneous

questions.q: A cell's ATP supply falls sharply. Predict what happens to intracellular Na+ and to cell volume.
options: Intracellular Na+ falls and the cell shrinks
Intracellular Na+ rises and the cell shrinks
Intracellular Na+ is unchanged, because the pump does not use ATP
Intracellular Na+ rises and the cell swells
questions.why: Without ATP the sodium potassium pump stops, so Na+ that leaks in is no longer extruded, it accumulates, and water follows the added solute osmotically into the cell. Falling intracellular Na+ would require a working pump. Rising intracellular solute draws water in rather than out, so the cell cannot shrink, and the pump is one of the largest ATP consumers in the body.
questions.answerText: Intracellular Na+ rises and the cell swells

questions.q: How does ATP most often transfer energy to a protein that is doing work?
options: By transferring its terminal phosphate to the protein, changing its shape
By donating an electron that chemically reduces the protein
By binding permanently to the protein and remaining in place
By raising the local temperature so that the protein moves faster
questions.why: Phosphorylation adds a bulky, doubly negative group that forces a conformational change, and that shape change is the work, whether it moves an ion, a filament, or a substrate. Electron transfer is what NADH and FADH2 do, a different energy carrier system. Permanent binding would leave the protein stuck in one state, and the energy is delivered chemically rather than as local heat.
questions.answerText: By transferring its terminal phosphate to the protein, changing its shape

questions.q: In rigor mortis, muscle stiffens because ATP production has stopped. What does this tell you about the role of ATP in the cross bridge cycle?
options: ATP is required only to start contraction, not to end it
ATP is required to keep calcium inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and its loss relaxes the muscle
ATP is required to break the actin filament apart after contraction
ATP binding is required for myosin to detach from actin, so without it the heads stay bound
questions.why: Detachment is the ATP dependent step, so the paradox is that relaxation, not contraction, is what fails first when ATP disappears. Saying ATP is needed only to begin contraction misses this. ATP does power the calcium pump of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, but losing that function causes sustained activation rather than relaxation, and actin filaments are not broken apart during normal cycling.
questions.answerText: ATP binding is required for myosin to detach from actin, so without it the heads stay bound

questions.q: A tissue increases its rate of active transport threefold. Predict the effect on its oxygen consumption.
options: Oxygen consumption falls, because transport uses ATP rather than oxygen
Oxygen consumption rises, because the ATP spent must be regenerated aerobically
Oxygen consumption is unchanged, because stored ATP covers the increase
Oxygen consumption rises only if the tissue is also contracting
questions.why: Cells hold only seconds of ATP, so any sustained increase in ATP use must be matched by an increase in ATP production, and in aerobic tissue that means burning more oxygen. Transport does use ATP, but replacing that ATP is precisely what consumes oxygen, so the two are linked rather than alternatives. Stored ATP is far too small to cover a sustained threefold increase, and mechanical work is not required for the demand to rise.
questions.answerText: Oxygen consumption rises, because the ATP spent must be regenerated aerobically

questions.q: A biosynthetic reaction has a free energy change of positive 5 kcal/mol. What must happen for it to proceed in a cell?
options: It must be catalyzed by an enzyme, which supplies the missing energy
It must be warmed above body temperature to supply the extra energy
It must be coupled to a more strongly exergonic reaction such as ATP hydrolysis
It will proceed on its own once enough substrate accumulates to overcome the barrier
questions.why: A positive free energy change means the reaction is uphill, and the only way for it to go forward is to be linked to a downhill reaction whose release exceeds its cost. Enzymes lower the activation energy and speed things up, but they never change the free energy of the reaction. Heating the cell is not a physiological option, and substrate accumulation shifts equilibrium only modestly and cannot substitute for energy coupling.
questions.answerText: It must be coupled to a more strongly exergonic reaction such as ATP hydrolysis

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes ATP as an energy carrier?
options: ATP is stored in large quantities in muscle and liver for later use
ATP is recycled continuously, with ADP rephosphorylated as fast as ATP is spent
ATP is produced once each day and then spent slowly over that day
ATP is exported into the blood so that other tissues can use it
questions.why: The cellular ATP pool is small and turns over extremely fast, so the body cycles through many times its own weight in ATP each day rather than stockpiling it. Muscle and liver store glycogen, and adipose stores triglyceride, but neither stores ATP in bulk. Slow use over a day contradicts the seconds long ATP reserve, and ATP is used where it is made rather than shipped through the blood.
questions.answerText: ATP is recycled continuously, with ADP rephosphorylated as fast as ATP is spent

questions.q: Cyanide blocks the final step of the electron transport chain. Trace the consequences for ATP, then for the Na+/K+ ATPase, then for the resting membrane potential.
options: ATP falls, the pump runs faster to compensate, and the membrane potential becomes more negative
ATP falls, the pump stops, and the membrane potential decays toward zero as gradients dissipate
ATP rises from glycolysis, the pump speeds up, and the membrane potential is unaffected
ATP falls, the pump stops, and the membrane potential immediately becomes more negative
questions.why: Oxidative phosphorylation supplies most ATP, so blocking it starves the pump, and once Na+ and K+ gradients dissipate there is no longer a chemical driving force to hold the membrane negative. The pump cannot speed up without the ATP it needs, so compensation is impossible. Glycolysis continues but yields far too little ATP to keep up, and loss of the K+ gradient depolarizes rather than hyperpolarizes the cell.
questions.answerText: ATP falls, the pump stops, and the membrane potential decays toward zero as gradients dissipate

questions.q: A sprinter accelerates from a standing start. Put the energy sources in the order the muscle draws on them over the first thirty seconds.
options: Anaerobic glycolysis, then stored ATP, then creatine phosphate
Stored ATP, then creatine phosphate, then anaerobic glycolysis
Creatine phosphate, then stored ATP, then oxidative phosphorylation
Oxidative phosphorylation, then stored ATP, then creatine phosphate
questions.why: The muscle spends the ATP already sitting in the cytosol within a couple of seconds, creatine phosphate then donates its phosphate to ADP for several more seconds, and glycolysis takes over before oxygen delivery has risen enough to matter. Glycolysis cannot come first because it takes time to ramp up and the existing ATP is used immediately. Creatine phosphate is a buffer that regenerates ATP rather than a source used before ATP itself, and oxidative phosphorylation is the slowest to respond, not the fastest.
questions.answerText: Stored ATP, then creatine phosphate, then anaerobic glycolysis

questions.q: In an ATP depleted intestinal cell, glucose still enters passively through GLUT transporters but Na+ dependent glucose uptake against a gradient fails. Explain the difference.
options: GLUT uptake is passive and needs only a glucose gradient, while Na+ dependent uptake spends the Na+ gradient the pump maintains
GLUT transporters generate their own ATP, while the Na+ dependent carrier must import ATP from the cytosol
Both are primary active transporters, but GLUT has a much lower ATP requirement per glucose molecule
The Na+ dependent carrier hydrolyzes ATP directly at its own binding site, while GLUT hydrolyzes it more slowly
questions.why: The Na+ glucose cotransporter never touches ATP itself, but it spends the Na+ gradient, and that gradient exists only because the Na+/K+ ATPase keeps rebuilding it, so ATP loss disables it one step removed. GLUT is a facilitated diffusion carrier that runs downhill and needs no energy input at all. No transporter generates its own ATP, and the cotransporter is secondary active rather than primary, which is exactly the distinction the scenario is testing.
questions.answerText: GLUT uptake is passive and needs only a glucose gradient, while Na+ dependent uptake spends the Na+ gradient the pump maintains

questions.q: A neuron extrudes 3 million Na+ ions per second at rest. The Na+/K+ ATPase moves 3 Na+ out per ATP hydrolyzed. How many ATP molecules per second does this consume, and what happens to that demand if the neuron fires rapidly?
options: 9 million ATP per second, and demand falls during firing because channels take over the work
1 million ATP per second, and demand is unchanged because the pump runs at a fixed rate
3 million ATP per second, and demand rises because one ATP is used per ion
1 million ATP per second, and demand rises because each action potential admits more Na+ to be pumped out
questions.why: Dividing 3 million ions by 3 ions per ATP gives 1 million ATP per second, and firing adds Na+ influx through voltage gated channels, so the pump must work harder to restore the gradient. Multiplying rather than dividing gives 9 million and reverses the stoichiometry. The pump responds to intracellular Na+ rather than running at a fixed rate, and using one ATP per ion ignores the 3 Na+ per cycle stoichiometry.
questions.answerText: 1 million ATP per second, and demand rises because each action potential admits more Na+ to be pumped out
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: What does a spectrophotometer measure in an enzyme assay?
options: How much light of a chosen wavelength the sample absorbs
The temperature of the reaction mixture in the cuvette
The pH of the reaction mixture in the cuvette
The total mass of enzyme present in the tube
questions.why: The instrument passes light of a set wavelength through the cuvette and reports absorbance, which tracks the concentration of a colored product or substrate. Temperature is set by a water bath and read with a thermometer, and pH is set by the buffer and read with a pH meter. Enzyme mass is known from how much you pipetted, not from the absorbance reading.
questions.answerText: How much light of a chosen wavelength the sample absorbs

questions.q: What is the purpose of blanking the spectrophotometer before an enzyme assay?
options: To warm the instrument and the cuvette holder to the assay temperature
To confirm that the enzyme sample is still active before the run begins
To remove any product that formed in the tube before timing began
To set absorbance to zero for everything in the tube except the product being measured
questions.why: The blank contains buffer and reagents but not the reaction product, so zeroing against it means every later reading reflects product formation and not the color of the solution itself. Warming is the job of the water bath, not the blank. Enzyme activity is what the assay itself measures, and blanking is an instrument setting that cannot remove anything from your reaction tubes.
questions.answerText: To set absorbance to zero for everything in the tube except the product being measured

questions.q: According to Beer's law, how does absorbance relate to the concentration of a colored product?
options: Absorbance is inversely proportional to concentration
Absorbance is proportional to the square of the concentration
Absorbance is directly proportional to concentration
Absorbance is independent of concentration once color appears
questions.why: A straight line relationship is what lets you read concentration off an absorbance value and lets a change in absorbance stand in for the amount of product made. An inverse relationship would describe transmittance, which falls as concentration rises. A squared relationship does not apply within the linear range, and if absorbance were independent of concentration the assay could not work at all.
questions.answerText: Absorbance is directly proportional to concentration

questions.q: In an experiment measuring enzyme activity across a range of temperatures, which variable belongs on the x-axis?
options: Temperature, since it is the variable you set
Reaction rate, since it is what you measured
Absorbance at the final time point
Time elapsed during the assay
questions.why: The independent variable, the one you deliberately changed, goes on the x-axis, and reaction rate as the dependent variable goes on the y-axis. Plotting rate on x reverses the two. Absorbance at a single time point is a raw reading rather than the variable being manipulated, and time is the x-axis only for a progress curve within one tube, not for a temperature series.
questions.answerText: Temperature, since it is the variable you set

questions.q: How is enzyme activity expressed from a colorimetric assay?
options: As the absorbance at the end of the run
As the volume of enzyme added to the tube
As the change in absorbance per unit time
As the wavelength that gives the highest absorbance
questions.why: Activity is a rate, so it must include time in the units, and the slope of absorbance against time is the standard way to report it. A single endpoint absorbance tells you how much product accumulated but not how fast, and two tubes can reach the same endpoint at very different rates. The volume pipetted is an experimental setting, and the wavelength is chosen to match the product's absorbance peak.
questions.answerText: As the change in absorbance per unit time

questions.q: On a plot of enzyme activity against pH, what identifies the optimum pH?
options: The pH where the curve crosses zero activity
The lowest pH tested, since acidity speeds all reactions
The pH at which the curve is steepest
The pH at the peak of the curve, where activity is highest
questions.why: The optimum is by definition the condition that produces the fastest rate, which is the top of the curve.
