Where the curve reaches zero the enzyme is inactive or denatured, the worst condition rather than the best. Acidity helps only enzymes whose optimum is acidic, and the steepest part of the curve marks where activity is changing fastest, not where it is greatest.
questions.answerText: The pH at the peak of the curve, where activity is highest

questions.q: What is the purpose of a control tube that contains substrate and buffer but no enzyme?
options: To provide extra substrate that can be added later if needed
To measure the maximum reaction rate the enzyme can reach
To calibrate the wavelength setting used by the spectrophotometer
To show how much change occurs without enzyme, so background can be subtracted
questions.why: Some substrates break down slowly on their own, and the no enzyme control tells you how much of the signal to credit to the enzyme rather than to spontaneous change. The maximum rate is measured in a tube with enzyme at optimal conditions, not in one without it. A control is not a reagent reservoir, and wavelength selection is based on the product's absorbance spectrum.
questions.answerText: To show how much change occurs without enzyme, so background can be subtracted

questions.q: Why are all tubes in a pH series kept in the same 37 C water bath?
options: To speed up every reaction so that the lab session finishes on time
To keep the buffer solutions from evaporating during the run
To ensure the enzyme denatures at the same rate in every tube
To hold temperature constant so that differences in rate can be attributed to pH
questions.why: Controlling every variable except the one under study is what lets you interpret the result, since a tube that was both warmer and more acidic would give an uninterpretable answer. Saving time is a side benefit, not the design reason. Evaporation is minor over a short assay, and you want to avoid denaturation in a pH experiment, not standardize it.
questions.answerText: To hold temperature constant so that differences in rate can be attributed to pH

questions.q: A student assays a human enzyme and records rates of 0.02, 0.09, 0.21, 0.08, and 0.01 absorbance units per minute at 5, 20, 37, 50, and 70 C. What is the optimum temperature?
questions.why: The highest rate, 0.21 per minute, occurs at 37 C, which matches the body temperature this enzyme evolved to work at. The rate at 20 C is still climbing toward the peak. Rates at 50 and 70 C are low because the enzyme is denaturing, so higher temperature does not keep improving performance.

questions.q: A pH series gives rates of 0.01, 0.05, 0.22, 0.19, and 0.03 absorbance units per minute at pH 3, 5, 7, 8, and 11. What is the optimum pH for this enzyme?
options: pH 5
pH 3
pH 11
pH 7
questions.why: The peak rate of 0.22 per minute falls at pH 7, with pH 8 close behind on the shoulder of the curve. Rates at pH 5 and pH 3 are low because the enzyme is progressively denatured on the acid side. pH 11 gives the near zero activity expected when strong alkali has unfolded the protein.
questions.answerText: pH 7

questions.q: Two tubes are plotted as absorbance against time. Tube A gives a steeper line than tube B. What does that tell you?
options: Tube A started with more product already present
Tube A contains a larger volume of solution
Tube A was read at a longer wavelength
The enzyme in tube A is producing product faster
questions.why: Slope is change in absorbance over change in time, which is exactly the definition of reaction rate, so a steeper line means faster product formation. Starting product would raise the intercept of the line rather than tilt it. Volume differences are eliminated by using matched cuvettes and standard volumes, and the wavelength is held constant for all tubes in an assay.
questions.answerText: The enzyme in tube A is producing product faster

questions.q: A student forgets to blank the spectrophotometer and instead zeroes it on air. Predict the effect on the recorded absorbance values and on the calculated rate.
options: All readings are shifted upward, but the rate calculated from the slope is largely unaffected
All readings are shifted upward, and the calculated rate is proportionally too high
All readings are shifted downward, and the calculated rate is too low
Readings are unaffected, since the blank matters only for color intensity
questions.why: A missing blank adds a constant offset from the buffer and cuvette to every reading, and a constant added to all points raises the line without changing its slope, so the rate survives even though the individual values are wrong. Treating the error as proportional confuses an additive offset with a multiplicative one. Adding the solution's own absorbance raises rather than lowers readings, and blanking affects the numbers regardless of how intense the color is.
questions.answerText: All readings are shifted upward, but the rate calculated from the slope is largely unaffected

questions.q: Predict the shape of the activity curve for a human enzyme as temperature rises from 0 C through 60 C.
options: A gradual rise to a peak near 37 C, then a steep drop as denaturation sets in
A steady rise all the way to 60 C
A symmetric bell with equally gradual rise and fall on both sides of 37 C
A flat line, since human enzymes are buffered against temperature change
questions.why: Below the optimum, rate climbs gradually as molecular motion increases, but above it the fold comes apart quickly and aggregation makes the loss abrupt and largely irreversible, so the curve is lopsided. A steady rise ignores denaturation entirely. A symmetric bell would imply the fall is as gentle as the rise, and a flat line would mean temperature does not matter, which is contradicted by any assay you run.
questions.answerText: A gradual rise to a peak near 37 C, then a steep drop as denaturation sets in

questions.q: With substrate at a saturating concentration, a student doubles the amount of enzyme added to the tube. Predict the slope of the absorbance versus time line.
options: Unchanged, because substrate is saturating
About twice as steep
About half as steep, because the enzyme molecules compete
Steeper at first and then flat within seconds
questions.why: Vmax is proportional to the number of active sites, so twice the enzyme converts substrate about twice as fast and the line rises twice as quickly. Saturating substrate means the enzyme is the limiting factor, which is exactly why adding enzyme helps here. Enzyme molecules do not interfere with each other, and with substrate in excess the reaction does not exhaust its supply within seconds.
questions.answerText: About twice as steep

questions.q: A lab group assays pepsin and trypsin across pH 1 to 10 and finds peak activity for pepsin near pH 2 and for trypsin near pH 8. What accounts for the difference?
options: Trypsin is the stronger enzyme, so it can work across a much wider range of pH values
Each enzyme's active site keeps its shape only near the pH of the compartment where it normally works
Pepsin is denatured at pH 2, so its apparent peak reflects nonenzymatic breakdown of the substrate
The buffers used at low pH absorb more light on their own, which artificially raises the pepsin reading
questions.why: Optimum pH is a property of the enzyme's own side chain charges, and each digestive enzyme is built to fold correctly in the compartment where it is secreted, which is why pepsin fails once it reaches the alkaline intestine. Strength is not a meaningful comparison between enzymes with different substrates. Pepsin is stable and active at pH 2, not denatured by it, and a properly blanked assay corrects for the absorbance of the buffer itself.
questions.answerText: Each enzyme's active site keeps its shape only near the pH of the compartment where it normally works

questions.q: A student's progress curve rises steeply for the first minute and then flattens, and she concludes the enzyme denatured. What is the more likely explanation, and how should the rate be reported?
options: The enzyme denatured, so the rate should be taken from the flat portion of the curve
The spectrophotometer drifted, so the whole run must be discarded
Substrate ran out, and the rate should be taken from the initial linear portion of the curve
Product inhibited the enzyme, so the rate should be averaged over the entire run
questions.why: A curve that flattens while conditions are held constant almost always means the substrate is exhausted, which is why initial velocity, measured while substrate is still plentiful, is the standard reported value. Denaturation would show as a decline over a series of temperature conditions rather than a plateau in a single tube at 37 C. Instrument drift would produce erratic or sloping baselines rather than a clean plateau, and averaging over a run that includes the plateau systematically underestimates the true rate.
questions.answerText: Substrate ran out, and the rate should be taken from the initial linear portion of the curve

questions.q: One enzyme sample is held at 5 C and another at 80 C, then both are returned to 37 C and assayed. The chilled sample works normally and the heated one shows no activity. What does this pair of results demonstrate?
options: Cold slows the enzyme reversibly, while high heat denatures it irreversibly
Both treatments denature the enzyme, but cold denaturation is slower to appear
The enzyme has two optima, one near 5 C and one near 37 C
Heat destroys the substrate rather than the enzyme, so no product can form
questions.why: The chilled enzyme simply lacked kinetic energy and recovers as soon as it is warmed, whereas the heated one unfolded and its exposed hydrophobic regions aggregated, so warming it back to 37 C cannot restore the fold. Cold does not denature the enzyme in this range, which is exactly why the chilled sample recovers. A single enzyme has one optimum, and the substrate was added fresh to both tubes after the temperature treatment.
questions.answerText: Cold slows the enzyme reversibly, while high heat denatures it irreversibly

questions.q: Tube A shows an absorbance change of 0.45 over 3 minutes and tube B shows 0.30 over 5 minutes. Calculate each rate and state which enzyme sample is more active.
options: Tube A is 0.15 per minute and tube B is 0.06 per minute, so tube B is more active
Tube B is more active, because its total absorbance change was measured over a longer time
Both are equally active, because absorbance eventually reaches the same value
Tube A is 0.15 per minute and tube B is 0.06 per minute, so tube A is more active
questions.why: Dividing each absorbance change by its own time gives 0.45 divided by 3, or 0.15 per minute, and 0.30 divided by 5, or 0.06 per minute, so tube A works more than twice as fast. Comparing raw absorbance changes without dividing by time is the usual error and would wrongly favor whichever tube ran longer. Reaching a similar endpoint eventually says nothing about rate, which is the quantity enzyme activity is defined by.
questions.answerText: Tube A is 0.15 per minute and tube B is 0.06 per minute, so tube A is more active

questions.q: What forms the continuous structural framework of the plasma membrane?
options: A phospholipid bilayer
A sheet of cholesterol molecules
A woven network of peripheral proteins
A surface layer of membrane carbohydrate
questions.why: The bilayer of phospholipids is the one component that is continuous around the whole cell, and it is what makes the membrane a barrier to water soluble substances. Cholesterol is inserted between phospholipids and does not form a sheet of its own. Peripheral proteins sit on the surfaces and can be removed without opening the cell. Membrane carbohydrate is attached to lipids and proteins on the outer face only, so it cannot be the framework.
questions.answerText: A phospholipid bilayer
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In an intact plasma membrane, where do the fatty acid tails of the phospholipids sit?
options: Facing the cytosol on both leaflets
Facing each other in the interior of the bilayer, away from water
Facing the extracellular fluid on both leaflets
Alternating with the phosphate heads along each membrane surface
questions.why: The tails are nonpolar, so water drives them together into the core of the membrane while the polar heads face the watery fluid on each side. Tails cannot face the cytosol or the extracellular fluid, because both are water and the tails are excluded from water. Tails do not alternate with the heads along the surface, because each phospholipid keeps its head at the surface and its tails pointing inward.
questions.answerText: Facing each other in the interior of the bilayer, away from water
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Calling a phospholipid amphipathic means that one molecule has which combination?
options: Two polar ends separated by a neutral middle
A charged head and a charged tail, both attracted to water
A polar head that interacts with water and nonpolar tails that do not
A nonpolar head and polar tails that face the cytosol
questions.why: Amphipathic means one molecule carries both a water loving and a water avoiding region, and that split is exactly what makes a bilayer form spontaneously. A molecule polar at both ends would dissolve rather than assemble into a sheet. A fully charged molecule would stay in solution. The head is the polar end and the tails are the nonpolar end, not the reverse.
questions.answerText: A polar head that interacts with water and nonpolar tails that do not
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which class of membrane protein extends completely through the bilayer and touches both the cytosol and the extracellular fluid?
options: Peripheral proteins bound to one membrane surface
Lipid anchored proteins tethered to a single leaflet
Secreted proteins that rest in the glycocalyx
Integral transmembrane proteins
questions.why: Only a transmembrane protein has a hydrophobic stretch long enough to cross the lipid core, which is what lets channels and transporters connect the two sides of the cell. Peripheral proteins bind to a surface and never enter the core. Lipid anchored proteins are attached to a fatty acid in one leaflet and stay on that side. Secreted proteins are outside the membrane entirely.
questions.answerText: Integral transmembrane proteins
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How is cholesterol positioned within the plasma membrane?
options: Wedged between phospholipids, with its hydroxyl near the polar heads
Floating free in the cytosol just under the inner leaflet
Coating the outer surface as a continuous waterproof film
Packed in the center of the bilayer with no contact with the heads
questions.why: Cholesterol is itself amphipathic, so its single hydroxyl group sits with the polar heads while its stiff ring structure sits among the fatty acid tails, and that position is what lets it control packing. Cytosolic cholesterol would not affect membrane fluidity. A surface film would block the transport proteins. Burying it entirely in the center would leave the hydroxyl group in the hydrophobic core, which it avoids.
questions.answerText: Wedged between phospholipids, with its hydroxyl near the polar heads
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On which face of the plasma membrane are the carbohydrate chains of glycolipids and glycoproteins found?
options: Only on the cytosolic face
Only on the extracellular face
Equally on both faces
Buried inside the hydrophobic core
questions.why: Carbohydrate is added in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi on the side of the membrane that becomes the outside, so the sugar coat always ends up facing the extracellular fluid where recognition happens. A cytosolic sugar coat would be useless for cell to cell identification. The asymmetry is maintained, so the two faces are not alike. Carbohydrate is strongly polar and cannot sit in the lipid core.
questions.answerText: Only on the extracellular face
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which membrane proteins can be released by changing the pH or salt concentration of the surrounding solution, without breaking up the bilayer?
options: Integral proteins that span the lipid core
Lipid anchored proteins covalently attached to a fatty acid
Peripheral proteins attached to a membrane surface
Glycoproteins with carbohydrate on the outer face
questions.why: Peripheral proteins are held on by ionic and hydrogen bonds to lipid heads or to other proteins, and those bonds are exactly what salt and pH changes disrupt. Integral proteins are held by hydrophobic contact with the lipid core, so they come out only when detergent breaks the bilayer. A lipid anchor is a covalent bond and is not undone by salt. Glycoproteins are typically integral proteins and stay put for the same reason.
questions.answerText: Peripheral proteins attached to a membrane surface
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What holds a phospholipid bilayer together?
options: Covalent bonds linking each phospholipid to its neighbors
Disulfide bridges between the embedded membrane proteins
Hydrogen bonds formed directly between the fatty acid tails
Hydrophobic interaction among the fatty acid tails
questions.why: The bilayer is held by weak, noncovalent forces, mainly the tendency of the nonpolar tails to cluster away from water while the polar heads stay in it, which is why the membrane can self seal and why its parts can move sideways. Covalent bonds between phospholipids would lock the membrane rigid and prevent that movement. Disulfide bridges stabilize some proteins but do not build the lipid sheet. Fatty acid tails are nonpolar and cannot form hydrogen bonds.
questions.answerText: Hydrophobic interaction among the fatty acid tails
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A membrane rich in cholesterol is cooled from 37 C to 20 C. Compared with the same membrane without cholesterol, what happens to its fluidity?
options: It stays more fluid, because cholesterol blocks tight packing of the tails
It becomes far more rigid, because cholesterol crystallizes with the tails
It is unchanged, because cholesterol acts only on the outer leaflet
It becomes completely liquid, because cholesterol dissolves the bilayer
questions.why: At low temperature the danger is that tails pack together and the membrane gels, and the bulky cholesterol ring gets in the way of that packing. Cholesterol does the opposite job at high temperature, where it restrains movement and reduces fluidity, so its effect depends on where you start. Cholesterol is present in both leaflets, not just the outer one. It never dissolves the membrane, since it is a structural part of it.
questions.answerText: It stays more fluid, because cholesterol blocks tight packing of the tails
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Two membranes are compared at 37 C. Membrane A has mostly saturated fatty acid tails and membrane B has mostly unsaturated tails. Which is more fluid?
options: Membrane A, because straight tails slide past each other easily
Membrane B, because kinks at the double bonds prevent close packing
Both are the same, because fluidity depends only on temperature
Membrane A, because saturated tails carry more cholesterol
questions.why: Every double bond puts a bend in the tail, so neighboring phospholipids cannot line up closely and the membrane stays loose and mobile. Straight saturated tails do the opposite, stacking neatly and stiffening the membrane. Temperature matters, but composition changes fluidity at any given temperature. Saturation does not determine how much cholesterol a membrane holds.
questions.answerText: Membrane B, because kinks at the double bonds prevent close packing
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A treatment makes a cell membrane much less fluid at body temperature. What happens to the rate of carrier mediated transport across it?
options: It rises, because a stiffer membrane holds carriers in the open position
It is unchanged, because carriers work independently of the lipid around them
It falls, because carrier proteins must change conformation inside the bilayer
It rises, because a rigid membrane brings carriers closer to their solute
questions.why: A carrier binds solute on one side, changes shape, and releases it on the other, and that shape change is resisted when the surrounding lipid is stiff. A rigid membrane does not lock carriers open, since the carrier cycles between two shapes and needs both. Carriers are embedded in lipid and are very much affected by it. Rigidity does not shorten the distance between carrier and solute, which is set by the fluid on each side.
questions.answerText: It falls, because carrier proteins must change conformation inside the bilayer
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A membrane protein can be released only by adding a detergent that breaks up the bilayer. What does that tell you about the protein?
options: It is held to the surface by ionic bonds, so it is a peripheral protein
It is a carbohydrate rich protein of the glycocalyx
It is a cytosolic protein that was contaminating the sample
It has a hydrophobic region in the lipid core, so it is an integral protein
questions.why: Detergent is needed only when the protein is held by hydrophobic contact with the fatty acid tails, which is the defining feature of an integral protein. A peripheral protein would have come off with a simple change in salt or pH. Glycocalyx carbohydrate faces the watery outside and does not require detergent to reach. A cytosolic contaminant would appear in the first wash, before any detergent was used.
questions.answerText: It has a hydrophobic region in the lipid core, so it is an integral protein
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An enzyme strips the carbohydrate chains from the outer surface of a cell but leaves the bilayer intact. Which function is most directly lost?
options: Recognition of the cell by other cells and by immune proteins
The barrier that keeps Na+ from leaking into the cell
The ability of the membrane to reseal after a small tear
The attraction between the phosphate heads and water
questions.why: The sugar coat is the cell's identity tag, so removing it interferes with recognition, adhesion, and immune identification while leaving the lipid seal untouched. The barrier to Na+ is a property of the hydrophobic core, which the enzyme never touches. Resealing is also a lipid property and is preserved. The phosphate heads are still polar and still face water after the sugars are gone.
questions.answerText: Recognition of the cell by other cells and by immune proteins
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A labeled phospholipid in the outer leaflet spreads sideways across the cell surface within seconds but takes hours to show up in the inner leaflet. What explains the difference?
options: The inner leaflet contains no phospholipid for the label to mix with
Sideways movement is easy, but flipping drags the head through the core
The label is destroyed by cytosolic enzymes as soon as it flips
Sideways movement uses ATP while flipping does not
questions.why: Lateral diffusion keeps each polar head in water the whole time, so it costs almost nothing, while a flip forces that head through the greasy core and is energetically expensive. The inner leaflet is also phospholipid, so there is plenty for the label to join. Destruction of the label would remove signal rather than delay it. Lateral diffusion is passive, and it is the flip that cells must speed up with ATP driven flippases.
questions.answerText: Sideways movement is easy, but flipping drags the head through the core
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A membrane sample turns out to be about 75 percent protein by mass, far above the usual value. What does that suggest about the membrane?
options: It is a poor barrier to water because protein has replaced the lipid seal
It has lost its cholesterol and has become unusually rigid
It carries out a great deal of transport and signaling work
It is an inactive storage membrane with little traffic across it
questions.why: Proteins are the working parts of a membrane, so a high protein fraction points to heavy transport, enzyme, or signaling activity, as seen in the inner mitochondrial membrane. The lipid bilayer is still continuous around the proteins, so the barrier remains intact. Protein content says nothing directly about cholesterol content or rigidity. A quiet storage membrane would be the low protein case, such as the myelin sheath.
questions.answerText: It carries out a great deal of transport and signaling work
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A drug removes most of the cholesterol from the plasma membrane of a cell held at 37 C. Follow the consequence through: what happens to fluidity, and then to the passive leak of small solutes?
options: Fluidity falls and passive leak falls, so pumps can slow down
Fluidity rises but leak is unchanged, because leak depends only on protein channels
Fluidity is unchanged, because cholesterol affects only membrane thickness
Fluidity rises and passive leak increases, so pumps must work harder to hold gradients
questions.why: At body temperature cholesterol restrains the tails, so taking it away loosens the packing, and a looser core lets small solutes and water slip through more easily. The pumps then run faster and burn more ATP to keep the same gradients. Losing cholesterol at 37 C increases fluidity rather than decreasing it. Leak is not purely a channel property, since the lipid core itself has a measurable permeability that packing controls.
questions.answerText: Fluidity rises and passive leak increases, so pumps must work harder to hold gradients
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A bacterium is moved from 37 C to 20 C but is genetically unable to change its fatty acid composition. Predict the state of its membrane and the effect on nutrient uptake.
options: The membrane stiffens toward a gel and carrier mediated uptake slows
The membrane becomes more fluid and uptake speeds up
The membrane is unaffected because bilayers are temperature independent
The membrane ruptures immediately because cold expands the bilayer
questions.why: Cooling lets the tails pack closer, and a cell that cannot add unsaturated tails or cholesterol has no way to counter it, so the membrane approaches a gel state. Carriers and pumps must flex to work, so their turnover falls and nutrients enter more slowly. Cooling reduces fluidity rather than increasing it. Bilayers do not rupture on cooling, they gel, and it is warming that eventually disorders them.
questions.answerText: The membrane stiffens toward a gel and carrier mediated uptake slows
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A newly sequenced membrane protein contains one stretch of about 20 hydrophobic amino acids flanked on both sides by charged residues. Where does that stretch sit, and what does the arrangement let the protein do?
options: It lies flat on the outer surface, so the protein can bind sugars
It spans the bilayer once, so the protein can link the outside to the inside
It coils inside the cytosol, so the protein can bind ATP
It is cleaved off in the Golgi, so the mature protein is secreted
questions.why: A run of about 20 hydrophobic residues is the right length to cross the lipid core, and charged residues at both ends anchor it at the two watery surfaces, which is the signature of a single pass transmembrane protein. That geometry is what lets a receptor bind a messenger outside and change something inside. A surface protein would not need a long hydrophobic run at all. A cytosolic domain would be flanked by cytosol on both sides, not by the membrane, and a cleaved signal sequence would leave no membrane anchor behind.
questions.answerText: It spans the bilayer once, so the protein can link the outside to the inside
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell is treated so that the carbohydrate of its glycocalyx is destroyed while the bilayer stays intact. Predict what happens to its permeability barrier and to its recognition by immune cells.
options: Both the barrier and recognition fail, since carbohydrate seals the membrane
The barrier fails but recognition is preserved, since sugars are only structural
The barrier is preserved but immune recognition is disturbed
Neither changes, since carbohydrate has no physiological role
questions.why: Sealing and recognition are done by different parts of the membrane, so this experiment separates them cleanly: the hydrophobic core still blocks ions and polar solutes, while the missing sugar coat is exactly what immune cells and neighboring cells read. Carbohydrate contributes nothing to the seal, so the barrier cannot fail here. Recognition cannot be preserved, because the surface markers are the thing that was destroyed. Blood group antigens are membrane carbohydrate, so the role is real and physiologically important.
questions.answerText: The barrier is preserved but immune recognition is disturbed
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which substance crosses a pure lipid bilayer most readily without help from a protein?
options: Sodium ion
Glucose
Chloride ion
Oxygen
questions.why: Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it dissolves in the fatty acid core and passes straight through. Na+ and Cl- are charged and carry a shell of water, which the hydrophobic core will not admit, so both need channels. Glucose is uncharged but large and heavily hydroxylated, so it needs a transporter such as GLUT.
questions.answerText: Oxygen
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which property of a molecule most increases its ability to cross a lipid bilayer unaided?
options: High lipid solubility
A large net negative charge
A high molecular weight
A large shell of bound water
questions.why: Crossing the membrane means dissolving into the fatty acid core and out again, so the more lipid soluble a molecule is, the faster it goes. Net charge does the opposite, since the nonpolar core repels charged particles. High molecular weight slows a molecule down at any given lipid solubility. A shell of bound water makes the effective particle much larger and more polar, which also slows crossing.
questions.answerText: High lipid solubility
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Why do charged particles cross the lipid core of a membrane so poorly?
options: They are all too large to fit between the phospholipids
The nonpolar core will not accept a charge or its water shell
They are repelled by the carbohydrate on the outer face
They bind irreversibly to cholesterol in the bilayer
questions.why: Stripping the water from an ion and pushing the bare charge into a greasy interior costs far more energy than an ion has at body temperature, so ions travel through protein channels instead. Size is not the problem, since ions like Na+ are far smaller than steroids that cross easily. The surface carbohydrate is a thin polar coat and does not repel ions. Ions do not bind cholesterol.
questions.answerText: The nonpolar core will not accept a charge or its water shell
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How does most water actually cross the plasma membrane of a cell that needs high water permeability?
options: By dissolving freely in the fatty acid core
By being pumped across using ATP
Through aquaporin channels
Bound to glucose on a shared transporter
questions.why: Water is small but polar, so a little crosses the lipid directly, and cells that must move a lot of water insert aquaporins to speed it up. Water is not lipid soluble, so free dissolution in the core is slow, not free. There is no ATP driven water pump in human cells, since water follows osmotic gradients instead. Water is not carried piggyback on the glucose transporter.
questions.answerText: Through aquaporin channels
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which of these substances requires a membrane protein in order to enter a cell at a useful rate?
options: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
A steroid hormone
Glucose
questions.why: Glucose is a fairly large polar molecule with many hydroxyl groups, so it needs a GLUT carrier or a sodium coupled transporter to move at physiological speed. CO2 and O2 are small nonpolar gases that dissolve in lipid and diffuse straight through. Steroid hormones are lipid derived and cross so freely that their receptors sit inside the cell.
questions.answerText: Glucose
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Steroid hormones cross the plasma membrane without a transporter mainly because they are what?
options: Lipid soluble
Very small and positively charged
Bound to plasma albumin
Broken down into amino acids first
questions.why: Steroids are made from cholesterol and dissolve readily in the membrane core, which is why their receptors are cytosolic or nuclear rather than on the surface. They are not small ions and carry no useful charge. Binding to albumin keeps a steroid in the blood, and it is the free fraction that crosses. Steroids are not proteins and are not digested into amino acids.
questions.answerText: Lipid soluble
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Two molecules are equally lipid soluble but one is much larger. How do their rates of simple diffusion across a bilayer compare?
options: The larger one crosses faster
The smaller one crosses faster
They cross at the same rate, since only lipid solubility matters
Neither crosses, since size blocks all simple diffusion
questions.why: Size and lipid solubility both matter, and when lipid solubility is held equal, the smaller molecule slips between the fatty acid tails more easily and diffuses faster. Larger molecules must push more tails apart, which slows them. Lipid solubility alone does not determine rate. Size slows diffusion but does not abolish it, as fairly large steroids still cross.
questions.answerText: The smaller one crosses faster
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What does it mean to call the plasma membrane selectively permeable?
options: It blocks every substance until a pump is activated
It allows anything smaller than a protein to pass freely
It lets some substances cross while restricting others
It allows movement in one direction only
questions.why: Selective permeability is the basis of every gradient in the body, because the membrane admits gases and lipid soluble molecules while holding back ions and large polar solutes. A membrane that blocked everything would not allow O2 uptake, which happens with no pump at all. Size is not the only filter, since small ions are blocked while much larger steroids pass. Simple diffusion has no built in direction, since it follows whichever gradient exists.
questions.answerText: It lets some substances cross while restricting others
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A new drug is small, uncharged, and highly lipid soluble. What do you predict about how it enters cells?
options: It needs a specific carrier protein and will saturate at high dose
It enters only by ATP driven pumping
It cannot enter cells and stays in the extracellular fluid
It diffuses straight through the bilayer without a transporter
questions.why: Small, uncharged, and lipid soluble is the exact profile that crosses by simple diffusion, so the rate will rise in proportion to the concentration gradient with no ceiling. A carrier would impose saturation, which simple diffusion does not show. No pump is needed for a molecule that has no charge to fight and no gradient to climb. Being lipid soluble is the opposite of being trapped outside.
questions.answerText: It diffuses straight through the bilayer without a transporter
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A weak acid drug exists as an uncharged molecule and as its negatively charged conjugate base. Which form crosses the lipid bilayer, and what does that mean in an acidic fluid?
options: The uncharged form crosses, and acid increases the uncharged fraction so more crosses
The charged form crosses, and acid increases the charged fraction so more crosses
Both forms cross equally, so pH has no effect
Neither form crosses without a transporter, so pH is irrelevant
questions.why: Charge is the main obstacle to crossing lipid, so only the protonated, uncharged form of a weak acid moves through the bilayer, and adding H+ pushes the equilibrium toward that form. The charged conjugate base is held back by the hydrophobic core. The two forms are not equivalent, which is why pH shifts drug movement so strongly. A transporter is not required, because the uncharged form is lipid soluble.
questions.answerText: The uncharged form crosses, and acid increases the uncharged fraction so more crosses
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: CO2 is more soluble in lipid than O2 is, and the two are similar in size. Which crosses the alveolar membrane faster for the same partial pressure difference?
options: O2, because it is the gas the body needs more urgently
CO2, because higher lipid solubility raises the diffusion rate
They cross at identical rates, since both are gases
Neither crosses, since gases require channel proteins
questions.why: Diffusion rate through a bilayer depends on how well the molecule dissolves in lipid, and CO2 is roughly twenty times more soluble than O2, so it moves much faster for the same driving pressure. Physiological need does not change the physical properties of a molecule. Being a gas is not enough, since gases still differ in solubility. Gases require no channels at all, since they dissolve directly in the membrane.
questions.answerText: CO2, because higher lipid solubility raises the diffusion rate
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An amino acid and a similarly sized uncharged molecule are offered to a cell whose transporters are all blocked. Which enters, and why?
options: The amino acid, because the cell needs it to build proteins
Both equally, because the two molecules are the same size
The uncharged molecule, because the amino acid is charged at body pH
Neither, because blocking the transporters stops all entry
questions.why: At pH 7.4 an amino acid is a zwitterion with charged amino and carboxyl groups, so the lipid core rejects it and blocking the transporters cuts off its route entirely. The cell's need for amino acids does not create a path across the lipid. Equal size does not mean equal permeability once charge differs. Simple diffusion continues for the uncharged molecule even with every transporter blocked.
questions.answerText: The uncharged molecule, because the amino acid is charged at body pH
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Aquaporins are inserted into a membrane that previously had none. What changes?
options: Both water and small solute permeability rise together
Water permeability rises and the cell begins to swell even in an isotonic solution
Water permeability falls, since the channels must first be activated by ATP
Water permeability rises sharply while solute permeability is essentially unchanged
questions.why: Aquaporins form a narrow pore that admits water in single file and excludes ions and solutes, so they change how fast water moves without changing what else can cross. They are not general pores, so solutes do not follow. Faster water movement does not by itself create swelling, because an isotonic solution offers no net driving force. Aquaporins are always open channels and do not need ATP.
questions.answerText: Water permeability rises sharply while solute permeability is essentially unchanged
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A fluorescent dye is injected into a cell and stays inside for hours. What does that tell you about the dye?
options: It is polar or charged and has no transporter to carry it out
It is highly lipid soluble and dissolves in the membrane
It is pumped inward continuously by the Na+/K+ ATPase
It has been covalently bonded to the phospholipid tails
questions.why: A dye that stays put is one the bilayer will not admit and no carrier recognizes, which is exactly why polar or charged dyes are chosen for this purpose. A lipid soluble dye would leak straight back out within minutes. The Na+/K+ ATPase moves only Na+ and K+, so it cannot trap a dye. Covalent bonding to tails would place the dye in the membrane rather than in the cytosol.
questions.answerText: It is polar or charged and has no transporter to carry it out
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Urea is small and uncharged but polar. What does that predict about how it crosses membranes?
options: It crosses as fast as O2, because small uncharged molecules all behave alike
It crosses slowly on its own, and cells needing speed use urea transporters
It cannot cross at all, because polar molecules are completely excluded
It crosses only when pumped against its gradient using ATP
questions.why: Polarity slows urea down without stopping it, so it leaks through the lipid over minutes, and the kidney medulla adds specific urea transporters where rapid movement matters. It is far slower than O2 because O2 is nonpolar and urea is not. Complete exclusion is wrong, and the fact that urea does eventually cross is what makes it behave as a penetrating solute in tonicity problems. No ATP is needed, since urea follows its gradient.
questions.answerText: It crosses slowly on its own, and cells needing speed use urea transporters
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A weakly basic drug is uncharged in plasma at pH 7.4 but becomes protonated and charged at pH 5. Predict what happens when it reaches a lysosome with an internal pH of 5.
options: It crosses in and back out equally, so its concentration matches the cytosol
It is excluded from the lysosome, because acidic compartments repel all drugs
It crosses in uncharged and becomes charged inside, so it is trapped and accumulates
It is pumped out of the lysosome by an ATPase specific for weak bases
questions.why: The uncharged form is lipid soluble and crosses the lysosomal membrane freely, but as soon as it picks up a proton inside it cannot cross back, so drug piles up in the acidic compartment. This is ion trapping, and it is why some drugs concentrate hundreds of times in acidic spaces. Equal movement in both directions would require the drug to stay uncharged inside, which the low pH prevents. Nothing repels the neutral form on the way in, and no general weak base pump is doing this work.
questions.answerText: It crosses in uncharged and becomes charged inside, so it is trapped and accumulates
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A local anesthetic must cross the axon membrane in its uncharged form and then block the Na+ channel from the cytosolic side in its charged form. Predict what happens when it is injected into inflamed tissue where the extracellular pH is low.
options: More drug is uncharged outside, so entry rises and the block is stronger
Entry is unchanged, because the membrane admits both forms equally
The drug is destroyed by acid, so it has no effect at any dose
Less drug is uncharged outside, so less enters the axon and the block is weaker
questions.why: Low pH pushes this weak base toward its protonated, charged form, and the charged form cannot cross the lipid core, so less drug reaches the inside where it acts. Acid does not increase the neutral fraction of a base, it decreases it. The membrane strongly favors the uncharged form, which is the whole reason pH matters here. The drug is not chemically destroyed, it is simply held on the wrong side.
questions.answerText: Less drug is uncharged outside, so less enters the axon and the block is weaker
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A synthetic bilayer containing no proteins is placed in a solution of oxygen, urea, glucose, and Na+. After ten seconds, which appear inside, and which are still essentially outside after an hour?
options: Oxygen enters at once, urea slowly, and glucose and Na+ not at all
All four enter within seconds, since a bilayer is freely permeable
Only Na+ enters, since ions are the smallest particles present
Glucose and Na+ enter first, since the cell needs them most
questions.why: Ranking by charge, then polarity, then size gives the order directly: nonpolar O2 dissolves in the core at once, small polar urea trickles through, large polar glucose needs GLUT, and charged Na+ needs a channel, and this bilayer has neither. A bilayer is selectively permeable, not freely permeable. Small size does not help Na+ because its charge and water shell are the barrier. A protein free membrane has no way to sense what a cell needs.
questions.answerText: Oxygen enters at once, urea slowly, and glucose and Na+ not at all
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell's glucose transporters are knocked out. Predict the effect on glucose entry and on the entry of a lipid soluble vitamin.
options: Both stop, since all entry into cells depends on transport proteins
Glucose entry nearly stops while the vitamin still enters by simple diffusion
Glucose entry is unchanged, since glucose can dissolve in the lipid core
Vitamin entry rises to compensate for the loss of glucose uptake
questions.why: Glucose depends completely on carriers because it is large and polar, so losing them cuts off its route, while a lipid soluble vitamin dissolves in the membrane and never needed a protein. Not everything entering a cell needs a protein, as gases and steroids show. Glucose is far too polar to dissolve in the core at any useful rate. Simple diffusion of the vitamin is driven by its own gradient and does not speed up because glucose uptake failed.
questions.answerText: Glucose entry nearly stops while the vitamin still enters by simple diffusion
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: According to Fick's law, increasing which variable increases the rate of diffusion across a membrane?
options: Membrane thickness
Molecular weight of the diffusing substance
Surface area available for exchange
Distance between the two compartments
questions.why: Rate is directly proportional to surface area, because more area means more parallel routes across the barrier. Thickness sits in the denominator, so increasing it slows transfer. Larger molecules diffuse more slowly, so molecular weight also works against rate. Greater distance slows diffusion for the same reason thickness does.
questions.answerText: Surface area available for exchange
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In Fick's law, the rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to which variable?
options: Concentration difference
Surface area
Temperature
Membrane thickness
questions.why: Thickness is the distance the molecule must travel, and it appears in the denominator, so doubling it halves the rate. Concentration difference is the driving force and multiplies the rate. Surface area also multiplies the rate. Warming speeds molecular motion, so temperature increases rather than decreases the rate.
questions.answerText: Membrane thickness
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What supplies the driving force for simple diffusion across a membrane?
options: The concentration gradient of the diffusing substance
Hydrolysis of ATP by a membrane pump
Binding of the substance to a carrier protein
The electrical charge on the membrane carbohydrate
questions.why: Simple diffusion is powered by the random thermal motion of molecules plus a difference in concentration, which is why it costs the cell nothing. ATP is required for active transport, which is a different process and can move solute uphill. Carrier binding describes facilitated diffusion and active transport, not simple diffusion. Surface carbohydrate does not drive movement of neutral solutes across the bilayer.
questions.answerText: The concentration gradient of the diffusing substance
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How does the size of a molecule affect its rate of diffusion, other things being equal?
options: Larger molecules diffuse more quickly
Larger molecules diffuse more slowly
Size has no effect on diffusion rate
Only molecules above 100 daltons diffuse at all
questions.why: A larger particle moves more sluggishly at a given temperature and has more trouble pushing between the phospholipid tails, so its diffusion coefficient is smaller. Larger molecules never move faster for the same driving force. Size is one of the main determinants of the diffusion coefficient, so it cannot be ignored. There is no size threshold below which diffusion stops, since very small molecules diffuse fastest of all.
questions.answerText: Larger molecules diffuse more slowly
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How does the time required for a molecule to diffuse a given distance change as that distance increases?
options: It increases in direct proportion to the distance
It decreases as distance increases
It increases with the square of the distance
It does not depend on distance
questions.why: Diffusion is a random walk, so doubling the distance multiplies the time by four, which is why diffusion is excellent over a few micrometers and hopeless over centimeters. Simple proportionality would make diffusion far more capable over distance than it actually is. Time cannot fall as distance rises. Distance is the single most important limit on diffusion, so it certainly matters.
questions.answerText: It increases with the square of the distance
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Net diffusion of a solute across a membrane stops when which condition is reached?
options: All molecular motion has ceased
The solute has all moved to one side
The membrane has become impermeable to the solute
The concentration is equal on both sides
questions.why: At equilibrium molecules still cross in both directions, but the two fluxes are equal, so there is no net movement. Molecular motion never stops at body temperature, which is what keeps the two way exchange going. Diffusion moves solute down its gradient, so it never piles everything on one side. The membrane's permeability does not change as equilibrium is approached.
questions.answerText: The concentration is equal on both sides
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which of these is not a variable in Fick's law of diffusion?
options: The amount of ATP available to the cell
The surface area of the barrier
The thickness of the barrier
The concentration difference across the barrier
questions.why: Fick's law describes a passive process, so energy supply never appears in it and diffusion continues in a cell with no ATP at all. Surface area, thickness, and the concentration difference are the three variables that physiology manipulates most often, in the lung, the gut, and the capillary bed. Recognizing that ATP is absent is the fastest way to tell diffusion apart from active transport.
questions.answerText: The amount of ATP available to the cell
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How does raising the temperature affect the rate of diffusion?
options: It decreases the rate
It increases the rate
It has no effect on the rate
It stops diffusion once the solution is warm
questions.why: Temperature is a measure of molecular kinetic energy, so warmer molecules move faster and spread more quickly. Cooling does the opposite and is why lab demonstrations run slowly in cold water. Temperature is one of the standard determinants of the diffusion coefficient, so it is never neutral. Nothing about warming halts diffusion.
questions.answerText: It increases the rate
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The surface area available for exchange doubles while everything else stays the same. What happens to the rate of diffusion?
options: It halves
It quadruples
It doubles
It is unchanged
questions.why: Surface area is in the numerator of Fick's law and enters as a simple multiplier, so twice the area gives twice the transfer. Halving would be the answer if the thickness had doubled instead. Quadrupling would require a squared relationship, which applies to diffusion time and distance, not to area. Area is a real variable, so the rate cannot stay put.
questions.answerText: It doubles
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Fluid collects in the space between the alveolus and the capillary, doubling the distance oxygen must travel. What happens to the rate of oxygen transfer, other things equal?
options: It doubles
It falls to about one quarter
It is unchanged, because the gradient is what matters
It falls to about half
questions.why: Thickness sits in the denominator of Fick's law, so doubling it cuts the transfer rate roughly in half, which is why pulmonary edema causes hypoxemia. Increasing the barrier thickness cannot increase transfer. The quarter answer would apply to the time for a molecule to random walk twice the distance, not to the steady state flux described by Fick's law. The gradient matters too, but it is not the only variable.
questions.answerText: It falls to about half
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The concentration difference across a membrane is tripled while area and thickness stay the same. What happens to the rate of diffusion?
options: It triples
It falls to one third
It is unchanged, since diffusion has a fixed maximum
It rises ninefold
questions.why: The concentration difference is the driving force and enters Fick's law as a direct multiplier, so three times the gradient gives three times the flux. A fall would require the gradient to be in the denominator, which it is not. Simple diffusion has no transport maximum, since there is no carrier to saturate, which is one way it differs from facilitated diffusion. Nothing in Fick's law is squared.
questions.answerText: It triples
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, so many small alveoli merge into fewer large ones. Which variable of Fick's law changes, and how does gas transfer respond?
options: Membrane thickness falls, so gas transfer rises
Surface area falls, so gas transfer falls
The concentration gradient rises, so gas transfer rises
The diffusion coefficient of oxygen falls, so gas transfer falls
questions.why: Merging many small sacs into a few large ones keeps the volume but loses an enormous amount of surface, and area multiplies the transfer rate directly. Wall destruction does not usefully thin the barrier, and even if it did, the loss of area dominates. The alveolar to capillary gradient is set by ventilation and blood flow, not by wall destruction. The diffusion coefficient is a property of oxygen and the tissue, and disease does not change it.
questions.answerText: Surface area falls, so gas transfer falls
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell increases in radius so that the distance from its surface to its center goes from 10 micrometers to 20 micrometers. How does the time for a solute to diffuse to the center change?
options: It doubles
It is halved
It increases about fourfold
It stays the same
questions.why: Diffusion time rises with the square of distance, so doubling the distance multiplies the time by four, and this is the main reason cells stay small. Doubling would be the answer only if time were directly proportional to distance. Time cannot fall as the distance grows. Distance is the dominant term here, so it certainly matters.
questions.answerText: It increases about fourfold
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A diffusion demonstration is repeated at 37 C instead of 20 C. What happens to the rate at which the dye spreads?
options: It decreases, because heat drives water out of the gel
It is unchanged, because Fick's law contains no temperature term
It increases only if the gradient is also increased
It increases, because molecules move faster at higher temperature
questions.why: Warming raises molecular kinetic energy and therefore the diffusion coefficient, so the same gradient produces faster spread. Heat does not push the dye backward or dry the gel appreciably over a demonstration. Temperature acts through the diffusion coefficient, so it is part of the law even when written as a single constant. The gradient can stay exactly the same and the rate will still rise.
questions.answerText: It increases, because molecules move faster at higher temperature
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The small intestine has villi and microvilli that raise its lining area many times over. Which term of Fick's law does this exploit, and with what result?
options: It raises surface area, so the rate of nutrient absorption rises
It lowers barrier thickness, so absorption rises
It raises the diffusion coefficient of glucose, so absorption rises
It raises the concentration gradient of nutrients, so absorption rises
questions.why: Folding the surface multiplies the area for exchange without needing a longer gut, and area multiplies the flux directly. The epithelium is not made thinner by folding it. The diffusion coefficient depends on the molecule and the medium and is unchanged by anatomy. The gradient is created by the meal and by transport out of the cell, not by folding.
questions.answerText: It raises surface area, so the rate of nutrient absorption rises
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In a diseased lung the alveolar surface area is cut in half, but supplemental oxygen doubles the alveolar to capillary oxygen gradient. Predict the net effect on oxygen transfer.
options: Transfer falls to about one quarter, since both changes reduce it
Transfer returns to about its original rate, since the two changes cancel
Transfer doubles, since the gradient change outweighs the area change
Transfer stops, since area is the only variable that matters
questions.why: Both area and the concentration difference are multipliers in the numerator of Fick's law, so multiplying by one half and by two returns the product to where it started, which is why supplemental oxygen helps in diffusion limited disease. Only the area change reduces transfer, so the two do not compound. The gradient does not outweigh area, since the two terms carry equal weight. Area is one of several variables and never acts alone.
questions.answerText: Transfer returns to about its original rate, since the two changes cancel
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A barrier becomes three times thicker while its surface area doubles. What happens to the rate of diffusion across it?
options: It rises to about six times the original rate
It falls to about one sixth of the original rate
It falls to about two thirds of the original rate
It is unchanged, since the two effects cancel exactly
questions.why: Area multiplies the rate and thickness divides it, so the new rate is the old rate times two divided by three, which is about 0.67 of the original. Multiplying the two factors together would treat thickness as if it helped, which it does not. Dividing by both would treat area as if it hurt. Exact cancellation would require the two factors to be equal, and two and three are not.
questions.answerText: It falls to about two thirds of the original rate
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A single cell of 10 micrometers relies entirely on diffusion for oxygen. A tissue 1 centimeter thick cannot. Explain the physiological consequence of the distance rule.
options: Diffusion stops entirely beyond 100 micrometers, so deep tissue relies on anaerobic metabolism alone
Diffusion slows in direct proportion to distance, so a centimeter takes only a thousand times as long as a micrometer
Diffusion is unaffected by distance, and deep tissue hypoxia results from low capillary density alone
Diffusion time rises with the square of distance, so large tissues need blood flow to bring oxygen close to every cell
questions.why: Because time scales with the square of distance, moving oxygen a centimeter by diffusion would take hours, so the circulation carries it by bulk flow to within about 50 micrometers of every cell and lets diffusion cover only the last short step. Diffusion does not have a hard cutoff, it simply becomes impractically slow. Simple proportionality would badly understate the penalty of distance. Distance is precisely the variable at issue here.
questions.answerText: Diffusion time rises with the square of distance, so large tissues need blood flow to bring oxygen close to every cell
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Two exchange surfaces are compared. Surface A has twice the area of B and half the thickness of B, and both face the same concentration difference. How do their diffusion rates compare?
options: A transfers about four times as fast as B
A transfers about twice as fast as B
A and B transfer at the same rate
A transfers half as fast as B
questions.why: Doubling area multiplies the rate by two and halving thickness multiplies it by two again, so the two changes compound to a factor of four. Counting only one of the two changes gives the twofold answer. The changes both favor A, so they cannot cancel. Nothing here slows A down, so it cannot be the slower surface.
questions.answerText: A transfers about four times as fast as B
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Osmolarity measures which property of a solution?
options: The number of particles that can cross the cell membrane
The total number of dissolved solute particles per liter of solution
The mass in grams of solute per liter of solution
The electrical charge carried by the dissolved solutes
questions.why: Osmolarity is a head count of particles and does not care what they are, so 300 mOsm/L of urea and 300 mOsm/L of NaCl have the same osmolarity. Counting only particles that cannot cross is tonicity, which is a different measurement. Mass per liter is concentration by weight, and a gram of glucose and a gram of NaCl give different particle counts. Charge is irrelevant, since uncharged glucose contributes just as much as an ion.
questions.answerText: The total number of dissolved solute particles per liter of solution
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the osmolarity of a solution of 150 mM NaCl, assuming complete dissociation?
options: 150 mOsm/L
75 mOsm/L
300 mOsm/L
450 mOsm/L
questions.why: Each NaCl unit separates into one Na+ and one Cl-, so 150 mmol of NaCl yields 300 mmol of particles per liter. Using 150 counts the formula units rather than the particles they produce. Halving to 75 would be right only if two NaCl combined into one particle, which does not happen. Reaching 450 would require three particles per formula unit, as with CaCl2.
questions.answerText: 300 mOsm/L
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Tonicity depends on the concentration of which solutes?
options: All dissolved solutes, whether or not they can cross
Only the charged solutes in the solution
Only the solutes that the cell can metabolize
Only the solutes that cannot cross the cell membrane
questions.why: Tonicity predicts what a solution does to cell volume, and only impermeant solutes can hold water on one side, so penetrating solutes such as urea do not count. Counting every solute gives osmolarity, and confusing the two is the single most common error in this topic. Charge does not decide the issue, since impermeant glucose counts and permeant urea does not. Metabolism is a separate matter, although a solute that is consumed inside the cell behaves as if it were penetrating.
questions.answerText: Only the solutes that cannot cross the cell membrane
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the approximate osmolarity of normal human body fluids?
options: About 300 mOsm/L
About 30 mOsm/L
About 1000 mOsm/L
About 150 mOsm/L
questions.why: Plasma, interstitial fluid, and intracellular fluid all sit near 300 mOsm/L, and that number is the reference point for calling a solution hyperosmotic or hyposmotic. A value near 30 would be close to distilled water and would lyse every cell. A thousand is nearer the concentrated urine of the kidney medulla, not general body fluid. The figure of 150 is the sodium concentration in millimoles per liter, which contributes about 300 mOsm/L once its accompanying anions are counted.
questions.answerText: About 300 mOsm/L
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the difference between osmolarity and osmolality?
options: Osmolarity counts impermeant particles and osmolality counts all particles
Osmolarity is per liter of solution and osmolality is per kilogram of water
Osmolarity applies to plasma and osmolality applies to intracellular fluid
Osmolarity is measured at 37 C and osmolality is measured at 0 C
questions.why: The two differ only in the denominator, and in dilute body fluids the numbers are nearly identical, which is why the terms are often used interchangeably in physiology. The permeant versus impermeant distinction separates osmolarity from tonicity, not osmolarity from osmolality. Both terms apply to any fluid compartment. Neither term is tied to a particular temperature, although volume based osmolarity does shift slightly with temperature.
questions.answerText: Osmolarity is per liter of solution and osmolality is per kilogram of water
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In osmosis, which way does water move across a selectively permeable membrane?
options: Toward the side with the lower total solute concentration
Toward the side with the higher hydrostatic pressure
Toward the side with the higher concentration of impermeant solute
Equally in both directions with no net movement under any conditions
questions.why: Water follows solute, because the side with more solute particles has a lower water concentration, and water diffuses down its own gradient. Moving toward the more dilute side would be backward. Hydrostatic pressure pushes water away from the high pressure side, which is filtration rather than osmosis. Water does cross in both directions constantly, but the two fluxes are unequal whenever a solute gradient exists.
questions.answerText: Toward the side with the higher concentration of impermeant solute
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Osmotic pressure of a solution is best described as what?
options: The pressure the solution exerts on the walls of its container
The force with which solute particles push each other apart
The pressure generated by dissolved gases in the solution
The pressure needed to stop net water movement into the solution
questions.why: Osmotic pressure is defined by the opposing pressure needed to hold water back, and it rises as the number of impermeant particles rises. Pressure on the container wall is hydrostatic pressure, which is a separate quantity. Solute particles do not repel each other in any meaningful way here, since the effect is colligative and depends on number alone. Dissolved gas pressure is unrelated to osmosis.
questions.answerText: The pressure needed to stop net water movement into the solution
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Tonicity is always stated relative to what?
options: A cell, since it describes the solution's effect on cell volume
Pure water, since that is the zero point of the scale
One liter of solution, since that is the standard volume
Plasma sodium, since sodium is the main extracellular ion
questions.why: Tonicity has no units and no meaning on its own, because it is a comparison: it tells you whether a cell placed in the solution will swell, shrink, or hold steady. Pure water is the reference for osmolarity being zero, not for tonicity. A liter is the volume basis for osmolarity. Sodium sets most of the extracellular osmolarity but is not the reference the term is defined against.
questions.answerText: A cell, since it describes the solution's effect on cell volume
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the osmolarity of a 300 mM glucose solution?
options: 600 mOsm/L
300 mOsm/L
150 mOsm/L
900 mOsm/L
questions.why: Glucose does not dissociate, so each molecule contributes one particle and the millimolar and milliosmolar numbers are the same. Doubling to 600 would apply to a salt that splits into two ions, such as NaCl. Halving is never correct, since dissolving cannot reduce the particle count. Tripling would apply to a salt like CaCl2 that yields three ions.
questions.answerText: 300 mOsm/L
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the osmolarity of a 100 mM CaCl2 solution, assuming complete dissociation?
options: 100 mOsm/L
200 mOsm/L
300 mOsm/L
400 mOsm/L
questions.why: Each CaCl2 unit gives one Ca2+ and two Cl-, so three particles per formula unit and 100 times 3 gives 300 mOsm/L. Using 100 counts formula units and ignores dissociation. Using 200 would be right for NaCl, which yields only two particles. The charge on calcium does not add a fourth particle, since osmolarity counts particles rather than charges.
questions.answerText: 300 mOsm/L
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A solution contains 150 mM NaCl plus 100 mM glucose. What is its total osmolarity?
options: 250 mOsm/L
500 mOsm/L
350 mOsm/L
400 mOsm/L
questions.why: NaCl contributes 300 mOsm/L because it dissociates into two particles, and glucose contributes 100 mOsm/L because it does not dissociate, giving 400 mOsm/L in total. The value of 250 comes from adding the millimolar figures without doubling the salt. The value of 500 would come from doubling the glucose as well, which does not dissociate. The value of 350 mixes the two errors.
questions.answerText: 400 mOsm/L
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A red blood cell with an internal osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L is placed in a 300 mOsm/L urea solution. Urea crosses the cell membrane. How is this solution best described?
options: Isosmotic but hypotonic
Isosmotic and isotonic
Hyperosmotic and hypertonic
Hyposmotic and hypotonic
questions.why: The total particle count matches the cell, so the solution is isosmotic, but urea enters the cell and stops holding water outside, leaving an effective impermeant osmolarity of zero, so the cell swells and eventually lyses. Calling it isotonic treats urea as if it were trapped outside, which is the classic error. It is not hyperosmotic, because 300 equals 300. It is not hyposmotic either, since the measured osmolarity is normal, and only its tonicity is low.
questions.answerText: Isosmotic but hypotonic
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell of 300 mOsm/L is placed in a 400 mOsm/L NaCl solution. How is this solution described?
options: Hyperosmotic but isotonic
Hyperosmotic and hypertonic
Isosmotic and isotonic
Hyperosmotic but hypotonic
questions.why: NaCl does not cross the membrane appreciably, so all 400 mOsm/L is effective and the solution both measures higher than the cell and pulls water out of it. A hyperosmotic solution is isotonic only when the excess above 300 is made of penetrating solute. It is not isosmotic, since 400 is not 300. It could be hypotonic only if its impermeant fraction were below 300, which it is not.
questions.answerText: Hyperosmotic and hypertonic
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A solution contains 300 mOsm/L NaCl plus 100 mOsm/L urea. A cell of 300 mOsm/L is placed in it. What is the correct description of the solution?
options: Hyperosmotic and hypertonic
Isosmotic and isotonic
Hyperosmotic but isotonic
Hyposmotic and hypotonic
questions.why: Total osmolarity is 400 mOsm/L, so the solution is hyperosmotic, but only the 300 mOsm/L of NaCl is impermeant, and 300 matches the cell, so after urea equilibrates the cell returns to its original volume. Calling it hypertonic counts the urea as if it were trapped outside. It is not isosmotic, since the measured total is 400. It is not hyposmotic in any sense, since both its total and its effective osmolarity are at or above the cell's.
questions.answerText: Hyperosmotic but isotonic
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A solution contains 200 mOsm/L NaCl plus 200 mOsm/L urea. A cell of 300 mOsm/L is placed in it. How is this solution described?
options: Hyperosmotic and hypertonic
Isosmotic but hypertonic
Hyposmotic and hypotonic
Hyperosmotic but hypotonic
questions.why: The total of 400 mOsm/L is above the cell, so the solution is hyperosmotic, but only the 200 mOsm/L of NaCl stays outside, and 200 is less than the cell's 300, so urea equilibrates and the cell ends up swollen. This is the case that shows most clearly that a hyperosmotic solution is not automatically hypertonic. It is not hypertonic, because its effective osmolarity is below the cell's. It is not isosmotic or hyposmotic, since its measured total is 400 mOsm/L.
questions.answerText: Hyperosmotic but hypotonic
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell with 300 mOsm/L of impermeant intracellular solute is placed in a solution of 200 mOsm/L NaCl plus 200 mOsm/L urea. Describe what happens to cell volume immediately and then after urea has equilibrated.
options: The cell shrinks briefly, then swells past its original volume
The cell swells at once and keeps swelling, since the solution is hyposmotic
The cell shrinks and stays shrunken, since the solution measures 400 mOsm/L
The cell does not change volume at any point, since 400 is above 300
questions.why: Immediately the total osmolarity outside is 400 against 300 inside, so water leaves for a moment, but urea then diffuses into the cell down its gradient and water follows it, and since only 200 mOsm/L of impermeant solute remains outside against 300 inside, the cell finishes larger than it started. It does not swell from the first instant, because the initial total gradient favors water leaving. It does not stay shrunken, because urea does not stay outside. Volume certainly changes, in both directions at different times.
questions.answerText: The cell shrinks briefly, then swells past its original volume
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Two patients each have a plasma osmolarity of 320 mOsm/L. In one it is raised by glucose that cannot enter most cells without insulin, and in the other by retained urea. Predict the effect on cell volume in each case.
options: Both patients' cells shrink equally, since both have the same osmolarity
The glucose patient's cells shrink and the urea patient's cells stay near normal volume
The urea patient's cells shrink and the glucose patient's cells stay normal
Both patients' cells swell, since 320 is above the normal 300
questions.why: Glucose that cannot enter cells acts as an impermeant solute, so it raises both osmolarity and tonicity and draws water out of cells, while urea crosses membranes freely and equilibrates, raising osmolarity without raising tonicity. Equal osmolarity does not mean equal effect, which is exactly the point of separating the two terms. The comparison is not reversed, since urea is the penetrating solute here. Neither patient's cells swell, because neither plasma is hypotonic.
questions.answerText: The glucose patient's cells shrink and the urea patient's cells stay near normal volume
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A liter of 5 percent dextrose in water is infused. It is close to isosmotic in the bag, but the glucose is taken up by cells and metabolized. Predict the eventual effect on the tonicity of the extracellular fluid and on cell volume.
options: It stays isotonic indefinitely, so cell volume is unchanged
It becomes hypertonic as glucose accumulates, so cells shrink
It ends up acting like pure water, so tonicity falls and cells swell
It stays entirely in the vascular space, so only blood volume changes
questions.why: Once the glucose is transported into cells and burned, the particles that made the solution isosmotic are gone, and what remains distributed through the body is free water, which dilutes the extracellular fluid and drives water into cells. It cannot stay isotonic, because that would require the glucose to stay outside the cells indefinitely. Glucose is consumed rather than accumulated, so the solution does not become hypertonic. Water distributes through all compartments rather than staying in the vessels, which is why isotonic saline and dextrose in water are used for different purposes.
questions.answerText: It ends up acting like pure water, so tonicity falls and cells swell
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Cells placed in an unknown solution shrink within seconds, then return to exactly their original volume over the next several minutes. Glycerol crosses cell membranes slowly and NaCl does not. Which composition explains this result?
options: 400 mOsm/L NaCl and no glycerol
200 mOsm/L NaCl plus 100 mOsm/L glycerol
300 mOsm/L NaCl and no glycerol
300 mOsm/L NaCl plus 100 mOsm/L glycerol
questions.why: The initial total of 400 mOsm/L pulls water out and the cell shrinks, and as glycerol crosses and equilibrates the effective impermeant osmolarity outside settles at 300, which matches the cell, so volume returns exactly to baseline. A pure 400 mOsm/L NaCl solution would leave the cell shrunken permanently, since none of it can enter. The 200 plus 100 mixture would leave only 200 mOsm/L impermeant outside, so the cell would end up swollen rather than back at baseline. A plain 300 mOsm/L NaCl solution would cause no shrinkage at all.
questions.answerText: 300 mOsm/L NaCl plus 100 mOsm/L glycerol
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: During osmosis, which way does water move across a membrane that blocks the solute?
options: Toward the side with more impermeant solute
Toward the side with less impermeant solute
Toward the side with the higher hydrostatic pressure
Toward the warmer side of the membrane
questions.why: Water diffuses down its own concentration gradient, and adding solute lowers the water concentration, so water always moves toward the more concentrated side. Moving toward the dilute side would be backward and would concentrate that solution further. Hydrostatic pressure pushes water away from the high pressure side, which is filtration rather than osmosis. Temperature changes how fast osmosis happens but not which way water goes.
questions.answerText: Toward the side with more impermeant solute
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What happens to a cell placed in a hypotonic solution?
options: It shrinks
It swells
Its volume does not change
It loses solute but keeps its volume
questions.why: Hypotonic means the effective impermeant solute outside is lower than inside, so water enters and the cell gains volume, and enough of it will burst a red blood cell. Shrinkage is the hypertonic result. No change is the isotonic result. Cells do lose some solute during volume regulation, but the immediate and defining response to a hypotonic solution is swelling.
questions.answerText: It swells
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What happens to a cell placed in a hypertonic solution?
options: It swells
