Its volume does not change
It shrinks
It bursts
questions.why: Hypertonic means more effective impermeant solute outside than inside, so water leaves the cell and it loses volume, which in a red blood cell is seen as crenation. Swelling and bursting are hypotonic results and require the opposite gradient. No change would require the two effective osmolarities to be equal.
questions.answerText: It shrinks
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What happens to a cell placed in an isotonic solution?
options: Water stops crossing the membrane entirely
Water moves in, then the cell pumps it back out
The cell slowly shrinks as solutes leak out
There is no net water movement and volume stays the same
questions.why: Isotonic means the effective impermeant osmolarity is equal on both sides, so water crosses in both directions at the same rate and volume holds steady. Water does not stop crossing, and the two way traffic continues constantly. No active pumping of water is involved, since there is no water pump. A steady leak of solutes is not what defines the isotonic case.
questions.answerText: There is no net water movement and volume stays the same
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which membrane protein greatly increases the rate at which water crosses a cell membrane?
options: Aquaporin
The Na+/K+ ATPase
GLUT4
The voltage gated Na+ channel
questions.why: Aquaporins are narrow channels that pass water in single file and exclude ions, and cells such as those of the kidney collecting duct insert them when water must move quickly. The Na+/K+ ATPase moves ions and sets up the gradients that water then follows, but it does not carry water. GLUT4 carries glucose. Voltage gated Na+ channels carry Na+ during an action potential.
questions.answerText: Aquaporin
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which ion contributes most to the osmolarity of the intracellular fluid?
options: Na+
K+
Cl-
Ca2+
questions.why: Potassium is the dominant intracellular cation, and with the organic anions and proteins it accompanies, it accounts for most of the particles inside the cell. Na+ is the main extracellular cation and is kept low inside by the pump. Cl- is largely extracellular as well. Free intracellular Ca2+ is held near 0.0001 mM, far too low to affect osmolarity.
questions.answerText: K+
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which ion contributes most to the osmolarity of the extracellular fluid?
options: K+
Ca2+
Na+
Mg2+
questions.why: Sodium and the anions that follow it make up most of the roughly 300 mOsm/L of extracellular fluid, which is why plasma sodium tracks so closely with plasma osmolarity. K+ is the main intracellular cation and sits near 4 mEq/L outside. Extracellular Ca2+ and Mg2+ are present at only a few milliequivalents per liter and contribute little to the total.
questions.answerText: Na+
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: When a cell has reached osmotic equilibrium with the fluid around it, how do intracellular and extracellular osmolarity compare?
options: Intracellular osmolarity is higher
Extracellular osmolarity is higher
They vary independently, since the membrane separates them
They are equal
questions.why: Water crosses cell membranes easily, so it moves until the osmolarity on the two sides matches, and body fluids sit at roughly 300 mOsm/L everywhere at equilibrium. A permanent difference cannot be maintained, because water would keep moving until it was erased. That is true whichever side is imagined to be higher. The membrane blocks solutes, not water, so the two compartments are osmotically linked.
questions.answerText: They are equal
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell with an internal osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L is placed in 150 mOsm/L NaCl. Which way does water move, and what happens to the cell?
options: Water enters and the cell swells
Water leaves and the cell shrinks
No net water movement occurs
Water enters and then leaves, so volume returns to normal
questions.why: The outside has fewer impermeant particles than the inside, so water moves toward the cell interior and volume rises. Water cannot leave, since that would require a higher effective osmolarity outside. There is a gradient here, so net movement occurs. Volume does not recover on its own in this case, because NaCl cannot enter the cell to erase the gradient.
questions.answerText: Water enters and the cell swells
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell with an internal osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L is placed in 600 mOsm/L NaCl. Predict the result.
options: Water enters and the cell swells
Water leaves and the cell shrinks
Volume is unchanged because NaCl cannot cross
NaCl enters until the two sides are equal
questions.why: With twice the impermeant solute outside, water moves out of the cell and the cell shrivels. Swelling would require the outside to be more dilute. The fact that NaCl cannot cross is precisely why the water gradient persists, so it does not protect volume. Sodium does leak slowly but is pumped back out, so it does not equilibrate the way urea does.
questions.answerText: Water leaves and the cell shrinks
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell with an internal osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L is placed in 300 mOsm/L NaCl. What happens to cell volume?
options: It rises slowly as NaCl enters
It falls slowly as water leaves
It stays the same
It rises sharply and the cell lyses
questions.why: The impermeant solute concentrations match on the two sides, so water crosses equally in both directions and the cell holds its volume, which is why 0.9 percent NaCl is used as an intravenous fluid. NaCl does not flood in, since the pump keeps intracellular Na+ low. There is no gradient to draw water out. Lysis requires a hypotonic solution.
questions.answerText: It stays the same
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell with an internal osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L is placed in a 300 mOsm/L urea solution. Predict what happens to cell volume.
options: Volume is unchanged, because the two osmolarities are equal
The cell shrinks, because urea pulls water out
Volume is unchanged, because urea cannot cross the membrane
The cell swells, because urea enters and stops holding water outside
questions.why: Urea crosses the membrane and equilibrates on both sides, so it stops contributing any osmotic pull, leaving the cell's own impermeant solutes to draw water in, and a red cell in this solution will lyse. Equal osmolarity is not enough, because tonicity depends only on the impermeant fraction. Urea cannot pull water out once it has equilibrated. Urea does cross, which is the whole reason this solution is hypotonic despite being isosmotic.
questions.answerText: The cell swells, because urea enters and stops holding water outside
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell is given many extra aquaporins and then placed in a hypotonic solution. How does this change the outcome?
options: The cell swells faster, but the final volume is the same
The cell swells to a larger final volume
The cell no longer swells, because aquaporins let solute escape
The cell shrinks instead, because water can now leave more easily
questions.why: Aquaporins change how quickly water moves, while the osmotic gradient decides how far it moves, so the endpoint is set by the solute concentrations and is unaffected. A larger endpoint would require a bigger gradient, which aquaporins do not create. Aquaporins pass water and exclude solute, so nothing escapes through them. Water moves both ways through aquaporins, and the net direction still follows the gradient, which favors entry here.
questions.answerText: The cell swells faster, but the final volume is the same
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A person becomes dehydrated and extracellular osmolarity rises from 300 to 320 mOsm/L. Predict the effect on intracellular volume.
options: Water enters the cells, so intracellular volume rises
Water leaves the cells, so intracellular volume falls
Intracellular volume is unchanged, since the membrane blocks water
Intracellular volume rises, since the cells make more solute
questions.why: Losing water from the extracellular fluid concentrates the solutes left behind, so the extracellular fluid becomes hypertonic to the cells and water follows the gradient out of them, shrinking every compartment. Water cannot enter against that gradient. Cell membranes are highly permeable to water, so the intracellular compartment always shares in an osmotic disturbance. Brain cells do generate organic osmolytes over hours, but that is a slow adaptation and not the immediate result.
questions.answerText: Water leaves the cells, so intracellular volume falls
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell placed in a hypotonic solution doubles its volume. What has happened to its intracellular osmolarity?
options: It has doubled, because the cell now holds twice as much fluid
It is unchanged, because osmolarity is a fixed property of the cell
It has fallen to about half, because the same solute is spread through twice the water
It has fallen to a quarter, because volume and osmolarity are squared terms
questions.why: The impermeant solutes cannot leave, so doubling the volume dilutes them to half their original concentration, and that dilution is what stops further water entry. Osmolarity cannot rise when water is added. It is not fixed, since it is a concentration and depends on the volume it is measured in. Osmolarity varies inversely with volume, with no squared relationship involved.
questions.answerText: It has fallen to about half, because the same solute is spread through twice the water
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A person drinks no water for a day and plasma osmolarity rises. Trace what happens to the extracellular and intracellular compartments once water has redistributed.
options: Only the extracellular compartment shrinks, since cell membranes block water
The intracellular compartment shrinks while the extracellular compartment returns to its original volume
Both compartments end up larger, since cells release solute to hold water
Both compartments end up smaller and more concentrated, since water leaves cells until the osmolarities match
questions.why: Water is lost from the extracellular fluid first, which raises its osmolarity, and because water crosses cell membranes freely it then moves out of cells until both sides are equal, so both compartments lose volume and both end above 300 mOsm/L. The intracellular compartment cannot be spared, since membranes are permeable to water. The extracellular compartment gains some water back from the cells but does not return to its starting volume, since total body water has fallen. Neither compartment can grow when water is being lost from the body.
questions.answerText: Both compartments end up smaller and more concentrated, since water leaves cells until the osmolarities match
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Compare infusing one liter of isotonic saline with infusing one liter of pure water. Predict where each ends up and what happens to cell volume.
options: Saline stays outside the cells while water spreads everywhere and swells them
Both stay extracellular, so neither changes cell volume
Both enter cells equally, so both swell the cells by the same amount
Saline enters cells and water stays extracellular, so saline swells the cells
questions.why: The Na+ in saline is held in the extracellular fluid by the pump, so it expands that compartment without creating an osmotic gradient across the cell membrane. Pure water adds no impermeant solute, so it dilutes the extracellular fluid and water then moves into cells until osmolarity is equal again. Saline cannot swell cells, because its solute cannot enter them. Water does not stay outside, because there is nothing holding it there.
questions.answerText: Saline stays outside the cells while water spreads everywhere and swells them
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell placed in a hypotonic solution swells at first, then over the next twenty minutes returns partway toward its original size while still in the same solution. What accounts for the recovery?
options: The cell pumps water back out using ATP
The cell exports K+, Cl-, and organic osmolytes, so water follows them out
The solution gradually becomes hypertonic on its own
The membrane becomes impermeable to water once the cell is stretched
questions.why: Since water cannot be moved directly, the only way for a cell to shed volume is to reduce its own impermeant solute content, and stretch activated channels release KCl and small organic solutes so water follows them out, a response called regulatory volume decrease. There is no ATP driven water pump anywhere in the body. The bathing solution is large and does not change measurably. Losing water permeability would freeze the cell at its swollen volume rather than shrink it.
questions.answerText: The cell exports K+, Cl-, and organic osmolytes, so water follows them out
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Cells are placed in two solutions that both measure 400 mOsm/L. Solution A is all NaCl. Solution B is 200 mOsm/L NaCl plus 200 mOsm/L glycerol, which slowly enters cells. Predict the final volume in each.
options: Both end up shrunken to the same degree, since both measure 400 mOsm/L
Cells in A end up swollen and cells in B end up shrunken
Cells in A end up shrunken, while cells in B end up swollen above their original volume
Both return to their original volume, since 400 mOsm/L is close to normal
questions.why: In A the entire 400 mOsm/L is impermeant, so water leaves and the cells stay shrunken, while in B only the 200 mOsm/L of NaCl stays outside, and once glycerol equilibrates that leaves 200 against the cell's 300, so water moves in and the cells finish larger than they started. Equal osmolarity does not predict equal volume change, because only impermeant solute counts. The pattern is not reversed, since it is B that contains the penetrating solute. Neither returns exactly to baseline, since neither effective osmolarity equals 300.
questions.answerText: Cells in A end up shrunken, while cells in B end up swollen above their original volume
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the diffusion and osmosis lab, dialysis tubing is used as a model of what?
options: A membrane that admits every solute equally
A membrane that actively pumps solutes across
A solid barrier that admits nothing
A selectively permeable membrane with pores of a fixed size
questions.why: Dialysis tubing lets small molecules through its pores and holds back large ones, which is why it models the size selectivity of a cell membrane. It is not freely permeable, since starch stays inside throughout the experiment. It has no proteins and no ATP, so it cannot pump anything. It is clearly not solid, since water and iodine cross it readily.
questions.answerText: A selectively permeable membrane with pores of a fixed size
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which indicator is used to detect starch, and what color change signals a positive result?
options: Iodine solution, which turns from amber to blue black
Benedict's reagent, which turns from blue to orange
Biuret reagent, which turns from blue to violet
Phenolphthalein, which turns from clear to pink
questions.why: Iodine slips into the coiled starch molecule and produces a deep blue black color, so any container that turns blue black contains starch. Benedict's reagent detects reducing sugars such as glucose. Biuret reagent detects protein. Phenolphthalein is a pH indicator and says nothing about carbohydrate.
questions.answerText: Iodine solution, which turns from amber to blue black
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A positive Benedict's test indicates the presence of what, and what does the positive result look like?
options: Starch, shown by a blue black color that appears without heating
A reducing sugar, shown by an orange to brick red color on heating
Protein, shown by a violet color that appears without heating
Lipid, shown by a translucent spot left on brown paper
questions.why: Benedict's reagent is reduced by the free aldehyde group of glucose when heated, and the deeper the color goes toward brick red, the more sugar is present. Starch gives no reaction with Benedict's and is detected with iodine instead. Protein is detected with Biuret. The translucent spot test is for lipid.
questions.answerText: A reducing sugar, shown by an orange to brick red color on heating
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A dialysis bag filled with starch solution is placed in a beaker of iodine solution. Which substance crosses the tubing?
options: Starch, because it is at higher concentration inside
Both cross at similar rates
Iodine, because it is much smaller than starch
Neither crosses, since the tubing is impermeable
questions.why: The pores admit small molecules such as iodine and exclude the large branched starch polymer, so the bag turns blue black while the beaker stays amber. Starch cannot cross regardless of its concentration, because size, not gradient, sets what fits through a pore. The two do not cross at similar rates, since one does not cross at all. The tubing is permeable, which is the point of using it.
questions.answerText: Iodine, because it is much smaller than starch
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Two dyes are placed in separate wells of an agar plate. Which one diffuses farther in a given time?
options: The dye with the larger molecular weight
The darker colored dye
The dye placed in the larger well
The dye with the smaller molecular weight
questions.why: Smaller molecules have larger diffusion coefficients, so they travel farther in the same amount of time, which is what this demonstration is designed to show. Larger molecules always lag behind. Color intensity affects how easy the ring is to see but not how fast the molecules move. Well size changes the amount of dye, not the speed of an individual molecule.
questions.answerText: The dye with the smaller molecular weight
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In a thistle tube osmometer, a sucrose solution is separated from distilled water by a selectively permeable membrane. Why does the fluid column rise?
options: Water moves into the sucrose solution by osmosis
Sucrose moves out into the distilled water
Air pressure pushes the column up the tube
The membrane actively pumps water upward
questions.why: Sucrose cannot cross the membrane, so water crosses toward the higher solute concentration and the added volume has nowhere to go but up the tube. Sucrose leaving would lower the column rather than raise it, and the membrane blocks it anyway. Air pressure is the same on both sides and does not drive the rise. Membranes in this setup are passive and have no pumping ability.
questions.answerText: Water moves into the sucrose solution by osmosis
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the appropriate control in a dialysis bag osmosis experiment?
options: A bag of concentrated sucrose placed in distilled water
A bag of distilled water placed in a beaker of distilled water
A bag of distilled water placed in concentrated sucrose
A beaker of sucrose with no bag in it at all
questions.why: The control has no osmotic gradient, so any change in its mass reveals handling error, evaporation, or a leaking bag rather than osmosis. The other bag setups all contain deliberate gradients and are experimental conditions rather than controls. A beaker with no bag has nothing to weigh and tests nothing.
questions.answerText: A bag of distilled water placed in a beaker of distilled water
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How is percent change in mass calculated for a dialysis bag?
options: Final mass divided by initial mass, times 100
Initial mass minus final mass, divided by final mass, times 100
Final mass minus initial mass, divided by initial mass, times 100
Final mass minus initial mass, times 100
questions.why: Percent change compares the change to where you started, so the difference is divided by the initial mass, and the sign then tells you whether the bag gained or lost water. Dividing final by initial gives percent of original rather than percent change, so an unchanged bag would read 100 instead of 0. Reversing the subtraction flips the sign of every result. Leaving out the denominator gives an answer that depends on the size of the bag rather than its relative change.
questions.answerText: Final mass minus initial mass, divided by initial mass, times 100
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A dialysis bag containing 30 percent sucrose is placed in a beaker of distilled water. What happens to the mass of the bag?
options: It decreases, because sucrose leaves the bag
It stays the same, because sucrose cannot cross
It decreases, because water moves out of the bag
It increases, because water moves into the bag
questions.why: The bag holds the higher solute concentration and sucrose cannot escape, so water enters by osmosis and the bag gains mass. Sucrose is too large for the pores, so it does not leave. The fact that sucrose cannot cross is exactly why water moves, so it does not keep the mass constant. Water moves toward solute, not away from it.
questions.answerText: It increases, because water moves into the bag
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A dialysis bag filled with distilled water is placed in a beaker of 30 percent sucrose. Predict the change in bag mass.
options: It decreases, because water leaves the bag
It increases, because sucrose enters the bag
It increases, because water enters the bag
It stays the same, because water crosses equally in both directions
questions.why: Now the higher solute concentration is outside, so water leaves the bag and it loses mass. Sucrose cannot enter through the pores, so it cannot add weight. Water moves toward the concentrated beaker, not into the dilute bag. Water does cross both ways, but the fluxes are unequal whenever a gradient exists.
questions.answerText: It decreases, because water leaves the bag
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A bag of 10 percent sucrose is placed in a beaker of 30 percent sucrose. What happens?
options: The bag gains mass, because it contains sucrose too
The bag loses mass, because the beaker is hypertonic to the bag
The bag is unchanged, because both contain the same solute
The bag gains mass, because water always moves into a bag
questions.why: What matters is the difference in concentration, not whether both sides contain sucrose, and the more concentrated beaker draws water out of the bag. Simply containing sucrose does not pull water in if the outside has more. Identical solutes at different concentrations still produce an osmotic gradient. Direction is set by the gradient, so there is no rule that bags always gain.
questions.answerText: The bag loses mass, because the beaker is hypertonic to the bag
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A dialysis bag weighs 20.0 g at the start and 23.0 g after 30 minutes. What is the percent change in mass?
options: An increase of 3 percent
An increase of 13 percent
An increase of 15 percent
An increase of 115 percent
questions.why: The gain of 3.0 g divided by the starting mass of 20.0 g is 0.15, or 15 percent. Reporting 3 percent uses the raw gain in grams and ignores the denominator. Using the final mass of 23.0 g as the denominator gives about 13 percent, which compares the change to where the bag ended rather than where it began. The figure of 115 percent is the final mass as a percentage of the initial mass, not the change.
questions.answerText: An increase of 15 percent
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A bag of starch solution sits in a beaker of iodine solution for 30 minutes. What do you expect to see?
options: The beaker turns blue black while the bag stays white
Both the bag and the beaker turn blue black
Neither changes color, since neither substance can cross
The bag contents turn blue black while the beaker stays amber
questions.why: Iodine is small enough to pass through the pores and meets the starch inside, so color develops in the bag, while starch is too large to reach the iodine outside. A blue black beaker would mean starch had escaped, which the pore size prevents. Both turning would require both molecules to cross. Iodine does cross, so a total absence of color change is not expected.
questions.answerText: The bag contents turn blue black while the beaker stays amber
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Potato cores are placed in a series of sucrose solutions and weighed. The concentration at which the mass change is zero tells you what?
options: The solution is isotonic to the potato cells
The solution contains no dissolved sucrose at all
The potato cells have died and stopped exchanging water
The cell membranes have become impermeable to water
questions.why: Zero net water movement means the outside and inside have the same effective osmolarity, so reading the crossover point off the graph is a way to measure the concentration of the potato cell sap. A zero sucrose solution would be distilled water and would cause the largest gain of all. Dead cells with leaky membranes usually lose solute and change mass rather than holding steady. A water impermeable membrane is not what is being demonstrated, and potato cells are quite permeable to water.
questions.answerText: The solution is isotonic to the potato cells
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The same osmosis setup is run at 40 C instead of 20 C. What changes?
options: The final mass change is much larger, since heat drives more water across
Equilibrium is reached sooner, but the final mass change is about the same
The bag loses mass instead of gaining it
Nothing changes, since osmosis is independent of temperature
questions.why: Warming speeds molecular movement, so water crosses faster and the curve reaches its plateau earlier, but the endpoint is set by the concentration gradient, which the temperature did not change. A larger endpoint would require a bigger gradient. The direction of water movement is set by solute concentration, so warming cannot reverse it. Temperature clearly affects the rate, so nothing changing is not right either.
questions.answerText: Equilibrium is reached sooner, but the final mass change is about the same
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A dialysis bag containing both starch and glucose is placed in distilled water. After 30 minutes the beaker water tests positive with Benedict's reagent and negative with iodine. What do these two results together tell you?
options: Both crossed, but starch is present at too low a concentration to detect
Neither crossed, and the Benedict's result came from the tubing itself
Glucose crossed and starch did not, so the pore size lies between the two molecules
Starch crossed and was digested to glucose in the beaker
questions.why: A positive sugar test outside proves glucose passed, and a negative iodine test outside proves starch stayed in, so the tubing discriminates by size between a monosaccharide and a large polysaccharide. If starch had crossed, iodine would have detected it, since the iodine test is sensitive. The tubing itself is not a reducing sugar and does not give a false positive here. There is no enzyme in the beaker, so starch cannot be broken down there.
questions.answerText: Glucose crossed and starch did not, so the pore size lies between the two molecules
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A dye diffuses 4 mm from an agar well in 20 minutes. About how far will it have traveled at 80 minutes, and why?
options: About 16 mm, because distance rises in proportion to time
About 4 mm, because diffusion stops once a ring has formed
About 32 mm, because the rate accelerates as the ring widens
About 8 mm, because distance rises with the square root of time
questions.why: Diffusion is a random walk, so time scales with the square of distance and distance with the square root of time, and quadrupling the time therefore only doubles the distance. Simple proportionality would predict 16 mm and badly overestimates how far diffusion can reach. Diffusion does not stop, it just slows as the gradient flattens. The process decelerates rather than accelerating, since the concentration difference falls as the dye spreads.
questions.answerText: About 8 mm, because distance rises with the square root of time
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A student predicts that her bag of 20 percent sucrose in distilled water will gain mass, but it loses 4 percent. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The bag leaked or was not sealed, so sucrose and fluid escaped
Water always leaves a bag placed in distilled water
Sucrose diffused into the bag from the beaker and displaced water
The beaker water was distilled, which prevents osmosis
questions.why: With sucrose inside and pure water outside the osmotic prediction is unambiguous, so a mass loss points to a mechanical failure, most often an unsealed clip or a puncture, and the fix is to check the seal and reweigh a control bag. Water moves toward solute, so it cannot routinely leave a bag placed in distilled water. There is no sucrose in the beaker to diffuse inward. Distilled water is the strongest osmotic driving condition in this experiment rather than a condition that prevents osmosis.
questions.answerText: The bag leaked or was not sealed, so sucrose and fluid escaped
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Two dialysis bags hold the same volume and the same sucrose concentration, but one is shaped so that it exposes twice as much surface to the beaker. Predict how their mass curves compare.
options: The wider bag reaches a larger final mass change, since more water can enter
The wider bag gains mass faster, but both reach the same final mass change
Both curves are identical, since surface area is not part of osmosis
The wider bag gains less, since the water is spread over more surface
questions.why: Surface area is a rate term in Fick's law, so more area means more water crossing per minute, while the endpoint is set by the sucrose gradient, which is the same in both bags. A larger endpoint would need a stronger gradient, not more area. Area is very much part of the rate, so identical curves are not expected. Spreading the same driving force over more area increases total flux rather than diluting it.
questions.answerText: The wider bag gains mass faster, but both reach the same final mass change
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the term for the shrunken, scalloped appearance of a red blood cell placed in a hypertonic solution?
options: Hemolysis
Agglutination
Crenation
Phagocytosis
questions.why: Water leaves the cell, the membrane loses its smooth curve, and the surface takes on spiky projections, which is crenation. Hemolysis is the opposite result and happens in hypotonic solutions. Agglutination is clumping caused by antibodies and has nothing to do with tonicity. Phagocytosis is engulfment by a white blood cell.
questions.answerText: Crenation
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What happens to a red blood cell placed in a strongly hypotonic solution?
options: It shrinks and crenates
It keeps its biconcave shape
It divides into two smaller cells
It swells and undergoes hemolysis
questions.why: Water enters until the membrane can stretch no further, and the cell bursts and releases its hemoglobin, which is hemolysis. Crenation requires water to leave, which needs a hypertonic solution. The biconcave shape is preserved only in an isotonic solution. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and do not divide at all.
questions.answerText: It swells and undergoes hemolysis
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which NaCl solution is isotonic to human red blood cells?
options: 0.9 percent NaCl
0.45 percent NaCl
3 percent NaCl
9 percent NaCl
questions.why: A 0.9 percent NaCl solution is about 154 mM, which gives roughly 300 mOsm/L once the salt dissociates, matching the cell and leaving volume unchanged. The 0.45 percent solution is half strength and is hypotonic, so cells swell. Both 3 percent and 9 percent are hypertonic and crenate cells, and 9 percent is ten times the isotonic concentration.
questions.answerText: 0.9 percent NaCl
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A tube of red blood cells that were suspended in a hypotonic solution now looks clear red rather than cloudy. What does that appearance indicate?
options: The cells have crenated and settled to the bottom
Hemolysis has occurred and hemoglobin is dissolved in the solution
The cells have clumped together into visible aggregates
The hemoglobin has been chemically destroyed by the solution
questions.why: Intact cells scatter light and make the suspension cloudy, so when they burst and release hemoglobin into solution the tube becomes transparent, and this laked appearance is the visual endpoint of hemolysis. Crenated cells are still intact and keep the suspension cloudy. Clumping produces visible flecks rather than clarity. The hemoglobin is released rather than destroyed, which is why the solution stays red.
questions.answerText: Hemolysis has occurred and hemoglobin is dissolved in the solution
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which substance is released into the surrounding fluid when a red blood cell hemolyzes?
options: Albumin
Fibrinogen
Hemoglobin
Bile
questions.why: Hemoglobin fills the cytoplasm of the red blood cell, so rupturing the membrane spills it into the surrounding fluid. Albumin and fibrinogen are plasma proteins made by the liver and are already outside cells. Bile is made in the liver and secreted into the gut, and it is not a red cell constituent.
questions.answerText: Hemoglobin
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the normal shape of a human red blood cell in an isotonic solution?
options: A perfect sphere
A flat square plate
A branched star
A biconcave disc
questions.why: The biconcave disc is the shape seen in plasma and in isotonic saline, and its dimpled sides give the cell extra surface area for its volume. A sphere is what a red cell becomes as it swells toward lysis, not its resting shape. Flat plates and star shapes are not red blood cell forms, though a crenated cell can look spiky.
questions.answerText: A biconcave disc
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the approximate osmolarity of the plasma in which red blood cells normally circulate?
options: About 300 mOsm/L
About 100 mOsm/L
About 600 mOsm/L
About 1200 mOsm/L
questions.why: Plasma sits near 300 mOsm/L, and the interior of the red blood cell matches it, which is why the cell holds its shape in the circulation. A value of 100 would be strongly hypotonic and would lyse the cells. Values of 600 and 1200 would be strongly hypertonic and would crenate them, and 1200 is closer to the concentrated interstitial fluid of the kidney medulla.
questions.answerText: About 300 mOsm/L
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What advantage does the biconcave shape give a red blood cell that is placed in a mildly hypotonic solution?
options: It allows the cell to pump the extra water back out using ATP
It gives the cell extra surface area, so it can swell before bursting
It makes the membrane completely impermeable to water
It lets the cell shed solute through pores in the dimples
questions.why: The dimpled disc holds less volume than a sphere of the same surface area, so the cell has slack to take on water and round up before the membrane is stretched to breaking. There is no water pump in any human cell. The membrane is highly water permeable, and that is why the cell swells at all. The dimples are shape, not openings, and no solute escapes through them.
questions.answerText: It gives the cell extra surface area, so it can swell before bursting
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Red blood cells are placed in 0.45 percent NaCl. Predict what happens.
options: They crenate, since the solution is hypertonic
They keep their normal shape, since the solution is isotonic
They swell and some may hemolyze, since the solution is hypotonic
They shrink at first and then return to normal
questions.why: Half strength saline is about 150 mOsm/L, well below the cell's 300 mOsm/L, so water moves into the cells and they round up and can burst. Crenation would require the outside to be more concentrated. Isotonic saline is 0.9 percent, twice this concentration. There is no initial shrinkage, because the gradient favors water entry from the first moment.
questions.answerText: They swell and some may hemolyze, since the solution is hypotonic
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Red blood cells are placed in 3 percent NaCl. Predict the result.
options: They gain water and hemolyze
They keep their normal biconcave shape
They gain water at first, then burst
They lose water and crenate
questions.why: A 3 percent solution is more than three times isotonic, so water leaves the cells and they shrivel with a scalloped edge. Water cannot enter against that gradient, so hemolysis will not occur. Normal shape is preserved only near 0.9 percent NaCl. There is no early swelling phase, since the solution is hypertonic from the start and NaCl does not enter the cell.
questions.answerText: They lose water and crenate
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Under the microscope a technician sees shrunken, spiky red blood cells. Which solution was most likely added?
options: 1.8 percent NaCl
0.9 percent NaCl
0.3 percent NaCl
Distilled water
questions.why: Crenation requires a hypertonic solution, and 1.8 percent NaCl is twice the isotonic concentration, so water leaves the cells. The 0.9 percent solution is isotonic and leaves the cells looking normal. Both 0.3 percent NaCl and distilled water are hypotonic and would swell or lyse the cells rather than shrink them.
questions.answerText: 1.8 percent NaCl
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Red blood cells sit in isotonic saline and show no change in volume. What is happening to water at the membrane?
options: Water has stopped crossing the membrane entirely
Water crosses both ways at equal rates, so there is no net movement
Water enters continuously and is broken down inside the cell
Water enters and is pumped back out by the Na+/K+ ATPase
questions.why: Osmotic equilibrium is a balance of two equal fluxes, not a halt, and water molecules keep moving through aquaporins constantly. A complete stop would require an impermeable membrane, which the red cell does not have. Water is not consumed inside the cell in any amount that matters here. The Na+/K+ ATPase moves ions and cannot pump water.
questions.answerText: Water crosses both ways at equal rates, so there is no net movement
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A blood sample is accidentally diluted with distilled water instead of isotonic diluent before the red blood cells are counted. Predict the effect on the count.
options: The count is falsely high, because the cells swelled and became easier to see
The count is unaffected, because dilution is corrected mathematically
The count is falsely low, because many cells lysed before being counted
The count is falsely high, because lysed cells break into countable fragments
questions.why: Distilled water is profoundly hypotonic, so cells take on water and burst, and a burst cell is no longer counted, which is exactly why isotonic diluents are required for cell counts. Swelling does not raise the count, since a cell that lyses disappears from the field. The dilution factor correction cannot recover cells that were destroyed. Red cell fragments and empty membranes are not counted as intact cells.
questions.answerText: The count is falsely low, because many cells lysed before being counted
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Red blood cells are suspended in a solution and the tube stays cloudy for an hour with the cells looking normal under the microscope. What can you conclude about the solution?
options: It must be distilled water, since nothing happened
It must be hypertonic, since the cells did not burst
It contains only penetrating solutes, since the cells stayed intact
It is isotonic to the cells, whatever its measured osmolarity
questions.why: Unchanged volume over time is the definition of an isotonic solution, and it tells you the impermeant solute concentration matches the cell even if the total measured osmolarity is higher. Distilled water would have lysed the cells within minutes. A hypertonic solution would have crenated them, which the microscope would show. A solution of only penetrating solutes would behave as hypotonic and lyse the cells.
questions.answerText: It is isotonic to the cells, whatever its measured osmolarity
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Two tubes each contain a 300 mOsm/L solution. Tube A is NaCl and tube B is urea. Red blood cells are added to both. Predict and explain the outcome in each tube.
options: Cells in A stay normal, while cells in B swell and hemolyze because urea enters the cell
Cells in both tubes stay normal, since both solutions are 300 mOsm/L
Cells in A crenate and cells in B stay normal
Cells in both tubes hemolyze, since 300 mOsm/L is below the cell osmolarity
questions.why: NaCl cannot cross the red cell membrane, so its full 300 mOsm/L holds water outside and volume is stable, while urea crosses freely, equilibrates on both sides, and leaves the cell's own impermeant solutes unopposed, so water follows in and the cell bursts. Equal osmolarity does not guarantee equal tonicity, and this pair is the clearest demonstration of that. NaCl at 300 mOsm/L matches the cell, so it cannot crenate it. The cell interior is about 300 mOsm/L, so 300 mOsm/L of impermeant solute is not hypotonic.
questions.answerText: Cells in A stay normal, while cells in B swell and hemolyze because urea enters the cell
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Red blood cells are placed in 5 percent dextrose in water, which measures close to 300 mOsm/L. Glucose enters red cells through GLUT1 and is metabolized. Predict what happens over the next hour.
options: The cells hold their volume indefinitely, because the solution is isosmotic
The cells swell and eventually hemolyze, because the glucose does not stay outside
The cells crenate, because glucose accumulates outside as water enters
The cells swell for a moment and then return exactly to normal volume
questions.why: Glucose that is transported into the cell and then consumed cannot act as an impermeant solute, so the effective osmolarity of the bathing solution falls toward zero and water moves in until the membrane fails. Being isosmotic in the bottle is not the same as being isotonic to a cell that takes up the solute. Glucose is consumed rather than concentrated outside, so crenation will not occur. Volume does not recover, because there is no impermeant solute left outside to pull water back.
questions.answerText: The cells swell and eventually hemolyze, because the glucose does not stay outside
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In an osmotic fragility test, spherocytes from a patient hemolyze in 0.65 percent NaCl while normal red cells survive until about 0.45 percent. Explain the difference.
options: Spherocytes contain more hemoglobin, so they draw in water faster
Spherocytes lack aquaporins, so water builds up against the membrane
Spherocytes have less surface area for their volume, so they burst sooner
Spherocytes are hypotonic to normal cells, so they gain water from them
questions.why: A normal biconcave cell can swell toward a sphere before its membrane is stretched, but a cell that is already spherical has used up that reserve, so even a mildly hypotonic solution pushes it past the breaking point. Hemoglobin content is not what sets the limit here, since the cell fails mechanically rather than osmotically. Fewer aquaporins would slow water entry rather than hastening lysis. The cells are suspended in the test solution, not in contact with normal cells, so no exchange between cell types is involved.
questions.answerText: Spherocytes have less surface area for their volume, so they burst sooner
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A technician adds red blood cells to 1.8 percent NaCl and sees crenation, then adds an equal volume of distilled water to the tube. Predict what the cells look like afterward.
options: They hemolyze, because distilled water was added to the tube
They stay crenated, because crenation cannot be reversed
They crenate further, because adding fluid raises the salt concentration
They return to their normal biconcave shape
questions.why: Adding an equal volume of water halves the salt concentration, taking 1.8 percent down to 0.9 percent, which is isotonic, so water moves back into the shrunken cells and they resume their normal shape. The distilled water is diluted by the saline already present, so the final solution is not hypotonic. Crenation is a reversible osmotic change as long as the membrane is intact. Adding water lowers the concentration rather than raising it.
questions.answerText: They return to their normal biconcave shape
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which membrane protein forms a continuous water filled pore that a solute passes through without binding to a transport site?
options: A carrier protein
A channel protein
An ATP driven pump
A membrane receptor
questions.why: A channel protein lines an aqueous pore, so solute flows through without a binding and release step. A carrier binds the solute and changes shape to deliver it, which is slower. A pump also binds solute but spends ATP to move it uphill. A receptor binds a ligand to start a signal and does not carry the ligand across.
questions.answerText: A channel protein
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What supplies the energy for facilitated diffusion of glucose into a cell?
options: Direct hydrolysis of ATP by the carrier
The concentration gradient of glucose itself
The Na+ gradient built by the Na+/K+ ATPase
Hydrolysis of GTP by a coupled G protein
questions.why: Facilitated diffusion is passive. The carrier only provides a path, and the glucose gradient does the work, so transport runs downhill and stops at equilibrium. Direct ATP use would make it primary active transport, and using the Na+ gradient would make it secondary active transport. GTP hydrolysis belongs to signaling proteins, not to GLUT carriers.
questions.answerText: The concentration gradient of glucose itself
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A carrier moves D-glucose across the membrane but will not move L-glucose. Which property is this?
options: Electrogenicity
Saturation
Competition
Specificity
questions.why: Specificity means the binding site fits some molecules and rejects others, which is why a mirror image sugar is turned away. Saturation is the plateau in rate when every site is busy. Competition happens when two molecules that both fit the site slow each other down. Electrogenicity refers to a transporter moving net charge, which this carrier does not.
questions.answerText: Specificity
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which substance crosses the lipid bilayer most readily by simple diffusion, with no membrane protein required?
options: An amino acid
Glucose
Na+
Oxygen
questions.why: Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it dissolves in the lipid core and crosses directly. Glucose and amino acids are polar and need carriers such as GLUT or amino acid transporters. Na+ carries a charge and drags a shell of water with it, so it needs a channel or a transporter and essentially never slips through the bilayer.
questions.answerText: Oxygen
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The GLUT family of transporters moves glucose across a cell membrane by which mechanism?
options: Primary active transport
Secondary active transport
Facilitated diffusion
Simple diffusion through the bilayer
questions.why: GLUT proteins are carriers that let glucose move down its own gradient, which is facilitated diffusion. Primary active transport would require GLUT to hydrolyze ATP, and secondary active transport would require it to be coupled to Na+, which is true of SGLT but not of GLUT. Simple diffusion is ruled out because glucose is polar and needs the protein.
questions.answerText: Facilitated diffusion
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: During facilitated diffusion of an uncharged solute, net movement stops at which point?
options: When the solute concentration is equal on both sides of the membrane
When every carrier has completed one cycle
When the cell runs out of ATP
When the membrane potential reaches zero
questions.why: Passive transport stops when the driving gradient is gone, so net flux ends at equal concentrations even though single molecules keep moving both ways. Carriers are reusable and are not consumed by a cycle. ATP is irrelevant because the process is passive, and membrane potential drives charged solutes, not an uncharged one like glucose.
questions.answerText: When the solute concentration is equal on both sides of the membrane
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the name for the maximum transport rate reached when every carrier binding site is occupied?
options: Transport maximum
Permeability coefficient
Equilibrium potential
Renal threshold
questions.why: The transport maximum is the ceiling set by the number of carriers, and once it is reached, adding more solute does not speed transport. The renal threshold is the plasma concentration at which a solute first appears in urine, a related but different idea. The permeability coefficient describes how easily a substance crosses by simple diffusion, and the equilibrium potential is a voltage, not a rate.
questions.answerText: Transport maximum
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Gating refers to which property of a membrane channel?
options: Binding one solute tightly and rejecting all others
Using ATP to move solute against its gradient
Opening and closing in response to a stimulus
Reversing direction when the gradient reverses
questions.why: A gated channel switches between open and closed states in response to voltage, a ligand, or mechanical stress, so the cell can control permeability moment to moment. Tight binding describes a carrier, not a channel pore. ATP use describes a pump. Reversing with the gradient is true of any passive pathway and is not what gating means.
questions.answerText: Opening and closing in response to a stimulus
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Extracellular glucose is raised from a very low value to twice that value while the GLUT carriers remain far from saturated. What happens to the rate of glucose entry?
options: It roughly doubles
It jumps immediately to the transport maximum
It stays the same
It falls by about half
questions.why: Well below saturation most carriers are free, so the rate rises in near proportion to the gradient and doubling the outside concentration roughly doubles entry. The rate would only stay flat if the carriers were already saturated. Nothing here reduces the gradient, so a fall makes no sense, and the transport maximum is reached only when carrier sites are fully occupied.
questions.answerText: It roughly doubles
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell is moved into a solution in which glucose is lower outside the cell than inside. Which way does GLUT move glucose?
options: Neither way, because a carrier needs ATP to run in reverse
Into the cell until the concentrations are equal
Into the cell, because carriers only work inward
Out of the cell, down its concentration gradient
questions.why: A facilitated diffusion carrier has no preferred direction. It simply follows the gradient, so with more glucose inside, net movement is outward. Carriers are not one way valves, and reversing does not cost ATP because no energy is being added in either direction. Inward movement would require glucose to climb its gradient, which passive transport cannot do.
questions.answerText: Out of the cell, down its concentration gradient
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Galactose is added at high concentration to a cell taking up glucose through a carrier that binds both sugars. What happens to glucose uptake?
options: It rises, because more total sugar is available
It is unchanged, because carriers handle only one sugar
It stops permanently
It falls, because galactose occupies the shared binding sites
questions.why: When two solutes fit the same site, they compete, and the more abundant one wins more cycles, so glucose uptake drops. Uptake does not rise because the number of carriers is fixed. It is not unchanged, because the premise says the carrier binds both sugars. The block is not permanent either, since raising glucose again would win back sites.
questions.answerText: It falls, because galactose occupies the shared binding sites
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Doubling the oxygen concentration outside a cell doubles the rate of oxygen entry, and the rate keeps climbing with no plateau at any concentration tested. Which process is this?
options: Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
Primary active transport
Secondary active transport
questions.why: A rate that keeps rising in direct proportion with no ceiling means there is no limited number of binding sites, which is the signature of simple diffusion through the lipid. Facilitated diffusion would plateau once carriers were saturated. Both active transport types would plateau as well and would also require an energy source, which a gas moving downhill does not use.
questions.answerText: Simple diffusion
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A treatment denatures every carrier protein in a cell membrane. Which solute still crosses at nearly its original rate?
options: A steroid hormone
Fructose
Glucose
An amino acid
questions.why: Steroid hormones are lipid soluble and dissolve straight through the bilayer, so losing carriers barely affects them. Glucose and fructose both depend on GLUT family carriers, and amino acids depend on their own carrier proteins, so all three would slow sharply. The general rule is that only small nonpolar or lipid soluble molecules are carrier independent.
questions.answerText: A steroid hormone
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Solute A enters a cell at a rate that rises in a straight line as its concentration rises. Solute B enters at a rate that rises and then levels off. What does the plateau for solute B indicate?
options: Solute B has reached equilibrium across the membrane
All the channels for solute B have closed
The carriers for solute B are saturated
Solute B is being pumped uphill with ATP
questions.why: A plateau means the transport proteins are the limiting factor, so every binding site is occupied and adding solute cannot speed things up. It does not imply ATP use, since facilitated diffusion saturates too. Equilibrium is ruled out because the outside concentration is being raised and net entry continues. Closed channels would drop the rate to near zero rather than hold it at a steady maximum.
questions.answerText: The carriers for solute B are saturated
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Ions cross through a single open channel at a far higher rate than solutes cross through a single carrier. What accounts for the difference?
options: The channel does not need a conformational change for each ion
The carrier binds only one solute at a time by chance
The carrier moves solute against its gradient
The channel is coupled to ATP hydrolysis
questions.why: An open channel is a pore, and ions stream through in single file with no cycle to complete, while a carrier must bind, change shape, release, and reset for every molecule. That cycling is the rate limiting step. Channels do not use ATP. Carriers do bind one solute at a time, but that is a consequence of the cycle rather than the cause, and facilitated carriers do not move solute uphill.
questions.answerText: The channel does not need a conformational change for each ion
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Insulin causes a muscle cell to insert many more GLUT4 carriers into its membrane. Extracellular glucose is held constant at a level high enough to saturate the carriers already present. Predict the effect on glucose uptake and on the transport rate curve.
options: Uptake is unchanged because the existing carriers are saturated
Uptake falls because the new carriers compete for glucose
Uptake rises and the maximum rate of the curve rises
Uptake rises but the maximum rate of the curve is unchanged
questions.why: The maximum rate is set by how many carriers are in the membrane, so adding carriers raises the ceiling and uptake climbs even at a saturating concentration. The maximum cannot stay fixed while carrier number changes, since that ceiling is exactly what carrier number determines. Saturation limits the old carriers, not the new ones, and carriers in the same membrane do not compete with each other in a way that lowers total flux.
questions.answerText: Uptake rises and the maximum rate of the curve rises
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A student measures uptake of a solute and finds three things: the rate plateaus at high concentration, a metabolic poison that removes ATP does not change the rate, and net uptake stops once the concentrations are equal on both sides. Which transport process is this?
options: Secondary active transport
Primary active transport
Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
questions.why: The plateau shows a limited number of transport proteins, and stopping at equal concentrations shows the process is passive, which together define facilitated diffusion. Simple diffusion is ruled out because it would not plateau. Primary active transport is ruled out by the ATP result. Secondary active transport is ruled out because it can keep pushing solute uphill past the point of equal concentration.
questions.answerText: Facilitated diffusion
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A mutation lowers the affinity of a glucose carrier for glucose but does not change how many carriers are in the membrane. Compare uptake at low glucose with uptake at very high glucose.
options: Uptake is higher at low glucose and the maximum rate is unchanged
Uptake is reduced at every concentration, including at the maximum rate
Uptake is unchanged at low glucose but the maximum rate is lower
Uptake is reduced at low glucose but the maximum rate is nearly normal
questions.why: Affinity determines how readily glucose binds, so at low concentrations fewer carriers are loaded and uptake drops. Flooding the system with glucose overcomes weak binding, so the ceiling, which depends on carrier number rather than affinity, is nearly normal. The maximum falls only if carriers are lost or inhibited in a way that flooding cannot overcome, and lower affinity can never raise uptake.
questions.answerText: Uptake is reduced at low glucose but the maximum rate is nearly normal
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A red blood cell takes up glucose through a carrier. When a nonmetabolized glucose analog is added at equal concentration, glucose uptake falls by about half, and raising glucose alone restores uptake nearly to its original value. What does this show about the carrier?
options: It is a wide channel that both sugars flow through freely
It is saturable and the two sugars compete for the same binding site
It uses ATP that the analog consumes
It has been permanently destroyed by the analog
questions.why: Both sugars fit the same limited set of binding sites, so they share cycles and uptake of each falls. The fact that extra glucose wins the sites back shows the interference is reversible competition, not damage. If the analog destroyed the carrier, raising glucose would not help. ATP is not involved in facilitated diffusion, and a freely permeable wide pore would show no competition at all.
questions.answerText: It is saturable and the two sugars compete for the same binding site
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How many K+ ions does the Na+/K+ ATPase bring into the cell per transport cycle?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
questions.why: Each cycle imports two K+ while exporting three Na+, so more positive charge leaves than enters. Three is the Na+ number, not the K+ number, and mixing the two up is the most common error with this pump. One and four do not match the stoichiometry and would not give the pump its small direct contribution to the resting membrane potential.
questions.answerText: Two
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How many molecules of ATP does the Na+/K+ ATPase hydrolyze per transport cycle?
options: Five
One
Two
Three
questions.why: One ATP powers one full cycle, which moves three Na+ out and two K+ in. Two and three are the ion counts, not the ATP count, so they are easy to grab by mistake. Five is the total number of ions moved per cycle and again is not the ATP requirement.
questions.answerText: One
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The Na+/K+ ATPase is called electrogenic. What does that mean?
options: It moves equal charge in each direction
It generates ATP as ions move down their gradients
It moves net positive charge out of the cell each cycle
It is activated by changes in membrane voltage
questions.why: Three positive charges leave and two enter, so each cycle exports one net positive charge and makes a small direct contribution to the negative resting potential. Being activated by voltage describes a voltage gated channel, not this pump. Equal charge exchange would make the pump electroneutral, which the three to two ratio rules out. The pump consumes ATP rather than making it.
questions.answerText: It moves net positive charge out of the cell each cycle
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which pair of gradients does the Na+/K+ ATPase maintain?
options: Ca2+ high outside and Na+ high inside
K+ high outside and Cl- high inside
Na+ high outside the cell and K+ high inside
Na+ high inside the cell and K+ high outside
questions.why: The pump pushes Na+ out and K+ in, so at rest Na+ is concentrated in the extracellular fluid and K+ is concentrated in the cytosol. The reversed version of that statement is the classic mix up and would give the wrong resting potential entirely. Ca2+ is indeed low inside, but it is handled by calcium pumps and exchangers, and Cl- is not a substrate of this pump.
questions.answerText: Na+ high outside the cell and K+ high inside
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What makes the Na+/K+ ATPase an example of primary active transport?
options: It hydrolyzes ATP directly to move ions against their gradients
It uses the Na+ gradient to move another solute uphill
It moves ions down their gradients through a pore
It works only when a hormone binds to it
questions.why: Primary means the transporter itself splits ATP and uses that energy immediately, which is exactly what this pump does for both ions. Using an existing Na+ gradient describes secondary active transport, such as SGLT. Downhill movement through a pore is a channel. Hormone dependence is a regulatory detail and is not part of the definition of primary active transport.
questions.answerText: It hydrolyzes ATP directly to move ions against their gradients
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which drug class inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase?
options: Loop diuretics such as furosemide
Beta blockers such as propranolol
Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin and ouabain
Calcium channel blockers such as verapamil
questions.why: Cardiac glycosides bind the extracellular face of the pump and lock it, which is why they are the standard experimental tool for stopping Na+ and K+ pumping. Beta blockers act on adrenergic receptors, calcium channel blockers act on voltage gated Ca2+ channels, and loop diuretics block the Na+/K+/2Cl- symporter in the loop of Henle. All three act on proteins other than this pump.
questions.answerText: Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin and ouabain
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the pump cycle, phosphorylation of the Na+/K+ ATPase by ATP does what?
options: Changes the pump's shape so the Na+ sites face outward and release Na+
Attaches K+ to the pump so it can be carried inward
Blocks the pump until a hormone removes the phosphate
Opens a permanent pore through the pump
questions.why: Adding the phosphate group drives a conformational change that swings the loaded Na+ sites to the outside and lowers their affinity, so Na+ is dropped into the extracellular fluid. The pump never forms an open pore, since that would let ions leak back down their gradients. K+ binds after the shape change, not because of phosphorylation, and dephosphorylation happens as part of the normal cycle rather than by hormone control.
questions.answerText: Changes the pump's shape so the Na+ sites face outward and release Na+
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Roughly what fraction of a typical resting cell's ATP use is spent on the Na+/K+ ATPase?
options: About 90 percent
About 1 percent
About 5 percent
About 25 percent
questions.why: Around a quarter of resting ATP consumption goes to this pump in a typical cell, and the share is even higher in neurons and kidney tubule cells, which is why these tissues fail fast without oxygen. One and five percent badly understate a continuous cost the cell pays every second to hold its gradients. Ninety percent leaves nothing for synthesis, contraction, or signaling, which cells clearly perform.
questions.answerText: About 25 percent
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Ouabain is applied to a cell. Predict what happens to intracellular Na+ over the next several minutes.
options: It rises, because Na+ leaks in and is no longer pumped out
It falls, because Na+ leaks out unopposed
It is unchanged, because the membrane is impermeable to Na+
It rises briefly and then returns to normal
questions.why: Na+ constantly leaks inward down a steep electrochemical gradient, and the pump is the only thing removing it, so blocking the pump lets Na+ pile up inside. It cannot fall, because there is no other route that carries Na+ out against the gradient. The membrane is leaky to Na+, not impermeable, and nothing restores the gradient while the pump stays blocked.
questions.answerText: It rises, because Na+ leaks in and is no longer pumped out
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell's Na+/K+ ATPase is blocked. What is the immediate effect on the resting membrane potential, before the ion gradients have had time to run down?
options: A small depolarization of a few mV
A small hyperpolarization of a few mV
No change at all under any circumstances
A large hyperpolarization of about 30 mV
questions.why: The pump exports one net positive charge per cycle, so it contributes a few mV of negativity directly. Removing that contribution makes the inside slightly less negative, a small depolarization. Losing an outward positive current cannot hyperpolarize the cell. The larger change comes later, as the K+ and Na+ gradients themselves decay, so saying nothing changes ignores both the direct and the delayed effect.
questions.answerText: A small depolarization of a few mV
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Intracellular Na+ rises in a working nerve cell after a burst of action potentials. What happens to the rate of the Na+/K+ ATPase?
options: It slows, because Na+ inhibits the pump
It stops until Na+ returns to baseline
It speeds up, because intracellular Na+ is the substrate that loads the pump
It is unaffected, because pump rate depends only on ATP
questions.why: Na+ inside the cell binds the pump's cytoplasmic sites, so more Na+ means more loaded pumps and a faster cycling rate. That is the built in feedback that restores gradients after activity. Na+ is a substrate, not an inhibitor, so slowing or stopping is backward. ATP matters, but at normal ATP levels the internal Na+ concentration is the variable that sets the pace.
questions.answerText: It speeds up, because intracellular Na+ is the substrate that loads the pump
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The Ca2+ ATPase of the sarcoplasmic reticulum hydrolyzes ATP to move Ca2+ from the cytosol into the SR against its gradient. How is this transporter classified?
options: Simple diffusion
Primary active transport
Facilitated diffusion
Secondary active transport
questions.why: The transporter itself splits ATP to drive uphill movement, which is the definition of primary active transport, the same category as the Na+/K+ ATPase. Secondary active transport would use an existing ion gradient rather than ATP, as the sodium calcium exchanger does. Both diffusion categories are passive and could never build a thousandfold Ca2+ gradient across the SR membrane.
questions.answerText: Primary active transport
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell is deprived of oxygen and its ATP level falls sharply. Predict what happens to cell volume.
options: The cell shrinks, because Na+ leaves and water follows it out
The volume holds steady, because the membrane is impermeable to water
The cell shrinks, because K+ is pumped in and drags water out
The cell swells, because Na+ accumulates inside and water follows
questions.why: Without ATP the pump stops, Na+ leaks in faster than K+ leaks out, and the added intracellular solute raises osmolarity so water follows and the cell swells. Shrinking would require solute to leave, which is the opposite of what a failed pump allows. Membranes are quite water permeable, and pumping K+ in requires the very ATP the cell no longer has.
questions.answerText: The cell swells, because Na+ accumulates inside and water follows
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Extracellular K+ falls well below normal in a tissue bath. What is the immediate effect on Na+/K+ ATPase activity?
options: It rises, because the K+ gradient is steeper
It slows, because external K+ is needed to load the pump's outward facing sites
It is unchanged, because the pump responds only to Na+
It stops entirely and cannot restart
questions.why: The pump needs K+ bound on the outside to complete its cycle, so lowering external K+ leaves those sites empty and slows the whole pump. A steeper gradient does not help, because a pump works against gradients rather than being driven by them. Internal Na+ is one substrate but not the only one, and the slowdown is graded and reversible rather than a permanent stop.
questions.answerText: It slows, because external K+ is needed to load the pump's outward facing sites
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the direction each ion moves relative to its own concentration gradient during one pump cycle?
options: Both Na+ and K+ move up their gradients
Both Na+ and K+ move down their gradients
Na+ moves down its gradient and K+ moves up its gradient
Na+ moves up its gradient and K+ moves down its gradient
questions.why: Na+ is already high outside and is pushed further out, and K+ is already high inside and is pushed further in, so both ions are moved uphill and that is why ATP is required. If either ion were moving downhill, that leg of the cycle would need no energy. If both moved downhill, the pump would be a channel and the gradients would collapse instead of being maintained.
questions.answerText: Both Na+ and K+ move up their gradients
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Digoxin partly inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase in a cardiac muscle cell. Trace the consequence: what happens to intracellular Na+, and then to intracellular Ca2+ handled by the sodium calcium exchanger?
options: Na+ falls, and Ca2+ rises because Ca2+ replaces the missing Na+ inside
Na+ falls, and Ca2+ falls because both pumps are blocked together
Na+ rises, and Ca2+ rises because the exchanger has a weaker gradient to work with
Na+ rises, and Ca2+ falls because the exchanger works harder than before
questions.why: Blocking the pump lets Na+ build up inside, which flattens the inward Na+ gradient that the sodium calcium exchanger uses as its power source. With less driving force the exchanger removes less Ca2+, so intracellular Ca2+ rises and each contraction becomes stronger. Na+ cannot fall when its only exit is blocked, and the exchanger cannot work harder when the gradient driving it has shrunk.
questions.answerText: Na+ rises, and Ca2+ rises because the exchanger has a weaker gradient to work with
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A neuron is deprived of oxygen for several minutes and ATP falls. Predict the sequence for the K+ gradient and then the membrane potential.
options: K+ is drawn inside by the pump reversing, so the potential becomes more negative
K+ is unchanged and the potential is set only by Cl-
K+ stays high inside and the potential becomes more negative
K+ leaks out and is not replaced, so the potential drifts toward zero
questions.why: With no ATP the pump cannot return the K+ that leaks out, so the K+ gradient dissipates, and since that gradient is the main source of the resting potential, the membrane depolarizes toward zero. The gradient cannot be preserved without pumping. A pump running backward to import K+ would still need energy input and does not happen here. Cl- distributes according to the potential in most cells rather than setting it.
questions.answerText: K+ leaks out and is not replaced, so the potential drifts toward zero
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Red blood cells are stored cold for hours. They gain Na+ and lose K+. They are then rewarmed to 37 C with glucose available, and the normal gradients are restored. What best explains both halves of this result?
options: Cold slowed pump activity, and warming with fuel restored ATP supply and pumping
Cold reversed the pump, and warming reversed it back
Cold destroyed the pumps, and warming caused new pumps to be synthesized in minutes
Cold opened Na+ channels, and warming closed them
questions.why: Cold slows metabolism and the pump much more than it slows passive leak, so ions drift down their gradients, and warming with glucose restores ATP so the pump can catch up and rebuild them. Gating of Na+ channels by temperature is not what drives this classic result, and a pump does not run backward simply because it is cold. Synthesizing new pumps would take far longer than the rapid recovery seen here.
questions.answerText: Cold slowed pump activity, and warming with fuel restored ATP supply and pumping
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An experimenter blocks the Na+/K+ ATPase and records membrane potential for an hour. The potential shifts by about 4 mV within seconds and then, over many minutes, drifts much further toward zero. What explains the two phases?
options: The fast shift is an action potential, and the slow drift is the cell repolarizing
The fast shift is loss of the pump's electrogenic current, and the slow drift is the gradients running down
The fast shift is the K+ gradient collapsing, and the slow drift is Cl- redistributing
Both phases reflect Ca2+ slowly entering the cell
questions.why: The pump exports net positive charge continuously, so removing it costs a few mV immediately. The much larger, slower change comes as Na+ leaks in and K+ leaks out with no pump to restore them, which erodes the gradients that generate the potential. Gradients cannot collapse in seconds given the small ion fluxes involved, and neither Ca2+ entry nor an action potential is described in this recording.
questions.answerText: The fast shift is loss of the pump's electrogenic current, and the slow drift is the gradients running down
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In a symport, the two transported solutes move in which directions?
options: Both move only when ATP is bound to the carrier
Both in the same direction across the membrane
In opposite directions across the membrane
One moves and the other stays bound to the carrier
questions.why: Symport, also called cotransport, carries both solutes the same way at once, as SGLT does when it brings Na+ and glucose into the cell together. Opposite directions define an antiport, such as the sodium calcium exchanger. A solute that stayed bound would never be delivered, and direct ATP binding would make the protein a primary active pump rather than a coupled carrier.
questions.answerText: Both in the same direction across the membrane
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In an antiport, the two transported solutes move in which directions?
options: Both into the cell
Both out of the cell
In opposite directions across the membrane
In the same direction, one after the other
questions.why: An antiport, also called an exchanger, moves one solute in while moving the other out, as the Na+/H+ exchanger does. Moving both the same way, whether in or out, describes a symport. Sequential same direction movement is still symport, since what defines antiport is opposing direction, not timing.
questions.answerText: In opposite directions across the membrane
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which ion's gradient directly powers SGLT, the sodium glucose cotransporter?
options: The K+ gradient
The Na+ gradient
The Ca2+ gradient
The Cl- gradient
questions.why: Na+ is kept low inside the cell, so it has a steep inward electrochemical gradient, and SGLT harnesses that inward rush to drag glucose in with it. K+ is high inside, so its gradient points outward and cannot pull glucose in. Ca2+ and Cl- gradients exist but are not coupled to this carrier.
questions.answerText: The Na+ gradient
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The sodium calcium exchanger moves how many Na+ into the cell for each Ca2+ it moves out?
options: Two
Three
Four
One
questions.why: Three Na+ enter for each Ca2+ that leaves, so the exchanger carries net positive charge inward and is electrogenic. One would not release enough energy to move Ca2+ out against its very steep gradient. Two is the K+ number for the Na+/K+ ATPase and is a common cross up. Four does not match the measured stoichiometry.
questions.answerText: Three
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The Na+/H+ exchanger brings Na+ into the cell while sending H+ out. How is it classified?
options: Antiport
