Primary active transport
Simple diffusion
Symport
questions.why: Opposite directions for the two solutes makes this an antiport, and because it runs on the Na+ gradient rather than on ATP, it is secondary active transport. A symport would carry both the same way. It is not primary active because the protein does not hydrolyze ATP. Simple diffusion would require no protein and could not move H+ uphill.
questions.answerText: Antiport
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the immediate energy source for secondary active transport?
options: GTP supplied by a G protein
Heat released by cell metabolism
ATP bound directly to the transporter
The electrochemical gradient of a driver ion, usually Na+
questions.why: The carrier lets one ion fall down its electrochemical gradient and uses that released energy to haul a second solute uphill, with no ATP touching the carrier itself. Direct ATP hydrolysis would make it primary active transport. GTP powers signaling proteins, and heat is not a usable energy source for directed transport in cells.
questions.answerText: The electrochemical gradient of a driver ion, usually Na+
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which pump ultimately supplies the energy that secondary active transport depends on?
options: The proton pump of the stomach
The Ca2+ ATPase of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
The H+/K+ ATPase of the kidney
The Na+/K+ ATPase
questions.why: The Na+/K+ ATPase spends ATP to keep intracellular Na+ low, which creates the inward Na+ gradient that every Na+ coupled carrier taps. That is why secondary active transport is called secondary. The gastric proton pump and the renal H+/K+ ATPase acidify secretions but do not set up the cell's Na+ gradient. The SR Ca2+ ATPase fills the SR with Ca2+ and likewise does not power SGLT or the exchanger.
questions.answerText: The Na+/K+ ATPase
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: SGLT moves Na+ and glucose into the cell together. Which category does SGLT belong to?
options: Facilitated diffusion of glucose alone
Antiport driven by ATP
Symport driven by the Na+ gradient
Channel gated by glucose
questions.why: Both solutes cross in the same direction, which makes it a symport, and the driving force is the Na+ gradient rather than ATP, which makes it secondary active. Calling it an antiport reverses the geometry. It is not a channel, because the carrier binds both solutes and cycles through conformations. Facilitated diffusion of glucose alone describes GLUT, which cannot move glucose uphill.
questions.answerText: Symport driven by the Na+ gradient
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Extracellular Na+ is replaced with choline, an impermeant cation, in a bath containing intestinal cells. Predict glucose uptake through SGLT.
options: It rises, because there is less competition for the carrier
It is unchanged, because glucose binds the carrier on its own
It falls sharply, because the Na+ gradient that drives the carrier is gone
It reverses, and glucose is pumped out of the cell
questions.why: SGLT only carries glucose when Na+ binds and moves inward down its gradient, so removing extracellular Na+ removes the driving force and uptake collapses. Na+ is a partner, not a competitor, so removing it cannot help. Glucose alone does not drive the cycle. Reversal would require a steep outward gradient for the driver ion, which choline cannot supply.
questions.answerText: It falls sharply, because the Na+ gradient that drives the carrier is gone
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A transporter in a cell membrane moves Cl- into the cell while moving HCO3- out. How should it be classified?
options: Primary active transport
Channel mediated diffusion
Symport
Antiport
questions.why: Two solutes crossing in opposite directions is the definition of an antiport, no matter which ions are involved. A symport would move both the same way. Nothing states that the protein hydrolyzes ATP, so primary active transport is not supported. A channel carries one species through a pore and does not couple two solutes to each other.
questions.answerText: Antiport
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Glucose enters an intestinal cell through SGLT even though intracellular glucose is already higher than luminal glucose. How is that possible?
options: Glucose is being carried uphill using energy released by Na+ moving downhill
Glucose has become lipid soluble inside the cell
The carrier hydrolyzes ATP for each glucose molecule
The glucose gradient must actually be reversed
questions.why: Coupled transport only needs the total energy change to be favorable, so a steep inward Na+ gradient can pay for glucose climbing its own gradient. Glucose does not change its chemical nature inside the cell. SGLT never hydrolyzes ATP itself, which is what separates secondary from primary active transport. The premise states the glucose gradient, so denying it does not answer the question.
questions.answerText: Glucose is being carried uphill using energy released by Na+ moving downhill
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The sodium calcium exchanger carries three Na+ in for each Ca2+ out. What is the net charge movement per cycle, and what does that do to the membrane potential?
options: Net two positive charges outward, a strong hyperpolarization
Net zero charge, no effect on potential
Net one positive charge inward, a slight depolarization
Net one positive charge outward, a slight hyperpolarization
questions.why: Three positive charges in and two positive charges out leave a net gain of one positive charge inside per cycle, which nudges the membrane potential toward less negative. Net zero would require the charges to balance, which three versus two does not. Any outward net movement reverses the actual direction, so the hyperpolarizing options describe the opposite of what happens.
questions.answerText: Net one positive charge inward, a slight depolarization
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The Na+ gradient across a cell membrane is reduced by half. Predict the effect on Ca2+ export by the sodium calcium exchanger.
options: Ca2+ export rises, so intracellular Ca2+ falls
Ca2+ export falls, so intracellular Ca2+ rises
Ca2+ export is unchanged, because the exchanger uses ATP
Ca2+ export stops completely and cannot resume
questions.why: The exchanger is powered by Na+ falling into the cell, so a shallower Na+ gradient supplies less energy and less Ca2+ is pushed out, letting cytosolic Ca2+ climb. Export cannot rise when its driving force has shrunk. The exchanger does not use ATP directly, and a partial reduction in gradient slows the exchanger rather than halting it permanently.
questions.answerText: Ca2+ export falls, so intracellular Ca2+ rises
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An amino acid is absorbed from the gut lumen by a Na+ coupled symporter. Removing Na+ from the lumen stops absorption. What does that experiment show?
options: Absorption depends on the Na+ gradient, so it is secondary active
The symporter hydrolyzes ATP directly for each amino acid
The amino acid uses the same carrier protein as glucose
The amino acid crosses the membrane by simple diffusion
questions.why: Absorption that fails without the driver ion identifies the Na+ gradient as the energy source, which is the definition of secondary active transport. Simple diffusion would be unaffected by removing Na+. Direct ATP use is not tested by this experiment and would make the carrier primary active. Sharing a carrier with glucose is a separate claim that removing Na+ does not address.
questions.answerText: Absorption depends on the Na+ gradient, so it is secondary active
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell becomes acidic inside. The Na+/H+ exchanger responds by moving H+ out. Which gradient pays for moving H+ against its concentration gradient?
options: The outward K+ gradient
The inward Cl- gradient
The outward HCO3- gradient
The inward Na+ gradient
questions.why: Na+ is far more concentrated outside than inside, so its inward movement releases energy the exchanger uses to push H+ out. K+ is concentrated inside, so its gradient points the wrong way to pull Na+ or H+ anywhere useful here. Cl- and HCO3- gradients drive other exchangers, such as the chloride bicarbonate antiport, but not this one.
questions.answerText: The inward Na+ gradient
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Ouabain is added to an intestinal epithelial cell. Trace the effect on intracellular Na+ and then on glucose uptake through SGLT at the apical membrane.
options: Intracellular Na+ is unchanged, because SGLT keeps it low
Intracellular Na+ rises, the Na+ gradient shrinks, and SGLT glucose uptake falls
Intracellular Na+ rises, the Na+ gradient steepens, and SGLT glucose uptake rises
Intracellular Na+ falls, and SGLT glucose uptake rises
questions.why: Ouabain stops the Na+/K+ ATPase, so Na+ accumulates inside and the inward Na+ gradient flattens, which removes the energy source that SGLT depends on and glucose uptake slows. Rising internal Na+ makes the gradient shallower, not steeper, so that option contradicts itself. Na+ cannot fall with its only exit blocked, and SGLT brings Na+ into the cell rather than removing it.
questions.answerText: Intracellular Na+ rises, the Na+ gradient shrinks, and SGLT glucose uptake falls
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: During ischemia a cardiac cell loses ATP, intracellular Na+ climbs, and the membrane depolarizes. The sodium calcium exchanger then begins running in reverse. What does reverse mode do, and what is the result?
options: It brings Ca2+ into the cell and imports more Na+, so both ions fall
It exports Ca2+ faster, so intracellular Ca2+ falls below normal
It stops all transport, so ion concentrations freeze where they are
It brings Ca2+ into the cell and exports Na+, so intracellular Ca2+ rises to harmful levels
questions.why: The exchanger has no fixed direction. It follows the combined Na+ gradient and membrane voltage, so when internal Na+ rises and the cell depolarizes, the favorable direction flips and Na+ leaves while Ca2+ enters, driving calcium overload. A transporter cannot move both coupled solutes inward at once. Faster export would require a steeper inward Na+ gradient, which ischemia destroys, and the exchanger keeps cycling rather than freezing.
questions.answerText: It brings Ca2+ into the cell and exports Na+, so intracellular Ca2+ rises to harmful levels
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A drug blocks SGLT2 in the proximal tubule, so filtered glucose that would normally be reabsorbed stays in the tubular fluid. Predict the effect on urine glucose and on urine volume.
options: Urine glucose rises and urine volume is unchanged, because water follows Na+ only
Urine glucose rises and urine volume rises, because glucose holds water in the tubule
Urine glucose rises and urine volume falls, because glucose absorbs water from the tubule
Urine glucose falls and urine volume rises
questions.why: Blocking the apical symporter leaves glucose in the tubular fluid, so it is excreted, and because the retained glucose is an osmotically active solute it holds water in the lumen and produces osmotic diuresis. Glucose in the lumen pulls water toward itself, so it cannot reduce urine volume. Glucose cannot fall when reabsorption is blocked, and water follows total osmotic gradients rather than Na+ alone.
questions.answerText: Urine glucose rises and urine volume rises, because glucose holds water in the tubule
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A student says that secondary active transport does not use ATP at all. What is the most accurate correction?
options: The carrier hydrolyzes ATP slowly rather than quickly
The carrier uses ATP only when moving solute downhill
The claim is completely correct, since no ATP is involved anywhere in the process
The carrier uses no ATP, but the Na+ gradient it spends was built by an ATP driven pump
questions.why: Secondary active transporters never touch ATP, which is what makes them secondary, but they spend a gradient the Na+/K+ ATPase paid for with ATP, so the process is ATP dependent one step upstream. Slow hydrolysis by the carrier would make it primary active. A carrier does not need energy to move solute downhill. Saying no ATP is involved anywhere ignores that the gradient collapses within minutes if the pump stops.
questions.answerText: The carrier uses no ATP, but the Na+ gradient it spends was built by an ATP driven pump
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What does the transport maximum of a carrier mediated system represent?
options: The rate at which the solute diffuses through the lipid bilayer
The rate at which the solute first appears in urine
The highest transport rate possible once all carriers are saturated
The concentration at which transport begins
questions.why: The transport maximum is the ceiling reached when every carrier binding site is occupied, so raising solute concentration further cannot speed transport. The concentration at which a solute first spills into urine is the renal threshold, a related idea measured in plasma units rather than rate units. Transport begins at any concentration above zero, and simple diffusion through lipid has no maximum at all.
questions.answerText: The highest transport rate possible once all carriers are saturated
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What physical feature of the membrane sets the value of the transport maximum?
options: The thickness of the lipid bilayer
The number of functioning carrier proteins available
The membrane potential
The temperature of the extracellular fluid
questions.why: Each carrier can only complete so many cycles per second, so the total ceiling is set by how many carriers are in the membrane. Bilayer thickness affects simple diffusion of lipid soluble substances, not carrier capacity. Membrane potential influences charged solutes but does not create or remove carriers. Temperature changes reaction rates broadly but is not what defines the maximum in a physiology curve.
questions.answerText: The number of functioning carrier proteins available
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: At about what plasma glucose concentration does glucose first begin to appear in the urine in a healthy adult?
options: About 400 mg/dL
About 80 mg/dL
About 120 mg/dL
About 180 mg/dL
questions.why: The renal threshold for glucose sits near 180 to 200 mg/dL, which is where the filtered load starts to exceed what some nephrons can reabsorb. Eighty and 120 mg/dL are ordinary fasting and fed values, so glucose is fully reabsorbed at both. By 400 mg/dL glucosuria is heavy and well past the point where it began.
questions.answerText: About 180 mg/dL
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The transport maximum for glucose reabsorption in the kidney of a healthy adult is closest to which value?
options: About 375 mg/min
About 1000 mg/min
About 125 mg/min
About 180 mg/min
questions.why: Roughly 375 mg/min is the standard figure for the combined capacity of the proximal tubule carriers. About 125 mg/min is the normal filtered load at a plasma glucose of 100 mg/dL, and 180 is the threshold expressed in mg/dL, so both numbers belong to different quantities in this same topic. A thousand mg/min far exceeds measured capacity.
questions.answerText: About 375 mg/min
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the term for glucose appearing in the urine?
options: Glucosuria
Proteinuria
Hyperglycemia
Diuresis
questions.why: Glucosuria names glucose in the urine, which happens once the filtered load exceeds the transport maximum. Proteinuria is protein in the urine and points to a filtration barrier problem instead. Hyperglycemia is high glucose in the blood, which is the cause here rather than the urinary finding. Diuresis is an increased urine volume, which often accompanies glucosuria but is not the same term.
questions.answerText: Glucosuria
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How is the filtered load of a freely filtered solute such as glucose calculated?
options: GFR multiplied by plasma concentration
GFR multiplied by urine concentration
Urine flow rate multiplied by plasma concentration
Plasma concentration divided by GFR
questions.why: Filtered load is the amount arriving in the tubule per minute, which is the volume filtered per minute times how much solute each volume carries, so GFR times plasma concentration. Dividing inverts the relationship and gives units that make no sense. Urine concentration reflects what escaped reabsorption, so it describes the excreted amount rather than the filtered amount.
questions.answerText: GFR multiplied by plasma concentration
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On a graph of glucose reabsorption rate against plasma glucose concentration, what does the curve do once the transport maximum is reached?
options: It rises more steeply than before
It continues to rise in a straight line
It becomes flat at a constant rate
It falls back toward zero
questions.why: Once every carrier is occupied, reabsorption cannot go faster, so the curve flattens into a horizontal plateau while any extra filtered glucose is excreted. A continued straight line would describe simple diffusion, which has no carriers to saturate. The rate does not fall, because the carriers keep working at capacity, and it certainly cannot steepen after saturation.
questions.answerText: It becomes flat at a constant rate
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In renal glucose handling, what does the term splay describe?
options: The complete loss of reabsorption at high plasma glucose
The delay between filtration and excretion
The sudden vertical jump in excretion at the threshold
The gentle rounding of the curve between threshold and transport maximum
questions.why: Splay is the rounded shoulder in the curve, and it exists because nephrons differ in their filtered loads and carrier numbers, so some spill glucose before others do. A sharp vertical jump is what the curve would look like if every nephron were identical. Reabsorption is not lost at high plasma glucose, since it continues at the maximum rate, and splay is a shape, not a time delay.
questions.answerText: The gentle rounding of the curve between threshold and transport maximum
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: GFR is 125 mL/min and plasma glucose is 100 mg/dL. What is the filtered load of glucose?
options: 12.5 mg/min
125 mg/min
375 mg/min
1250 mg/min
questions.why: A plasma glucose of 100 mg/dL is 1 mg/mL, so 125 mL/min carries 125 mg/min into the tubule. The 12.5 value comes from slipping a decimal place during the dL to mL conversion. The 375 value is the transport maximum rather than the filtered load, and 1250 would require a plasma glucose ten times higher than the one given.
questions.answerText: 125 mg/min
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: GFR is 125 mL/min and plasma glucose is 400 mg/dL. The transport maximum for glucose is 375 mg/min. How much glucose is excreted per minute?
options: 500 mg/min
0 mg/min
125 mg/min
375 mg/min
questions.why: The filtered load is 4 mg/mL times 125 mL/min, or 500 mg/min, and the carriers can reclaim only 375 mg/min, so 125 mg/min is left in the tubule and excreted. Zero would require the filtered load to stay under the maximum. The 375 figure is what is reabsorbed, and 500 is what was filtered, so both are steps in the calculation rather than the answer.
questions.answerText: 125 mg/min
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A person has a plasma glucose of 120 mg/dL with a normal GFR. Will glucose appear in the urine?
options: No, because the filtered load is well below the transport maximum
No, because glucose is too large to be filtered
Yes, because any glucose in plasma spills into urine
Yes, because 120 mg/dL exceeds the transport maximum
questions.why: At 120 mg/dL the filtered load is about 150 mg/min, comfortably under the 375 mg/min capacity, so the proximal tubule reclaims all of it. Plasma glucose is always present in the filtrate without spilling into urine, so the idea that any plasma glucose appears in urine is wrong on its face. The transport maximum is a rate, not a plasma concentration, so 120 mg/dL cannot exceed it. Glucose is small and is freely filtered.
questions.answerText: No, because the filtered load is well below the transport maximum
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An experimental treatment doubles the number of glucose carriers in the proximal tubule. Predict the effect on the transport maximum for glucose.
options: It roughly doubles
It is halved
It is unchanged, because the maximum depends on GFR
It falls to zero, because carriers interfere with each other
questions.why: The maximum is the sum of what all carriers can move per minute, so doubling the carriers roughly doubles the ceiling. Halving is the opposite of adding capacity. GFR determines how much glucose arrives, not how much the carriers can handle, so the maximum is not fixed by GFR. Carriers work independently and do not disable one another.
questions.answerText: It roughly doubles
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A person has a steady plasma glucose of 300 mg/dL with a GFR of 125 mL/min and a normal transport maximum of 375 mg/min. What is the rate of glucose reabsorption?
options: 0 mg/min
125 mg/min
375 mg/min, the transport maximum
300 mg/min
questions.why: The filtered load is 3 mg/mL times 125 mL/min, or 375 mg/min, which exactly matches capacity, so the carriers reabsorb at the maximum and essentially nothing is excreted. The 125 value would be the filtered load at a normal plasma glucose. The 300 figure is the plasma concentration in different units and is not a rate. Reabsorption cannot be zero while functioning carriers are present.
questions.answerText: 375 mg/min, the transport maximum
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On a renal glucose curve, the excretion line stays at zero and then begins to rise. What does the point where it starts to rise represent?
options: The transport maximum
The renal threshold
The filtered load
The splay
questions.why: The plasma concentration where glucose first shows up in urine is the renal threshold, which is reached before the transport maximum because some nephrons saturate earlier than others. The transport maximum is where the reabsorption curve flattens, at a higher plasma concentration. Filtered load is the rising straight line of delivery, and splay is the rounded region between threshold and maximum rather than a single point.
questions.answerText: The renal threshold
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Plasma glucose is 600 mg/dL, GFR is 100 mL/min, and the transport maximum for glucose is 375 mg/min. How much glucose is excreted per minute?
options: 125 mg/min
600 mg/min
375 mg/min
225 mg/min
questions.why: The filtered load is 6 mg/mL times 100 mL/min, or 600 mg/min. Carriers reclaim 375 mg/min, so 600 minus 375 leaves 225 mg/min in the urine. Six hundred is the filtered load, which would only all be excreted if reabsorption were zero, and 375 is the reabsorbed amount. The 125 value comes from a different case with a normal GFR and a plasma glucose of 400 mg/dL.
questions.answerText: 225 mg/min
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Two people both have a plasma glucose of 500 mg/dL and a normal transport maximum of 375 mg/min. One has a GFR of 125 mL/min and the other has a GFR reduced to 60 mL/min. Compare their glucose excretion.
options: Both excrete the same amount, because plasma glucose is equal
The person with the higher GFR excretes more, and the one with the low GFR may excrete none
The person with the lower GFR excretes more, because filtration is impaired
Neither excretes glucose, because the transport maximum is normal in both
questions.why: Excretion depends on filtered load compared with capacity. At a GFR of 125 mL/min the filtered load is 625 mg/min, which exceeds 375 and leaves 250 mg/min in the urine, while at 60 mL/min the load is only 300 mg/min, which the carriers can fully reclaim. Equal plasma glucose does not mean equal delivery once GFR differs. A low GFR delivers less glucose, not more, and normal capacity does not prevent spillage when delivery is high.
questions.answerText: The person with the higher GFR excretes more, and the one with the low GFR may excrete none
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In uncontrolled hyperglycemia, glucose that exceeds the transport maximum remains in the tubular fluid. Trace what this does to water handling and then to the person's thirst.
options: Retained glucose holds water in the tubule, urine volume rises, body water falls, and thirst increases
Retained glucose draws water out of the tubule, urine volume falls, and thirst decreases
Retained glucose has no osmotic effect, so urine volume and thirst are unchanged
Retained glucose is reabsorbed later in the collecting duct, so nothing changes
questions.why: Unreabsorbed glucose is osmotically active and holds water in the lumen, producing osmotic diuresis, and the resulting loss of body water raises plasma osmolarity and stimulates thirst. Solute in the tubule pulls water toward itself rather than out of the lumen. Glucose is a strong osmotic particle, so no effect is not an option. The collecting duct has no glucose carriers, so glucose escaping the proximal tubule is lost in the urine.
questions.answerText: Retained glucose holds water in the tubule, urine volume rises, body water falls, and thirst increases
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A drug lowers the transport maximum for glucose from 375 mg/min to 150 mg/min. With a GFR of 125 mL/min and a plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL, how much glucose is excreted per minute?
options: 50 mg/min
100 mg/min
250 mg/min
0 mg/min
questions.why: The filtered load is 2 mg/mL times 125 mL/min, or 250 mg/min, and only 150 mg/min can now be reabsorbed, so 100 mg/min is excreted. Zero would be right with the normal maximum of 375, which is the point of the comparison. The 250 value is the filtered load before any reabsorption, and 50 comes from subtracting in the wrong direction.
questions.answerText: 100 mg/min
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which form of endocytosis takes in large solid particles such as bacteria and cell debris?
options: Exocytosis
Pinocytosis
Phagocytosis
Receptor mediated endocytosis
questions.why: Phagocytosis extends pseudopods around a solid particle and encloses it in a large vesicle, which is how a macrophage clears a bacterium. Pinocytosis takes in droplets of extracellular fluid, not solid particles. Receptor mediated endocytosis takes in specific molecules bound to surface receptors. Exocytosis moves material out of the cell rather than in.
questions.answerText: Phagocytosis
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Pinocytosis brings which kind of cargo into the cell?
options: Only lipid soluble hormones
Solid particles the size of bacteria
Small droplets of extracellular fluid and whatever is dissolved in them
Only molecules bound to specific surface receptors
questions.why: Pinocytosis, sometimes called cell drinking, pinches off small vesicles of extracellular fluid, so the cargo is whatever happens to be dissolved nearby and the process is nonselective. Solid particles of bacterial size go by phagocytosis. Selection by receptor is receptor mediated endocytosis. Lipid soluble hormones cross the bilayer directly and need no vesicle at all.
questions.answerText: Small droplets of extracellular fluid and whatever is dissolved in them
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which protein coats the membrane pit that forms during receptor mediated endocytosis?
options: Myosin
Tubulin
Actin
Clathrin
questions.why: Clathrin assembles into a cage on the cytosolic face of the pit and helps curve the membrane into a vesicle, which is why these are called clathrin coated pits. Actin and myosin generate movement and shape change more broadly, including the pseudopods of phagocytosis, but they are not the coat here. Tubulin builds microtubules that carry vesicles once they have formed.
questions.answerText: Clathrin
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which particle is the classic example of cargo taken up by receptor mediated endocytosis?
options: Low density lipoprotein
Oxygen
Na+
Carbon dioxide
questions.why: LDL binds to specific LDL receptors that gather in coated pits, which is how cells obtain cholesterol from the blood. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are small nonpolar gases that diffuse straight through the bilayer. Na+ crosses through channels and transporters. None of those three needs a vesicle, and none binds a receptor for uptake.
questions.answerText: Low density lipoprotein
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What does exocytosis accomplish?
options: It moves single molecules through a channel in the membrane
It engulfs bacteria and debris into a large vesicle
It fuses a vesicle with the plasma membrane and releases the contents
It pulls droplets of extracellular fluid into the cell
questions.why: In exocytosis a secretory vesicle merges with the plasma membrane, so its contents empty into the extracellular fluid without ever crossing the bilayer. Engulfing bacteria is phagocytosis and taking in fluid is pinocytosis, both of which move material inward. Channel transport moves individual dissolved solutes and cannot handle proteins or packaged transmitter.
questions.answerText: It fuses a vesicle with the plasma membrane and releases the contents
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which ion entering an axon terminal triggers exocytosis of neurotransmitter?
options: Na+
K+
Ca2+
Cl-
questions.why: Ca2+ entering through voltage gated calcium channels binds the vesicle sensor protein and sets off fusion, which is why blocking Ca2+ entry silences transmitter release. Na+ entry carries the depolarization that opens those calcium channels, but Na+ is not the fusion trigger itself, which is the most common mix up here. K+ efflux repolarizes the terminal, and Cl- is not part of this release step.
questions.answerText: Ca2+
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How much ATP does vesicular transport require?
options: ATP is required, because membrane remodeling and vesicle movement need energy
ATP is required only for exocytosis and not for any form of endocytosis
ATP is required only when the cargo is a charged molecule
None, because vesicles move passively down gradients
questions.why: Bending membrane, assembling coats, moving vesicles along the cytoskeleton, and driving fusion all consume ATP, so every form of vesicular transport is an active process. Vesicles do not follow concentration gradients, so calling the process passive misses the point. Endocytosis is just as energy dependent as exocytosis, and the cost has nothing to do with whether the cargo carries a charge.
questions.answerText: ATP is required, because membrane remodeling and vesicle movement need energy
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which family of proteins catalyzes the fusion of a secretory vesicle with the plasma membrane?
options: Aquaporins
Cadherins
SNARE proteins
Integrins
questions.why: SNARE proteins on the vesicle and on the target membrane zipper together and pull the two bilayers close enough to fuse. Integrins anchor cells to the extracellular matrix, and cadherins hold neighboring cells together, so both are adhesion proteins rather than fusion machinery. Aquaporins are water channels and play no role in vesicle fusion.
questions.answerText: SNARE proteins
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A neutrophil extends pseudopods around a bacterium and encloses it in a vesicle. Which process is this?
options: Exocytosis
Pinocytosis
Receptor mediated endocytosis
Phagocytosis
questions.why: Surrounding a large solid target with pseudopods and sealing it into a vesicle is phagocytosis, the specialty of neutrophils and macrophages. Pinocytosis brings in fluid droplets rather than particles this large. Receptor mediated endocytosis concentrates specific molecules in coated pits and does not use pseudopods. Exocytosis would send material outward instead.
questions.answerText: Phagocytosis
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A liver cell binds LDL particles to surface receptors that cluster in coated pits, then internalizes them. Which process is this?
options: Receptor mediated endocytosis
Phagocytosis
Pinocytosis
Simple diffusion
questions.why: Binding to a specific receptor and concentrating in a coated pit before internalization defines receptor mediated endocytosis, which lets the cell gather scarce cargo efficiently. Phagocytosis handles large particles with pseudopods and is not receptor selective in this way. Pinocytosis is nonselective fluid uptake. A lipoprotein particle is far too large to diffuse through the bilayer.
questions.answerText: Receptor mediated endocytosis
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Voltage gated Ca2+ channels at a nerve terminal are blocked while the action potential still arrives. Predict neurotransmitter release.
options: Release is unchanged, because depolarization alone triggers fusion
Release falls sharply, because Ca2+ entry is the trigger for vesicle fusion
Release reverses, and transmitter is taken back into the vesicle
Release increases, because the terminal stays depolarized longer
questions.why: Depolarization normally works by opening calcium channels, and it is the Ca2+ that binds the vesicle sensor and triggers fusion, so with the channels blocked the vesicles stay put. Longer depolarization does not help when the trigger ion cannot enter. Believing depolarization alone is sufficient is the common misconception this card targets. Exocytosis is not a reversible step in this sense.
questions.answerText: Release falls sharply, because Ca2+ entry is the trigger for vesicle fusion
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A cell is treated so that ATP production stops. Which process continues at close to its normal rate?
options: Phagocytosis of bacteria
Exocytosis of secretory granules
Receptor mediated endocytosis of LDL
Diffusion of oxygen across the membrane
questions.why: Oxygen crosses by simple diffusion down its own partial pressure gradient, so it needs no cellular energy. All three vesicular processes require ATP for membrane remodeling, coat assembly, and fusion, so each of them slows or stops when ATP is gone. That shared energy requirement is what groups them together as active transport.
questions.answerText: Diffusion of oxygen across the membrane
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A person's cells lack functional LDL receptors. Predict what happens to LDL in the blood.
options: LDL rises, because cells can no longer clear it efficiently by receptor mediated endocytosis
LDL is unchanged, because LDL diffuses into cells through the bilayer
LDL rises only after the cells stop making ATP
LDL falls, because cells take it in by pinocytosis instead
questions.why: Receptor mediated endocytosis is the main route by which cells remove LDL from plasma, so losing the receptor leaves LDL circulating and plasma levels climb. Pinocytosis is far too slow and nonselective to substitute. An LDL particle is a large lipid protein complex and cannot diffuse through the membrane. The problem is the missing receptor, not an energy shortage.
questions.answerText: LDL rises, because cells can no longer clear it efficiently by receptor mediated endocytosis
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which vesicular process is the most selective about what it brings into the cell?
options: Phagocytosis, because the particles are large
Receptor mediated endocytosis, because cargo must bind a specific receptor first
Exocytosis, because it chooses which granules to release
Pinocytosis, because it samples fluid continuously
questions.why: Requiring the cargo to fit a specific receptor makes receptor mediated endocytosis highly selective and lets a cell concentrate a molecule present at low levels outside. Pinocytosis takes whatever is dissolved nearby, which is the opposite of selective. Phagocytosis targets particles but is far less molecule specific. Exocytosis moves cargo out and therefore is not an uptake route at all.
questions.answerText: Receptor mediated endocytosis, because cargo must bind a specific receptor first
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins in motor nerve terminals. Trace the effect on acetylcholine release and then on the muscle.
options: Ca2+ entry stops, so acetylcholine is released without a trigger
Vesicles cannot fuse, acetylcholine release fails, and the muscle becomes weak or paralyzed
Vesicles fuse faster, acetylcholine floods the synapse, and the muscle contracts continuously
Vesicles fuse normally but acetylcholine is destroyed, so the muscle is unaffected
questions.why: SNARE proteins are the fusion machinery, so cleaving them leaves docked vesicles unable to merge with the membrane and the terminal cannot release transmitter, which leaves the muscle unstimulated and flaccid. Destroying the fusion machinery cannot increase release. If release failed, the muscle would certainly be affected. The claim that stopping Ca2+ entry causes release without a trigger contradicts itself.
questions.answerText: Vesicles cannot fuse, acetylcholine release fails, and the muscle becomes weak or paralyzed
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A mutation prevents clathrin coated pits from forming but leaves membrane ruffling and pseudopod formation intact. Predict which processes fail and which continue.
options: Only exocytosis fails, because vesicles cannot leave the Golgi
Receptor mediated endocytosis fails while phagocytosis and pinocytosis continue
All forms of endocytosis fail together
Phagocytosis fails while receptor mediated endocytosis continues
questions.why: Clathrin builds the coat that curves the pit in receptor mediated endocytosis, so that route is lost, while phagocytosis and pinocytosis rely on actin driven membrane movement that the mutation spares. That difference is exactly why the three routes are studied as separate mechanisms. Phagocytosis does not depend on clathrin, and exocytosis uses SNARE mediated fusion rather than clathrin coated pits at the plasma membrane.
questions.answerText: Receptor mediated endocytosis fails while phagocytosis and pinocytosis continue
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A pancreatic cell releases secretory granules by exocytosis at a high rate for hours, yet its surface area does not keep growing. What accounts for this?
options: The added membrane is digested by extracellular enzymes
Exocytosis does not add membrane, because the vesicle contents pass through a pore only
The cell divides each time its surface area increases
The added membrane is retrieved by endocytosis and recycled to form new vesicles
questions.why: Every fusion event adds vesicle membrane to the cell surface, and cells balance that by pulling equivalent membrane back in as endocytic vesicles, so surface area stays roughly constant and membrane components are reused. Extracellular digestion of the cell's own membrane would breach the barrier. Full fusion genuinely inserts the vesicle membrane, and cell division is far too slow and drastic to serve as membrane bookkeeping.
questions.answerText: The added membrane is retrieved by endocytosis and recycled to form new vesicles
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In a cell line, endosomes fail to acidify after internalization, so receptors and their bound ligands do not separate. Predict the effect on receptor recycling and on further uptake of that ligand.
options: Uptake continues unchanged, because ligand enters by pinocytosis instead
Receptors are not returned to the surface, so uptake of the ligand declines over time
Receptors return to the surface faster, so uptake rises over time
Receptors are unaffected, because separation happens at the cell surface
questions.why: The drop in endosomal pH is what makes the receptor release its ligand so the receptor can be shuttled back to the plasma membrane for another round. Without that separation, receptors are trapped with their cargo, surface receptor numbers fall, and uptake declines. Failing to release cargo cannot speed recycling. Separation occurs inside the endosome, not at the surface, and pinocytosis is far too slow to replace a receptor based route.
questions.answerText: Receptors are not returned to the surface, so uptake of the ligand declines over time
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In a polarized epithelial cell, the apical membrane faces which compartment?
options: The adjacent epithelial cell
The lumen
The interstitial fluid
The capillary blood
questions.why: The apical surface is the one exposed to the lumen, such as the inside of the intestine or the kidney tubule, and it is where absorbed material first enters the cell. Interstitial fluid and blood lie on the other side, which is served by the basolateral membrane. The surface contacting a neighboring cell is the lateral membrane and is where junctions form.
questions.answerText: The lumen
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The basolateral membrane of an intestinal epithelial cell faces which compartment?
options: The interstitial fluid on the blood side
The lumen of a secretory vesicle
The inside of the nucleus
The gut lumen
questions.why: The basolateral membrane lines the sides and base of the cell and faces the interstitial fluid, so solutes crossing there are on their way into the blood. The lumen is served by the apical membrane on the opposite face. Vesicle membranes are internal compartments, and the nucleus is not part of the transport route across an epithelium.
questions.answerText: The interstitial fluid on the blood side
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In an intestinal or proximal tubule cell, where is the SGLT sodium glucose cotransporter located?
options: The mitochondrial inner membrane
The basolateral membrane
The apical membrane
The nuclear envelope
questions.why: SGLT sits on the apical membrane, which is where it can pull glucose out of the lumen using the inward Na+ gradient. Putting it on the basolateral side would drag glucose from the interstitial fluid instead of absorbing it. The nuclear envelope and mitochondrial membranes handle internal traffic and have nothing to do with transepithelial absorption.
questions.answerText: The apical membrane
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where is GLUT2, the carrier that lets absorbed glucose leave the epithelial cell, located?
options: In the tight junction itself
The apical membrane
The basolateral membrane
Both membranes equally
questions.why: GLUT2 is basolateral, so glucose that has accumulated inside the cell can move down its gradient toward the interstitial fluid and blood. If GLUT2 were apical, absorbed glucose would leak straight back into the lumen. Equal distribution would defeat the whole point of polarity, and tight junctions are sealing structures, not transport proteins.
questions.answerText: The basolateral membrane
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In a polarized absorptive epithelial cell, where is the Na+/K+ ATPase found?
options: Only in the tight junction
Only on the apical membrane
Only on the basolateral membrane
Evenly on both membranes
questions.why: The pump is restricted to the basolateral membrane, where it moves absorbed Na+ toward the blood and, by keeping intracellular Na+ low, maintains the gradient that apical carriers depend on. An apical pump would push Na+ back into the lumen. An even distribution would cancel any net direction of transport, and junction proteins do not pump ions.
questions.answerText: Only on the basolateral membrane
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What do tight junctions between epithelial cells accomplish?
options: They supply ATP to nearby membrane transporters
They pump Na+ from the lumen into the cell using ATP
They seal the space between cells and keep the two membrane domains distinct
They open wide to allow proteins to pass into the blood
questions.why: Tight junctions seal the space between neighboring cells and act as a fence that prevents membrane proteins from drifting between the apical and basolateral domains, which is what makes directional transport possible. They do not transport ions themselves, so pumping is not their role. They restrict rather than permit protein passage, and they have no role in energy supply.
questions.answerText: They seal the space between cells and keep the two membrane domains distinct
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is transcellular transport?
options: Movement of solute inside a blood vessel
Movement of solute through the cells, crossing both the apical and basolateral membranes
Movement of solute between adjacent cells through the tight junction
Movement of solute along the surface of the epithelium
questions.why: Transcellular means through the cell, so the solute enters at one membrane and exits at the other, which is the route glucose takes during absorption. Slipping between cells is the paracellular route. Movement along the surface is not transport across the epithelium at all, and flow inside a vessel is bulk transport rather than membrane transport.
questions.answerText: Movement of solute through the cells, crossing both the apical and basolateral membranes
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What does it mean to say an epithelium is polarized?
options: The apical and basolateral membranes contain different transport proteins
The cells are aligned with the magnetic field of the body
All the cells face the same direction but have identical membranes
The cells carry a net electrical charge on one side
questions.why: Polarity means the two faces of the cell are equipped differently, and that difference in transporters is what allows solute to move in one direction across the sheet. A net charge on one side describes a membrane potential rather than polarity in this sense. Magnetic alignment is not a physiological concept. Identical membranes would give no net direction, which is exactly what polarity provides.
questions.answerText: The apical and basolateral membranes contain different transport proteins
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Glucose enters an intestinal epithelial cell from the lumen. Which type of transport is that first step?
options: Facilitated diffusion
Secondary active transport
Primary active transport
Simple diffusion
questions.why: Glucose is carried in by SGLT together with Na+, using the Na+ gradient rather than ATP, which makes the apical step secondary active transport and lets glucose move against its own gradient. Facilitated diffusion happens later, at the basolateral membrane through GLUT2. Simple diffusion cannot move polar glucose, and primary active transport would require the carrier itself to hydrolyze ATP.
questions.answerText: Secondary active transport
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Glucose leaves the epithelial cell across the basolateral membrane on its way to the blood. Which type of transport is that step?
options: Facilitated diffusion through GLUT2
Secondary active transport through SGLT
Primary active transport by an ATPase
Vesicular transport by exocytosis
questions.why: Apical uptake concentrates glucose inside the cell, so glucose can then move downhill through GLUT2, a passive carrier that needs no energy. SGLT is on the apical side and works in the opposite direction. No ATPase carries glucose, and packaging glucose into vesicles would be a wasteful way to move a small sugar.
questions.answerText: Facilitated diffusion through GLUT2
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Phlorizin blocks apical SGLT in the proximal tubule. Predict the effect on glucose reabsorption from the tubular fluid.
options: Reabsorption falls, because glucose can no longer be pulled out of the lumen
Reabsorption is unchanged, because glucose crosses the apical membrane by diffusion
Reabsorption reverses, and glucose is pumped from blood into the cell
Reabsorption rises, because GLUT2 compensates
questions.why: The apical step is the entry point for the entire pathway, so blocking SGLT strands glucose in the tubular fluid and it is excreted. GLUT2 sits on the basolateral membrane and cannot reach luminal glucose. Glucose is polar and does not cross the apical membrane by simple diffusion. Blocking a carrier does not create transport in the opposite direction.
questions.answerText: Reabsorption falls, because glucose can no longer be pulled out of the lumen
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Ouabain is applied only to the basolateral side of an intestinal epithelium. Predict the effect on glucose uptake at the apical membrane.
options: It falls only if glucose is also removed from the lumen
It rises, because Na+ inside the cell increases
It falls, because the Na+ gradient that drives apical SGLT is lost
It is unchanged, because ouabain acts only on the side where it is applied
questions.why: The basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase keeps intracellular Na+ low, and that low internal Na+ is what makes the apical Na+ gradient steep enough to power SGLT. Blocking the pump on one side therefore shuts down transport on the other side, which shows how the two membranes work as one system. Rising intracellular Na+ weakens rather than strengthens the driving force, and luminal glucose is not the limiting factor here.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the Na+ gradient that drives apical SGLT is lost
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which membrane of an absorptive epithelial cell holds the transporter that keeps intracellular Na+ low?
options: The basolateral membrane
Both membranes equally
Neither, since Na+ is kept low by binding proteins in the cytosol
The apical membrane
questions.why: The basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase exports Na+ toward the interstitial fluid, which is what holds cytosolic Na+ low and sustains apical Na+ coupled uptake. An apical pump would return Na+ to the lumen and defeat absorption. Equal distribution would eliminate directionality, and cytosolic binding proteins are not how cells maintain their Na+ gradient.
questions.answerText: The basolateral membrane
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Sodium is absorbed across an intestinal epithelium and water follows. What drives the water movement?
options: Water is carried inside vesicles with the Na+
Water moves because tight junctions actively squeeze it through
Water is pumped by an ATP driven water pump
Water follows the osmotic gradient created by solute absorption
questions.why: Moving Na+ and its accompanying solutes to the blood side raises osmolarity there, and water follows passively through aquaporins and between cells. There is no water pump in human cell membranes, since water movement is always driven by osmotic and hydrostatic forces. Vesicular carriage would be far too slow for the volumes involved, and junctions are passive seals rather than motors.
questions.answerText: Water follows the osmotic gradient created by solute absorption
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Na+ moves from the lumen into an intestinal epithelial cell across the apical membrane. Relative to its electrochemical gradient, how does Na+ move at that step?
options: Uphill, which is why ATP is required at the apical membrane
Neither, because Na+ is at equilibrium across the apical membrane
Uphill, powered by the glucose gradient
Downhill, because intracellular Na+ is low and the cell interior is negative
questions.why: The basolateral pump keeps intracellular Na+ low and the inside of the cell negative, so Na+ entering from the lumen is moving downhill and releases energy. That released energy is what SGLT harnesses to carry glucose uphill. No ATP is spent at the apical membrane. Na+ is far from equilibrium there, and it is Na+ that powers glucose transport, not the reverse.
questions.answerText: Downhill, because intracellular Na+ is low and the cell interior is negative
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Put the steps of glucose absorption in the correct order from gut lumen to blood.
options: Na+/K+ ATPase at the apical membrane, then SGLT at the basolateral membrane, then the capillary
Simple diffusion across both membranes, then the capillary
GLUT2 at the apical membrane, then SGLT at the basolateral membrane, then the capillary
SGLT at the apical membrane, then GLUT2 at the basolateral membrane, then the capillary
questions.why: Glucose is pulled from the lumen by apical SGLT using the Na+ gradient, accumulates inside the cell, and then exits downhill through basolateral GLUT2 into the interstitial fluid, from which it enters the capillary. Swapping the two carriers puts each on the wrong face and would move glucose out of the blood instead of into it. The pump is basolateral, and glucose is too polar to diffuse through either membrane.
questions.answerText: SGLT at the apical membrane, then GLUT2 at the basolateral membrane, then the capillary
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A toxin blocks basolateral GLUT2 in an intestinal epithelial cell while apical SGLT stays intact. Predict what happens to intracellular glucose and then to apical glucose uptake.
options: Intracellular glucose rises, and apical uptake speeds up to compensate
Intracellular glucose is unchanged, because SGLT stops immediately
Intracellular glucose rises, and apical uptake slows as the internal gradient steepens
Intracellular glucose falls, and apical uptake speeds up to compensate
questions.why: With its exit blocked, glucose piles up in the cytosol, and SGLT then has to push glucose against an increasingly steep internal gradient, so uptake slows even though the carrier is undamaged. Glucose cannot fall when entry continues and exit is blocked. There is no mechanism by which a rising internal load speeds the apical carrier, and SGLT does not stop the instant GLUT2 is blocked, so intracellular glucose does change.
questions.answerText: Intracellular glucose rises, and apical uptake slows as the internal gradient steepens
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Suppose an epithelial cell mistakenly placed its Na+/K+ ATPase in the apical membrane instead of the basolateral membrane. Predict the effect on net Na+ absorption from the lumen.
options: Net absorption would be unchanged, because the pump works the same on either face
Na+ would be absorbed but glucose would not
Net absorption would rise, because the pump would be closer to the lumen
Net Na+ absorption would fail, because the pump would push Na+ back into the lumen
questions.why: The pump always moves Na+ from cytosol to the side it faces, so an apical pump would return absorbed Na+ to the lumen and no net transfer to the blood would occur. Proximity to the lumen does not help when the direction of pumping is wrong. Location is exactly what determines the direction of transepithelial transport, so this could never be a neutral change, and glucose uptake would also fail once the Na+ gradient collapsed.
questions.answerText: Net Na+ absorption would fail, because the pump would push Na+ back into the lumen
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Cholera toxin causes intestinal cells to secrete Cl- across the apical membrane at a high rate. Trace what happens next to Na+ and to water in the lumen.
options: Na+ moves into the blood and water follows it, so the stool becomes dry
Na+ stays in the cell and water moves into the blood
Only Cl- accumulates in the lumen, since water cannot cross the epithelium
Na+ follows Cl- into the lumen and water follows osmotically, producing watery diarrhea
questions.why: Secreted Cl- makes the lumen electrically negative, so Na+ follows through the paracellular route, and the added NaCl raises luminal osmolarity so water is pulled in as well, which is the mechanism of secretory diarrhea. Absorption into the blood is the opposite of what secretion does. Na+ does not sit trapped in the cell, and the epithelium is highly water permeable, which is precisely why the fluid loss is so large.
questions.answerText: Na+ follows Cl- into the lumen and water follows osmotically, producing watery diarrhea
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In a membrane transport simulation, which transport type stops when a metabolic poison removes ATP from the model cell?
options: Active transport
Osmosis of water
Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
questions.why: Only active transport spends ATP, so it is the one process the poison shuts down. Simple and facilitated diffusion run on the solute gradient and keep going, which is why the poison run is the standard test for distinguishing them. Osmosis is likewise passive and follows the water gradient regardless of ATP.
questions.answerText: Active transport
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the simulation, which transport type shows no plateau no matter how high the solute concentration is raised?
options: Primary active transport
Secondary active transport
Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
questions.why: Simple diffusion has no carriers to saturate, so its rate keeps rising as long as the gradient rises. All three of the other processes depend on a limited number of transport proteins, so each one flattens into a plateau once every binding site is occupied. Watching for that plateau is how the simulation separates protein mediated transport from movement through the lipid.
questions.answerText: Simple diffusion
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the simulation, the concentration gradient for a passively transported solute is reversed. What happens to the direction of net movement?
options: It stays the same, because carriers have a fixed direction
It reverses, because passive transport always follows the gradient
It stops permanently
It becomes random with no net direction at any concentration
questions.why: Passive transport has no preferred direction, so flipping which side has more solute flips the direction of net flux. Carriers used in facilitated diffusion are not one way valves. Transport does not stop, since a gradient still exists, and net movement is only zero when the two sides are equal, not whenever the gradient is reversed.
questions.answerText: It reverses, because passive transport always follows the gradient
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the simulation, what is the defining behavior of active transport that neither type of diffusion shows?
options: It works only at a temperature of 37 C
It can move solute uphill, from the low side to the high side
It moves solute faster than diffusion at every concentration
It requires a membrane containing wide open pores
questions.why: Moving solute uphill against its gradient is the behavior that requires an energy input, and it is what marks a run as active transport. Speed alone does not distinguish the processes, since an open channel can outpace a pump. Pores are features of channels, which are passive, and temperature affects all of the processes rather than defining any one of them.
questions.answerText: It can move solute uphill, from the low side to the high side
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the purpose of running a control condition in the transport simulation?
options: To confirm that the solute is present
To increase the transport rate in later runs
To make the membrane thicker for later trials
To provide a baseline rate against which the treated runs are compared
questions.why: The control gives the untreated transport rate, so any change seen after adding poison, reversing the gradient, or changing carrier number can be attributed to that one variable. Confirming the solute is present is a setup check, not the reason for a control. A control does not alter later runs, and it does not change the properties of the simulated membrane.
questions.answerText: To provide a baseline rate against which the treated runs are compared
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: You build a curve of transport rate against solute concentration in the simulation. Which variable is the independent variable?
options: The number of carriers in the membrane
The temperature of the bath
The transport rate
The solute concentration you set
questions.why: The independent variable is the one you set on purpose, which here is the solute concentration plotted along the horizontal axis. Transport rate is the dependent variable, since it is the outcome you measure. Carrier number and temperature are held constant in this particular run, which makes them controlled variables rather than the independent one.
questions.answerText: The solute concentration you set
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the simulation, which factor does not affect the rate of simple diffusion of a solute across the membrane?
options: The surface area of the membrane
The lipid solubility of the solute
The number of carrier proteins in the membrane
The size of the concentration gradient
questions.why: Simple diffusion goes straight through the lipid, so carrier number is irrelevant to it, and adding carriers changes only the carrier mediated runs. The gradient sets the driving force, larger surface area gives more room to cross, and greater lipid solubility lets the solute dissolve into the bilayer more readily, so all three of those do change the rate.
questions.answerText: The number of carrier proteins in the membrane
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the simulation, which two transport types require a transport protein to be present in the model membrane?
options: Simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion
Osmosis and active transport only
Simple diffusion and osmosis
Facilitated diffusion and active transport
questions.why: Facilitated diffusion needs a carrier or channel, and active transport needs a pump, so removing the protein sets both rates to zero. Simple diffusion needs no protein at all, which is why it is the process that continues in a bare lipid membrane. Osmosis of water can occur through the lipid as well, though aquaporins speed it up.
questions.answerText: Facilitated diffusion and active transport
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In a simulation run, a solute continues to move from the compartment with the lower concentration into the compartment with the higher concentration. What does this tell you about the transport?
options: It is facilitated diffusion through a carrier protein
It is active transport, since energy is moving solute uphill
It is osmosis of water across the membrane
It is simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
questions.why: Uphill movement cannot occur without an energy input, so a run that builds a gradient rather than erasing one must be active transport. Both forms of diffusion stop at equal concentrations and can never push past that point. Osmosis describes water movement, not the solute movement measured here.
questions.answerText: It is active transport, since energy is moving solute uphill
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In a simulation run, doubling the solute gradient doubles the transport rate, and the rate keeps rising with no ceiling at any concentration tested. Which process is this?
options: Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
Primary active transport
Secondary active transport
questions.why: A rate that rises in direct proportion with no ceiling means nothing is saturating, which points to movement through the lipid rather than through a limited set of proteins. Facilitated diffusion would flatten once the carriers were full. Both active transport types would also flatten and would require energy, which a strictly gradient driven result does not indicate.
questions.answerText: Simple diffusion
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A metabolic poison is added in the simulation and the transport rate for solute X does not change. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Solute X is being actively transported
Solute X is moving by a passive process
Solute X must be crossing without any protein
Solute X is being moved against its gradient
questions.why: Insensitivity to ATP loss rules out active transport and marks the process as passive, but the poison test alone cannot say whether the passive route is simple or facilitated diffusion. Deciding between those two requires the saturation test. Uphill movement is also ruled out, since a passive process cannot build a gradient.
questions.answerText: Solute X is moving by a passive process
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the simulation you increase the number of carrier proteins in the membrane while keeping the solute concentration high enough to saturate them. Predict the effect on the transport rate.
options: The maximum rate falls, because carriers interfere with each other
The rate is unchanged, because saturation is already reached
The rate becomes linear with concentration
The maximum rate rises, because more carriers can work at once
questions.why: The saturated rate is the sum of what all carriers can move, so adding carriers raises the ceiling. Carriers in the same membrane operate independently and do not obstruct each other. Saturation limits the carriers that were already present, not the new ones. The curve keeps its saturating shape, since more carriers only shift the plateau upward.
questions.answerText: The maximum rate rises, because more carriers can work at once
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the simulation you double the surface area of the membrane while holding the concentration gradient constant. Predict the effect on the rate of simple diffusion.
options: It is unchanged, because the gradient did not change
It falls to zero
It roughly doubles
It is halved
questions.why: Diffusion rate is proportional to the area available for crossing, so twice the area gives roughly twice the flux even with the same driving gradient. Adding area cannot slow diffusion or stop it. Saying nothing changes ignores area as a determinant, which is exactly the variable this run isolates.
questions.answerText: It roughly doubles
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the simulation, the pore size of a channel is set smaller than the solute molecule. Predict the transport rate for that solute through the channel.
options: It stays the same, because pore size affects only water
It falls to essentially zero, because the solute cannot fit through the pore
It reverses direction
It rises, because the solute is forced through faster
questions.why: A channel is a size selective pore, so a solute larger than the opening simply cannot pass and flux through that route drops to nearly nothing. Narrowing a pore cannot accelerate passage. Pore size restricts every solute, not only water, and blocking a path does not create movement in the opposite direction.
questions.answerText: It falls to essentially zero, because the solute cannot fit through the pore
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the simulation, solute X shows these results: the transport rate plateaus at high concentration, a metabolic poison does not change it, and reversing the gradient reverses the direction of net movement. Which transport type is solute X using?
options: Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
Primary active transport
Osmosis
questions.why: The plateau shows a limited number of transport proteins, while ATP independence and gradient following both show the process is passive, which together identify facilitated diffusion. Simple diffusion is ruled out by the plateau. Active transport is ruled out by the poison result and by the willingness to reverse with the gradient. Osmosis refers to water rather than a solute.
questions.answerText: Facilitated diffusion
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the simulation, solute Y shows these results: the transport rate plateaus at high concentration, a metabolic poison stops transport, and the solute continues to move into the compartment that already has more of it. Which transport type is solute Y using?
options: Active transport
Movement through a leaky junction
Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
questions.why: Uphill movement plus dependence on ATP identifies active transport, and the plateau confirms a limited number of pump proteins. Simple diffusion would neither plateau nor need ATP. Facilitated diffusion plateaus but is ATP independent and cannot build a gradient. A leak pathway is passive and would erase the gradient rather than deepen it.
questions.answerText: Active transport
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Two solutes both plateau at high concentration in the simulation, so both are protein mediated. Which single additional run best separates facilitated diffusion from active transport?
options: Add more solute to the high concentration side
Raise the temperature of the bath
Add the metabolic poison and see which transport stops
Increase the surface area of the membrane
questions.why: Active transport depends on ATP and facilitated diffusion does not, so the poison run separates them cleanly in a single test. Temperature speeds up both processes and distinguishes neither. Extra membrane area raises both rates. Adding still more solute only confirms the plateau you have already seen, which both processes share.
questions.answerText: Add the metabolic poison and see which transport stops
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In the simulation a student sees a solute moving into the compartment that already has more of it, even though ATP is not being supplied to the transport protein itself. What is the best explanation?
options: The simulation is measuring simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
The transport protein is producing its own ATP as it carries the solute
The gradient in the simulation must actually point the other way
A coupled carrier is using another solute's gradient, so this is secondary active transport
questions.why: A carrier can move one solute uphill by letting a second solute run downhill, so no ATP touches the protein even though the process is still active transport, one step removed from the pump that built the driver gradient. Simple diffusion could never move solute uphill. Transport proteins consume energy rather than producing ATP, and dismissing the observed gradient avoids the question instead of explaining it.
questions.answerText: A coupled carrier is using another solute's gradient, so this is secondary active transport
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In which part of the cell does glycolysis take place?
options: The mitochondrial matrix
The cytosol
The inner mitochondrial membrane
The outer mitochondrial membrane
questions.why: The ten glycolytic enzymes are soluble proteins dissolved in the cytosol, which is why a cell with no mitochondria at all can still run glycolysis. The mitochondrial matrix holds the citric acid cycle enzymes, and the inner mitochondrial membrane holds the electron transport chain. The outer mitochondrial membrane is freely permeable to small molecules and carries no ATP producing pathway.
questions.answerText: The cytosol

questions.q: When oxygen is plentiful, what is the end product of glycolysis?
options: Lactate
Acetyl CoA
Pyruvate
Oxaloacetate
questions.why: Glycolysis splits one six carbon glucose into two three carbon pyruvate molecules regardless of oxygen; oxygen only decides what happens to the pyruvate next. Lactate is the product when oxygen is short and pyruvate must be reduced to regenerate NAD+. Acetyl CoA is made one step later by pyruvate dehydrogenase inside the mitochondrion, and oxaloacetate is the four carbon molecule that accepts acetyl CoA into the citric acid cycle.
questions.answerText: Pyruvate

questions.q: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per molecule of glucose?
options: Two ATP
Four ATP
Six ATP
Thirty two ATP
questions.why: Glycolysis spends two ATP in the early priming steps and makes four by substrate level phosphorylation later, so the net gain is two. Four is the gross yield before you subtract the investment, a very common slip. Thirty two is the approximate total for complete aerobic oxidation of glucose, most of which comes from oxidative phosphorylation rather than glycolysis itself.
questions.answerText: Two ATP

questions.q: Where in the cell does the citric acid cycle operate?
options: In the cytosol
In the inner mitochondrial membrane
In the smooth endoplasmic reticulum
In the mitochondrial matrix
questions.why: The citric acid cycle enzymes float in the matrix, the fluid space enclosed by the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is why pyruvate has to be carried into the mitochondrion before the cycle can use it. The cytosol is where glycolysis runs. The inner membrane is protein studded with the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, not with cycle enzymes. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum handles lipid synthesis and calcium storage.
questions.answerText: In the mitochondrial matrix
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Where are the electron transport chain complexes located?
options: In the inner mitochondrial membrane
In the mitochondrial matrix
In the cytosol
In the outer mitochondrial membrane
questions.why: The complexes are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane so they can pump H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space and build the gradient that ATP synthase uses. If they sat in the matrix there would be no membrane to pump across and no gradient. The cytosol holds glycolysis, and the outer membrane is too leaky to hold any gradient at all.
questions.answerText: In the inner mitochondrial membrane
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: What molecule accepts the electrons at the end of the electron transport chain?
options: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
NAD+
Pyruvate
questions.why: Oxygen takes the spent electrons and combines with H+ to form water, which is the only reason the chain keeps flowing and the only place oxygen is directly used in metabolism. Carbon dioxide is a waste product released by the citric acid cycle, not an electron acceptor. NAD+ carries electrons into the chain rather than accepting them at the end, and pyruvate accepts electrons only in the anaerobic side reaction that makes lactate.
questions.answerText: Oxygen

questions.q: Which ATP producing pathway can run with no oxygen present at all?
options: The citric acid cycle
Oxidative phosphorylation
Glycolysis
Beta oxidation
questions.why: Glycolysis needs no oxygen because it regenerates its own NAD+ by reducing pyruvate to lactate, so it keeps producing two ATP per glucose in an oxygen free cell. The citric acid cycle stops without oxygen because its NADH has nowhere to unload. Oxidative phosphorylation requires oxygen by definition as the terminal electron acceptor, and beta oxidation feeds acetyl CoA into that same oxygen dependent machinery.
questions.answerText: Glycolysis

questions.q: About how many ATP does the complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule yield?
options: About 2 ATP
About 12 ATP
About 32 ATP
About 100 ATP
questions.why: Most texts give roughly 30 to 32 ATP per glucose, with only 2 from glycolysis and 2 from the citric acid cycle; the rest comes from oxidative phosphorylation harvesting NADH and FADH2. Two is the anaerobic yield from glycolysis alone. Twelve is far too low for full oxidation, and one hundred is well above what the proton gradient can pay for.
questions.answerText: About 32 ATP

questions.q: A mature red blood cell has no mitochondria. Which pathway supplies its ATP?
options: The citric acid cycle
Oxidative phosphorylation
Beta oxidation
Anaerobic glycolysis
questions.why: Glycolysis is entirely cytosolic, so it is the only pathway a red cell can run, and the pyruvate it makes is converted to lactate and exported. The citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and beta oxidation all require mitochondrial compartments the red cell does not have. This is also why a red cell cannot consume any of the oxygen it carries.
questions.answerText: Anaerobic glycolysis
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Cyanide blocks the final complex of the electron transport chain. Which ATP producing process can still run?
options: Oxidative phosphorylation
Proton pumping by complex I
The citric acid cycle in the matrix
Glycolysis producing lactate
questions.why: Glycolysis survives the block because it makes ATP by substrate level phosphorylation and regenerates its own NAD+ by reducing pyruvate to lactate. Oxidative phosphorylation is exactly what cyanide stops. Complex I halts as well, because with the chain blocked downstream the carriers stay reduced and cannot accept more electrons, and for the same reason NADH piles up and the citric acid cycle stalls.
questions.answerText: Glycolysis producing lactate

questions.q: Why must a muscle working without enough oxygen convert pyruvate to lactate?
options: To regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running
To make two extra ATP in the reaction itself
To feed acetyl CoA into the citric acid cycle
To consume the protons pumped by complex IV
questions.why: Glycolysis consumes NAD+ at the glyceraldehyde 3 phosphate step, and with the electron transport chain unavailable the only way to get NAD+ back is to dump the electrons on pyruvate, making lactate. The lactate reaction itself yields no ATP; it simply keeps the earlier ATP producing steps supplied. Acetyl CoA production goes down, not up, when oxygen is short, and complex IV is not pumping at all under these conditions.
questions.answerText: To regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running

questions.q: How many turns of the citric acid cycle occur per glucose molecule that is fully oxidized?
options: One turn, because glucose enters as a single acetyl CoA
Four turns, because four carbons enter the cycle
Two turns, because glucose yields two pyruvate
Six turns, one for each carbon in glucose
questions.why: One glucose is split into two pyruvate, each becomes one acetyl CoA, and each acetyl CoA drives one turn, so the cycle turns twice per glucose. Forgetting the doubling is the single most common arithmetic error in ATP tallies. Four and six come from counting carbons rather than acetyl CoA units, and only two of glucose's six carbons enter the cycle per turn.
questions.answerText: Two turns, because glucose yields two pyruvate
