questions.q: A chemical makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to H+. What happens to ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation?
options: It rises, because electron transport speeds up
It falls, because the H+ gradient is dissipated
It is unchanged, because ATP synthase is intact
It stops, because oxygen can no longer be used
questions.why: ATP synthase is powered by H+ flowing back through it, so a leak that lets H+ return by another route removes the driving force and ATP output falls even though every protein is still functional. Electron transport does speed up, but that only burns more fuel and releases the energy as heat instead of ATP. Oxygen consumption continues and in fact increases, which is why this is called uncoupling rather than inhibition.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the H+ gradient is dissipated
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A tissue loses its oxygen supply and must rely on anaerobic metabolism. By roughly what factor does ATP yield per glucose fall?
options: About 100 fold
About 16 fold
About 4 fold
About 2 fold
questions.why: Complete aerobic oxidation gives about 32 ATP per glucose and anaerobic glycolysis gives 2, so the yield falls roughly sixteen fold. This is why an oxygen starved tissue must consume glucose many times faster just to hold its ATP steady, and why it produces so much lactate. Two fold and four fold badly understate the loss, and one hundred fold overstates it because glycolysis still contributes real ATP.
questions.answerText: About 16 fold

questions.q: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is deficient, so pyruvate cannot be converted to acetyl CoA. Which substance accumulates in the blood?
options: Lactate
Citrate
Acetyl CoA
Glucose
questions.why: With the door into the mitochondrion shut, pyruvate backs up in the cytosol and is reduced to lactate, so plasma lactate climbs. Acetyl CoA is downstream of the block and therefore falls, and citrate falls with it because the cycle is starved of its two carbon input. Glucose sits upstream of glycolysis and is consumed faster, not accumulated, as the cell tries to compensate.
questions.answerText: Lactate

questions.q: Blood flow to a leg muscle is occluded while the muscle keeps contracting. Predict the ATP yield per glucose and the lactate concentration in that muscle.
options: ATP per glucose stays near 32 and lactate rises
ATP per glucose falls to about 2 and lactate rises
ATP per glucose falls to about 2 and lactate falls
ATP per glucose rises and lactate stays unchanged
questions.why: No blood flow means no oxygen, so the electron transport chain stops and only glycolysis makes ATP, dropping the yield from about 32 to 2 per glucose. To keep glycolysis running the cell must reduce pyruvate to lactate, and with no blood flow the lactate cannot be washed away, so it accumulates locally. Holding the yield near 32 would require oxidative phosphorylation, and a falling lactate would require either oxygen or perfusion to remove it.
questions.answerText: ATP per glucose falls to about 2 and lactate rises

questions.q: Brown adipose tissue expresses UCP1, a protein that lets H+ leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Predict oxygen consumption, ATP made per oxygen consumed, and heat production.
options: Oxygen use falls, ATP per oxygen rises, heat falls
Oxygen use is unchanged, ATP per oxygen falls, heat falls
Oxygen use rises, ATP per oxygen rises, heat rises
Oxygen use rises, ATP per oxygen falls, heat rises
questions.why: The leak keeps the gradient small, so electron transport runs fast and consumes oxygen quickly, but little of that energy reaches ATP synthase and most is released as heat. That is precisely the point of brown fat, which exists to warm the body rather than to make ATP. Any answer with heat falling misses that uncoupled transport dissipates energy thermally, and ATP per oxygen cannot rise when the gradient driving ATP synthase is being short circuited.
questions.answerText: Oxygen use rises, ATP per oxygen falls, heat rises
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A toxin blocks ATP synthase but leaves the electron transport chain complexes intact. Predict the H+ gradient across the inner membrane and the rate of oxygen consumption.
options: The gradient builds up and oxygen consumption falls
The gradient collapses and oxygen consumption rises
The gradient builds up and oxygen consumption rises
The gradient collapses and oxygen consumption falls
questions.why: With ATP synthase blocked, the H+ that the chain pumps out has no way back in, so the gradient grows until it opposes further pumping and electron flow slows, which in turn slows oxygen consumption. This coupling of oxygen use to ATP demand is called respiratory control. A collapsing gradient with rising oxygen use describes an uncoupler such as UCP1, the opposite manipulation, and a gradient that builds while oxygen use rises is self contradictory because the gradient itself is what holds the pumps back.
questions.answerText: The gradient builds up and oxygen consumption falls

questions.q: A patient has a normal resting lactate, but mild exercise sends lactate climbing steeply and peak oxygen consumption is very low. Which step is limited?
options: Glucose uptake into muscle
Glycolysis in the muscle cytosol
Oxidative phosphorylation
Oxygen carriage by hemoglobin
questions.why: Muscle that cannot use oxygen at the mitochondria meets any extra ATP demand by accelerating glycolysis, so lactate rises out of proportion to a low workload while peak oxygen consumption stays small. A glycolytic block would do the opposite and produce little or no lactate. Limited glucose uptake would lower fuel supply rather than force lactate production, and a hemoglobin problem would limit oxygen delivery but would also lower venous oxygen content, whereas a mitochondrial defect leaves venous oxygen unusually high.
questions.answerText: Oxidative phosphorylation

questions.q: Which hormone dominates the absorptive state?
options: Insulin
Glucagon
Cortisol
Epinephrine
questions.why: The absorptive state is the two to four hours after a meal when nutrients are entering the blood from the gut, and insulin is the hormone that moves them into cells for use and storage. Glucagon dominates the postabsorptive state, when the job is releasing stored fuel instead of storing it. Cortisol and epinephrine are counter regulatory hormones that raise plasma glucose, which is the opposite of what the fed state calls for.
questions.answerText: Insulin

questions.q: Which pancreatic cells secrete insulin?
options: Alpha cells of the islets
Delta cells of the islets
Beta cells of the islets
Acinar cells
questions.why: Beta cells make up the bulk of each pancreatic islet and secrete insulin directly into the blood. Alpha cells in the same islet secrete glucagon, the hormone with the opposite job, and delta cells secrete somatostatin, which damps both. Acinar cells are the exocrine pancreas and secrete digestive enzymes into the duct system, not hormones into the blood.
questions.answerText: Beta cells of the islets

questions.q: What is the main stimulus for insulin secretion after a meal?
options: A fall in plasma glucose
A rise in plasma free fatty acids
A rise in plasma glucose
A fall in plasma amino acids
questions.why: Beta cells sense glucose directly, and a rising plasma glucose is the primary signal that triggers insulin release; amino acids and gut incretin hormones add to it. A falling glucose does the opposite and shuts insulin secretion off while turning glucagon on. Free fatty acids rise during fasting when insulin is low, and falling amino acids are not a fed state signal at all.
questions.answerText: A rise in plasma glucose

questions.q: In what form is absorbed glucose stored in liver and skeletal muscle?
options: As free glucose
As triglyceride
As glucose 6 phosphate
As glycogen
questions.why: Glucose is polymerized into glycogen, a branched storage polysaccharide, which lets the cell hold thousands of glucose units without raising its osmolarity. Storing free glucose would draw water into the cell osmotically. Triglyceride is the storage form of excess energy once glycogen stores are full, mostly in adipose tissue, and glucose 6 phosphate is only the brief intermediate on the way into glycogen.
questions.answerText: As glycogen
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: In what particles do absorbed long chain fats leave the small intestine?
options: In low density lipoproteins
As free fatty acids bound to albumin
In high density lipoproteins
In chylomicrons
questions.why: Enterocytes reassemble absorbed fatty acids into triglyceride, package it into chylomicrons, and release these into lacteals so they travel by lymph and enter the blood at the thoracic duct. Low density lipoprotein and high density lipoprotein are made by the liver and by remodeling in plasma, not by the intestine. Free fatty acids bound to albumin are what adipose tissue releases during fasting, the opposite state.
questions.answerText: In chylomicrons

questions.q: Which glucose transporter does insulin recruit to the membrane of muscle and adipose cells?
options: GLUT1
GLUT4
GLUT2
SGLT1
questions.why: GLUT4 sits in intracellular vesicles until insulin signals them to fuse with the plasma membrane, which is what makes glucose uptake into muscle and fat insulin dependent. GLUT1 is the constitutive transporter present in most cells, including red blood cells and the blood brain barrier. GLUT2 is the high capacity, insulin independent transporter of liver and beta cells, and SGLT1 is the sodium coupled transporter of the intestinal and renal epithelium.
questions.answerText: GLUT4

questions.q: Once glycogen stores are full, what happens to the glucose still arriving from a large meal?
options: It is excreted in the urine
It is converted to triglyceride and stored
It is converted to glycogen in the brain
It is converted to protein in muscle
questions.why: Glycogen capacity is limited to a few hundred grams, so surplus glucose is routed through acetyl CoA into fatty acid synthesis and stored as triglyceride, which has no practical upper limit. Urinary loss only starts if plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold, which does not happen in a healthy person after a meal. The brain stores essentially no glycogen, and glucose carbon cannot be made into the essential amino acids that protein synthesis requires.
questions.answerText: It is converted to triglyceride and stored

questions.q: What does insulin do to amino acids arriving after a protein containing meal?
options: It promotes their uptake and protein synthesis
It blocks their entry into muscle cells
It converts them to urea in the liver
It promotes their release from muscle
questions.why: Insulin is an anabolic hormone across all three fuel classes: it drives amino acids into cells and stimulates protein synthesis while inhibiting protein breakdown. Blocking entry and promoting release from muscle are effects of cortisol during fasting, not of insulin during absorption. Deamination and urea formation happen mostly when amino acids are in excess or when they are being used as fuel, which is the postabsorptive pattern.
questions.answerText: It promotes their uptake and protein synthesis

questions.q: Insulin increases the activity of lipoprotein lipase on the capillary walls of adipose tissue. What does this do to fat handling after a meal?
options: It increases fatty acid uptake into adipocytes
It releases stored fat into the blood
It moves chylomicrons intact into adipocytes
It converts fatty acids into glucose
questions.why: Lipoprotein lipase sits on the endothelium and strips triglyceride out of circulating chylomicrons, freeing fatty acids that diffuse into the adipocyte and are re esterified for storage. Releasing stored fat is the job of hormone sensitive lipase inside the adipocyte, which insulin inhibits rather than stimulates. Whole chylomicrons are far too large to cross the capillary wall, and fatty acids with an even number of carbons cannot be converted to glucose.
questions.answerText: It increases fatty acid uptake into adipocytes

questions.q: A person eats a large carbohydrate meal. Predict what happens to glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase activity in the liver.
options: Both activities rise together
Synthase falls and phosphorylase rises
Both activities fall together
Synthase rises and phosphorylase falls
questions.why: Insulin drives dephosphorylation of both enzymes, which activates glycogen synthase and inactivates glycogen phosphorylase, so the liver stores glucose instead of releasing it. Running both at once would create a futile cycle that burns ATP and stores nothing. Synthase down with phosphorylase up is exactly the fasting pattern set by glucagon, and shutting both down would leave the liver unable to handle the meal at all.
questions.answerText: Synthase rises and phosphorylase falls

questions.q: In a person whose muscle GLUT4 vesicles cannot fuse with the plasma membrane, what happens to plasma glucose after a meal?
options: It falls faster than normal
It is unaffected, because the liver compensates
It stays elevated longer than normal
It falls below the fasting value
questions.why: Skeletal muscle is the largest single sink for a glucose load, and it takes glucose up only when insulin puts GLUT4 into the membrane, so blocking that step leaves glucose in the plasma much longer. This is the mechanism behind insulin resistance in muscle. The liver takes up glucose through insulin independent GLUT2, but liver uptake alone cannot substitute for the muscle mass, so glucose cannot fall faster or below fasting.
questions.answerText: It stays elevated longer than normal
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Why does plasma sometimes look milky a few hours after a fatty meal?
options: Free fatty acids released from adipose scatter light
Cholesterol crystals precipitate out of plasma
Bile salts absorbed from the gut scatter light
Chylomicrons entering from the lymph scatter light
questions.why: Long chain fats leave the intestine as chylomicrons through the lymphatics and enter the bloodstream at the thoracic duct, and these large triglyceride rich particles scatter light enough to make plasma turbid until lipoprotein lipase clears them. Free fatty acids rise in fasting, are bound to albumin, and do not cloud plasma. Cholesterol does not precipitate in normal plasma, and bile salts are reabsorbed into the portal blood at a concentration far too low to be visible.
questions.answerText: Chylomicrons entering from the lymph scatter light

questions.q: A person eats a meal of pure protein with almost no carbohydrate. Why does glucagon rise along with insulin?
options: Glucagon helps move amino acids into cells
Glucagon prevents insulin from lowering glucose too far
Glucagon stimulates further insulin release
Glucagon slows amino acid absorption from the gut
questions.why: Amino acids stimulate insulin secretion, but with no carbohydrate in the meal that insulin would push plasma glucose down; the simultaneous glucagon rise stimulates hepatic glucose output and holds glucose steady. This is a nice example of two opposing hormones being co secreted to achieve a net result neither could achieve alone. Glucagon does not move amino acids into cells, does not slow their absorption, and its islet effect on insulin is minor compared with the glucose it liberates.
questions.answerText: Glucagon prevents insulin from lowering glucose too far

questions.q: Oral glucose triggers more insulin release than an intravenous infusion that produces the same plasma glucose. Why?
options: Oral glucose is absorbed as a different sugar
Portal blood bypasses the pancreas after infusion
Gut incretin hormones amplify insulin secretion
Intravenous glucose is cleared before reaching the islets
questions.why: As glucose passes through the small intestine it triggers release of incretins such as GIP and GLP-1, which prime beta cells to secrete more insulin for any given plasma glucose. This is the incretin effect and it means the body starts storing before glucose has even peaked. Oral glucose is absorbed as glucose either way, the pancreas sees arterial blood in both cases, and infused glucose is certainly not cleared before it circulates.
questions.answerText: Gut incretin hormones amplify insulin secretion

questions.q: Insulin stimulates the Na+/K+ ATPase in muscle and liver cells. Predict the effect of an insulin surge on plasma K+.
options: Plasma K+ falls as K+ moves into cells
Plasma K+ rises as K+ leaves cells
Plasma K+ is unchanged, since insulin acts only on glucose
Plasma K+ rises because the kidney retains K+
questions.why: A more active Na+/K+ ATPase pumps K+ into cells, so a large insulin surge shifts K+ out of the plasma and lowers its concentration. This is a redistribution between compartments, not a change in total body K+, and it happens within minutes. Potassium leaving cells is what happens when insulin is absent, and the kidney response is far too slow to explain a change on this timescale.
questions.answerText: Plasma K+ falls as K+ moves into cells

questions.q: A person with untreated type 1 diabetes, who makes no insulin, eats a carbohydrate meal. Predict muscle glucose uptake, plasma glucose, and urinary glucose.
options: Uptake low, plasma glucose high, no glucose in urine
Uptake low, plasma glucose high, glucose in urine
Uptake normal, plasma glucose high, glucose in urine
Uptake low, plasma glucose normal, no glucose in urine
questions.why: Without insulin the GLUT4 transporters stay inside muscle and fat cells, so the meal's glucose has nowhere to go and plasma glucose climbs steeply. Once it passes the renal threshold of roughly 180 mg/dL the filtered load exceeds what the tubule can reabsorb and glucose spills into the urine, dragging water with it. Uptake cannot be normal without insulin, and plasma glucose cannot stay normal when its main disposal route is closed.
questions.answerText: Uptake low, plasma glucose high, glucose in urine

questions.q: A person with an inherited deficiency of lipoprotein lipase eats a fatty meal. Predict plasma triglyceride, adipose fat storage, and how long the plasma stays cloudy.
options: Triglyceride high, storage increased, plasma clears quickly
Triglyceride normal, storage poor, plasma clears quickly
Triglyceride high, storage poor, plasma cloudy for hours
Triglyceride low, storage poor, plasma cloudy for hours
questions.why: Lipoprotein lipase is the enzyme that unloads chylomicron triglyceride at the capillary wall, so without it the particles circulate uncleared, plasma triglyceride stays high, and the plasma stays turbid long after a meal. Because the fatty acids are never freed, they never reach the adipocyte and storage is poor rather than increased. Plasma triglyceride cannot be normal or low when the only route for clearing it is missing.
questions.answerText: Triglyceride high, storage poor, plasma cloudy for hours

questions.q: Insulin is infused into a healthy person who has been fasting overnight. Predict what happens to plasma glucose, plasma free fatty acids, and plasma ketones.
options: Glucose falls, fatty acids rise, ketones rise
Glucose falls, fatty acids fall, ketones rise
Glucose falls, fatty acids fall, ketones fall
Glucose rises, fatty acids fall, ketones fall
questions.why: Insulin drives glucose into muscle and fat and shuts down hepatic glucose output, so plasma glucose falls. It also inhibits hormone sensitive lipase, so adipose tissue stops releasing free fatty acids, and with less fatty acid reaching the liver, ketone production falls as well. Insulin is the single most powerful antilipolytic hormone in the body, so any answer with fatty acids or ketones rising has the fed state backwards.
questions.answerText: Glucose falls, fatty acids fall, ketones fall

questions.q: A blood sample shows high insulin, low glucagon, low free fatty acids, and essentially no ketones. Which metabolic state does this describe, and what is the liver doing?
options: Postabsorptive state, liver releasing glucose
Prolonged fast, liver making ketones
Postabsorptive state, liver making glucose from amino acids
Absorptive state, liver storing glucose as glycogen
questions.why: A high insulin to glucagon ratio is the signature of the fed state, and low free fatty acids confirm that lipolysis is suppressed while ketones are absent because the liver has no fatty acid substrate and no signal to make them. Under those hormonal conditions the liver takes glucose up and builds glycogen rather than exporting it. All three wrong options describe fasting, when insulin would be low and glucagon high, and the prolonged fast option additionally requires ketones to be high.
questions.answerText: Absorptive state, liver storing glucose as glycogen

questions.q: Which process supplies blood glucose during the first several hours of a fast?
options: Ketogenesis
Hepatic glycogenolysis
Gluconeogenesis
Lipolysis in adipose tissue
questions.why: The liver breaks its stored glycogen back down to glucose and exports it, and this is the fastest and first source once absorption ends. Gluconeogenesis is running too but contributes little at first and only takes over as glycogen runs down. Lipolysis supplies fatty acids, which most tissues can burn but which cannot be turned into glucose, and ketogenesis becomes important only after a day or more of fasting.
questions.answerText: Hepatic glycogenolysis

questions.q: About how long can liver glycogen alone sustain the blood glucose concentration during a fast?
options: About one day
About one hour
About four hours
About one week
questions.why: The liver holds roughly 100 g of glycogen and the body uses glucose at a rate that exhausts this in something like 24 hours, which is why gluconeogenesis has to be ramping up the whole time. An hour or four hours is far too short; glycogenolysis easily carries a person through an overnight fast. A week is far too long, and by then the body is running on gluconeogenesis and ketones instead.
questions.answerText: About one day

questions.q: Which organ can release free glucose into the bloodstream?
options: The liver
Skeletal muscle
Adipose tissue
The brain
questions.why: The liver is the body's glucose exporter because it has the enzyme needed to strip the phosphate off glucose 6 phosphate, letting free glucose leave the cell. Skeletal muscle stores more glycogen than the liver in total but keeps every glucose unit for itself. Adipose tissue stores fat rather than glycogen, and the brain is a pure consumer of glucose with essentially no store of its own.
questions.answerText: The liver

questions.q: Which enzyme does skeletal muscle lack, so that it cannot contribute glucose to the blood?
options: Glycogen phosphorylase
Glucose 6 phosphatase
Hexokinase
Glycogen synthase
questions.why: Glucose 6 phosphatase removes the phosphate group, and only liver and kidney have it, so only they can release free glucose into blood. Muscle does have glycogen phosphorylase and breaks its glycogen down normally, but the glucose 6 phosphate produced is charged, cannot cross the membrane, and is burned on site. Hexokinase and glycogen synthase both point the other way, trapping and storing glucose rather than releasing it.
questions.answerText: Glucose 6 phosphatase
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which pancreatic cells secrete glucagon?
options: Beta cells of the islets
Delta cells of the islets
Acinar cells
Alpha cells of the islets
questions.why: Alpha cells occupy the periphery of each islet and release glucagon when plasma glucose falls. Beta cells in the same islet release insulin, the hormone with the opposite effect, and the ratio between the two rather than either alone sets the metabolic state. Delta cells secrete somatostatin, which restrains both, and acinar cells belong to the exocrine pancreas and secrete digestive enzymes.
questions.answerText: Alpha cells of the islets

questions.q: Which hormone dominates the postabsorptive state?
options: Insulin
Aldosterone
Calcitonin
Glucagon
questions.why: Once absorption ends and plasma glucose starts to drift down, insulin secretion falls and glucagon rises, and glucagon is the main signal telling the liver to break down glycogen and make new glucose. Insulin is the absorptive state hormone and its job is the reverse. Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium handling in the kidney, and calcitonin acts on calcium, so neither has a role in setting fuel traffic.
questions.answerText: Glucagon

questions.q: Which product of fat breakdown can be converted into glucose by the liver?
options: Palmitic acid
Acetyl CoA from fatty acids
Glycerol
Acetoacetate
questions.why: A triglyceride yields three fatty acids and one glycerol, and only the glycerol backbone can enter the gluconeogenic pathway. Fatty acids with an even number of carbons, such as palmitic acid, are broken down to acetyl CoA, and there is no pathway in humans that converts acetyl CoA back to pyruvate or glucose. Acetoacetate is a ketone body made from that same acetyl CoA and is a fuel, not a glucose precursor.
questions.answerText: Glycerol

questions.q: Where are ketone bodies produced, and from what substrate?
options: In muscle, from amino acids
In adipose tissue, from glycerol
In the kidney, from lactate
In the liver, from fatty acids
questions.why: When fatty acids flood into the liver during fasting, acetyl CoA is produced faster than the citric acid cycle can handle it and the liver condenses the excess into acetoacetate and beta hydroxybutyrate for export. The liver makes ketones but cannot use them, which is exactly what makes them available to other tissues. Muscle, adipose and kidney consume ketones rather than producing them, and lactate and glycerol feed gluconeogenesis instead.
questions.answerText: In the liver, from fatty acids

questions.q: A person has fasted for 36 hours. Which process is now the main supplier of plasma glucose?
options: Hepatic glycogenolysis
Muscle glycogenolysis
Gluconeogenesis
Intestinal absorption
questions.why: Liver glycogen is essentially gone by about 24 hours, so beyond that point the liver has to build glucose from lactate, glycerol and amino acids. Muscle glycogenolysis never contributes glucose to the blood because muscle lacks glucose 6 phosphatase. Intestinal absorption stopped when the last meal was absorbed, which is what started the postabsorptive state in the first place.
questions.answerText: Gluconeogenesis

questions.q: Working muscle sends lactate to the liver, which converts it back to glucose and returns it to the blood. What is this loop called?
options: The urea cycle
The Cori cycle
The citric acid cycle
The enterohepatic cycle
questions.why: The Cori cycle lets muscle unload the lactate it makes during anaerobic work and lets the liver recycle that carbon into glucose, at a net cost in ATP that the liver pays. The urea cycle disposes of the nitrogen from amino acid breakdown, not of lactate carbon. The citric acid cycle oxidizes acetyl CoA inside mitochondria, and the enterohepatic circulation recycles bile salts between gut and liver.
questions.answerText: The Cori cycle

questions.q: Adipose tissue breaks down triglyceride during a fast. What happens to the fatty acids released into the blood?
options: Most tissues oxidize them, sparing glucose
They are converted to glucose by the liver
They are taken up and stored by muscle
They are used by the brain as its main fuel
questions.why: Free fatty acids travel bound to albumin and are burned by heart, skeletal muscle, liver and most other tissues, which is called glucose sparing because it leaves the limited glucose supply for tissues that need it. Fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose because acetyl CoA cannot go backwards to pyruvate. The brain cannot use free fatty acids at all, since they do not cross the blood brain barrier in useful amounts; it uses ketones instead.
questions.answerText: Most tissues oxidize them, sparing glucose

questions.q: After several days of fasting, which fuel does the brain begin to rely on heavily?
options: Free fatty acids
Lactate from muscle
Ketone bodies
Amino acids from muscle
questions.why: Ketone bodies are water soluble, cross the blood brain barrier readily, and after several days can supply well over half the brain's energy, which sharply reduces how much glucose the body must manufacture. That in turn slows the breakdown of muscle protein and is the main reason a person can survive a long fast. Free fatty acids do not cross into the brain, and lactate and amino acids are not brain fuels in any meaningful quantity.
questions.answerText: Ketone bodies

questions.q: A frightened person releases a surge of epinephrine. Predict its effect on liver glycogenolysis and plasma glucose.
options: Glycogenolysis falls and glucose falls
Glycogenolysis rises and glucose falls
Glycogenolysis falls and glucose rises
Glycogenolysis rises and glucose rises
questions.why: Epinephrine is a counter regulatory hormone that acts through beta receptors and cyclic AMP to activate glycogen phosphorylase, so hepatic glucose output and plasma glucose both climb, readying the body for exertion. Epinephrine also drives glycogenolysis in muscle, though that glucose stays in the muscle. Any option pairing more glycogen breakdown with a falling plasma glucose ignores that the liver exports the glucose it liberates.
questions.answerText: Glycogenolysis rises and glucose rises

questions.q: Cortisol rises during a prolonged fast. What does it do to skeletal muscle protein?
options: It promotes synthesis of new muscle protein
It promotes breakdown, releasing amino acids
It blocks amino acid release from muscle
It converts muscle protein directly to glucose
questions.why: Cortisol is catabolic in muscle and anabolic for hepatic glucose production, breaking protein down so amino acids such as alanine can travel to the liver and be built into glucose. This is why prolonged fasting or long term cortisol excess wastes muscle. Cortisol does not promote muscle protein synthesis, and the conversion to glucose happens in the liver, not inside the muscle cell itself.
questions.answerText: It promotes breakdown, releasing amino acids
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: As a fast continues, the insulin to glucagon ratio falls. Predict the effect on hormone sensitive lipase in adipose tissue.
options: Activity increases and lipolysis speeds up
Activity decreases and fat storage speeds up
Activity is unchanged, since it responds only to epinephrine
Activity increases but lipolysis slows
questions.why: Insulin is the main brake on hormone sensitive lipase, so as insulin falls and glucagon and catecholamines rise the enzyme is disinhibited and triglyceride breakdown accelerates, pouring fatty acids and glycerol into the blood. Storage requires insulin and lipoprotein lipase, the fed state pattern. Epinephrine does stimulate the enzyme, but the insulin to glucagon ratio is the tonic control, and an active lipase by definition means faster lipolysis.
questions.answerText: Activity increases and lipolysis speeds up

questions.q: A healthy person has fasted for three days. Predict liver glycogen content, the rate of gluconeogenesis, and plasma ketone concentration.
options: Glycogen depleted, gluconeogenesis low, ketones high
Glycogen depleted, gluconeogenesis high, ketones high
Glycogen normal, gluconeogenesis high, ketones low
Glycogen depleted, gluconeogenesis high, ketones low
questions.why: Liver glycogen is spent within roughly a day, so by day three the liver is making glucose from glycerol, lactate and amino acids at a high rate. At the same time the low insulin state has adipose tissue releasing fatty acids so fast that the liver converts the excess acetyl CoA into ketone bodies, and plasma ketones climb. Gluconeogenesis cannot be low when it is the only glucose source left, and ketones cannot stay low when fatty acid delivery to the liver is maximal.
questions.answerText: Glycogen depleted, gluconeogenesis high, ketones high

questions.q: A child with a deficiency of glucose 6 phosphatase is fasted overnight. Predict plasma glucose, liver glycogen content, and plasma lactate.
options: Glucose falls, glycogen is depleted, lactate falls
Glucose is normal, glycogen accumulates, lactate rises
Glucose falls, glycogen accumulates, lactate rises
Glucose rises, glycogen accumulates, lactate falls
questions.why: Without glucose 6 phosphatase the liver can break glycogen down but cannot free the glucose to export it, so plasma glucose falls during any fast while glucose 6 phosphate and glycogen pile up inside hepatocytes. The trapped glucose 6 phosphate is pushed on through glycolysis to pyruvate and lactate, so plasma lactate rises. Glycogen cannot be depleted when the exit is blocked, and glucose cannot stay normal or rise when the liver's only export route is closed.
questions.answerText: Glucose falls, glycogen accumulates, lactate rises

questions.q: Glucagon is injected into one person who fasted overnight and into another who has fasted three days. The first shows a large rise in plasma glucose and the second almost none. Why?
options: Glucagon receptors are destroyed by prolonged fasting
The three day faster has more insulin opposing glucagon
Glucagon acts only on muscle glycogen after a long fast
The three day faster has no liver glycogen left
questions.why: Glucagon's fastest and largest effect is to trigger hepatic glycogenolysis, so its acute glucose raising power depends on there being glycogen to break down, and after three days there is none. Its slower action on gluconeogenesis is already running near maximum in that person, so extra hormone adds little. Receptors are not destroyed by fasting, insulin is lower rather than higher after three days, and glucagon has no significant action on muscle glycogen at any time.
questions.answerText: The three day faster has no liver glycogen left

questions.q: A person with type 1 diabetes stops taking insulin. Trace the effect on adipose lipolysis, hepatic ketone production, and blood pH.
options: Lipolysis accelerates, ketones rise, pH falls
Lipolysis slows, ketones fall, pH rises
Lipolysis accelerates, ketones rise, pH rises
Lipolysis slows, ketones rise, pH falls
questions.why: Insulin is the brake on hormone sensitive lipase, so removing it lets adipose tissue release fatty acids without restraint, and the liver converts the flood of acetyl CoA into acetoacetate and beta hydroxybutyrate. Those ketone bodies are acids, so as they accumulate they consume bicarbonate and blood pH falls, producing a metabolic acidosis. Note the paradox worth remembering: plasma glucose is very high, yet the cells behave as though they are starving, because without insulin they cannot use that glucose.
questions.answerText: Lipolysis accelerates, ketones rise, pH falls

questions.q: What is the normal fasting plasma glucose concentration in a healthy adult?
options: About 200 to 260 mg/dL
About 140 to 180 mg/dL
About 70 to 100 mg/dL
About 20 to 40 mg/dL
questions.why: Fasting plasma glucose is held in a narrow band around 70 to 100 mg/dL, and the tightness of that band is the point: it is defended from both sides by opposing hormones. Values around 20 to 40 mg/dL cause loss of consciousness because the brain cannot function on so little. Values of 140 and above are what a healthy person reaches only briefly after a meal, and sustained values in the 200s mean glucose regulation has failed.
questions.answerText: About 70 to 100 mg/dL

questions.q: In a healthy person, how high does plasma glucose usually rise after a carbohydrate meal?
options: It peaks below about 140 mg/dL
It stays completely unchanged
It peaks near 250 mg/dL
It falls immediately after eating
questions.why: Glucose does rise after a meal, typically peaking somewhere under 140 mg/dL at about one hour and coming back down toward fasting by two hours as insulin does its work. It does not stay flat, because absorption is faster than disposal for a while. A peak near 250 mg/dL indicates failed disposal, and an immediate fall would mean the meal was never absorbed.
questions.answerText: It peaks below about 140 mg/dL

questions.q: Which organ depends on a continuous glucose supply and uses roughly 120 g of glucose per day?
options: The brain
The liver
Skeletal muscle
Adipose tissue
questions.why: The brain has almost no fuel store, cannot use free fatty acids, and consumes about 120 g of glucose a day, which is why plasma glucose is defended so aggressively. The liver is a net supplier of glucose in the fasting state rather than an obligate consumer. Skeletal muscle can burn fatty acids and ketones freely, and adipose tissue stores fuel instead of demanding glucose.
questions.answerText: The brain

questions.q: Which hormone is the only one that lowers plasma glucose?
options: Growth hormone
Cortisol
Glucagon
Insulin
questions.why: Insulin stands alone on the glucose lowering side, while several hormones raise glucose, an asymmetry that reflects how much more dangerous a low glucose is than a high one in the short term. Growth hormone and cortisol both oppose insulin and raise plasma glucose over hours. Glucagon is the fastest acting glucose raising hormone and is insulin's direct partner in the islet.
questions.answerText: Insulin

questions.q: Which group of hormones is called counter regulatory because they oppose insulin?
options: Aldosterone, ADH, renin, and ANP
Glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, and growth hormone
Thyroid hormone, PTH, calcitonin, and vitamin D
Somatostatin, gastrin, secretin, and CCK
questions.why: These four all raise plasma glucose, by mobilizing glycogen, driving gluconeogenesis, or reducing tissue glucose uptake, and together they defend against hypoglycemia. Aldosterone, ADH, renin and ANP regulate salt and water. Thyroid hormone, PTH, calcitonin and vitamin D handle metabolic rate and calcium, and the last set are gastrointestinal hormones controlling digestion rather than plasma glucose.
questions.answerText: Glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, and growth hormone

questions.q: In the beta cell, what does a rising internal ATP concentration do to the ATP sensitive K+ channel?
options: It opens the channel
It closes the channel
It converts it into a Ca2+ channel
It has no effect on the channel
questions.why: When glucose enters the beta cell and is metabolized, ATP rises and binds the ATP sensitive K+ channel, closing it. With less K+ leaving, the cell depolarizes, voltage gated Ca2+ channels open, and Ca2+ entry triggers insulin exocytosis. Opening the channel would hyperpolarize the cell and stop secretion, and a K+ channel does not become a Ca2+ channel; these are separate proteins acting in sequence.
questions.answerText: It closes the channel

questions.q: At about what plasma glucose concentration does glucose start to appear in the urine?
options: About 500 mg/dL
About 300 mg/dL
About 180 mg/dL
About 100 mg/dL
questions.why: The renal threshold sits near 180 mg/dL, the point at which the filtered glucose load exceeds what the proximal tubule transporters can reabsorb, so the excess stays in the tubule and is excreted. Below that, essentially all filtered glucose is reclaimed, which is why healthy urine contains none at 100 mg/dL. Waiting until 300 or 500 mg/dL would mean the transporters had far more reserve than they actually do.
questions.answerText: About 180 mg/dL

questions.q: Which hormone is the body's first hormonal defense when plasma glucose starts to fall?
options: Cortisol
Glucagon
Growth hormone
Thyroid hormone
questions.why: Glucagon responds within minutes and acts on the liver at once, which makes it the front line defense, with epinephrine as the immediate backup. Cortisol and growth hormone also raise glucose but work through changes in enzyme expression and take hours, so they matter in prolonged fasting rather than in a sudden fall. Thyroid hormone sets the overall metabolic rate and is not part of the acute glucose response.
questions.answerText: Glucagon

questions.q: In a glucose tolerance test, plasma glucose two hours after the drink is 165 mg/dL. How is this value classified?
options: Impaired glucose tolerance
Normal glucose tolerance
Hypoglycemia
Normal fasting glucose
questions.why: A normal two hour value is under 140 mg/dL, and values from 140 up to 199 fall in the impaired range, meaning disposal is slower than it should be but not yet in the diabetic range of 200 or above. The value is far too high to be hypoglycemia, and it cannot be called a fasting value at all because the person deliberately drank glucose two hours earlier.
questions.answerText: Impaired glucose tolerance

questions.q: Closure of the ATP sensitive K+ channel in a beta cell has what immediate effect on its membrane potential?
options: The cell hyperpolarizes
The membrane potential is unchanged
The cell repolarizes toward the K+ equilibrium potential
The cell depolarizes
questions.why: Resting membrane potential is negative largely because K+ leaks out, so closing a K+ channel removes that outward positive current and the interior becomes less negative, which is depolarization. Hyperpolarization would require more K+ leaving, not less. Moving toward the K+ equilibrium potential is the same thing as hyperpolarizing, since that potential is more negative than rest, so it is the opposite of what happens here.
questions.answerText: The cell depolarizes

questions.q: Contracting skeletal muscle takes up glucose even when insulin is low. What does regular exercise therefore do to a person's insulin requirement?
options: It raises it
It lowers it
It has no effect on it
It abolishes the need for glucose entirely
questions.why: Muscle contraction moves GLUT4 into the membrane by a pathway independent of insulin, so working muscle pulls glucose out of the blood without insulin having to force it, and less insulin is needed for the same disposal. Exercise also increases insulin sensitivity for hours afterward. Muscle still needs glucose, and indeed uses much more of it during exercise, so the demand for the fuel rises even as the demand for the hormone falls.
questions.answerText: It lowers it
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: During a prolonged fast, plasma glucose settles near 60 to 70 mg/dL rather than continuing to fall. What holds it there?
options: Gluconeogenesis matched to reduced glucose demand
Continued absorption of glucose from the gut
Renal reabsorption of glucose above the threshold
Release of glucose from muscle glycogen
questions.why: The liver keeps building glucose from glycerol, lactate and amino acids while most tissues switch to fatty acids and the brain switches partly to ketones, so supply and a shrinking demand meet at a low but stable value. Absorption from the gut ended long ago. Renal reabsorption prevents loss but adds no new glucose, and muscle cannot release glucose to the blood at any time because it lacks glucose 6 phosphatase.
questions.answerText: Gluconeogenesis matched to reduced glucose demand

questions.q: A person with a falling plasma glucose becomes shaky, sweaty, and anxious before feeling confused. Which hormone produces those early symptoms?
options: Insulin
Cortisol
Epinephrine
Growth hormone
questions.why: Falling glucose triggers a sympathetic discharge and adrenal epinephrine release, and tremor, sweating, palpitations and anxiety are the recognizable warning signs of that surge. Insulin is suppressed rather than released when glucose falls, so it cannot be causing symptoms. Cortisol and growth hormone rise too, but they act slowly through gene expression and produce no acute symptoms; the confusion that follows comes from the brain itself running short of glucose.
questions.answerText: Epinephrine

questions.q: A person skips breakfast after eating dinner the night before. Predict the insulin to glucagon ratio by late morning.
options: High, because insulin has risen
Unchanged, because both hormones fall together
High, because glucagon has fallen further than insulin
Low, because insulin has fallen and glucagon has risen
questions.why: With no nutrients arriving, plasma glucose drifts down, beta cells quiet and alpha cells become active, so the ratio of insulin to glucagon falls and the liver switches from storing glucose to exporting it. The two hormones move in opposite directions rather than together, which is what makes the ratio such a useful summary of metabolic state. A high ratio is the signature of the fed state, not of a skipped meal.
questions.answerText: Low, because insulin has fallen and glucagon has risen

questions.q: An intravenous glucose bolus produces a sharp insulin spike within two minutes, followed by a slower sustained rise. What explains the first phase?
options: Transcription of new insulin genes
Recruitment of new beta cells into the islet
Release of preformed insulin from granules
Slower breakdown of insulin in the liver
questions.why: Beta cells keep a ready pool of insulin containing granules docked at the membrane, and Ca2+ entry dumps them within seconds, giving the sharp first phase. The slower second phase reflects newly synthesized and mobilized insulin and lasts as long as glucose stays high. Transcription is far too slow for a two minute response, beta cell number does not change acutely, and a change in hepatic clearance would alter the level without producing a spike.
questions.answerText: Release of preformed insulin from granules

questions.q: A glucose tolerance test shows a fasting value of 95 mg/dL, a one hour peak of 210 mg/dL, and a two hour value of 190 mg/dL. What does the shape of this curve indicate?
options: Complete absence of insulin secretion
Excessive insulin secretion with hypoglycemia
Normal glucose handling throughout
Normal fasting glucose with impaired disposal
questions.why: The fasting value is normal because the liver and the remaining insulin can still hold baseline, but the high peak and the failure to come down by two hours show that tissue uptake of a load is slow, the pattern of insulin resistance with limited beta cell reserve. Total absence of insulin would leave the fasting value high as well, not at 95. Excessive insulin would drive glucose below fasting, and a normal curve would be back under 140 by two hours.
questions.answerText: Normal fasting glucose with impaired disposal

questions.q: A person has a tumor that secretes insulin regardless of plasma glucose. After an overnight fast, predict plasma glucose, plasma ketones, and hepatic glucose output.
options: Glucose low, ketones high, hepatic output high
Glucose low, ketones low, hepatic output suppressed
Glucose low, ketones high, hepatic output suppressed
Glucose high, ketones low, hepatic output high
questions.why: Unregulated insulin keeps driving glucose into tissues and keeps telling the liver not to release any, so plasma glucose falls even though the person is fasting. The same insulin blocks hormone sensitive lipase, so fatty acids never reach the liver in bulk and ketones stay low, which is the giveaway: a normal person that hypoglycemic from fasting alone would have high ketones. Hepatic output cannot be high while insulin is elevated, and glucose cannot be high when insulin is unopposed.
questions.answerText: Glucose low, ketones low, hepatic output suppressed

questions.q: Compare moderate exercise performed one hour after breakfast with the same exercise after a twelve hour fast. Predict the dominant fuel and the dominant hormone in each case.
options: Fed uses glucose under insulin, fasted uses fatty acids under glucagon
Both use mostly fatty acids under glucagon
Fed uses fatty acids under insulin, fasted uses glucose under glucagon
Both use mostly glucose under insulin
questions.why: One hour after a meal, insulin is still high, glucose is plentiful, and lipolysis is suppressed, so working muscle burns mostly carbohydrate. After twelve hours insulin has fallen and glucagon and epinephrine have risen, adipose tissue is releasing fatty acids, and muscle shifts toward fat while conserving the remaining glucose for the brain. The two states cannot use the same fuel mix because the hormonal signals pointing at that mix are opposite.
questions.answerText: Fed uses glucose under insulin, fasted uses fatty acids under glucagon

questions.q: A person who has fasted for 24 hours eats a large carbohydrate meal. Trace what happens to the insulin to glucagon ratio, to hepatic glycogen phosphorylase, and to plasma free fatty acids.
options: Ratio rises, phosphorylase inactivated, fatty acids fall
Ratio rises, phosphorylase activated, fatty acids fall
Ratio falls, phosphorylase inactivated, fatty acids rise
Ratio rises, phosphorylase inactivated, fatty acids rise
questions.why: Absorbed glucose stimulates insulin and suppresses glucagon, so the ratio swings upward and the liver's enzymes are dephosphorylated: glycogen phosphorylase switches off and glycogen synthase switches on, turning the liver from an exporter into a storer of glucose within minutes. The same insulin rise inhibits hormone sensitive lipase, so free fatty acids drop sharply. Phosphorylase cannot stay active while insulin is high, and fatty acids cannot rise when the strongest antilipolytic signal in the body has just been released.
questions.answerText: Ratio rises, phosphorylase inactivated, fatty acids fall

questions.q: What does basal metabolic rate measure?
options: Energy used during moderate exercise
Total energy used over a full day of activity
Energy used at rest, awake, and postabsorptive
Energy stored as fat over a day
questions.why: Basal metabolic rate is the cost of simply staying alive, measured under standardized conditions: awake but at rest, twelve hours after eating so digestion is not adding to it, and in a thermoneutral room so no energy goes to warming or cooling. Exercise energy and total daily expenditure both include activity and are larger numbers. Energy stored is what remains after expenditure, not the expenditure itself.
questions.answerText: Energy used at rest, awake, and postabsorptive

questions.q: About what fraction of resting energy expenditure does the brain account for in an adult?
options: About 2 percent
About 20 percent
About 50 percent
About 80 percent
questions.why: The brain is about 2 percent of body mass but consumes roughly a fifth of resting energy, which is why plasma glucose is defended so tightly. Two percent would match its mass rather than its metabolism. Fifty percent overstates it, since liver, kidney, heart and skeletal muscle together account for most of the rest, and eighty percent would leave almost nothing for every other organ.
questions.answerText: About 20 percent

questions.q: What is a typical basal metabolic rate for an average adult?
options: About 9000 to 10000 kcal per day
About 3800 to 4200 kcal per day
About 1500 to 1800 kcal per day
About 150 to 180 kcal per day
questions.why: Most adults sit near 1500 to 1800 kcal per day at basal conditions, roughly 1 kcal per minute, with total daily expenditure higher once activity and the cost of digesting food are added. A rate near 150 kcal per day would not keep a person alive. About 4000 kcal is closer to a full day of heavy physical work than to a basal value, and 10000 kcal exceeds even that.
questions.answerText: About 1500 to 1800 kcal per day

questions.q: Which hormone is the most important long term determinant of basal metabolic rate?
options: Insulin
Aldosterone
Antidiuretic hormone
Thyroid hormone
questions.why: Thyroid hormone acts on nearly every cell, increasing the number of Na+/K+ ATPase pumps and mitochondrial enzymes, and it sets the resting rate of energy use over weeks and months. Insulin directs which fuel is used and whether it is stored, but does not set the overall rate. Aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone regulate sodium, potassium and water balance and have no direct effect on metabolic rate.
questions.answerText: Thyroid hormone

questions.q: About how many kilocalories are released per liter of oxygen consumed on a mixed diet?
options: About 0.5 kcal per liter
About 4.8 kcal per liter
About 20 kcal per liter
About 100 kcal per liter
questions.why: The caloric equivalent of oxygen is close to 4.8 kcal per liter for a mixed diet, and it varies only slightly with fuel, which is exactly what makes indirect calorimetry work: measure oxygen and you know energy use. Many texts round it to 5 for quick estimates. The other values are off by roughly an order of magnitude in one direction or the other and would give absurd daily totals.
questions.answerText: About 4.8 kcal per liter

questions.q: How is the respiratory quotient defined?
options: Carbon dioxide produced divided by oxygen consumed
Oxygen consumed divided by carbon dioxide produced
Carbon dioxide produced divided by minute ventilation
Oxygen consumed divided by body surface area
questions.why: The respiratory quotient is the volume of CO2 produced divided by the volume of O2 consumed over the same period, and its value tells you which fuel is being oxidized. Inverting the ratio gives a number that moves in the opposite direction and would be read backwards. Dividing by ventilation or by body surface area gives other useful quantities but not a fuel indicator.
questions.answerText: Carbon dioxide produced divided by oxygen consumed

questions.q: What is the respiratory quotient for the oxidation of pure carbohydrate?
questions.why: Carbohydrate is already partly oxidized, so burning it produces exactly as much CO2 as the oxygen it consumes, giving a quotient of 1.0. Fat is hydrogen rich and oxygen poor, needs proportionally more oxygen, and gives about 0.7, while protein falls near 0.8. A value above 1.0 is not produced by burning any single fuel and usually signals extra CO2 from buffering acid or from converting carbohydrate to fat.

questions.q: What does indirect calorimetry actually measure in order to estimate energy expenditure?
options: Heat released from the body surface
Core body temperature over time
Calories eaten over a full day
Oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange
questions.why: Indirect calorimetry infers energy release from gas exchange, because oxygen consumption is tightly proportional to energy production in aerobic metabolism. Measuring heat directly is direct calorimetry, which requires an insulated chamber and is rarely practical. Core temperature reflects the balance between heat production and loss rather than the rate of energy use, and dietary intake tells you what went in, not what was expended.
questions.answerText: Oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange

questions.q: Metabolic rate rises about 10 percent for each 1 C rise in body temperature. If a person with a basal rate of 1500 kcal per day develops a fever 2 C above normal, what is the approximate new rate?
options: About 3000 kcal per day
About 1800 kcal per day
About 1650 kcal per day
About 1550 kcal per day
questions.why: Two degrees at roughly 10 percent each is about a 20 percent increase, and 20 percent of 1500 is 300, giving about 1800 kcal per day. This is a real clinical burden: a sustained fever measurably increases energy and fluid needs. About 1650 would correspond to only 1 C, and 3000 would require a doubling, which no realistic fever produces.
questions.answerText: About 1800 kcal per day

questions.q: Two people weigh the same, but one has considerably more skeletal muscle and less fat. Predict their basal metabolic rates.
options: The person with more fat has the higher rate
The person with more muscle has the higher rate
The rates are identical because body mass is equal
The rates cannot differ unless thyroid hormone differs
questions.why: Basal metabolic rate tracks lean body mass because muscle, liver and other lean tissues are metabolically active even at rest, while stored triglyceride uses very little energy. This is also why basal rate tends to be higher in men and to fall with age as lean mass is lost. Equal total mass does not mean equal active mass, and body composition changes metabolic rate without any change in thyroid hormone.
questions.answerText: The person with more muscle has the higher rate
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A patient secretes far too little thyroid hormone. Predict their basal metabolic rate, heat production, and tolerance of cold.
options: Rate down, heat down, cold tolerated poorly
Rate up, heat up, cold tolerated well
Rate down, heat up, cold tolerated well
Rate unchanged, heat down, cold tolerated poorly
questions.why: Thyroid hormone sets the resting rate at which cells burn fuel, so too little slows metabolism, reduces the heat generated as a byproduct, and leaves the person intolerant of cold, often with weight gain and fatigue. Heat production cannot rise while metabolic rate falls, since the heat is a byproduct of that same metabolism. An unchanged rate would not explain the symptoms at all.
questions.answerText: Rate down, heat down, cold tolerated poorly

questions.q: A person who has fasted overnight has a measured respiratory quotient of 0.71. Which fuel are they mainly burning?
options: Carbohydrate
Protein
An equal mix of carbohydrate and fat
Fat
questions.why: A quotient near 0.7 means CO2 output is well below oxygen uptake, which is the signature of fat oxidation because fatty acids are hydrogen rich and require extra oxygen. Pure carbohydrate gives 1.0 and protein about 0.8. An even mix would land near 0.85, so 0.71 tells you this person has already shifted almost entirely to fat, exactly as expected after an overnight fast.
questions.answerText: Fat

questions.q: A resting subject consumes oxygen at 0.25 L/min. Using 4.8 kcal per liter of oxygen, what is their approximate daily energy expenditure?
options: About 7200 kcal per day
About 3400 kcal per day
About 1700 kcal per day
About 850 kcal per day
questions.why: Multiply 0.25 L/min by 4.8 kcal/L to get 1.2 kcal/min, then by 1440 minutes in a day to get about 1730 kcal. That result lands squarely in the normal adult range, which is a good check that the arithmetic is right. Half or double that value would come from dropping or doubling a factor, and 7200 kcal per day is beyond even sustained heavy labor.
questions.answerText: About 1700 kcal per day

questions.q: A person cuts daily intake sharply for several weeks and loses weight, then finds the loss slows even though intake has not changed. What has happened to metabolic rate?
options: It has risen to burn the remaining fat
It is unchanged, so the plateau must be miscounted intake
It has fallen only because thyroid hormone was destroyed
It has fallen from lost mass and adaptive suppression
questions.why: There are two effects: a smaller body has less tissue to maintain, and prolonged restriction lowers thyroid hormone signaling and sympathetic activity so that each remaining kilogram burns less, which is called adaptive thermogenesis. Together they narrow the gap between intake and expenditure until weight stabilizes. Metabolic rate does not rise during restriction, and the thyroid gland is not destroyed, only downregulated, which reverses when eating resumes.
questions.answerText: It has fallen from lost mass and adaptive suppression

questions.q: A patient has lost weight despite a large appetite, feels hot in a cool room, and has an elevated resting oxygen consumption. Trace the mechanism from the likely hormone to the heat.
options: Excess insulin drives storage and releases heat
Excess thyroid hormone raises pump activity and oxidation
Deficient cortisol slows gluconeogenesis and releases heat
Excess ADH raises water reabsorption and releases heat
questions.why: Thyroid hormone increases the number of Na+/K+ ATPase pumps and mitochondrial enzymes across the body, so cells consume more ATP and more oxygen at rest and more of that energy escapes as heat, which raises oxygen consumption, produces heat intolerance, and burns stored fuel faster than appetite can replace it. Excess insulin would promote storage and weight gain rather than loss. Cortisol deficiency lowers rather than raises metabolic rate, and ADH acts on water handling with no meaningful thermal effect.
questions.answerText: Excess thyroid hormone raises pump activity and oxidation

questions.q: A subject exercises hard enough to produce lactate. Why does indirect calorimetry underestimate their true energy expenditure during that period?
options: Lactate binds oxygen and hides it from the analyzer
Ventilation falls during heavy exercise
Anaerobic ATP is produced without consuming oxygen
Carbon dioxide production stops during anaerobic work
questions.why: Indirect calorimetry assumes all ATP comes from oxidative metabolism, so any ATP made by anaerobic glycolysis is energy released that the oxygen measurement never sees, and the estimate comes in low. Part of that debt is paid back after exercise, when oxygen consumption stays elevated. Lactate does not bind oxygen, ventilation rises steeply rather than falling, and CO2 output actually increases as bicarbonate buffers the acid load.
questions.answerText: Anaerobic ATP is produced without consuming oxygen

questions.q: A subject's respiratory quotient falls from 0.85 shortly after breakfast to 0.72 twenty four hours later. Explain the fuel shift and name the hormonal change driving it.
options: A shift from mixed fuel to mostly fat, driven by falling insulin
A shift from fat to carbohydrate, driven by rising insulin
A shift from protein to carbohydrate, driven by rising cortisol
No real fuel shift, only a change in ventilation
questions.why: A quotient of 0.85 reflects a mix of carbohydrate and fat shortly after eating, and 0.72 is close to pure fat oxidation, so over the fast the body has switched fuels. The driver is the falling insulin to glucagon ratio, which releases hormone sensitive lipase from inhibition and floods the circulation with fatty acids while glucose is conserved for the brain. A shift toward carbohydrate would raise rather than lower the quotient, and while ventilation can transiently change the measured value, a sustained change of this size over a day reflects real substrate use.
questions.answerText: A shift from mixed fuel to mostly fat, driven by falling insulin

questions.q: A person expends about 2700 kcal per day but eats about 2200 kcal per day. Given that roughly 3500 kcal are stored in a pound of adipose tissue, estimate their weekly weight change.
options: A loss of about 0.5 pound per week
A loss of about 3 pounds per week
A loss of about 1 pound per week
No change, because the body adjusts immediately
questions.why: The daily deficit is 2700 minus 2200, or 500 kcal, and 500 times seven days is 3500 kcal, which is about one pound of adipose tissue. Working the arithmetic this way shows why the arithmetic of energy balance is so unforgiving, and also why plausible sounding deficits produce slow change. Three pounds a week would require a deficit of about 1500 kcal a day, and the adaptive fall in metabolic rate blunts the loss over weeks rather than canceling it immediately.
questions.answerText: A loss of about 1 pound per week

questions.q: Which brain region is the integrating center for body temperature?
options: The medulla oblongata
The cerebellum
The thalamus
The hypothalamus
questions.why: The preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus compares incoming temperature information with a set point and drives the effector responses, which makes it the classic example of a negative feedback control center. The medulla houses the cardiovascular and respiratory centers. The cerebellum coordinates movement, and the thalamus relays sensory information to the cortex without setting a regulated variable.
questions.answerText: The hypothalamus

questions.q: What is the normal regulated core body temperature in an adult?
options: About 30 C
About 34 C
About 37 C
About 41 C
questions.why: Core temperature is held near 37 C, with a normal daily swing of a few tenths of a degree that is lowest in the early morning. Values near 34 C and below define hypothermia, at which shivering and then consciousness begin to fail. A core of 41 C is a dangerous hyperthermia at which proteins begin to denature, not a normal value.
questions.answerText: About 37 C

questions.q: Where are the thermoreceptors that report the temperature of the blood itself?
options: In the skin
In the hypothalamus
In the carotid bodies
In the spinal ganglia
questions.why: Central thermoreceptors sit in the hypothalamus alongside the integrating neurons and monitor the temperature of blood perfusing the brain, which is the variable actually being regulated. Skin thermoreceptors are the peripheral set and give early warning of a changing environment before core temperature has moved. The carotid bodies sense oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH, and spinal ganglia contain the cell bodies of sensory neurons rather than a temperature sensing center.
questions.answerText: In the hypothalamus

questions.q: Which mechanism removes the most heat when the environment is hotter than the skin?
options: Evaporation of sweat
Radiation to the surroundings
Conduction to nearby surfaces
Convection into moving air
questions.why: Radiation, conduction and convection all move heat down a temperature gradient, so when the surroundings are warmer than the skin they add heat to the body rather than removing it. Evaporation is the only route that still works, because it depends on water changing phase rather than on a temperature difference. This is why humidity, which limits evaporation, is so much more dangerous than heat alone.
questions.answerText: Evaporation of sweat

questions.q: Which of these is an effector response to cold?
options: Shivering by skeletal muscle
Sweating by eccrine glands
Cutaneous vasodilation
Increased respiratory rate
questions.why: Shivering is rapid involuntary skeletal muscle contraction whose only useful product is heat, and it can raise metabolic heat production several fold. Sweating and cutaneous vasodilation are heat loss responses used when the body is too warm. Respiratory rate is controlled mainly by carbon dioxide and is not a major human thermoregulatory effector, though panting serves that role in some other species.
questions.answerText: Shivering by skeletal muscle
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: Which route of heat transfer moves heat as electromagnetic waves without any physical contact?
options: Conduction
Convection
Evaporation
Radiation
questions.why: Radiation transfers heat between any two objects at different temperatures without touching, and it accounts for a large share of resting heat loss into a cool room. Conduction requires direct contact between surfaces, and convection is conduction into air or water that then moves away carrying heat with it. Evaporation carries heat away in the latent heat of vaporized water and does not require a temperature gradient at all.
questions.answerText: Radiation

questions.q: Which molecules act as endogenous pyrogens during infection?
options: Cytokines such as interleukin 1 and 6
Catecholamines such as epinephrine
Thyroid hormones such as T3 and T4
Mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone
questions.why: Macrophages responding to infection release interleukin 1, interleukin 6 and tumor necrosis factor, which signal the hypothalamus to raise the set point through prostaglandin E2. Epinephrine and thyroid hormone both increase heat production, but they do so without moving the set point, which is why they cause hyperthermia rather than fever. Aldosterone acts on renal sodium handling and has no thermoregulatory role.
questions.answerText: Cytokines such as interleukin 1 and 6

questions.q: What does an endogenous pyrogen do to the hypothalamic temperature set point?
options: It raises the set point
It lowers the set point
It abolishes the set point entirely
It leaves the set point unchanged and blocks sweating
questions.why: A fever is a regulated rise: prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus moves the target upward, and the normal control mechanisms then work hard to reach the new, higher target. That distinguishes fever from hyperthermia, where the set point is normal and the body is simply overwhelmed. Lowering the set point would produce heat loss responses, and the set point is not abolished during fever, only reset.
questions.answerText: It raises the set point

questions.q: Cold exposure triggers cutaneous vasoconstriction. How does this conserve heat?
options: It increases the insulating fat layer
It reduces blood flow to the skin surface
It raises the metabolic rate of skin cells
It closes the sweat ducts mechanically
questions.why: Skin blood flow is the main variable resistor in heat loss, and constricting those vessels keeps warm blood in the core where its heat cannot escape by radiation or convection. The fat layer is a fixed insulator and does not change acutely. Skin metabolism contributes very little heat either way, and sweat production is controlled by sympathetic cholinergic fibers to the glands rather than by mechanical closure of ducts.
questions.answerText: It reduces blood flow to the skin surface

questions.q: A person stands in still air at 40 C, which is above their skin temperature. Which mechanism can still remove heat from the body?
options: Radiation
Convection
Conduction
Evaporation
questions.why: When the surroundings are hotter than the skin, radiation, convection and conduction all run backwards and deliver heat into the body. Evaporation works against that gradient because vaporizing water absorbs heat regardless of which way the temperature difference points. This is why sweating becomes the sole defense in a very hot environment, and why fluid replacement becomes critical.
questions.answerText: Evaporation

questions.q: Two people exercise at the same intensity at 32 C, one in dry air and one in very humid air. Predict how core temperature differs.
options: It rises more in the dry condition
It rises equally in both, since air temperature is the same
It rises more in the humid condition
It falls in the humid condition
questions.why: Sweat only cools when it evaporates, and evaporation depends on the water vapor gradient between skin and air, so humid air lets sweat drip off without taking heat with it. The person in humid air therefore loses less heat despite sweating just as much or more, and core temperature climbs faster. Air temperature alone does not determine heat loss when evaporation is the dominant route.
questions.answerText: It rises more in the humid condition

questions.q: Vigorous shivering begins in a cold room. Predict what happens to oxygen consumption and metabolic rate.
options: Both decrease as the body conserves energy
Oxygen consumption rises while metabolic rate falls
Both increase substantially
Both stay the same, since no external work is done
questions.why: Shivering is muscle contraction, and contraction costs ATP, so shivering can raise metabolic rate and oxygen consumption several fold above basal. Because no useful external work is done, essentially all of that energy appears as heat, which is exactly the point of the response. Metabolic rate and oxygen consumption cannot move in opposite directions in aerobic tissue, and the absence of external work makes the response more thermally efficient, not free.
questions.answerText: Both increase substantially

questions.q: During the rising phase of a fever, why does the patient shiver and feel cold even though their temperature is already above normal?
options: The thermoreceptors are damaged by the infection
The hypothalamus stops responding during infection
Sweating has cooled the skin below core temperature
Core temperature is still below the raised set point
questions.why: The pyrogen raises the set point first, so the hypothalamus reads the current temperature as too low and calls for heat gain: shivering, vasoconstriction, and the subjective sense of cold. The person feels chilled at 38.5 C because their control system is now aiming at 39.5 C. Thermoreceptors and the hypothalamus are working normally throughout, which is precisely why the responses are so vigorous and so well coordinated.
questions.answerText: Core temperature is still below the raised set point

questions.q: A drug inhibits cyclooxygenase and blocks prostaglandin E2 production in the hypothalamus of a febrile patient. Predict the immediate effect.
options: The set point rises further and shivering intensifies
The set point returns to normal and heat loss begins
Core temperature falls below normal within minutes
Heat production rises while heat loss stays blocked
questions.why: Prostaglandin E2 is the molecule that actually shifts the hypothalamic set point, so blocking its synthesis returns the target to normal while core temperature is still elevated, and the hypothalamus responds with vasodilation and sweating until the two match again. Shivering stops rather than intensifying, because the body is now too warm relative to its target. Temperature falls over hours rather than minutes, and it stops at normal because the set point itself is intact.
questions.answerText: The set point returns to normal and heat loss begins

questions.q: A person sweats heavily for two hours in the heat without drinking. Predict what happens to plasma volume and to their ability to keep losing heat.
options: Plasma volume falls and heat loss is impaired
Plasma volume rises and heat loss improves
Plasma volume is unchanged because sweat comes from cells
Plasma volume falls but heat loss improves
questions.why: Sweat is drawn ultimately from extracellular fluid including plasma, so prolonged unreplaced sweating shrinks plasma volume, which reduces both the sweat rate the glands can sustain and the skin blood flow needed to deliver heat to the surface. The body is then forced to choose between defending blood pressure and defending temperature. Losing volume cannot improve heat loss, and sweat certainly does not leave the extracellular compartment untouched.
questions.answerText: Plasma volume falls and heat loss is impaired

questions.q: A runner competes in hot, humid weather. Trace the consequences of maximal cutaneous vasodilation plus heavy sweating for plasma volume, skin blood flow, and core temperature.
options: Plasma volume falls, skin blood flow rises, core temperature falls
Plasma volume rises, skin blood flow rises, core temperature falls
Plasma volume falls, skin blood flow falls, core temperature falls
Plasma volume falls, skin blood flow falls, core temperature climbs
questions.why: Sweating without replacement drains plasma volume while working muscle demands a huge share of cardiac output, so the skin circulation eventually loses the competition and heat delivery to the surface falls. Humid air already limits evaporation, so with both routes compromised heat production outruns heat loss and core temperature rises. Skin blood flow cannot be sustained on a shrinking volume, and core temperature cannot fall while heat production is high and both loss routes are failing.
questions.answerText: Plasma volume falls, skin blood flow falls, core temperature climbs

questions.q: A fever breaks: the patient suddenly flushes and sweats profusely. Explain what changed at the hypothalamus and what the effectors are now doing.
options: The set point rose further, triggering heat loss
Thermoreceptors stopped reporting core temperature
The set point fell to normal, so heat loss responses fire
Heat production rose, forcing compensatory sweating
questions.why: Once the pyrogen is cleared and prostaglandin E2 falls, the set point drops back to about 37 C while core temperature is still at 39 C or higher, so the hypothalamus now sees the body as far too hot and drives maximal vasodilation and sweating. That is the flushed, drenched crisis phase. A further rise in set point would produce shivering instead, and the thermoreceptors are reporting accurately the whole time, which is why the switch is so abrupt.
questions.answerText: The set point fell to normal, so heat loss responses fire

questions.q: A person taking a drug that blocks muscarinic receptors works outdoors on a hot day. Predict sweating, evaporative heat loss, and core temperature.
options: Sweating rises, evaporative loss rises, temperature falls
Sweating is blocked, evaporative loss falls, temperature falls
Sweating is normal, evaporative loss rises, temperature rises
Sweating is blocked, evaporative loss falls, temperature rises
questions.why: Eccrine sweat glands are unusual in being sympathetic but cholinergic, so a muscarinic blocker shuts sweating down even though the sympathetic nerves are firing hard. With the only effective route of heat loss in a hot environment disabled, heat accumulates and core temperature climbs, the mechanism behind drug related heat illness. Core temperature cannot fall when the dominant heat loss route is closed, and sweating cannot be normal when its receptor is blocked.
questions.answerText: Sweating is blocked, evaporative loss falls, temperature rises

questions.q: A cold newborn cannot shiver effectively but still raises heat production. Trace the pathway from sympathetic activation through brown fat to heat.
options: Norepinephrine drives lipolysis and UCP1 releases the energy as heat
Insulin drives fat storage and the storage reaction releases heat
Thyroid hormone contracts brown fat cells like muscle
Norepinephrine constricts brown fat vessels and friction warms the blood
questions.why: Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto brown adipocytes, which activates lipolysis and also UCP1, a protein that lets H+ leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Fatty acid oxidation then runs fast without producing much ATP, so nearly all of the energy is released as heat directly into the blood perfusing the tissue. Insulin promotes storage rather than heat, brown fat does not contract, and no meaningful heat is generated by vascular friction.
questions.answerText: Norepinephrine drives lipolysis and UCP1 releases the energy as heat

questions.q: In a metabolic rate lab, which quantity does the equipment measure in order to estimate energy expenditure?
options: The heat radiated from the skin
The volume of oxygen consumed per minute
The volume of blood pumped per minute
The number of calories eaten that day
questions.why: Indirect calorimetry measures oxygen consumption, usually alongside carbon dioxide production, and converts it to energy using the known caloric equivalent of oxygen. Measuring radiated heat is direct calorimetry and needs a sealed chamber. Cardiac output rises with metabolic rate but is not a calorimetric measurement, and food intake tells you what was consumed, not what was expended.
questions.answerText: The volume of oxygen consumed per minute

questions.q: What conversion factor turns oxygen consumption into energy expenditure?
options: About 4.8 kcal per liter of carbon dioxide
About 4.8 kcal per liter of oxygen
About 4.8 kcal per breath
About 4.8 kcal per gram of glucose
questions.why: Roughly 4.8 kcal of energy is released for every liter of oxygen consumed on a mixed diet, and many labs round this to 5 for quick estimates. The factor is tied to oxygen because oxygen use is nearly constant per unit energy across fuels, whereas the same is not true per liter of carbon dioxide. A per breath figure would depend entirely on tidal volume, and the energy content of glucose is a separate number, about 4 kcal per gram.
