There is no voltage gated glucose channel, since glucose crosses by carrier mediated transport. Transcription would take hours and would not match insulin's speed, and GLUT4 carries glucose down its gradient without using ATP.
questions.answerText: Moving GLUT4 transporters into the plasma membrane
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: What is the name of the DNA sequence that an activated steroid receptor complex binds?
options: A second messenger promoter
A ligand binding domain
A synaptic cleft consensus site
A hormone response element
questions.why: A hormone response element is the short regulatory DNA sequence near a target gene where the hormone receptor complex docks to change transcription. The ligand binding domain is a part of the receptor protein, not a piece of DNA. The other two options are invented terms that mix vocabulary from unrelated parts of the pathway.
questions.answerText: A hormone response element

questions.q: A hormone increases an enzyme's activity within 5 minutes, and the effect survives treatment with a protein synthesis inhibitor. Which receptor type is it using?
options: A receptor enzyme in the plasma membrane
A cytosolic steroid receptor
A nuclear thyroid hormone receptor
A receptor bound to a hormone response element
questions.why: Speed plus independence from the ribosome means the hormone is modifying proteins that already exist, which is what a membrane bound receptor kinase does. All three other options are transcription linked receptors whose effects appear slowly and vanish when protein synthesis is blocked. Those receptors would fit a response measured over hours instead.
questions.answerText: A receptor enzyme in the plasma membrane
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A mutation removes the kinase activity of the insulin receptor but leaves the insulin binding site intact. Predict the results of a binding assay and of a glucose uptake assay.
options: Both binding and glucose uptake are normal
Insulin binding is normal and glucose uptake fails to increase
Insulin binding fails and glucose uptake increases normally anyway
Both binding and glucose uptake fail
questions.why: Binding and signaling are separate functions of the same protein, so an intact extracellular site still captures insulin while the dead kinase cannot start the cascade that moves GLUT4. Normal uptake would require the kinase, which is exactly what is missing. Binding failure would require damage to the extracellular domain, which the mutation spared.
questions.answerText: Insulin binding is normal and glucose uptake fails to increase

questions.q: Cells are treated with a transcription inhibitor. Cortisol's effect disappears but insulin's effect on glucose uptake remains. Why?
options: Insulin is a steroid hormone and is therefore resistant to any inhibitor of gene transcription
Cortisol binds a surface receptor that the inhibitor happens to block as well
Cortisol works only by making new proteins, while insulin modifies transporters the cell already has
Insulin reaches the nucleus faster than cortisol does in these cultured cells
questions.why: The experiment separates the two mechanisms cleanly: a gene mediated response depends on transcription and a kinase mediated response does not. Cortisol uses an intracellular receptor rather than a surface receptor. Insulin is a peptide, not a steroid, and it never enters the nucleus, since its receptor works from the plasma membrane.
questions.answerText: Cortisol works only by making new proteins, while insulin modifies transporters the cell already has

questions.q: Both hormones are washed out of a culture after a brief exposure. Which effect is more likely to persist for hours and why?
options: The insulin effect, because phosphate groups are permanent
Both equally, because washing removes only free hormone
Neither effect, because both depend on the continuous presence of their hormone
The steroid effect, because the proteins it induced remain until they are degraded
questions.why: Gene mediated responses leave behind physical protein molecules with lifetimes of hours to days, so the effect outlasts the hormone. Phosphate groups are quickly removed by phosphatases, so kinase driven effects reverse within minutes. Persistence after washout is exactly what distinguishes the two hormones, so answers claiming that neither effect persists or that both persist equally miss the difference in mechanism.
questions.answerText: The steroid effect, because the proteins it induced remain until they are degraded

questions.q: A receptor has its ligand binding site facing the extracellular fluid and a catalytic domain projecting into the cytosol. How should it be classified?
options: A receptor enzyme
An intracellular receptor
A G protein coupled receptor
A ligand gated ion channel
questions.why: A single protein that both binds ligand outside and catalyzes a reaction inside is the definition of a receptor enzyme, the family that includes the insulin receptor. An intracellular receptor would have no extracellular domain at all. A G protein coupled receptor has no catalytic domain of its own, and an ion channel forms a conducting pore rather than a catalytic site.
questions.answerText: A receptor enzyme

questions.q: A mutation damages the DNA binding domain of a receptor. Which hormone's signaling would be impaired?
options: Insulin
Cortisol
Epinephrine
Acetylcholine
questions.why: Only receptors that act as transcription factors have a DNA binding domain, so a steroid such as cortisol is the one that loses its pathway. Insulin acts through a membrane kinase and epinephrine through a G protein, neither of which touches DNA directly. Acetylcholine works through ion channels or G protein coupled receptors, also without a DNA binding step.
questions.answerText: Cortisol

questions.q: A steroid receptor mutation leaves ligand binding intact but prevents the complex from entering the nucleus. Predict what a researcher would find for hormone uptake into the cell, receptor binding, and messenger RNA levels.
options: Uptake reduced, binding reduced, and no change in messenger RNA
Uptake normal, binding absent, and messenger RNA increased
Uptake normal, binding normal, and no change in messenger RNA
Uptake normal, binding normal, and messenger RNA increased as usual
questions.why: The hormone still crosses the membrane by lipid solubility and still binds its receptor, but a complex stuck in the cytosol never reaches the DNA, so transcription is unchanged. Uptake does not depend on the receptor, so reduced uptake does not follow. Binding was explicitly preserved, and a normal messenger RNA rise would require the nuclear step that the mutation blocks.
questions.answerText: Uptake normal, binding normal, and no change in messenger RNA
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: After a meal, insulin lowers blood glucose within minutes. Cortisol raises blood glucose over hours by increasing the enzymes of gluconeogenesis. What accounts for the difference in time course?
options: Insulin is far more potent per molecule than cortisol is when the two act on the same tissue
Insulin circulates through the blood faster than cortisol does after a meal
Cortisol must first be converted into a peptide before it can act on the cell
Insulin modifies existing transporters and enzymes, while cortisol must produce new enzyme molecules
questions.why: Time course follows mechanism: phosphorylation and vesicle insertion are fast because the machinery is already built, while transcription and translation take time to accumulate enough enzyme to matter. Potency describes how much hormone is needed, not how quickly it works. Cortisol is not converted to a peptide, and both hormones reach tissues in the same circulation within seconds.
questions.answerText: Insulin modifies existing transporters and enzymes, while cortisol must produce new enzyme molecules

questions.q: A cell is exposed to cortisol for several hours and then given epinephrine. The cyclic AMP response to epinephrine is larger than in an untreated cell. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Cortisol increased transcription of beta receptors, so more receptors were present for epinephrine
Cortisol bound the beta receptor directly and added its own signal to that of epinephrine
Cortisol inhibited adenylyl cyclase, which made the later response rebound higher
Cortisol converted the beta receptor into a nuclear receptor during those hours
questions.why: A gene mediated hormone can change how a cell responds to a later signal by altering how many receptors or downstream proteins it expresses, and the hours long delay fits transcription. Cortisol does not bind adrenergic receptors, so it cannot add a direct signal. Inhibiting the cyclase would blunt rather than amplify the response, and receptors are not converted from one class to another.
questions.answerText: Cortisol increased transcription of beta receptors, so more receptors were present for epinephrine

questions.q: A phosphatase inhibitor is added to cells stimulated with insulin. Predict what happens to the insulin response after the hormone is washed away, and explain why.
options: The response ends sooner, because phosphatases are needed to sustain signaling
The response persists longer than normal, because the phosphates placed by the receptor kinase are not removed
The response is unchanged, because washing removes the receptor along with the hormone
The response becomes gene mediated, because prolonged signaling recruits nuclear receptors to the pathway
questions.why: Kinase driven signals are normally brief because phosphatases strip the phosphate groups off within minutes, so blocking that removal leaves target proteins phosphorylated and active after the hormone is gone. Phosphatases terminate rather than sustain the signal. Washing removes free hormone but leaves receptors in the membrane, and a receptor enzyme does not turn into a nuclear receptor.
questions.answerText: The response persists longer than normal, because the phosphates placed by the receptor kinase are not removed

questions.q: What does signal amplification mean in a cell signaling pathway?
options: The receptor increases its affinity for the ligand as the signal continues
The ligand concentration in the blood rises during the response
One bound ligand molecule leads to a much larger number of product or response molecules
The response spreads from one cell to neighboring cells through gap junctions
questions.why: Amplification is a numerical idea: each step multiplies the number of active molecules, so a single binding event ends in thousands or millions of product molecules. Rising ligand concentration in blood is a change in the input, not amplification inside the cell. Increased affinity would change binding rather than multiply output, and spread between cells is a separate phenomenon from cascade gain.
questions.answerText: One bound ligand molecule leads to a much larger number of product or response molecules

questions.q: In a G protein coupled receptor pathway, where does amplification begin?
options: One ligand binds many receptors at once
One second messenger molecule binds many receptors at the surface
One G protein binds many ligands
One activated receptor activates many G protein molecules
questions.why: A single occupied receptor can cycle through and switch on many G proteins before the ligand leaves, so the first multiplication happens right at the membrane. A single ligand molecule occupies one receptor at a time, so binding itself does not amplify. G proteins do not bind ligand, and second messengers act downstream on kinases rather than back on receptors.
questions.answerText: One activated receptor activates many G protein molecules

questions.q: Why does one activated adenylyl cyclase molecule amplify the signal?
options: Because it is an enzyme and converts many ATP molecules into cyclic AMP while it stays active
Because it binds many G proteins at once and adds their signals together
Because it is consumed in the reaction, releasing all of the signal molecules it had stored
Because it doubles in number every time a G protein activates it again
questions.why: Catalysis is the source of gain, since an enzyme is not used up and keeps turning over substrate for as long as it remains active. Binding many G proteins at once is not how the cyclase works, and one activating G protein is enough. Enzymes are not consumed in their reactions, and they do not replicate themselves during signaling.
questions.answerText: Because it is an enzyme and converts many ATP molecules into cyclic AMP while it stays active

questions.q: Which feature of a cascade makes it capable of large amplification?
options: Each step uses a different second messenger
Each active enzyme acts catalytically on many substrate molecules
Each step is reversible, so signal can flow both directions
Each step requires a new receptor to be synthesized
questions.why: Turnover number is the engine of amplification: one enzyme molecule handles many substrate molecules per second, and stacking such steps multiplies the gain. Using different messengers adds versatility but not gain by itself. Cascades flow in one direction under normal conditions, and no step waits for new receptor synthesis, which would slow rather than amplify the signal.
questions.answerText: Each active enzyme acts catalytically on many substrate molecules

questions.q: Which step in a signaling pathway does not amplify the signal?
options: An enzyme generating second messenger molecules
A kinase phosphorylating many target proteins
A ligand binding to one receptor
A G protein activating an amplifier enzyme that then works repeatedly
questions.why: Binding is a one to one event, so it converts a single ligand into a single occupied receptor with no multiplication. Enzymes making messengers and kinases phosphorylating many targets are both catalytic steps with high gain. A G protein activating an enzyme that then turns over substrate repeatedly also multiplies, because the gain comes from the enzyme it switches on.
questions.answerText: A ligand binding to one receptor

questions.q: When a pathway has several amplifying steps in series, how do their individual gains combine?
options: They add
Only the largest one counts
They average
They multiply
questions.why: Each step takes the output of the step before it as its input, so gains compound and three modest steps can produce a very large final number. Adding them would badly underestimate the output. Averaging is not how sequential processes combine, and every step contributes, which is why a single step with no gain can hold the whole pathway back.
questions.answerText: They multiply

questions.q: Roughly how many glucose molecules can be released from liver glycogen as a result of one epinephrine molecule binding its receptor?
options: On the order of a hundred million
About one thousand
About ten
Exactly one, since binding is one to one
questions.why: Textbook estimates for this cascade land near 10 to the eighth power glucose molecules, because four or five catalytic steps multiply together. Ten or a thousand would describe a single step, not the whole chain. One to one holds only at the binding event itself, which is precisely the step the cascade exists to overcome.
questions.answerText: On the order of a hundred million

questions.q: Amplification explains how a hormone can act at what kind of plasma concentration?
options: Concentrations similar to plasma sodium
Extremely low concentrations, in the nanomolar or picomolar range
Concentrations similar to plasma glucose
Only concentrations high enough to saturate every receptor
questions.why: Because each binding event is multiplied many times inside the cell, hormones can be effective at concentrations far below those of ordinary solutes. Sodium sits near 140 mEq/L and glucose near 5 mmol/L, both millions of times higher than typical hormone levels. Saturating every receptor is not required, since a modest fraction of occupied receptors already produces a large response.
questions.answerText: Extremely low concentrations, in the nanomolar or picomolar range

questions.q: One receptor activates 10 G proteins, and each activated adenylyl cyclase makes 100 cyclic AMP molecules. How many cyclic AMP molecules result from one binding event?
questions.why: The two steps multiply, so 10 times 100 gives 1,000 second messenger molecules from a single ligand. Adding the two numbers gives 110 and misses the compounding that defines a cascade. Ten thousand would require another tenfold step, and 100 counts only the last step while ignoring the G protein stage.

questions.q: A pathway has three amplifying steps with gains of 10, 100, and 100. What is the total amplification?
questions.why: Multiplying 10 by 100 by 100 gives 10 to the fifth power, or 100,000. The sum of 210 treats sequential steps as if they were independent contributions. One thousand and ten thousand each drop one of the hundredfold steps, which shows how quickly the estimate collapses when a step is left out.

questions.q: In a pathway with gains of 20, 50, and 200, a drug doubles the gain of the middle step. What happens to total amplification?
options: It doubles
It increases by 50
It increases fourfold
It is unchanged, because the other steps are limiting
questions.why: Because the steps multiply, doubling any single factor doubles the product, no matter which step it is. Adding 50 would apply if the steps summed, which they do not. A fourfold rise would require two steps to double, and no step is limiting in a simple multiplicative chain, so the total cannot be unchanged.
questions.answerText: It doubles

questions.q: One step in a cascade is replaced by a stoichiometric binding step with a gain of 1. What happens to the overall output compared with the original pathway?
options: It falls to zero, because the pathway is broken
It falls by the factor that step used to contribute
It is unchanged, because a gain of 1 passes the signal through
It rises, because the step no longer consumes substrate
questions.why: A gain of 1 still transmits the signal, but the product loses whatever multiplier that step used to supply, so a step that once gave a hundredfold gain costs the pathway a factor of 100. The signal is not blocked, so output does not fall to zero. Output is not unchanged, because the lost multiplier mattered, and removing gain never increases the final number.
questions.answerText: It falls by the factor that step used to contribute

questions.q: Two pathways start with the same ligand concentration. Pathway A has two catalytic steps and pathway B has four, with similar gain at each step. Which produces the larger response and why?
options: Pathway A, because fewer steps means less signal is lost along the way
They are equal, because the ligand concentration sets the response
Pathway B, because each additional catalytic step multiplies the output again
Pathway A, because shorter pathways always have higher gain per step
questions.why: More catalytic steps mean more multiplications, so the longer chain reaches a larger final number even though it takes slightly longer to develop. Signal is not lost step by step in the way the shorter is better answer imagines, since each step is a fresh round of catalysis. Ligand concentration sets the input rather than the gain, and step count does not by itself change the gain of an individual step.
questions.answerText: Pathway B, because each additional catalytic step multiplies the output again

questions.q: Only 2 percent of a cell's receptors are occupied by hormone, yet the cell shows a near maximal response. Which property of the pathway explains this?
options: Direct entry of the hormone into the nucleus, bypassing the surface receptors entirely
Very high hormone concentration in the plasma, saturating the available receptors
Receptor up regulation occurring within seconds of the hormone arriving at the cell
Cascade amplification, so a small number of occupied receptors generates a large internal signal
questions.why: When each occupied receptor is multiplied through several catalytic steps, a small fraction of receptors is enough to saturate the downstream machinery, which is the basis of spare receptors. Low occupancy tells you the plasma concentration is well below saturating, not high. Up regulation takes hours and requires new protein, and a hormone using surface receptors does not enter the nucleus.
questions.answerText: Cascade amplification, so a small number of occupied receptors generates a large internal signal

questions.q: One receptor activates 20 G proteins, each activated cyclase makes 200 cyclic AMP molecules, and each protein kinase A molecule phosphorylates 100 target enzymes. Estimate the number of enzymes affected by one binding event.
options: About 400,000
About 4,000
About 320
questions.why: Multiplying 20 by 200 by 100 gives 4 times 10 to the fifth power, so roughly four hundred thousand enzyme molecules are modified from a single ligand. The value 320 comes from adding the three numbers instead of multiplying them. Four thousand drops the hundredfold kinase step, and forty million would need another hundredfold factor that this pathway does not have.
questions.answerText: About 400,000

questions.q: A cascade has gains of 10, then 50, then a final step where each activated molecule binds one target molecule. Total gain and limiting feature?
options: Total gain is 500, and the first step is the limiting one
Total gain is 500, and the final one to one step adds no multiplication
Total gain is 61, because the steps add
Total gain is 25,000, because a binding step counts as a fiftyfold gain
questions.why: Only the two catalytic steps multiply, giving 10 times 50 equals 500, and multiplying by 1 leaves the total unchanged, so the stoichiometric step is where gain stops accruing. The tenfold first step is not limiting compared with a step that contributes nothing. Steps multiply rather than add, and a one to one binding step cannot be counted as a fiftyfold gain.
questions.answerText: Total gain is 500, and the final one to one step adds no multiplication

questions.q: A mutation makes protein kinase A dephosphorylate itself faster, so each active molecule modifies half as many targets before shutting off. Predict the effect on final output and on the time to peak response.
options: Output doubles because faster cycling means more turnover
Output is unchanged but the response lasts longer
Output falls by about half and the response peaks and fades sooner
Output falls to zero because the kinase can no longer phosphorylate anything
questions.why: Gain at a catalytic step is set by how many substrate molecules each active enzyme handles before it is switched off, so halving that number halves the step's contribution and shortens its active window. Duration cannot lengthen when the enzyme turns off sooner. Faster inactivation reduces rather than increases total turnover, and the kinase still works, just for less time.
questions.answerText: Output falls by about half and the response peaks and fades sooner

questions.q: Compare a ligand gated ion channel with a cyclic AMP cascade started by the same number of ligand molecules. Which produces greater molecular amplification, and what is the tradeoff?
options: The channel amplifies more, because millions of ions cross it, and it is also slower to begin
The cascade amplifies less, because each enzyme handles only one substrate molecule at a time
They amplify to the same degree, since both are driven by the same ligand concentration at the cell surface
The cascade amplifies more through catalytic steps, while the channel is faster but limited to one pore's ion flow
questions.why: A cascade multiplies at every catalytic step and can reach many orders of magnitude, but it costs tens of seconds, while a channel opens in milliseconds with its output capped by the ions one pore can pass. Calling the channel both larger and slower reverses both halves of the comparison. Identical amplification would ignore the catalytic steps entirely, and enzymes handle many substrate molecules rather than one.
questions.answerText: The cascade amplifies more through catalytic steps, while the channel is faster but limited to one pore's ion flow

questions.q: What is an agonist?
options: A molecule that binds a receptor and activates it, producing the same response as the natural ligand
A molecule that binds a receptor and prevents it from producing any response to the natural ligand
A molecule that increases the number of receptors displayed on a target cell
A molecule that destroys the natural ligand before it can reach the receptor
questions.why: An agonist both binds and switches the receptor on, so it mimics the endogenous signal. A molecule that binds and blocks is an antagonist, the opposite case. Changing receptor number is up regulation, a slower change in the cell, and destroying the ligand ends the signal without touching the receptor at all.
questions.answerText: A molecule that binds a receptor and activates it, producing the same response as the natural ligand

questions.q: What is an antagonist?
options: A molecule that activates a receptor more strongly than the natural ligand does at the same site
A molecule that binds a receptor without activating it and prevents the natural ligand from acting
A molecule that increases the affinity of the receptor for its natural ligand
A molecule that speeds degradation of the second messenger inside the cell
questions.why: An antagonist occupies the binding site but produces no signal, so its effect is entirely to keep the agonist out. Activating more strongly than the natural ligand describes a potent agonist. Raising receptor affinity is a form of modulation rather than blockade, and destroying second messengers acts downstream of the receptor rather than at it.
questions.answerText: A molecule that binds a receptor without activating it and prevents the natural ligand from acting

questions.q: What defines competitive inhibition at a receptor?
options: The inhibitor binds a different site and permanently changes the receptor shape
The inhibitor destroys the receptor so it must be replaced
The inhibitor binds the same site as the ligand, so more ligand can outcompete it
The inhibitor blocks the second messenger rather than the receptor
questions.why: Competition means the two molecules fight for one site, so raising ligand concentration shifts the odds and restores the response. Binding at a different site with a lasting shape change describes noncompetitive inhibition, which more ligand cannot overcome. Destroying the receptor and blocking a second messenger are both different mechanisms that do not involve competition for the binding site.
questions.answerText: The inhibitor binds the same site as the ligand, so more ligand can outcompete it

questions.q: What does down regulation of receptors mean?
options: The receptor binds ligand but sends a stronger signal
The target cell decreases the amount of ligand it secretes
The receptor changes into a different receptor subtype
The target cell decreases the number of receptors it displays
questions.why: Down regulation is a change in the target cell, usually receptor internalization and degradation, that lowers receptor number and makes the cell less sensitive. Reduced secretion is a change at the signaling cell, not the target. Receptors do not convert into other subtypes, and a stronger signal per receptor is the opposite of what down regulation produces.
questions.answerText: The target cell decreases the number of receptors it displays

questions.q: What does up regulation of receptors mean?
options: The target cell increases the number of receptors it displays, becoming more sensitive
The gland increases the amount of hormone it releases
The receptor's affinity falls so more ligand is needed
The second messenger is produced in larger amounts per receptor that is occupied
questions.why: Up regulation adds receptors to the membrane, so the same ligand concentration produces a larger response. Increased hormone release is a change in the signal rather than in the target cell's sensitivity. Falling affinity would reduce responsiveness, and more second messenger per receptor describes a downstream change rather than receptor number.
questions.answerText: The target cell increases the number of receptors it displays, becoming more sensitive

questions.q: Chronic exposure to a high concentration of a hormone usually causes what change in its target cells?
options: Up regulation of the receptors
Down regulation of the receptors
No change, since receptor number is fixed
Conversion of surface receptors into intracellular receptors
questions.why: Persistently high signal leads the cell to internalize and degrade receptors, which protects it from overstimulation and lowers sensitivity. Up regulation is the response to chronically low signal, not high. Receptor number is continuously adjusted rather than fixed, and receptor class does not change with exposure.
questions.answerText: Down regulation of the receptors

questions.q: Chronic absence of a signal, as when a muscle loses its nerve supply, tends to produce what change at the target cell?
options: Down regulation, with fewer receptors remaining
No change, because receptor number depends only on genetics
Up regulation, with more receptors appearing in the membrane
Loss of the ability to respond to the ligand permanently
questions.why: When stimulation falls, the cell adds receptors so it can detect whatever ligand remains, which is why denervated muscle becomes hypersensitive to acetylcholine. Down regulation follows excess signal rather than deficiency. Receptor number is regulated, not fixed by genetics alone, and the increased sensitivity shows the response capacity is preserved rather than lost.
questions.answerText: Up regulation, with more receptors appearing in the membrane

questions.q: What does the affinity of a receptor for its ligand describe?
options: How many receptors the cell has
How quickly the second messenger is degraded
How large the maximal response can be
How tightly the receptor binds the ligand
questions.why: Affinity is about binding strength, so a high affinity receptor holds its ligand at low concentrations and needs less ligand for half maximal effect. Receptor number is a separate variable that mostly sets the size of the maximal response. Maximal response and messenger degradation are downstream properties and can change without any change in affinity.
questions.answerText: How tightly the receptor binds the ligand

questions.q: A drug binds beta 1 receptors on cardiac cells but produces no change in heart rate, and it prevents norepinephrine from acting. How should it be classified?
options: An antagonist
A full agonist
A partial agonist
An up regulator
questions.why: Binding with no response of its own plus blockade of the natural ligand is the definition of an antagonist. A full agonist would raise heart rate on its own. A partial agonist would produce some response, just less than the full agonist, and up regulation refers to receptor number rather than to a drug action at the binding site.
questions.answerText: An antagonist

questions.q: A competitive antagonist is present. What happens if the agonist concentration is raised high enough?
options: The maximal response stays permanently reduced
The full response can still be reached
The receptor is destroyed and cannot respond
The antagonist becomes an agonist at high concentration
questions.why: Competition is a matter of odds at a shared site, so flooding the system with agonist wins back the receptors and restores the maximum, though it takes more agonist to do it. A permanently reduced maximum is what a noncompetitive or irreversible blocker produces. Competitive binding is reversible and does not destroy receptors, and an antagonist does not change into an agonist with concentration.
questions.answerText: The full response can still be reached

questions.q: An inhibitor binds a site other than the ligand binding site and locks the receptor in an inactive shape. What happens when agonist concentration is raised?
options: The full response is restored, exactly as it is with any receptor inhibitor
The receptor's affinity for the agonist increases enough to compensate for the blockade
The maximal response stays reduced, because the agonist is not competing for the same site
The inhibitor is displaced as soon as the agonist concentration is doubled
questions.why: Noncompetitive inhibition removes receptors from the functional pool regardless of how much agonist is present, so the ceiling falls and cannot be restored by more ligand. Full restoration is the hallmark of competitive inhibition instead. Affinity does not rise to compensate, and displacement requires the two molecules to occupy the same site, which they do not.
questions.answerText: The maximal response stays reduced, because the agonist is not competing for the same site

questions.q: A person has chronically elevated insulin levels for months. Predict what happens to insulin receptor number and to target cell sensitivity.
options: Receptor number rises and sensitivity increases
Receptor number is unchanged and sensitivity increases
Receptor number falls but sensitivity increases
Receptor number falls and sensitivity decreases
questions.why: Sustained ligand excess drives internalization and degradation of receptors, so the cell reads the same insulin level as a weaker signal, which is one contributor to insulin resistance. Rising receptor number is the response to chronic deficiency instead. Fewer receptors cannot make a cell more sensitive, so any answer pairing falling or unchanged receptor number with increased sensitivity has the relationship backward.
questions.answerText: Receptor number falls and sensitivity decreases

questions.q: Cells are cultured with a beta receptor antagonist for two days, then the antagonist is washed away and a standard dose of agonist is applied. Predict the response compared with untreated cells.
options: A larger response, because receptor number increased during the blockade
A smaller response, because the receptors were damaged by the antagonist
The same response, because the antagonist has been removed
No response, because the antagonist permanently occupies the receptors
questions.why: Blocking receptors makes the cell read the signal as absent, so it up regulates receptor number, and the extra receptors are exposed once the blocker is gone. A competitive antagonist does not damage receptors, so the smaller response does not follow. The response is not identical, precisely because the cell adapted during the two days, and a washed out antagonist no longer occupies the sites.
questions.answerText: A larger response, because receptor number increased during the blockade

questions.q: Which change would make a target cell more sensitive to a given hormone concentration?
options: An increase in the rate of receptor internalization
An increase in the number of receptors on the cell
A decrease in the affinity of the receptor for the hormone
An increase in the rate of hormone degradation in plasma
questions.why: More receptors means more binding events at any given concentration, so the same signal produces a larger response. Faster internalization lowers receptor number and reduces sensitivity. Lower affinity requires more hormone for the same effect, and faster plasma degradation lowers the concentration reaching the cell rather than changing how the cell responds.
questions.answerText: An increase in the number of receptors on the cell

questions.q: A drug binds the same receptor as the natural ligand and produces a response, but its maximum is only 40 percent of the natural ligand's maximum even at saturating concentration. What is it?
options: A competitive antagonist
A noncompetitive inhibitor
A partial agonist
A full agonist with low affinity
questions.why: Producing a real but submaximal effect at full occupancy defines a partial agonist, since the ceiling is set by how well it activates the receptor rather than by how much is present. A competitive antagonist would produce no response of its own. A noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and produces no activation, and a low affinity full agonist would eventually reach the full maximum at high enough concentration.
questions.answerText: A partial agonist

questions.q: An agonist is infused continuously for a week, then stopped, and a standard test dose is given. Predict the receptor number and the size of the test response, and name the mechanism.
options: More receptors and a larger response, because the pathway was exercised repeatedly
Fewer receptors but a larger response, because each remaining receptor becomes supersensitive to ligand
Unchanged receptors and an unchanged response, because receptor number is set genetically
Fewer receptors and a smaller response, because sustained stimulation drove internalization and degradation
questions.why: Chronic excess signal leads the cell to pull receptors out of the membrane and degrade them, so the test dose finds fewer targets and produces less effect. Repeated stimulation does not build receptor number, and the up regulation option describes what happens after chronic blockade instead. Receptor number is dynamically regulated, and the surviving receptors do not become individually supersensitive enough to overcome the loss.
questions.answerText: Fewer receptors and a smaller response, because sustained stimulation drove internalization and degradation

questions.q: Two preparations are treated, one with a competitive antagonist and one with an irreversible antagonist. In each, the agonist dose is then increased tenfold. Predict the outcomes.
options: The competitive preparation regains its full maximal response, while the irreversible preparation does not
Both regain their full maximal response, since more agonist always wins
The irreversible preparation regains its full response, since covalent binding is quickly reversed
Neither shows any response, since antagonists abolish signaling permanently
questions.why: Raising agonist concentration shifts a competitive equilibrium back toward agonist binding, but an irreversibly blocked receptor is out of the pool no matter how much agonist is added, so its ceiling stays low. More agonist does not always win, which is exactly what distinguishes the two kinds of blockade. Irreversible binding is not quickly reversed, and unblocked receptors in both preparations still respond.
questions.answerText: The competitive preparation regains its full maximal response, while the irreversible preparation does not

questions.q: A person has produced almost no thyroid hormone for months. When a normal dose is finally given, the tissues respond more strongly than expected. What explains the exaggerated response?
options: The hormone became more potent during storage in the deficient state
The chronic deficiency up regulated receptors, so the same dose now finds more binding sites
The tissues switched to a faster surface receptor pathway during the months of deficiency
The dose given was larger than the tissues had ever seen before
questions.why: Cells starved of a signal add receptors, so responsiveness climbs, and when the hormone returns at normal levels the enlarged receptor pool produces an outsized effect. The molecule itself does not gain potency, since potency is a property of the hormone and its receptor. Receptor class does not switch with hormone levels, and the dose was described as normal rather than large.
questions.answerText: The chronic deficiency up regulated receptors, so the same dose now finds more binding sites

questions.q: During prolonged agonist excess a cell has lost half its receptors. Why does raising the agonist dose further give only a limited improvement in response?
options: Extra ligand competitively inhibits the very receptors it binds, so it cancels itself out
The remaining receptors have lost all their affinity, so no ligand can bind at all
With fewer receptors the maximal response is lower, so extra ligand cannot recover what is missing
The pathway now runs in reverse, so adding more ligand reduces the response
questions.why: Down regulation removes receptors from the pool, which lowers the ceiling in the same way an irreversible blocker does, so more ligand can only push the surviving receptors toward their own maximum. The remaining receptors still bind ligand normally, since down regulation changes number rather than affinity. A ligand does not competitively inhibit its own receptor, and signaling pathways do not reverse direction with dose.
questions.answerText: With fewer receptors the maximal response is lower, so extra ligand cannot recover what is missing

questions.q: Which enzyme ends the action of acetylcholine at a synapse?
options: Monoamine oxidase
Phosphodiesterase
Adenylyl cyclase
Acetylcholinesterase
questions.why: Acetylcholinesterase sits in the synaptic cleft and splits acetylcholine into acetate and choline within milliseconds, which is why each nerve impulse produces a separate muscle response. Phosphodiesterase degrades cyclic AMP inside the cell. Adenylyl cyclase makes a second messenger rather than ending a signal, and monoamine oxidase breaks down catecholamines, not acetylcholine.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholinesterase

questions.q: Which enzyme terminates a cyclic AMP signal?
options: Phosphodiesterase
Adenylyl cyclase
Protein kinase A
Phospholipase C
questions.why: Phosphodiesterase hydrolyzes cyclic AMP to AMP, so the messenger disappears within seconds once production stops. Adenylyl cyclase makes cyclic AMP, the opposite job. Protein kinase A is the target of cyclic AMP, and phospholipase C belongs to a different branch of signaling entirely.
questions.answerText: Phosphodiesterase

questions.q: What kind of enzyme reverses the changes a protein kinase has made?
options: A cyclase
A phosphatase
A protease
A ligase
questions.why: Phosphatases remove the phosphate groups kinases add, returning target proteins to their resting activity and ending the response. Cyclases make cyclic nucleotides rather than removing phosphate from proteins. A protease would destroy the protein instead of resetting it, and a ligase joins molecules together.
questions.answerText: A phosphatase

questions.q: How is a calcium signal in the cytosol normally terminated?
options: Calcium is degraded by an enzyme in the cytosol
Calcium binds permanently to calmodulin in the cytosol and is inactivated
Calcium ATPase pumps move calcium back into stores and out of the cell
Calcium diffuses into the nucleus where it has no effect
questions.why: Calcium is an element, so it cannot be broken down and must instead be physically moved, which the endoplasmic reticulum and plasma membrane pumps do at the cost of ATP. There is no enzyme that degrades an ion. Calmodulin binding is reversible and is part of the signal rather than its end, and calcium entering the nucleus does not remove it from the cytosolic pool.
questions.answerText: Calcium ATPase pumps move calcium back into stores and out of the cell

questions.q: What is reuptake as a mechanism of signal termination?
options: The neurotransmitter diffuses out of the cleft into the blood
An enzyme in the cleft splits the neurotransmitter into inactive pieces
The receptor is pulled into the cell along with its ligand
A transporter carries the neurotransmitter back into the cell that released it
questions.why: Reuptake uses a membrane transporter to recapture intact transmitter for reuse, which both clears the cleft and saves the cell the cost of making more. Enzymatic splitting in the cleft is degradation, a separate mechanism. Pulling in the receptor is internalization, which removes the receptor rather than the ligand, and simple diffusion away is a third and slower route.
questions.answerText: A transporter carries the neurotransmitter back into the cell that released it

questions.q: Which built in property of the G protein alpha subunit shuts off a G protein coupled pathway?
options: Its GTPase activity, which hydrolyzes bound GTP to GDP
Its ability to bind a second ligand
Its phosphatase activity, which removes phosphate from the receptor
Its ability to leave the cell after activation
questions.why: The alpha subunit is a timer as well as a switch, since it slowly hydrolyzes its own GTP and then reassembles with the beta and gamma subunits in the inactive state. G protein subunits do not bind ligand, which is the receptor's job. They are not phosphatases, and they remain anchored at the membrane rather than leaving the cell.
questions.answerText: Its GTPase activity, which hydrolyzes bound GTP to GDP

questions.q: How does receptor internalization help end a signal?
options: It destroys the ligand inside the endosome before it can bind
It pulls receptors out of the membrane so the ligand outside can no longer reach them
It converts the receptor into an enzyme that degrades second messengers in the cytosol
It increases the affinity of the remaining receptors
questions.why: Removing receptors from the surface lowers the number of binding sites available, so the same extracellular concentration produces less signal. Ligand degradation can occur after internalization, but the termination comes from the loss of surface receptors. Receptors are not converted into degrading enzymes, and raising affinity would prolong rather than end the response.
questions.answerText: It pulls receptors out of the membrane so the ligand outside can no longer reach them

questions.q: Which of the following ends a chemical signal?
options: Increased secretion of the ligand by the signaling cell
Up regulation of receptors on the target cell
Enzymatic degradation of the ligand
Activation of the amplifier enzyme
questions.why: Breaking the ligand down removes the molecule that carries the message, which is one of the three standard termination routes along with reuptake and diffusion away. Increased secretion sustains the signal rather than ending it. Up regulation makes the cell more responsive, and activating the amplifier enzyme is a step in transmitting the signal, not in stopping it.
questions.answerText: Enzymatic degradation of the ligand

questions.q: A drug inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction. Predict what happens to acetylcholine in the cleft and to the muscle fiber.
options: Acetylcholine is cleared faster and the muscle relaxes sooner
Acetylcholine is converted to norepinephrine, changing the receptor used
Acetylcholine release stops, so the muscle cannot contract at all
Acetylcholine accumulates and the muscle is stimulated repeatedly instead of once
questions.why: Without the esterase, transmitter lingers and rebinds its receptors, so a single nerve impulse produces prolonged and repeated activation of the fiber. Clearance cannot speed up when the clearing enzyme is blocked. Release from the nerve terminal is unaffected by the drug, and acetylcholine is not converted into another transmitter.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine accumulates and the muscle is stimulated repeatedly instead of once
review: territory tagged automatically from wording

questions.q: A phosphodiesterase inhibitor is given to a cell already stimulated by a Gs coupled agonist. Predict the effect on cyclic AMP level and on the duration of the response.
options: Cyclic AMP rises higher and the response lasts longer
Cyclic AMP falls and the response ends sooner
Cyclic AMP is unchanged but the response is stronger
Cyclic AMP rises but the response ends sooner because of desensitization
questions.why: Concentration reflects the balance of production and destruction, so blocking the only enzyme that destroys cyclic AMP raises its level and stretches out its action. A fall would require either less production or more degradation, neither of which the drug causes. The level cannot stay unchanged when its degradation is blocked, and desensitization develops over minutes to hours rather than immediately shortening the response.
questions.answerText: Cyclic AMP rises higher and the response lasts longer

questions.q: A drug blocks the transporter that carries norepinephrine back into the presynaptic terminal. Predict the effect at the synapse.
options: Norepinephrine is released in smaller amounts, weakening the signal
Norepinephrine stays in the cleft longer and its effect on the target cell is prolonged
Norepinephrine is degraded faster in the cleft to compensate, which shortens the signal
The postsynaptic receptors are blocked, ending the signal
questions.why: Reuptake is the main clearance route for catecholamines, so blocking it leaves more transmitter in the cleft for longer and amplifies the postsynaptic response. Release from the terminal is a separate step and is not reduced by a transporter blocker. Enzymatic degradation does not automatically increase to compensate, and the drug acts on a transporter rather than on postsynaptic receptors.
questions.answerText: Norepinephrine stays in the cleft longer and its effect on the target cell is prolonged

questions.q: A toxin inhibits the calcium ATPase of the endoplasmic reticulum in a smooth muscle cell. Predict the effect on cytosolic calcium and on contraction.
options: Cytosolic calcium falls quickly and the cell relaxes
Cytosolic calcium is unchanged, because the plasma membrane pump is enough
Cytosolic calcium stays elevated and the cell stays contracted
Cytosolic calcium rises but contraction stops, because calcium inhibits myosin
questions.why: Relaxation depends on removing calcium from the cytosol, so disabling the main pump leaves calcium high and the contractile machinery engaged. Calcium cannot fall when the pump that lowers it is inhibited. The plasma membrane pump alone works too slowly to compensate, and calcium activates rather than inhibits smooth muscle contraction through calmodulin.
questions.answerText: Cytosolic calcium stays elevated and the cell stays contracted

questions.q: Why does a toxin that destroys the GTPase activity of a G protein prevent normal signal termination?
options: The receptor cannot release its ligand, so binding continues without end
The cell can no longer make new G proteins to replace the ones already used
Phosphodiesterase is destroyed along with the GTPase activity of the subunit
The alpha subunit cannot hydrolyze its GTP, so it stays in the active form indefinitely
questions.why: Hydrolysis of GTP to GDP is the off switch built into the G protein, so removing it leaves the amplifier enzyme running long after ligand has gone. Ligand release from the receptor is a separate event and is unaffected. Phosphodiesterase is a different enzyme that the toxin does not touch, and the problem is too much activity rather than too few G proteins.
questions.answerText: The alpha subunit cannot hydrolyze its GTP, so it stays in the active form indefinitely

questions.q: Why does a signal that cannot be terminated tend to produce pathology?
options: Because the response no longer matches the stimulus, so regulated processes run to harmful extremes
Because the ligand itself becomes toxic once it remains in the blood too long
Because an unterminated signal always destroys its receptor and eventually kills the whole cell
Because the cell cannot make any ATP while a signal remains active in it
questions.why: Homeostasis depends on responses that turn off when the stimulus does, so a stuck pathway drives secretion, contraction, or metabolism far past the point that is useful. Most ligands are not chemically toxic in themselves, which is why the harm comes from the sustained response. Receptor destruction is not required for damage, and cells continue making ATP during prolonged signaling, sometimes to the point of depleting substrates.
questions.answerText: Because the response no longer matches the stimulus, so regulated processes run to harmful extremes

questions.q: An organophosphate irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Trace the consequences at the neuromuscular junction from the cleft to the muscle.
options: Acetylcholine is cleared normally but the receptors are blocked, so the muscle is flaccid from the start
Acetylcholine accumulates, the endplate stays depolarized, receptors desensitize, and the muscle stops responding
Acetylcholine release stops, the endplate hyperpolarizes, and the muscle relaxes completely
Acetylcholine accumulates but the endplate potential is unchanged, so nothing happens at the muscle
questions.why: The story has three linked steps: loss of degradation raises cleft transmitter, continuous receptor occupancy holds the endplate depolarized, and sustained depolarization inactivates sodium channels and desensitizes receptors so further impulses fail. The drug inhibits an enzyme rather than blocking receptors, so flaccidity from the start does not fit. Release is unaffected, and accumulating transmitter must change the endplate potential rather than leave it untouched.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine accumulates, the endplate stays depolarized, receptors desensitize, and the muscle stops responding

questions.q: Cholera toxin locks Gs in the active state in intestinal cells. Trace the pathway from that lesion to the massive watery diarrhea that follows.
options: The toxin opens water channels in the cell directly, so water moves into the lumen without any solute movement
Cyclic AMP falls, sodium absorption stops, and water is left behind in the lumen unabsorbed
Adenylyl cyclase runs continuously, cyclic AMP stays high, chloride secretion continues, and water follows osmotically
Protein kinase A is destroyed, so the cell can no longer reabsorb the fluid it normally secretes
questions.why: Each step follows from the one before: a Gs protein that cannot switch off keeps cyclic AMP elevated, protein kinase A holds chloride channels open, and the osmotic gradient created by luminal chloride and sodium pulls liters of water out of the body. Cyclic AMP rises rather than falls when Gs is locked on. Water does not move without an osmotic driving force, and protein kinase A is activated by the excess cyclic AMP rather than destroyed.
questions.answerText: Adenylyl cyclase runs continuously, cyclic AMP stays high, chloride secretion continues, and water follows osmotically

questions.q: Synapse A clears its transmitter by enzymatic degradation in the cleft within about one millisecond. Synapse B clears its transmitter by reuptake over tens of milliseconds. Predict how each behaves during rapid repeated stimulation.
options: Neither can follow rapid stimulation, since all synapses need seconds to recover
Synapse B produces distinct responses to each impulse, while synapse A blurs its responses together
Both behave identically, since the amount of transmitter released is the same
Synapse A produces distinct responses to each impulse, while synapse B shows summed and prolonged responses
questions.why: How fast a cleft is cleared sets how quickly a synapse can reset, so millisecond degradation supports one to one following while slower reuptake lets transmitter accumulate and responses merge. Reversing the two contradicts the clearance times given. Release amount is not the variable being changed here, and many synapses follow stimulation at rates far faster than once per second.
questions.answerText: Synapse A produces distinct responses to each impulse, while synapse B shows summed and prolonged responses

questions.q: A cell is unable to pump calcium out of its cytosol. Predict the immediate signaling consequence and then the consequence for the cell itself.
options: Calcium dependent responses stay switched on, and the high calcium activates degradative enzymes that damage the cell
Calcium dependent responses shut down immediately, and the cell becomes unresponsive to any further signal
Calcium leaks harmlessly into the nucleus, so no change in signaling occurs in the cell
The cell compensates by making more calmodulin, so the response returns to normal within seconds
questions.why: Termination of a calcium signal is entirely a transport problem, so losing the pumps leaves effectors continuously engaged, and prolonged high calcium activates proteases and lipases that injure the cell. Responses cannot shut down when the activating ion remains elevated. Calcium entering the nucleus does not neutralize it, and making more calmodulin would extend rather than end calcium signaling, and could not happen within seconds.
questions.answerText: Calcium dependent responses stay switched on, and the high calcium activates degradative enzymes that damage the cell

questions.q: On a dose response curve, what is plotted on the horizontal axis?
options: The magnitude of the response
The dose or concentration of the drug, usually on a log scale
The time since the drug was given
The number of receptors present on the target cell membrane
questions.why: Dose is the independent variable and goes on the horizontal axis, and a log scale is used because effective doses span several orders of magnitude. Response magnitude is the dependent variable and belongs on the vertical axis. Time belongs on a time course plot, and receptor number is a property of the tissue rather than something varied along the axis.
questions.answerText: The dose or concentration of the drug, usually on a log scale

questions.q: On a dose response curve, what is plotted on the vertical axis?
options: The concentration of the drug that is present in the tissue bath
The time to reach steady state
The size of the measured response, often as a percent of maximum
The affinity of the receptor
questions.why: The vertical axis carries the biological output, such as tension developed or percent of maximal response, so the curve shows how output changes with dose. Drug concentration is the horizontal axis variable. Time to steady state and receptor affinity are separate measurements that do not appear as the plotted response.
questions.answerText: The size of the measured response, often as a percent of maximum

questions.q: What is the threshold dose on a dose response curve?
options: The dose that produces half the maximal response
The dose at which toxicity begins
The dose above which the response no longer increases
The lowest dose that produces a detectable response
questions.why: Threshold marks the left foot of the curve, where enough receptors are occupied for the response to rise above baseline noise. The dose giving half of maximum is the EC50, a point in the middle of the curve. The dose beyond which the response stops rising defines the plateau, and toxicity is a separate curve measured on a different endpoint.
questions.answerText: The lowest dose that produces a detectable response

questions.q: What does the plateau of a dose response curve represent?
options: The maximal response, beyond which more drug produces no further effect
The point at which half of the receptors are occupied by drug
The dose at which the drug first begins to work on the tissue
The point at which the drug starts to be degraded in the bath
questions.why: The flat top shows that the system is saturated, so adding drug cannot recruit any more response from the tissue. Half occupancy corresponds to the EC50 region, not the plateau. The point where the drug begins to work is the threshold, and drug degradation happens throughout the experiment rather than starting at the plateau.
questions.answerText: The maximal response, beyond which more drug produces no further effect

questions.q: What does EC50 mean?
options: The concentration that occupies 50 percent of the receptors permanently
The concentration that produces 50 percent of the maximal response
The concentration that is effective in 50 percent of tissues tested
The concentration at which the response first becomes detectable
questions.why: EC50 is read off the curve at the halfway point of the response axis, and it is the standard measure of potency, so a lower EC50 means a more potent drug. Receptor occupancy is a related but separate measurement, and it is not permanent. The fraction of tissues responding is a different kind of statistic, and first detectable response defines threshold.
questions.answerText: The concentration that produces 50 percent of the maximal response

questions.q: Why is dose usually plotted on a logarithmic scale?
options: Because the size of the measured response is itself logarithmic, so both axes must use the same scale
Because a log axis removes the need to identify the threshold dose anywhere on the curve
Because effective doses span several orders of magnitude, and a log axis makes the curve a readable sigmoid
Because it converts the whole curve into a straight line from threshold to plateau
questions.why: Doses from threshold to maximum often differ by a hundredfold or more, so a linear axis crushes the low doses against the origin while a log axis spreads them out into the familiar S shape. The response itself is measured in ordinary units, not log units. The threshold is still visible on a log plot, and the curve is straight only through its middle portion, not across its full range.
questions.answerText: Because effective doses span several orders of magnitude, and a log axis makes the curve a readable sigmoid

questions.q: How does the curve of a partial agonist differ from that of a full agonist on the same axes?
options: It rises without ever reaching a plateau
It reaches the same plateau but always at a lower dose
It has no threshold, so it works at any dose
It reaches a lower plateau, even at saturating concentrations
questions.why: A partial agonist activates each receptor it occupies less effectively, so its ceiling sits below the full agonist's maximum no matter how much is added. Reaching the same plateau at a lower dose would describe a more potent full agonist. Every agonist has a threshold, and all agonist curves plateau once the system saturates.
questions.answerText: It reaches a lower plateau, even at saturating concentrations

questions.q: What shape does a typical dose response curve take when dose is plotted on a log scale?
options: A sigmoid, or S shaped, curve
A straight line with constant slope
A U shaped curve
A curve that falls steadily as dose rises
questions.why: On a log dose axis the response rises slowly near threshold, steeply through the middle, and flattens at the maximum, producing the classic S. A perfectly straight line would mean equal response increments for every dose increment, which fails at both ends. A U shape and a falling curve do not describe an agonist producing a graded response.
questions.answerText: A sigmoid, or S shaped, curve

questions.q: A tissue reaches a maximal tension of 80 grams. At what tension would you read the EC50 off the curve?
options: 80 grams
40 grams
20 grams
8 grams
questions.why: EC50 is defined against the maximal response of that same preparation, so half of 80 grams is 40 grams and the corresponding dose is read down to the horizontal axis. Eighty grams is the maximum itself. Twenty grams is one quarter of maximum, and 8 grams is 10 percent, neither of which is the halfway point.
questions.answerText: 40 grams

questions.q: Adding a drug shifts an agonist's dose response curve to the right without lowering its plateau. What does that tell you?
options: The agonist has become more potent, since the curve has moved along the dose axis
The tissue has permanently lost receptors, lowering what it can achieve
More agonist is now needed for the same effect, but the full response is still achievable
The agonist has been converted into a partial agonist at the same receptor
questions.why: A parallel rightward shift with an unchanged maximum is the signature of competitive inhibition: potency falls, seen as a higher EC50, while efficacy is preserved. Increased potency would shift the curve to the left instead. Permanent receptor loss would drop the plateau, as would conversion to a partial agonist.
questions.answerText: More agonist is now needed for the same effect, but the full response is still achievable

questions.q: Two drugs act at the same receptor. Drug A has an EC50 of 1 nanomolar and drug B an EC50 of 100 nanomolar. Which statement is correct?
options: Drug B is more potent, because it acts at a higher concentration
Drug B must be a partial agonist
Drug A must also produce a larger maximal response
Drug A is one hundred times more potent than drug B
questions.why: Potency is inversely related to EC50, so needing one hundredth as much drug for the same fractional effect makes drug A one hundred times more potent. Requiring a higher concentration means less potent, not more. Potency and efficacy are independent, so nothing about the maximal response or partial agonism follows from EC50 alone.
questions.answerText: Drug A is one hundred times more potent than drug B

questions.q: A drug's curve has reached its plateau. Why does doubling the dose again produce no further response?
options: The receptors and the downstream machinery are already saturated
The drug has been fully metabolized by the tissue at that dose
The receptor affinity falls as dose rises
The response axis cannot record higher values
questions.why: Once essentially every available receptor is occupied and the response system is running at capacity, extra drug molecules have nothing left to bind or drive. Metabolism does not switch on selectively at the plateau dose. Affinity is a fixed property of the drug receptor pair at a given condition, and the flat top is a biological ceiling rather than a limit of the measuring device.
questions.answerText: The receptors and the downstream machinery are already saturated

questions.q: In a bath experiment, doses of 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 micromolar produce responses of 0, 0, 18, and 62 percent of maximum. What is the best estimate of the threshold dose?
options: About 0.1 micromolar
About 10 micromolar
About 1 micromolar
About 100 micromolar
questions.why: Threshold is the lowest tested dose that produces a measurable response, and 10 micromolar is the first dose to move the response off zero. The two lower doses produced nothing at all, so neither can be the threshold. One hundred micromolar produces a large response but is well above the point where the response first appeared.
questions.answerText: About 10 micromolar

questions.q: A second drug produces a curve whose plateau is only half as high as the first drug's plateau, even at very high doses. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The second drug was tested at doses below threshold
The second drug has a higher affinity for the receptor
The second drug is a partial agonist at that receptor
The second drug is a competitive antagonist
questions.why: A lower ceiling that persists at saturating doses reflects lower efficacy, which is what defines a partial agonist. Higher affinity would move the curve left rather than lower its plateau. Doses below threshold would produce no response at all, and a competitive antagonist produces no response of its own to plot.
questions.answerText: The second drug is a partial agonist at that receptor

questions.q: A tissue gives these responses as percent of maximum: 1 nM produces 5, 10 nM produces 25, 30 nM produces 50, 100 nM produces 90, 300 nM produces 100, and 1000 nM produces 100. Identify the threshold, the EC50, and the dose that first produces the maximal response.
options: Threshold 30 nM, EC50 300 nM, maximum first reached at 1000 nM
Threshold 10 nM, EC50 100 nM, maximum first reached at 1000 nM
Threshold 1 nM, EC50 100 nM, maximum first reached at 300 nM
Threshold 1 nM, EC50 30 nM, maximum first reached at 300 nM
questions.why: The first dose with any measurable effect is 1 nM, the response is 50 percent of maximum at 30 nM, and the plateau is first reached at 300 nM since 1000 nM adds nothing. Calling 10 nM the threshold ignores the response already present at 1 nM. Reading EC50 at 100 nM confuses the 90 percent point with the halfway point, and 300 nM is where the plateau begins rather than the EC50.
questions.answerText: Threshold 1 nM, EC50 30 nM, maximum first reached at 300 nM

questions.q: On the same axes, drug A reaches 100 percent maximal response with an EC50 of 10 nM, and drug B reaches only 60 percent with an EC50 of 1 nM. Compare their potency and efficacy.
options: Drug B is more potent, and drug A is more efficacious
Drug A is more potent and more efficacious
Drug B is both more potent and more efficacious
Drug A is more potent, and drug B is more efficacious
questions.why: Potency is read from the horizontal position of the curve, so the lower EC50 of drug B makes it more potent, while efficacy is read from the height of the plateau, where drug A wins. Saying drug A is more potent misreads a higher EC50 as an advantage. The two properties are independent, which is why one drug can lead on one measure and trail on the other.
questions.answerText: Drug B is more potent, and drug A is more efficacious

questions.q: A competitive antagonist is added to the bath before repeating a full agonist dose response curve. Predict the change in the curve and explain why it takes that form.
options: The curve shifts left with an unchanged plateau, because the antagonist increases the affinity of the receptor for agonist
The curve shifts right with an unchanged plateau, because extra agonist can outcompete the antagonist for the shared site
The plateau drops with no horizontal shift, because receptors are permanently removed
The curve disappears entirely, because the antagonist blocks all responses
questions.why: Competition raises the agonist concentration needed at every response level, which moves the curve right, but the maximum is preserved because enough agonist eventually occupies the receptors. A leftward shift would mean increased potency, the opposite of blockade. A dropped plateau without a shift is the pattern for a noncompetitive or irreversible blocker, and a competitive antagonist reduces potency rather than abolishing all response.
questions.answerText: The curve shifts right with an unchanged plateau, because extra agonist can outcompete the antagonist for the shared site

questions.q: A tissue is already producing its maximal response to a full agonist. A large dose of a partial agonist acting at the same receptor is added. Predict the effect on the response and explain why.
options: The response rises above the previous maximum, because two different agonists are now bound at once
The response is unchanged, because both molecules are agonists at the same receptor
The response falls toward the partial agonist's lower maximum, because it displaces the full agonist
The response falls to zero, because a partial agonist behaves as a pure antagonist here
questions.why: When both molecules compete for one site, a large excess of the weaker activator takes over most receptors and the tissue output drifts down to what the partial agonist alone can produce. Occupancy is limited by receptor number, so adding a second agonist cannot push output above the system maximum. The response does change, since the two agonists differ in efficacy, and it stops at the partial agonist's plateau rather than falling to zero.
questions.answerText: The response falls toward the partial agonist's lower maximum, because it displaces the full agonist
